# P versus NP: unconventional idea ledger

Started: 23 September 2026  
Working rule: Re-read this file at the start of each research continuation. After every serious attempt, record what was formalized, what was tested, what failed, and the next proof obligation. Keep theorem, experiment, conjecture, and speculation separate. Imaginative language is welcome; an idea advances only when its definitions and proof obligations survive scrutiny.
Failure-to-next-idea rule: after each failed attempt, extract a reusable constraint from the exact failed step, then make the next idea satisfy that constraint at the definition, encoding, witness, and runtime levels before expanding it. A failed proof route should narrow the search space, not be treated as evidence that P versus NP is impossible to solve.

## What counts as progress

- Breakthrough: a complete, independently checkable proof of P = NP or P != NP, with complexity and uniformity steps justified.
- Theorem: a correct lemma or theorem that materially advances a route, with proof and scope recorded.
- Lead: a precise conjecture or reduction whose next proof obligation can be attacked.
- Refuted / blocked: a counterexample, known barrier, quantifier mismatch, or reduction to an already open problem.

Experiments can falsify constructions or check finite cases; they cannot establish asymptotic complexity claims.

## Durable starting point

The project audit is `P_VS_NP_PROJECT_AUDIT_2026-08-24.md`; the current synthesis is `P_vs_NP_Research_Synthesis_2026-09-23.docx`. The conventional route studies lower bounds for semi-filter covers connected to Gap-MCSP hardness magnification. Sections 23-25 of the audit eliminate broad binary and q-ary Reed-Muller feature-span families as candidates: under stated conditions, one disjoint pair covers all relevant anchors. Section 26 records a necessary finite-geometry blocker bound but no pair-count lower bound. The missing step remains a superlinear all-semi-filter cover lower bound, or a different route to a P-versus-NP theorem.

This ledger starts with one final finite-geometry check, then turns to self-reference, foundations, and new descriptive language. It does not claim access to the complete P-versus-NP literature or to unexported ChatGPT project conversations.

## Idea 0 - Split-flat shadows and obstruction geometry

Source: final check of the Reed-Muller feature-span route.  
Status: exact necessary condition; no complexity lower bound.

For binary degree-d Reed-Muller features, minimum-weight supports are affine flats of codimension d. If anchor a is outside endpoint E and its feature vector lies in the affine span of E, then E-a must meet every (N-d)-dimensional linear subspace. Otherwise the indicator polynomial of a missed flat separates a from E. The Bose-Burton theorem gives the minimum blocker size 2^(d+1)-1, attained by all nonzero vectors in a fixed (d+1)-dimensional subspace.

For endpoints E,H, define the split-flat shadow as anchors a for which there is a minimum-support flat F through a with F intersecting E and H separately but missing E intersect H. Such a flat witnesses that E and H pass the feature-span test while their intersection fails, assuming E and H belong to that anchored filter. This captures one kind of pair coverage, not every possible higher-degree separator. The blocker bound concerns endpoint size, not number of pairs; the existing disjoint information-set construction still covers the entire relevant anchor family with one pair below half degree.

The exhaustive script `experiment_split_flat_blocking.py` checked all candidate blockers below the theorem's bound for (N,d)=(2,1),(3,1),(3,2),(4,1),(4,2). All matched the bound. The general theorem comes from Bose-Burton, not the finite checks. References: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021980066800078 and https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.2554.

Next test: seek useful bounds on split-flat shadows for arbitrary intersecting endpoint pairs. Do not reopen the feature-span family absent a genuinely new invariant.

## Idea 1 - Self-reference as a quantifier pump

Status: initial attempt blocked at the exact quantifier step; retain as a diagnostic for diagonal arguments.

Try to make a SAT instance refer to its own encoding and assert that every small circuit fails to decide its satisfiability. A fixed-point theorem can arrange self-reference, but does not turn a global statement over all circuits into an NP witness. For fixed x, the desired condition has the form: for every circuit C of size at most s, C(x) differs from SAT(x). If C(x)=1, verifying disagreement requires proving x has no satisfying assignment; if C(x)=0, disagreement needs a satisfying assignment. Finding one bad circuit does not establish that every circuit fails.

This is the quantifier cost behind the liar-paradox intuition. For a proposed global decider C, the map D_C(z)=1-C(z) is easy to compute when C is polynomial-time, but it depends on C and is not one fixed NP language that diagonalizes against all such deciders. Defining a language on descriptions by D(code(C))=1-C(code(C)) creates a representation-size problem: a circuit of size n^k need not fit in an n-bit self-description. Giving a circuit a succinct description of an exponentially larger SAT instance can move the problem to Succinct-3SAT, which is NEXP-complete; it does not produce an ordinary NP verifier. See https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jswright/papers/re.pdf for the standard succinct-3SAT completeness fact.

Current verdict: no route to P != NP. Self-reference does not erase a universal quantifier or its resource cost. Next test: look for a certificate compressing the universal sweep, and derive its exact complexity before using it in a diagonal proof.

## Idea 2 - ZFC reflection as a resource boundary

Status: foundation probe; no independence claim.

Keep separate: (1) P = NP is true in the standard natural numbers; (2) a named formal theory proves or refutes it; (3) a proof system has short proofs of all tautologies. P = NP is an arithmetic statement: it can be expressed using quantification over machine descriptions, polynomial bounds, finite inputs, and finite verifier witnesses. Failure to find a proof in ZFC would not settle the mathematical question. A P-versus-NP independence result for ZFC would itself require a metamathematical theorem; there is no basis here for assuming independence.

Quantifier sketch: fix a polynomial-time verifier R for 3-SAT and quantify over a deterministic machine M and exponent k. Its correctness can be written in the form `exists M,k forall formula phi, witness w0, exists witness w1` with a bounded-arithmetic predicate saying (i) if M rejects phi then w0 is not a valid satisfying assignment, and (ii) if M accepts phi then w1 is a valid satisfying assignment. Together with the polynomial running-time bound, this gives a Sigma-3 arithmetic sentence for 3-SAT in P, hence for P = NP. This is only an upper bound on the quantifier complexity, not an independence result.

Also keep the proof-system implications precise: P = NP implies NP = coNP, which implies existence of a polynomially bounded Cook-Reckhow proof system. A polynomially bounded proof system gives NP = coNP, not P = NP. The Baker-Gill-Solovay oracle constructions show both relativized outcomes, but oracle separation is a barrier to relativizing proofs, not independence from ZFC. Ordinary set forcing preserves the natural numbers of a transitive model, so it cannot by itself flip an arithmetic sentence such as P = NP between that model and its forcing extension. Scott Aaronson's survey describes actual P-versus-NP independence as an unprecedented kind of result, not an accepted explanation for the problem's difficulty.

Fresh question: can one define a natural uniform measure of the proof resources needed to reflect a computation's correctness, and show that a polynomial-time decider forces a forbidden short reflection scheme? Likely trap: the reflection statement may already encode the original hardness.

Next test: formalize one candidate proof system and derive the exact implication chain. Compare the attempt against the relativization, natural-proofs, and algebrization barriers in the main audit. Do not use "unprovable," "true," and "hard to prove" interchangeably.

## Idea 3 - Empty-fiber geometry: language for witnesses and anti-witnesses

Status: new organizing vocabulary; definitions only, not a theorem.

For a polynomially verifiable relation R(x,w), define the witness fiber W_x = {w : R(x,w)}. NP asks whether W_x is nonempty. An accepting witness is a point certificate. An unsatisfiability proof, or a P algorithm's "empty" answer, must account for the whole fiber and is an anti-witness certificate. A family of local constraints can be viewed as a cover of candidate witnesses by regions where R fails. The gap is succinctness: the local cover may have a short description while checking complete coverage remains coNP-hard.

Terms for use in this ledger:

- Fiber: W_x, the set of valid witnesses.
- Separator: a test distinguishing a proposed witness from W_x.
- Anti-witness cover: a compact object whose verified coverage proves W_x is empty.
- Cover debt: the cost of turning a succinct local description into a sound, efficiently checkable global emptiness certificate.

First test: apply this to 3-SAT. Each clause's falsifying assignments form a subcube; UNSAT means these subcubes cover the Boolean cube. A resolution step from A or x and B or not-x to A or B is sound geometrically: the falsifying cube of the resolvent is contained in the union of the parents' falsifying cubes. A resolution refutation therefore grows a DAG certificate that the initial clause cubes cover every assignment.

The four-clause formula (x or y), (not-x or y), (x or not-y), (not-x or not-y) covers the four assignments. Resolving the first pair gives y, the second gives not-y, and the final resolution gives the empty clause. The script `experiment_antiwitness_cube_resolution.py` checked the cube-containment condition for 3,178 pivot-clause pairs through four variables and checked this example. All pass. This is a useful geometric reading of resolution, but the correspondence is known: see the University of Washington proof-complexity notes, https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse599s/20au/notes/Proof_Complexity_Notes.pdf. The ledger's vocabulary has not yet found a new invariant.

Next test: compare a candidate coverage invariant to width, size, and standard closure measures, and determine whether it extends beyond resolution while remaining polynomially verifiable.

## Idea 4 - Topology of the missing witness

Status: speculation with an immediate representation obstacle.

Represent partial assignments as cells, with satisfying assignments as compatible maximal cells. A hoped-for topological invariant would vanish exactly when no satisfying assignment exists and be computable from a succinct formula. The obstacle is that the full cell complex can be exponentially large. A polynomial-size circuit naming incidence rules does not make its homology polynomial-time computable; succinct homology may be harder than explicit homology.

Test: define a particular complex K(F), specify its facets and boundary maps, and prove (i) its empty/nonempty signature, (ii) a polynomial-size succinct representation, and (iii) polynomial-time computation of the invariant from that representation. If (iii) is missing, this is an encoding of SAT, not an algorithm.

## Idea 5 - Physics-inspired zero-energy witness audit

Status: speculation; likely repackages SAT unless a new local-to-global theorem appears.

Encode each clause as a local penalty and let H_F(x) be the number of violated clauses. SAT is equivalent to minimum energy zero. The partition function Z_F(beta) = sum_x exp(-beta H_F(x)) contains witness-count information, but calling it a partition function does not make it easier to compute. For finite beta, Z is never zero; the relevant zero-temperature quantity is ground energy or a limiting free energy.

Test: specify the observable oracle and its cost. Then identify exactly where the proposed access is stronger than a SAT oracle. A useful new route would need a theorem deriving a zero-energy certificate or positive lower bound from local observables in polynomial time for every instance.

## Idea 6 - Modular witness resonance

Status: first version refuted as a decision method; a possible new route would need fast modular counting, which is itself a major complexity problem.

Let N_F be the number of satisfying assignments. Then F is satisfiable exactly when the integer N_F is positive. A tempting arithmetic/quantum analogy is to calculate N_F modulo primes and interpret a nonzero residue as a surviving witness amplitude. A zero residue is not an UNSAT certificate: the 2-variable formula (not-x or not-y) has exactly 3 satisfying assignments, so its count vanishes modulo 3; the empty 1-variable formula has 2 and vanishes modulo 2. The script `experiment_modular_witness_resonance.py` checks these examples by exhaustive enumeration.

Chinese remaindering would recover the exact count if residues were available for enough primes that their product exceeds 2^n. But computing those residues for arbitrary CNFs is the hard part; fast exact counting would solve a #P-complete task. A future angle would need a structural reason that the relevant residues are easy without already giving a #SAT algorithm.

## Idea 7 - Bounded consistency as a self-reference mirror

Status: speculative foundation connection; no contradiction or independence result.

For a formal theory T, let Con_T(n) say that no T-proof of contradiction of length at most n exists. Bounded proof search is an NP relation: a proposed proof is a polynomially checkable witness. If P = NP, bounded proof-existence for any fixed efficiently checkable proof system would have a polynomial-time decision algorithm, and positive instances would have efficiently findable proof witnesses. It is tempting to feed that solver statements about its own correctness, or to use all answers Con_T(n) to extract global consistency.

The obvious argument stops at the quantifier boundary. Answering every finite Con_T(n) query does not provide one finite proof of the universal statement for all n. Goedel incompleteness does not turn a fast bounded checker into a contradiction; any claim that it does must identify the exact formalized soundness or reflection principle being derived. A possible lead is to study whether a P = NP algorithm for a self-referential proof predicate forces a short reflection scheme in a weak arithmetic theory.

Next test: choose a small, explicit proof system and weak base theory, encode its bounded proof search, and write the proposed reflection implication as a formal sentence. Check whether it proves only each finite case or genuinely yields uniform reflection. Do not infer ZFC independence from failure of a particular proof attempt.

## Idea 9 - Finite combinatorics as a ZFC barometer

Status: literature lead, not a P-versus-NP result; the key independence claim is explicitly conjectural in the source. Its connection to ordinary binary Turing complexity has an input-size mismatch.

S. Gill Williamson's short preprint translates Friedman's Jump Free Theorem into a subset-sum statement. It proves a finite-function regularity theorem by invoking the Jump Free Theorem, then states that P = NP implies a related corollary about polynomial-time solvability of paired subset-sum instances. The abstract and final section conjecture that this corollary is independent of ZFC; they do not prove that independence. The corollary follows from the regularity theorem because the constructed F and H agree as sets; if interpreted as lists indexed by points of E^k, the same regularity argument removes the middle-block positions. Even if independence were established and the implication formalized in ZFC, it would only rule out a ZFC proof of P = NP, assuming ZFC consistency. It would not prove P != NP or establish the actual truth of the corollary.

This is a plausible wacky direction because an arithmetic statement about finite structures can require strong set-theoretic axioms, and complexity reductions can transfer consequences from P = NP to that statement. The missing task is exact: prove the corollary independent, or find a direct standard-model contradiction between P = NP and its actual truth value. The fact that a parent theorem uses large cardinals does not by itself make every corollary independent; a simpler proof may exist. The papers formally define the constructed instances as sets and count subsets of distinct integer values; the earlier ledger multiplicity objection was too strong under that convention. The 2024 note additionally says the sets have size p^k "as multisets"; that phrase should be made precise if the list interpretation is operationally relevant. The script experiment_subset_sum_multiplicity.py is only a convention demonstration, not a counterexample to the set-based count. The durable issue is the runtime measure: the papers count O(p^(kt)) comparisons and use p^k as instance size, but ordinary P = NP supplies time polynomial in total binary encoding length. The 2024 paper allows arbitrary bijections gamma:N -> Z without effectiveness or growth bounds; no uniform bit-length bound is supplied for the selected sequence of instances. Therefore the implication to the stated item-count runtime is not established in the standard Turing model as written. This is a model/encoding gap, not a refutation of the finite regularity theorem.

Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00468. For the distinction between oracle relativization and foundational independence, see Baker-Gill-Solovay, https://doi.org/10.1137/0204037, and Aaronson's survey, https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp.pdf.

Next test: formalize the exact implication from P = NP to the subset-sum corollary, including bit lengths of gamma-mapped integers and the set/list convention. The current reading finds this bridge under-specified in the standard binary input model. Then look for a direct proof of the corollary that avoids the Jump Free theorem. If it is independent, record only the resulting non-provability consequence.

## Idea 10 - The quine that outruns its own description (23 September 2026)

Status: a sharpened self-reference attempt; blocked by a size fixed point, with the obstruction written as an explicit recurrence.

Take a proposed deterministic polynomial-time SAT decider M with running time O(n^d). Try to use a recursion theorem or quine to build a SAT formula F whose satisfiability is the negation of M(code(F)). If an ordinary formula could uniformly encode that self-referential computation, then correctness of M would yield a contradiction. The key distinction is that Kleene fixed points give a program index that can refer to itself; they do not automatically give a Boolean formula whose own syntax is a fixed point of a semantic construction.

For an input string e of length n, a clocked simulation of M(e) may run for T=n^d steps. The generic Cook-Levin construction translates this bounded computation into a formula of size polynomial in T, so the output formula has length m=poly(n^d). The SAT-decider input in the desired contradiction must instead be the code of that output formula, of length m. A naive attempt to identify the two inputs therefore leads to a size equation m=poly(m^d), which does not close for d>1. This is an obstruction to the generic tableau/quine construction, not a proof that all self-reference fails: M might have a special compressed simulation on the relevant inputs, or a different fixed-point representation might avoid storing the tableau. Succinctly naming the tableau changes the input problem to succinct-SAT and does not preserve ordinary NP.

This is a formal diagnosis of this particular quine construction, not a theorem ruling out every self-referential P-vs-NP proof. The tableau-size claim concerns the canonical generic encoding; no unconditional lower bound is known here against every possible compression. Any claimed escape must identify a polynomial-size, uniformly constructible way to express the relevant computation without asking SAT to verify a longer transcript.

Next test: write down the exact language and encoding for a proposed fixed-point diagonal, distinguish an ordinary formula from a succinct formula, and compare input length, simulated runtime, and witness length before using recursion. Reject any version whose size recurrence is m >= poly(m^d) for d>1 unless it proves a new compression theorem.

## Idea 8 - Minimax violation margin

Status: exact characterization with a sharp gap; computational bottleneck is the original optimization problem.

For a CNF with m>=1 clauses C_1,...,C_m, let v_j(x)=1 when assignment x falsifies clause C_j and 0 otherwise. Define

    gamma(F) = max over weights w in the m-simplex of min over assignments x of sum_j w_j v_j(x).

If F is satisfiable, a satisfying assignment makes the inner sum zero for every w, so gamma(F)=0. If F is unsatisfiable, every assignment violates at least one clause; uniform weights therefore give gamma(F) at least 1/m. Thus SAT versus UNSAT is exactly the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial margin test gamma(F)=0 versus gamma(F)>=1/m.

The clause-free formula is trivially satisfiable and can be handled separately.

This turns SAT into a zero-sum game: one player chooses clause weights, the other chooses an assignment. Because the gap is 1/m, a polynomial-time additive approximation with error below 1/(3m) would decide SAT and hence imply P = NP. The LP has exponentially many assignment constraints. A separation oracle for those constraints must find an assignment minimizing a weighted number of violated clauses, which is weighted MaxSAT. If P = NP, that separation problem becomes polynomial-time and the ellipsoid method can optimize the LP. So efficient computation of this convex margin is another formulation equivalent to the target collapse; it does not yet yield an algorithm.

The SciPy LP experiment `experiment_violation_margin.py` checked the sign of gamma against satisfiability for all 512 CNFs over two variables, including a unique-solution formula, and confirmed the 1/m unsatisfiable lower bound. It also measured margins 1/2 for contradictory unit clauses and 1/4 for the four-cube cover. These finite checks support the implementation only; the gap proof above is elementary.

Possible next direction: replace assignments by low-degree pseudo-distributions or a restricted strategy class, then measure the degree needed to force positive margin on UNSAT formulas. That likely enters existing Sum-of-Squares and proof-complexity territory. A new result would need a structural theorem that computes or lower-bounds the restricted margin efficiently without hiding a SAT/MaxSAT oracle.

## Idea 11 - Semantic evidence, syntax leakage, and the neutral-atom trap (23 September 2026)

Status: a precise audit failure in a recent claimed proof architecture; it does not resolve P versus NP. The useful new language is a candidate repair framework, not yet a lower-bound method.

Audit target: Ben Goertzel, [A Quantale-Weakness Route to P != NP via CD Evidence Normalization and Gauge-Buffered Locked Ensembles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08814), v2 dated 22 April 2026. The paper's upper-bound implication is standard in outline: if a polynomial-time verifier has a satisfying assignment whose readout is the same message for every assignment, then P=NP gives a polynomial-time SAT self-reduction that finds an assignment and reads the message. The problem is the lower-bound ensemble and evidence interface needed for the contradiction.

The appendix defines an abstract locked core, then lists as hypotheses: lock satisfiability (D.7), rigidity of the message over all lock completions (D.8), balance of target coordinates (D.12), atom completeness (D.33), and existence of specially compatible opposite-message couplings (D.48). The main interface theorem 4.31 explicitly imports hidden-gauge product behavior and atom completeness as hypotheses; D.54 assumes the lock, buffer, syntax, atom-completeness, and coupling properties before it yields the sampler interface. The witnessed sampler does not instantiate the lock: it calls a lock sampler that already outputs a satisfying completion. The buffer appendix also assumes guarded remoteness and finite-geometry approximation (E.18-E.19), while bounded readout overlap is a hypothesis (F.36) with a remark about how a construction could enforce it. I found no concrete lock family or derivation discharging these assumptions in the paper's construction appendix.

The more structural concern is the public-input model. The paper says the observer sees the entire public SAT instance, but its primitive evidence interface has only declared public-template/surface reads, safe probes, and gauge literals; it excludes a primitive operation that simply runs a program on Y. The observer-to-evidence theorem expands a decision tree over that chosen interface. It does not establish that every ordinary polynomial-time machine on the full bit string Y has an evidence trace whose normalized target-relevant leaves are only safe-buffer or gauge atoms. That completeness is separately assumed (4.22/D.33).

The paper's Hypothesis 7.5 makes the interface problem sharper: every normalized neutral atom must be pair-neutral for every switched target under the fixed opposite-message coupling. If public syntax atoms cover every field of the full SAT instance Y, then pair-neutrality forces the two endpoints to agree on Y. But rigidity makes B_j a function of Y, so opposite-message endpoints cannot have the same Y. Hence the following fork is unavoidable: either neutral atoms expose the whole public input, in which case neutral coherence is inconsistent with opposite phases; or they expose only a target-independent quotient/skeleton, in which case the observer-to-evidence theorem has not shown that ordinary Turing machines inspecting the omitted public fields are represented. A proof could escape only by precisely defining an input encoding and proving a nontrivial completeness theorem that resolves this fork.

There is also a useful information-theoretic identity. Since rigidity makes B_j a deterministic function of Y on the ensemble support, the conditional public-input laws for B_j=0 and B_j=1 have disjoint supports, hence total variation distance exactly one. This does not provide a polynomial-time decoder: the optimal distinguishing set may have high circuit complexity. But it means that ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“public syntax is neutralÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â cannot mean the full public string is statistically phase-independent. The intended theorem must be about computational indistinguishability of a particular encoding, which is the missing hardness property.

Why this matters: ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“there is no field literally named target bitÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â does not imply that the target is hard to compute from all public fields. The script `experiment_public_neutral_leak.py` finds an invertible 12-by-12 linear encoding over GF(2) such that no set of at most three public bits determines any individual message bit, but Gaussian elimination on the full public vector recovers the entire message. If ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“no public decoderÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â bans every polynomial-time computation of public syntax, it assumes the desired hardness property; if it bans only declared tags or fixed template maps, it leaves ordinary computations like this inverse outside the proof's charge system. A valid proof must resolve this distinction and supply the missing construction, not just rename public reads as neutral.

Candidate language: for a fixed coupling ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ_j of worlds with opposite target bit, define the semantic derivative of an observation A by

    d_j(A) = Pr_(ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°0,ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°1)~ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ_j[A(ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°0) != A(ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°1)].

Call A neutral only when d_j(A)=0 under every relevant surviving pair relation, rather than because its syntax class is called neutral. A derived circuit f(A_1,...,A_k) can separate a pair only if some input observation separates it, so

    d_j(f(A_1,...,A_k)) <= sum_i d_j(A_i).

This finite union-bound fact is sound but currently weak: observing the whole public input may have large total derivative, and polynomial running time permits reading all of it. The novel obligation is to find a representation-independent measure that charges the computation of a target from public syntax by its *algorithmic* cost, while remaining composable through arbitrary circuits and useful against SAT self-reduction. No such measure has been found here.

The stronger coupling check also exposes a trap: the seeded 12-bit transform has no predictive subset of at most three public coordinates for any single target, yet for each target there is a coupling of opposite phases that pairs public strings differing in exactly one coordinate. Pick a public coordinate in the target's inverse-parity support and translate every phase-0 string by that unit vector; this is a bijection onto phase 1. Thus one fixed coupling can make one public atom separate every paired world even though that atom's marginal distribution is identical in the two phases. Pairwise disagreement under an arbitrary coupling is not the same as predictive advantage. An informative semantic norm must optimize over couplings for the *whole transcript* (equivalently, use its total variation), or directly use a circuit distinguishing norm. The latter is familiar pseudorandomness/average-case hardness, not a new lower-bound technique; the unresolved part is constructing the required hard distribution.

The follow-up literature check points to the right scale of the difficulty. Grollmann and Selman prove that one-way functions exist iff P != UP ([SIAM Journal on Computing](https://doi.org/10.1137/0217018)). Liu and Pass show that mild average-case hardness of a natural conditional time-bounded Kolmogorov problem characterizes one-way functions ([IACR ePrint 2021/513](https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/513)). There is an exact reduction behind the analogy. Let a fixed-length random tape r drive a deterministic witnessed sampler G(r)=(Y,W), let f(r)=Y, and suppose all valid witnesses for the same Y have a common message M(Y). An inverter I for f gives a predictor: on input Y, run I(Y) to obtain r', check f(r')=Y, rerun G(r'), and output its message. Whenever inversion succeeds, rigidity makes the output equal to M(Y). Thus hard-to-predict messages on one fixed uniform generator imply one-wayness of f. This is a diagnostic, not a proved implication for the arXiv construction: its ensemble parameters are chosen after fixing a clock exponent, so one must first build a single sampler family secure against all polynomial clocks before concluding it yields an OWF.

Experiment result: a seeded search found an invertible 12-bit linear encoding after two candidates. Every subset of at most three public coordinates was checked algebraically: its span contains none of the 12 message-coordinate vectors, so no such subset reveals any individual target bit on a uniform message. The inverse was checked on all 2^12 messages. For every target coordinate, the script also constructs an opposite-phase coupling changing exactly one public coordinate. Thus bounded-arity leakage checks and Hamming coupling cost can both miss the high-order parity structure, even though Gaussian elimination recovers the message in polynomial time.

Next proof task: see Idea 122. The exact coupling/total-variation identity is now proved. Continue by asking whether a full-input trace theorem can charge ordinary input-bit reads without assuming locality; the linear parity encoding is an explicit stress test.

## Idea 12 - Diagonal sampler and the logarithmic input-length wall (23 September 2026)

Status: direct brute-force diagonalization has a sharp size/time tradeoff. A generic explicit-tableau self-reference cannot close the size equation; a hidden-seed construction would need to evade the resulting public-decoding barrier.

Try to sample a public string Y of length N and a t-bit message M(Y) that no program of length at most a t computes from Y within N^D steps. Assume the public sampler uniformly knows t=t(N) with polynomial overhead. For the counting construction to have an absent t-bit output, take a fixed 0<a<1 and sufficiently large t: then there are at most 2^{a t+O(1)} candidate programs, fewer than the 2^t possible messages. The direct construction would enumerate every such program, run it on Y for the clock, and choose M to be the first t-bit string absent from their outputs. This naive method costs about 2^{at}N^D universal-machine steps, up to polynomial overhead.

The threshold is exact for this direct method. If t=O(log N), then 2^{a t} is polynomial in N, so the brute-force diagonal is polynomial-time computable from Y. The diagonalizer itself is a fixed short program producing M(Y), with some exponent E>D; it defeats any claimed lower bound whose clock is at least E. If t/log N grows without bound, this direct enumeration becomes superpolynomial in N; this is a limitation of the proposed method, not a general lower bound against every possible sampler. A sampler might know M from hidden randomness while Y conceals it. But arranging that separation is one-way-function-like: the sampler's knowledge cannot be converted into a public-input decoding program.

The fixed-point variant inherits Idea 10's tableau-size problem. This can be stated as a no-go lemma for the *padded explicit-tableau construction*. Let the public input have length N, let the diagonalizer enumerate K=2^{a t+O(1)} descriptions, and deliberately clock-pad every simulation to N^D steps, with D>=1. Its universal computation then uses T=Theta(K N^D) steps up to fixed interpreter constants. A Cook-Levin encoding that explicitly records one tableau row per simulated step has length at least cT for a fixed c>0. If that output formula is required to be its own public input, then N>=c K N^D. For superlogarithmic t, K is superpolynomial in N, so this inequality fails for all sufficiently large N. If the enumeration is not padded, the actual tableau size depends on the run times of the listed programs; the inequality is then conditional on the actual transcript length and does not follow from the clock upper bound alone. This rules out the padded explicit fixed-point encoding; it is not a lower bound against all possible formula encodings or all self-reference.

The parameter split is now explicit. If t=O(log N), then K N^D is polynomial in N, and the sampler's diagonalizer is itself a fixed polynomial-time public decoder for M(Y), with some exponent E. That contradicts any proposed hardness claim at clocks at least N^E. If t/log N tends to infinity, the explicit tableau needed for the same sweep is longer than N, so it cannot be the formula whose code was the diagonalizer's input. Intermediate t=c log N still gives polynomial enumeration and hence falls on the first side, with the polynomial exponent depending on c. A route that handles every polynomial clock using one fixed sampler would need something beyond this brute-force enumeration.

Succinctly naming the tableau is not a generic escape. For arbitrary succinct 3-CNF inputs, satisfiability is NEXP-complete: a circuit can describe an exponentially long Cook-Levin formula, and the standard tableau construction for a nondeterministic exponential-time computation yields such a circuit in polynomial time. Therefore a general polynomial-time compiler from arbitrary succinct 3-SAT to ordinary SAT would put NEXP in NP, contradicting Cook's nondeterministic time hierarchy theorem. A compiler for only a special structured family of tableaux is not ruled out by this argument; it would need its own explicit construction and proof. The change of input model is the known point of this avenue, not a new separation.

Result: a theorem-level obstruction for the naive explicit-tableau quine and a clean two-regime diagnosis for direct diagonal sampling. No new complexity-class separation follows. The theorem does not exclude length-preserving fixed points of a different form, nor a special succinct compiler; both remain precise proof obligations rather than assumed impossibilities. Background references: Papadimitriou and Yannakakis, [A Note on Succinct Representations of Graphs](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(86)80009-2), and Cook, [A Hierarchy for Nondeterministic Time Complexity](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-0000(73)80028-5). The succinct-3SAT NEXP-completeness consequence follows by the usual Cook-Levin tableau argument for nondeterministic exponential time.

## Idea 13 - Lawvere fixed points with resource-indexed evaluation (23 September 2026)

Status: a fresh conceptual lens for the self-reference branch; it identifies the missing resource-preservation theorem but does not yet provide one.

Lawvere's fixed-point theorem packages diagonal arguments categorically. In one standard form, if an evaluation map e:A -> B^A is weakly point-surjective, then every endomorphism f:B -> B has a fixed point. For B={0,1}, choosing f to be negation shows that a universal evaluator cannot simultaneously enumerate every Boolean function and remain in a setting where such total evaluation is available. This unifies the familiar diagonal move, but it does not say that a fixed point has a short SAT encoding.

The P-vs-NP adaptation would need a resource-indexed evaluation object: inputs describe candidate polynomial-time SAT solvers, the evaluator runs the described solver within its declared clock, and a diagonal object negates that answer while remaining an ordinary polynomial-size SAT instance with the intended truth value. The fixed-point theorem supplies no size or runtime bounds for this translation. The known gap reappears as failure to prove that the evaluator, diagonal flip, and SAT encoding all fit within one polynomial resource bound. If that construction succeeded uniformly against every polynomial clock, it would prove P != NP; calling the evaluator a categorical object does not discharge that burden.

Finite check: circuits of size at most s on n input bits have at most K=2^{O(s log(n+s))} descriptions, while a full truth table on n bits has 2^n entries. A brute-force census that evaluates every candidate on every input has KÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â·2^n entries/work, and is only polynomial in the truth-table length in regimes where K is polynomial in 2^n. This census is deliberately simple; a diagonal function may admit a more economical construction, so the count is not a lower bound. It does show that Lawvere's theorem alone gives no small evaluator or truth table. If a succinct circuit replaces the table, membership of the resulting diagonal language and the uniform circuit construction need separate analysis. This reproduces the representation-size wall as a diagnostic, not a theorem ruling out a better construction. The conceptual gain is a checklist: identify the evaluator, the diagonal endomap, the represented function class, and the exact resource bound at each map.

Primary reference: Lawvere, [Diagonal Arguments and Cartesian Closed Categories](https://www.tac.mta.ca/tac/reprints/articles/15/tr15abs.html) (1969). Status after this test: useful organizing language, not a new lower-bound invariant. The next step is to try a genuinely different resource measure or a special circuit family for which point-surjectivity can be quantified without writing the full truth table.

## Idea 14 - The GÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¶del numbering may be the hidden resource (Kozen's subrecursive indexings)

Status: unusually relevant literature lead; only the abstract and bibliographic record have been checked so far, so the theorem's exact scope is not yet audited.

Dexter Kozen's 1980 paper [Indexings of Subrecursive Classes](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3975(80)90017-1) studies a complexity class together with a programming system/GÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¶del numbering for its functions. The abstract says the paper relates uniform simulation, diagonalization, membership and halting, and characterizes diagonalization power for subrecursive classes. It also says that if $P\r\ne NP$ is provable at all, it is provable by diagonalization. This is a striking clue: perhaps the obstacle is not absence of fixed points, but the choice of how candidate polynomial-time algorithms are indexed and simulated.

Do not read the abstract as a proof of $P\r\ne NP$, as a claim that every proof must look like the textbook liar argument, or as a construction of an NP diagonal language. The exact indexing axioms and the precise meaning of ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“provable by diagonalizationÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â must be recovered from the paper.

There is a useful conditional reindexing lemma behind the abstract-level claim. Let $C$ be an effectively enumerable class of total Boolean functions on binary strings that contains constants and is closed under finite changes. If a computable Boolean function $g$ is outside $C$, then there is a computable surjective indexing $\varphi_e$ of $C$ whose diagonal is exactly $g$: $g(e)=1-\varphi_e(e)$, with each index string also used as the input string. Start with a total effective enumeration $\psi_j$ of $C$. Since $g\r\notin C$, each $\psi_j$ disagrees with $g$ on infinitely many strings; otherwise $g$ would be a finite change of $\psi_j$ and hence belong to $C$. In a fixed length-lexicographic order, choose an increasing sequence of code strings $e_j$ with $\psi_j(e_j)=1-g(e_j)$. Set $\varphi_{e_j}=\psi_j$, and for every unused code string $e$, set $\varphi_e$ to the constant function $1-g(e)$. The indexing is computable: to determine whether $e$ is one of the reserved $e_j$, generate the increasing sequence until it reaches or passes $e$. It is surjective because every $\psi_j$ gets a reserved index, and every index satisfies the diagonal identity by construction.

For $C=P$ and any hypothetical $g\in NP\setminus P$, the lemma would yield a computable numbering of P whose diagonal is that NP language. This is a conditional repackaging, not a way to find $g$: the reindexing procedure itself uses $g$ to locate the reserved codes, and no polynomial runtime bound follows. In fact, if the universal evaluator $U(e,x)=\varphi_e(x)$ for this numbering were in P, then $g(e)=1-U(e,e)$ would be in P, contradiction. The separation is therefore stored in the indexing/evaluation cost. The construction proves only a computable surjective numbering; whether it satisfies all of Kozen's axioms remains unverified until the paper is available.

There is also a precise benchmark for the ordinary clocked-machine indexing. Let $U(p,x)$ be the deterministic universal evaluator that parses $p=\langle M,1^k\r\nangle$ and accepts iff $M$ accepts $x$ within $|x|^k$ steps; define $\mathrm{UEVAL}=\{\langle p,x\r\nangle:U(p,x)=1\}$. Every fixed program code $p$ gives a polynomial-time function, and all of P occurs among the sections. On an input of total length $m$, $k\le m$ and $|x|\le m$, so universal simulation takes at most $m^m=2^{O(m\log m)}$ steps up to polynomial simulation overhead; hence $\mathrm{UEVAL}\in EXP$. Conversely, for any fixed $L\in EXP$ decided in time $2^{n^c}$ by $M_L$, map $x$ of length $n\ge2$ to $\langle\langle M_L,1^{n^c}\r\nangle,x\r\nangle$. This is a polynomial-time reduction, and $n^{n^c}\ge2^{n^c}$, so $\mathrm{UEVAL}$ is EXP-hard. Thus this standard universal evaluator is EXP-complete. If it were in NP, EXP would be contained in NP; since NP is contained in EXP, this would give NP=EXP, and then P\r\ne NP follows from the deterministic time hierarchy P\subsetneq EXP. This does not establish that upper bound; it shows that proving an NP bound for this universal evaluator would already be a stronger-than-needed breakthrough.

The associated diagonal language gives a sharper concrete target. Let $D_U(p)=1-U(p,p)$ for valid clocked-program codes $p$, with any fixed convention on malformed strings. Then $D_U\in EXP$, and $D_U\r\notin P$: if a polynomial-time decider for $D_U$ had clocked code $p_D$, then $D_U(p_D)=U(p_D,p_D)$ by correctness, while the definition gives $D_U(p_D)=1-U(p_D,p_D)$. In fact $D_U$ is EXP-hard. Given any $L\in EXP$, hardwire $x$ into a clocked machine $M_x$ that ignores its input and decides the complement of $L$ on $x$; choose a unary clock exponent $k=|x|^c$. The code $p_x=\langle M_x,1^k\r\nangle$ has polynomial length, and its clock $|p_x|^k$ exceeds the $2^{|x|^c}$ simulation time. Thus $D_U(p_x)=L(x)$. Therefore $D_U$ is EXP-complete and outside P. Showing $D_U\in NP$ would immediately prove P\r\ne NP (indeed NP=EXP). This is a precise target language, but its NP membership remains entirely open.

The toy experiment [experiment_kozen_reindexing_toy.py](experiment_kozen_reindexing_toy.py) instantiates the construction for the class of eventually constant Boolean sequences and $g(e)=e\bmod 2$. It verifies the diagonal identity across a finite prefix and checks that the first enumerated base functions receive distinct reserved codes. This checks the implementation, not the infinite lemma; the infinite argument is the proof above.

Next test: obtain and read Kozen's full 1978 conference/1980 journal text; formalize the theorem's hypotheses and check whether the custom reindexing lemma meets them. The standard universal evaluator is EXP-complete, so focus on a special diagonal restriction whose NP verification does not imply an NP upper bound for the full evaluator. The 1992 paper by Jones and Regan on delayed diagonalization and fixed-point theorems for subrecursive classes is a companion lead, not yet analyzed: https://doi.org/10.1016/0890-5401(92)90040-M.

## Idea 15 - Clock entropy and the uniform verifier budget (23 September 2026)

Status: a precise resource-profile lemma and a useful failure diagnosis. It does not put a diagonal language in NP.

Let a program index be a pair p=<M,1^k>, where the unary component declares a time limit. Take a polynomial-time computable, nondecreasing, unbounded clock ceiling h(n) (for example, ceil(log n)); define U_h(p,x) to simulate M(x) for |x|^k steps only when k<=h(|p|), and define D_h(p)=1-U_h(p,p). Allow arbitrary ignored padding in program codes. If h is unbounded, every fixed polynomial-time decider M has some padded index p=<M,1^k> with k large enough to bound M's runtime and k<=h(|p|). If D_h were in P, apply this to a polynomial-time decider for D_h; on its padded index p, U_h(p,p)=D_h(p), while the definition says D_h(p)=1-U_h(p,p), a contradiction. Hence D_h is outside P for every such unbounded ceiling h.

The construction's direct simulation uses n^{O(h(n))} time for length-n codes, up to universal-interpreter overhead (assuming the ceiling is efficiently evaluable and h(n)<=n). For h(n)=ceil(log n), this is quasipolynomial time 2^{O(log^2 n)} and still outside P. The ceiling can grow arbitrarily slowly, but if it is unbounded then the direct deterministic computation can have length n^{h(n)}, which is not bounded by n^c for any one fixed c. An explicit tableau has at least one row per simulated step (and the standard full tableau can be quadratic in the step count), so an NP verifier cannot simply include that full trace as its witness. This is only an obstacle to the explicit-trace certificate: a different, compressed certificate could exist. For the unrestricted unary clock k<=n, the evaluator returns to Idea 14's EXP-complete universal language; placing that full evaluator or its diagonal in NP would imply EXP=NP and therefore P!=NP.

The underlying quantifier mismatch is now explicit. P is the union over all fixed polynomial exponents, while one NP verifier must use one fixed witness exponent across all inputs. Diagonalizing against the first family forces the code to carry unbounded k; a literal computation certificate then inherits that unbounded exponent. A successful self-reference proof must exhibit a certificate whose verification cost is uniform in k without checking the full n^k-step computation.

Indexing literature adds a separate restriction. Bhaskar and Simonsen summarize one of Kozen's subrecursive-indexing axioms as a polynomial-time compiler that, from codes of f and g, outputs a code for f composed with g ([Read/write factorizable programs](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0956796823000023), Section 9, footnote 18). The conditional reindexing in Idea 14 is only computable and deliberately uses the hypothetical diagonal g to reserve indices. It has not been shown to meet this efficient composition requirement, constant-generation requirements, or Kozen's complete axiom list. Efficient composability is exactly where the tailored numbering may fail; no impossibility theorem for that custom indexing has been established.

Padding rescue attempt: encode a short machine/index core x together with a much longer ignored padding string, hoping the physical input length will make the simulated run |x|^k polynomially certifiable. Padding does make a transcript for a computation on x short relative to the padded input p. But to diagonalize against a decider M_D of the resulting language, one needs M_D(p) to equal the simulated value on x. A natural way to ensure this is to make the language invariant under padding; then any decider can be normalized to strip the padding and run on x. The problem moves to the canonical short input x: padding invariance forces D(x)=D(p), so NP membership must still provide a polynomial-size certificate for that same diagonal truth value on x. If instead short inputs are declared inactive, padding invariance and the needed equality fail. Thus padding alone does not compress the diagonal certificate; it merely transfers the unresolved certificate obligation to the shortest representative. A non-trace certificate for that short representative remains a possible lead, but none is known.

Next test: recover the precise Kozen axioms and diagonal theorem from the full text or a reliable transcription. Then test whether any polynomial-time compositional indexing can make its diagonal NP-verifiable without putting the whole EXP-complete evaluator in NP. Treat this as a conjectural obstruction until proved; the observed clock/certificate gap rules out only the direct tableau witness.

## Idea 16 - Incompressible strings under a self-referential clock

Status: literature-grounded attempt; the search gives a polynomial-time generator under P=NP for each fixed clock, but the generator's polynomial degree need not fit that clock. No separation follows.

For a fixed polynomial clock f(n), let K^f(x) be the length of the shortest program that prints x within f(|x|) steps. The language Upper_f={(x,s): K^f(x)<=s} is in NP when s<=|x|+O(1): guess a program of length s and simulate it for f(|x|) steps. Its complement Lower_f is in coNP. If P=NP, both predicates are in P, so binary search over s computes K^f(x) deterministically in polynomial time.

Try to turn that fact into a diagonal string. For a prefix u, ask whether there exists a completion x of length n extending u with K^f(x)>s. This is an existential quantifier over a coNP property, hence a Sigma_2^P predicate. Under P=NP, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to P, so this prefix-extension test is in P. Set s=n-2: by counting, some n-bit string has K^f(x)>s, since there are fewer than 2^{n-1} programs of length at most n-2. Repeatedly querying the prefix test can construct such a string x_n. The generator has fixed code plus the binary encoding of n, so an unclocked program can print x_n using O(log n) description bits.

The attempted contradiction needs more: that this generator itself runs within the same clock f(n)=n^d. Its polynomial exponent a_f can depend on f and on the collapse algorithms. A Cook-Levin encoding of the n^d-step bounded-output predicate and a P algorithm for the resulting formula can multiply the exponent; P=NP gives no linear or degree-preserving running-time bound. If a_f<d (or a concrete runtime bound fits f), then the generator with n hardwired (O(log n) bits) prints x_n within f(n), contradicting K^f(x_n)>n-2. But choosing a larger clock changes the predicate and may change the generator's exponent again. Thus we have no fixed point ensuring a_f<d. This is the same clock debt as Idea 15, now expressed as a time-bounded incompressibility problem.

This is close to existing literature, not a new theorem. Hromkovic proves conditional disjunctions: either P!=NP, or deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial-time compression differ in a specified way; another corollary says P=NP would make time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity computable in deterministic polynomial time for each fixed polynomial clock. The report's discussion explicitly says its argument cannot rule out an unbounded sequence of deterministic compression improvements, because the descriptions of the successive compressors may keep growing. See the [ECCC report and revision](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2021/049/) and the published [2024 Theoretical Computer Science article](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tcs.2024.114747). These are implications and proposed indications, not an accepted proof of P!=NP.

Next test: formalize the prefix-extension language with explicit encodings and reductions, bound the generator's code length and time exponent as functions of the clock exponent d, and see whether a degree-neutral compression theorem can hold for a restricted universal machine model. Without a bound making the generator fit inside its own fixed clock (or another sound self-reference relation), discard the contradiction route.

## Idea 17 - High nondeterministic-complexity strings as a separation target

Status: a concrete target extracted from a very recent meta-complexity lower bound. The target would prove P!=NP if constructed, but its NP verifier is precisely the missing difficulty.

Goldberg, Hu, Lu, Lyu, and Oliveira (ECCC report TR25-215, revised February 2026) prove that for every fixed gamma>1/2, every dense language L contained in R_nKt[gamma n] lies outside NTIME(2^{epsilon n}) intersect coNTIME(2^{epsilon n}) for some epsilon>0. Here R_nKt[gamma n] consists of strings x whose nondeterministic time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity nKt(x) is at least gamma|x|. They also show that the associated estimation problem is NEXP-hard under nonuniform reductions and lies in P^NEXP.

This gives a clean conditional route: if one could construct a *dense uniform NP language* L contained in R_nKt[gamma n], then P!=NP. Under P=NP, L would be in P; every P language is in NTIME(2^{epsilon n}) intersect coNTIME(2^{epsilon n}), contradicting the theorem. The same implication works for a dense coNP subset. This route turns P!=NP into a verifiable anti-compression certificate problem: certify, in NP, that each accepted string cannot be generated by any shorter nondeterministic program within its declared time.

The missing certificate is substantial. nKt's definition has an existential choice of program and time bound together with a universal condition over all nondeterministic paths, so the low-complexity predicate carries a high quantifier cost. This review found no dense NP or coNP subset of the high-complexity set. The NEXP-hardness result alone does not solve this: its reductions are nonuniform, and under P=NP an NP upper bound would yield NEXP subset P/poly, whose impossibility is itself open. Thus do not turn the paper's lower bound into a P-vs-NP separation.

Foundations/proof-system variant: for each x, write a succinct bounded-arithmetic or propositional claim saying that no description of cost <gamma|x| uniquely generates x. Let L_S contain x when it has a short proof of that claim in a sound proof system S with a polynomial-time checker on the chosen succinct encoding. Then L_S is in NP, and soundness gives L_S subset R_nKt[gamma n]. If L_S were dense, the ECCC theorem would prove P!=NP. The missing step is a density theorem for *short proofs*: counting proves that most x are high-nKt, but it gives no polynomial-size certificate for an individual x. Also, a proof system for succinct formulas must verify soundness in polynomial time without expanding the exponentially long computation statement. This is a precise way to connect the ZFC/proof-complexity theme to the recent meta-complexity result, but neither proof-size nor succinct-verifier obligation is met yet.

Primary source: [Goldberg et al., Synergies Between Complexity Theory and Nondeterministic Kolmogorov Complexity](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/215/), especially Theorem 1.1 and the definition of R_nKt. The authors explicitly describe a superpolynomial circuit lower bound for the deterministic version as a breakthrough-level missing result. This idea is distinct from the Hromkovic time-bounded-compression disjunction in Idea 16: the actionable target here is a dense NP subset of a language already proved hard for subexponential NP intersect coNP.

Next test: determine the exact uniform upper-bound class and density of R_nKt[gamma n], then search for a natural NP-verifiable restriction whose members are provably high nKt. In particular, define a sound proof system for the succinct anti-generator statement and bound its proof-checking cost; then separately prove that polynomial-size certificates cover a dense subset. Any candidate must rule out *all* shorter nondeterministic generators; a witness that only hides the output from a selected family is insufficient.

## Idea 18 - Information debt, worst-case symmetry, and an average-to-worst bootstrap

Status: sharp conditional P-vs-NP target from recent literature; an attempted shortcut from average-case to worst-case fails because the counterexample search still costs exponential time. No separation is proved.

For pnKt (probabilistic nondeterministic time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity), the exact worst-case statement is: for some fixed c>0 and every sufficiently large n, all x,y in {0,1}^n satisfy

    pnKt(x,y) >= pnKt(x) + pnKt(y | x) - log^c(n).

Goldberg, Hu, Lu, Lyu, and Oliveira prove that this statement implies UNSAT is not in AMTIME[2^(log^d n)] for every d>=1. If P=NP, then PH=P and AM is contained in P, so UNSAT would be in P and hence in AMTIME[2^(log^2 n)], contradicting the theorem for d=2. Therefore proving the displayed worst-case inequality would prove P!=NP. This is a remarkably focused target: a resource-bounded chain rule for description length that is strong enough to rule out short interactive proofs for UNSAT.

The same authors prove an average-case version for every polynomial-time samplable pair distribution. It holds with high probability, with an O(log n + log k) loss at failure probability 1/k, and its first term is pKt(x) rather than pnKt(x). A tempting bootstrap is to assume P=NP, search for a pair violating worst-case symmetry, and feed the pair to this average-case theorem as a sampler. That does not presently work. The paper's own gap-testing routine for pnKt thresholds enumerates all candidate programs of budget at most m/2 and makes SAT queries, taking 2^{O(m)} time. The possible pnKt values relevant to the worst-case inequality can be linear in string length, so collapsing SAT to P removes the oracle but not this exponential description search. Average-case symmetry only covers polynomial-time samplers; the violating pair has not been shown polynomial-time generable.

The proof's mechanism suggests a useful new vocabulary. Under a hypothetical short AM proof system for UNSAT, it constructs a sequence x_1,...,x_ell with each conditional pnKt(x_i | x_1,...,x_{i-1}) at least m/2, while the joint sequence has much smaller randomized nondeterministic time-bounded description. Call the accumulated excess the *information debt*: a chain-rule inequality would force the short joint description to pay for each increment, but the construction makes the unpaid debt grow with ell. This is a metaphor for the algebra in the proof, not a new invariant. The theorem extracts a pair (u,v) with a polylogarithmic violation from this sequence; the pair family is not shown to be efficiently samplable.

The telescoping proof reveals a narrower target than full worst-case symmetry. Let u_i=x_1||...||x_{i-1}, and let v_i be x_i padded with zeros to |u_i| bits. It is enough to have, for these particular append pairs, pnKt(u_i,v_i) >= pnKt(u_i)+pnKt(v_i|u_i)-delta(n), with delta(n)=o(m) and with encoding losses O(log n) absorbed. Summing over i would charge at least about m/2-delta(n) per new block, contradicting the paper's short joint description when ell is large. The pairs are generated using a pseudorandom set and an AMÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©coAM oracle under the contradictory assumption UNSATÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â AMTIME[n^polylog(n)]; their generation procedure enumerates exponentially many m-bit candidates. So this restricted statement is not yet easier, but it isolates exactly where a proof could exploit special structure instead of all pairs.

Related extension to test: average-case SoI is proved for polynomial-time samplers. Could it be extended to a carefully bounded class of slower samplers while charging their description/time overhead explicitly? A direct extension to arbitrary samplers cannot be assumed: time-bounded symmetry is known to fail for related measures, and the sequence's generator may be far above polynomial time in its output length. Any useful theorem would need an overhead smaller than the m-scale conditional-complexity increments in this construction.

Important variant check: the target must use pnKt. A 2026 ECCC paper proves that the analogous symmetry of information fails for rKt and pKt, so swapping in ordinary randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity does not work. Also, the 2025-215 paper constructs an oracle under which every listed measure (rKt, pKt, nKt, rnKt, pnKt) has pairs with a linear violation. Thus a proof of the needed unrelativized worst-case theorem must use a nonrelativizing ingredient.

Primary sources: [Goldberg et al., TR25-215, Theorem 5.3 and Sections 5.1-5.4](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/215/); [Hu, Manor, and Oliveira, TR26-021](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/021/). The latter establishes failure for rKt and pKt, not pnKt.

Next test: isolate the weakest restricted SoI statement actually used in Theorem 5.3's telescoping argument. Test whether it can be proved for the append pairs (u_i,v_i) from the paper's sequence using a nonrelativizing property of its pseudorandom-set construction. In parallel, test a slower-sampler version of average-case SoI with an explicit log-runtime loss and see whether that loss is below m/2 for these sequences. Do not assume the generator is polynomial in output length or that P=NP removes its 2^m candidate sweep. Any route must overcome the oracle barrier.

## Idea 19 - Random-seed collapse under P=NP

Status: proved conditional lemma about descriptions; not a P-vs-NP separation. It clarifies what the P=NP hypothesis does and does not buy in Idea 18.

Claim: if P=NP, then every string x with rnKt(x)<=B also has deterministic time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity Kt(x)=O(B), with a constant depending on the assumed polynomial algorithms. Here rnKt uses a program ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â , a time bound t, a public random string r of length t, and a nondeterministic string w of length t. On at least 2/3 of random tapes r, all nondeterministic paths output either x or ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¦Ã‚Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥ and at least one path outputs x.

For a fixed encoded pair (ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â ,1^t,r), define GOOD to mean there is a witness w whose computation outputs a non-bottom string z and every other witness outputs either z or ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¦Ã‚Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥. A witness w together with a universal check over w' gives a Sigma_2^P predicate. The current Revision #1 of Hirahara and Nanashima's TR25-092 (accepted 8 April 2026) substantially changed the earlier report. ## Idea 21 - Output-spectrum calculus for ambiguous descriptions

Status: new bookkeeping language and a concrete extraction question; not a new complexity measure theorem yet.

For a clock T, advice y, program-size bound s, and random tape r, define the output spectrum

    S_{T,s}(y,r) = { z : some program pi of length at most s outputs z from (y,r) within T steps }.

For a target x, its support in this spectrum is

    supp_{T,s}(x|y) = Pr_r[x in S_{T,s}(y,r)].

This makes the pK-to-pnKt gap visible. Probabilistic pK measures high support of x. Probabilistic nondeterministic pnKt additionally requires a compact uniform mechanism that marks x as the unique live element of the spectrum on most relevant r. Call the extra description required to perform that isolation the selector debt. The term is only a proposed analysis device; define it relative to an explicit selector machine, clock, and error before using it in a theorem.

Sanity checks: if S_{T,s}(y,r)={x} on every r, selector debt is O(1), and the pK description immediately induces a unique-output description. If every S_{T,s}(y,r) contains both x and an unrelated y, pK supports both equally; the spectrum alone cannot identify the intended target. Encoding x itself always isolates it at cost |x|+O(log T), so the naive bound is linear and consumes the sequence's m/2-scale gain. A random hash can isolate x from at most 2^s competitors with about s fingerprint bits, but a general pairwise-independent hash on m-bit outputs also needs a seed describing an m-by-s map; this is not a sublinear selector without extra structure. No finite experiment can decide whether the paper's spectra have the needed structure.

There is an exact toy lower bound against a general sublinear selector theorem. Let the universe be strings x_u=0^k||u for uÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â {0,1}^k and let S_r={x_u:uÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â {0,1}^k} for every random tape r. Then every target has support 1 and every seed has the same spectrum. A selector that sees only S_r and a b-bit target-specific advice string can name at most 2^b members of this 2^k-element family; selecting an arbitrary prescribed target therefore requires bÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥k in the worst case. This spectrum is realizable by k-bit programs that hardwire u. It shows that high pK support alone cannot force sublinear selector debt; any improvement must use a structural property of the actual TR25-215 spectra.

The promising question is narrower than inventing another entropy: in the TR25-215 sequence, do the public-randomness/pseudorandom-set construction and the AMÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©coAM predicate force S_r to be nearly single-valued on the sequence's actual prefix-conditioned blocks? If yes, a selector could convert conditional pnKt lower bounds into the pK lower bounds needed by Idea 20. If no, exhibit a spectrum family consistent with every stated property but with linear selector debt. Either outcome would sharpen the exact obstruction.

Next test: the sequence's A procedure is deterministic once T_s and the AMÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©coAM oracle L are fixed; it picks the first x whose estimated test acceptance exceeds 1/3+1/10. Its output is already single-valued. The ambiguity is instead in a hypothetical short pK description of one such x. The two-test co-selection has a counting plausibility argument, but it does not pay the pKt-to-q_t clock conversion. Reopen only with a bound that makes the conversion loss and the actual 2^poly(m) generator runtime smaller than the per-block gain. Do not infer single-valuedness from the words "pseudorandom set" or "AMÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©coAM".

## Idea 22 - The degree ladder in a self-referential SAT instance

Status: the diagonal has a clean size equation, but no fixed polynomial encoding closes it for an arbitrary P decider. Succinct encodings that do close the size equation move the language out of NP.

Fix an encoding E_c that maps an n-bit description x to an ordinary CNF ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â _x of length at most n^c, where c is a fixed constant. The language L_c={x: ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â _x is satisfiable} is in NP: guess an assignment of length at most n^c, generate ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â _x, and check it. Suppose a proposed P decider D for L_c runs in n^k time. A self-reference diagonal would like ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â _x to assert that D rejects x. A Cook-Levin tableau for D(x) has size n^{O(k)}. It fits in E_c's expansion only if c is at least the tableau exponent, which can be larger than c. Since c is fixed before D is known, this does not diagonalize against every polynomial-time decider.

Allowing c to be chosen in the input does not solve the problem: if c(x) is unbounded, the verifier may need n^{c(x)} time and witness bits, so the language need not be in NP. Padding x to make it longer also pads D's input and raises its simulated time to |x|^k; it does not create a fixed point. An exponentially succinct tableau does fit in a short description, but satisfiability of an exponentially expanded formula has exponentially long witnesses and is an NEXP problem. The resource equation is d_new ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â  kÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â·d_old: for k>1, no finite polynomial degree d is a fixed point. This equation summarizes the failed construction; it is not a general lower-bound theorem.

Tested variants: recursion-theorem self-reference produces a program index, not an explicitly expanded SAT formula; polynomially bounded expansion leaves the unknown exponent mismatch; exponential expansion changes the witness class. A useful new construction would need a representation with all three properties at once: short self-reference, ordinary polynomial-size certificates, and verifier time bounded by one fixed polynomial independent of D's exponent. No such representation is identified.

The same mismatch appears in total search. For a fixed polynomial-time bit function f, the relation R_f(x,b)=[bÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â f(x)] is a total P relation, and f is not its solver. To diagonalize against every solver in one fixed language, encode a machine M, input x, and a unary clock 1^t, and accept b exactly when b differs from M(x)'s output within t steps (with a default answer if M does not halt). This relation is itself polynomial-time in the explicit clock length. But a proposed solver S may take N^k time on the whole encoded input of length N, while the verifier only simulates S for tÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¤N steps. Setting t=N^k requires the unary clock field to have length N^k, after which S's runtime is (N^k)^k. The diagonal condition again has no finite fixed point for k>1. Binary clocks would make the bounded simulation potentially exponential and leave NP.

Next test: revisit only if a representation offers a verifiable local constraint system of polynomial size whose witness checks the full D(x) computation without writing its tableau. State the witness length and checking time explicitly; a succinct generator alone is not enough.

## Idea 23 - Bounded consistency as a nonstandard reflection ladder

Status: the bounded statements collapse under P=NP, but the missing finite-to-global step is exactly the unbounded reflection problem.

Let T be a fixed recursively axiomatized theory with a polynomial-time proof checker, and let Con_T(1^N) assert that no T-proof of contradiction has length at most N. Given 1^N, a counterexample proof is an NP witness, so Con_T(1^N) is coNP. Under P=NP, each bounded consistency question has a deterministic polynomial-time decider in the explicit input length N. The global statement Con(T) is ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬N Con_T(1^N), however. Fast answers for every finite bound do not give a single finite proof of all bounds, nor do they imply that T is consistent.

A GÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¶del-style sentence saying "there is no T-proof of this sentence below N^k" can be checked against a polynomial cutoff, but proving the required lower bound on T-proof length is a proof-complexity lower bound. If the cutoff is exponential in the sentence length, the certificate/search encoding can leave NP. Thus the informal move from P=NP to global reflection silently changes either the quantifier range or the resource bound. No independence claim follows from this observation.

Next test: choose one explicit weak arithmetic theory and proof system, formalize its bounded reflection sentence, and determine whether any finite-to-global principle is already equivalent to a known open proof-length lower bound. Only continue if a genuinely new compression theorem appears.

## Idea 24 - SAT as a zero-temperature phase transition

Status: cross-field translation with a precise failure point; no physical lower bound on abstract running time follows.

For a 3-CNF formula ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  on n variables, define E_ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â (a) as the number of violated clauses and the partition function Z_ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â (ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â²)=ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â£_{aÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â {0,1}^n} exp(-ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â² E_ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â (a)). Then ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  is satisfiable exactly when the ground-state energy min_a E_ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â (a) is zero, equivalently when the zero-temperature free energy reaches zero. The same object can be viewed as a weighted sum over the vertices of a solution-space complex or as a tensor-network contraction.

This rephrasing exposes several known resource costs: exact Z_ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  contains #SAT information; low-temperature approximation may require exponentially fine precision; tensor contraction depends on graph width; local homology only sees the represented complex if its chain groups and boundary maps can be constructed within the allowed input size. None of these facts gives a lower bound against unrestricted polynomial-time algorithms. Landauer's principle constrains irreversible physical erasure, while a complexity lower bound concerns abstract computation and can be modeled reversibly. Converting the physical intuition into a proof would require a theorem connecting a SAT-instance invariant to a superpolynomial lower bound in a standard computational model; that theorem would itself be the breakthrough.

Next test: reject proposals based only on energy-landscape ruggedness or observed phase transitions. Continue only with a concrete invariant computable from the formula encoding and a proven relation between its precision/representation cost and a standard time lower bound.

## Idea 25 - Nonstandard polynomial time from ultraproducts

Status: a foundations diagnostic; nonstandard polynomial bounds do not transfer to standard P or P/poly.

Take finite structures of increasing size and imagine an ultraproduct in which a solver is described as taking n^K steps for an internal exponent K. If K is nonstandard, then this bound can exceed n^c for every standard constant c while still looking polynomial inside the nonstandard model. A nonstandard finite truth table for SAT can likewise be hidden in a circuit whose size is n^K. This may make P=NP appear true internally without producing a standard algorithm with any fixed polynomial exponent.

The transfer obligation is a standard exponent bound: prove that the internal K is bounded by a standard integer, and separately extract a uniform machine or circuit family. Compactness and ultraproducts do not supply either fact. If a proposed argument only shows that every finite initial segment has some solver, the solver and its exponent may vary with the segment; choosing a lookup table is the trivial example. This route currently explains a common nonstandard-model mirage rather than solving P versus NP.

Next test: for any ultraproduct or forcing construction, write the exact transfer theorem that turns internal correctness and internal polynomiality into one standard uniform decider. If the theorem assumes a standard bound on K or a uniform code, it has already assumed the missing complexity control.
