A polynomial bound on ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Âº_F(n) implies Range(F)ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â P. This gives a reusable design test: any candidate whose output is determined by a short header and then releases the rest of its seed has an efficiently findable missing set; a universal NP-hitting generator must avoid polynomial cylinder-cover descriptions. The measure is project-defined, not a standard named complexity class.

Fundamental diagnosis: several failed ideas tried to carry a proof identity through a one-bit stretch by adding labels, but labels either consume output capacity or create an enumerable cylinder family. The invariant they need is not merely ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“many outputs are missingÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â; it is ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“the missing set contains no infinite NP-definable family.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â Range size gives the first statement for free, while cylinder decomposability can destroy the second by making the complement P. For subsequent constructions, reject any polynomial cylinder cover of the range: it makes the complement an infinite P set. ## Idea 54 - The identity-transport trilemma and the hole-resistance profile

Status: a synthesis of proved constraints from Ideas 50ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ53, useful as a design filter. It is not a P versus NP proof and does not rule out generators that transform the entire seed in a nontrivial way.

Identity-transport heuristic: the recent proof-tag diagonals need an output to retain enough information to identify which formula ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ generated a missing-proof choice. Three attempted transports have each paid a distinct cost. If ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ is discarded, an NP verifier for the proposed counterexample cannot ensure its proof claim matches the generator's ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ (Idea 50's unrelated-tag failure). If ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ is carried as an output tag while arbitrary suffixes are preserved, the image tends to be a polynomial union of cylinders and the range becomes P (Idea 53). If only selected prefixes are permitted to encode ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦, a cylinder language can concentrate all its infinite mass on an excluded prefix, so the generic infinite-fiber argument breaks (Idea 51). These are established failures of those specific encodings, not an exhaustive theorem about every possible identity code.

New bookkeeping language: for a polynomial-time map G, call $H_G=\{0,1\}^*\setminus\operatorname{Range}(G)$ its hole set. Its hole-resistance profile records, for each NP verifier and polynomial resource bound, whether H_G contains an infinite language recognized by that verifier. Universal NP-hitting is exactly the statement that this profile is empty. A range-size deficit only proves that H_G is large at each length; the suffix-replay lemma shows how a polynomial cylinder cover makes its profile immediately nonempty (indeed H_G is then an infinite P language). This separates ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“many holesÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â from ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“holes no NP language can systematically select.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â The term is project vocabulary, not a standard complexity measure.

Design consequence to test: bijective suffix scrambling cannot improve a cylinder construction, because it preserves the full suffix image. Any useful new construction must either create a genuinely nontrivial suffix image or couple the header choice to the whole input; then its first proof obligation is to prevent an infinite NP subset of the holes. Test toy maps against that obligation before attempting diagonalization. Preserve the identity-transport costs above as a rejection checklist, not as a no-go theorem.

Next test: build a small family of suffix maps h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦} and classify when their range is still P by an explicit inverse/decider, then identify the first map in the family whose range complexity is not explained by a cylinder cover. Do not treat a hard inversion problem as evidence of NP-immunity; separately look for an NP subset of its complement.

## Idea 55 - Suffix scrambling does not buy range hardness for free

Status: simple variants tested analytically and rejected. This is a boundary result for suffix-only transforms, not an impossibility theorem for all generators.

Test family: on a formula cylinder ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦s, replace the copied suffix s by h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦}(s), retaining a header w_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦}. If each h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦} is a bijection on suffixes of the same length, its image is still the full suffix cube even if computing h^{-1} is difficult; the output remains the same easy prefix cylinder. A length-dependent XOR mask is a concrete instance. If h is many-to-one but its image has a polynomial-time membership test, a polynomial union of branch images is again P. Appending parity or another P-computable checksum also fails: the image is described by a P-checkable relation, and its complement is an infinite P set. Thus invertibility hardness alone is irrelevant, while ordinary local redundancy produces publicly recognizable holes.

The unresolved transform must make the image membership hard enough that no infinite NP language can live in its complement. Merely making range membership NP-hard is insufficient: an NP-hard range can still have an infinite, easily recognized P subset in its complement. Under a cylinder decomposition into polynomially many branches, this obligation is already present for each branch image and cannot be supplied by the header bookkeeping. This moves the hard part from ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“scramble the formula identityÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â to ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“construct an NP range with an NP-immune complement,ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â which is essentially the strong-generator problem itself.

Learning: any transform with an explicit P image description makes holes easy to select. Any transform whose only proposed merit is one-way inversion has not addressed the universal-hitting quantifier. The next creative step must change the geometry of the image and prove an immunity property, not just hide a preimage.

## Idea 56 - Density-padding extractor and the length-alignment barrier

Status: a precise reduction in the non-stretch setting; the attempt to recover one-bit stretch fails at an exact length quantifier. This is a fresh connection to demi-bit generators, not a P versus NP result.

Literature trigger: Ren, Wang, and Zhong (ITCS 2026) define demi-bits security by forbidding NP/poly tests that accept a noticeable fraction of uniform outputs while accepting no generator output. They show that sufficiently stretched demi-bits generators make range avoidance hard for SearchNP, and under stronger parameters yield pseudo-surjective proof-complexity generators. Those results are conditional cryptographic evidence and do not give the uniform one-bit-stretch universal hitter required by the strong-generator conjecture.

Own density-padding lemma: for an NP language A, define

    Pad(A) = { enc(|x|) x z : x in A, z in {0,1}* },

where enc(k) is a self-delimiting code, for example 1^k0. Pad(A) is in NP. If A is nonempty, fix any x in A of length k. At every sufficiently large output length m, all strings with prefix 1^k0x belong to Pad(A), so its length-m density is at least 2^-(2k+1), a positive constant depending on the chosen member. A generator that hits every dense NP language therefore has an output y in Pad(A); a uniform deterministic decoder parses enc(|x|) and returns xÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â A. Thus composing that generator with the decoder yields a polynomial-time map whose range intersects every nonempty NP language. This is no separation: without a stretch requirement, the identity map already has this universal range-hitting property.

Failed upgrade: to force the decoded x to have length exactly n+1 when the seed has length n, replace Pad(A) by the set encoding only AÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©{0,1}^{n+1}. Its density at length m is proportional to |AÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©{0,1}^{n+1}|/2^{n+1}, which may be zero for infinitely many n or exponentially tiny along a sparse infinite NP language. Concrete stress test: A={0^{2^k}: kÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥1} is an infinite P language, but AÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¹Ã¢â‚¬Â Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©{0,1}^{n+1} is empty at every length n+1 that is not a power of two. The padding trick gives a fixed-member cylinder, but that cylinder only decodes a fixed short x; it does not align the decoded member's length with the seed length. The one-bit stretch cannot be restored by appending arbitrary bits, since the appended string need not remain in A.

Learning: dense-set security plus a self-delimiting decoder is a powerful way to turn density hitting into member extraction, but it spends the length surplus as padding and decoder metadata. The missing theorem is a length-alignment principle that yields members at precisely the generator's output length without making the test sparse. Any proposed repair must prove that principle for every infinite NP language; assuming dense NP sets are representative of all infinite NP sets silently drops the hardest quantifier.

Next test: investigate whether length alignment can be obtained by a selector over many input lengths with a single polynomially bounded clock, and whether sparse length spectra can be covered without making the target test's density negligible. Reject a proposal if it yields only a prefix in A rather than an output that itself belongs to A.

Source: [Ren, Wang, and Zhong, ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“Hardness of Range Avoidance and Proof Complexity Generators from Demi-Bits,ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â ITCS 2026](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.111).

## Idea 57 - Three-color escape bound and the non-additive witness frontier

Status: a proved short-cover theorem closes the one-uniform-majority-witness-per-anchor family, independent of support overlap. The attempted extension to every semi-filter fails for a precise reason: semi-filters need not be representable by additive weights. This is a route boundary and a new encoding for the next attempt, not a P versus NP result.

### The proved part: overlap-independent cover

Proposition 18.9 in the project audit uses a random three-coloring $U=A\sqcup B\sqcup C$ and the pair $E=A\cup B$, $H=A\cup C$. Its intersection is $A$. For any majority measure with collision mass $h=\sum_u\mu(u)^2\le1/48$, Chebyshev gives at least $1/2$ probability that both $E,H$ have mass above one half while $A$ has mass at most one half. For a uniform measure on any support size $3\le t<48$, one explicit color pattern has probability at least $3^{-47}$ and gives the same strict inequalities; for $t\ge48$, the collision bound applies. Independent repetitions and a union bound give an $O(\log M)$ list for any selected family of $M$ filters, regardless of support overlap.

Applied to one selected filter per Gap-MCSP anchor, where $M=2^{O(N^\beta)}$ and fixed $\beta<1$, the cover length is $O(N^\beta)=o(N)$. The argument removes support disjointness and low-overlap assumptions from this particular witness strategy. Its tiny absolute constant for uniform supports below 48 is immaterial asymptotically.

### Why this does not reach all semi-filters

A semi-filter is an arbitrary nonempty upward-closed family of subsets of $U$ that excludes the empty set. Equivalently, it is a monotone Boolean function on $2^U$. A probability measure gives only a weighted-threshold subclass. The random-coloring proof exploits linear mass, its expectation, and its collision variance; it has no automatic extension to a monotone family with no additive representation.

Concrete four-point obstruction to the additive representation: on $U=\{1,2,3,4\}$, let $\mathcal F$ consist of all sets containing at least one of $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{1,3\},\{2,4\}$. This is a semi-filter. If it were represented as $\mathcal F=\{W:\sum_{i\in W}w_i>1/2\}$ for nonnegative weights summing to one, the four winning-pair inequalities would sum to $2\sum_i w_i>2$, contradicting $\sum_iw_i=1$. This proves that majority measures do not exhaust the semi-filters. The example is itself easy to cover, for instance by $(\{1,2\},\{3,4\})$ whose intersection is empty; it demonstrates a representation gap, not a hard instance.

### New language: witness antichains and fusion resistance

For finite $U$, let $\mathcal A(\mathcal F)$ be the antichain of inclusion-minimal members of a semi-filter. Then $W\in\mathcal F$ exactly when some witness $S\in\mathcal A(\mathcal F)$ is contained in $W$. A pair $(E,H)$ covers $\mathcal F$ exactly when each side contains a witness from $\mathcal A(\mathcal F)$ but their intersection contains none. This replaces scalar mass with a hypergraph of minimal certificates.

For an anchor $a$, an anchored antichain must ensure that every required generator $G_{a,i}=U\cap\{z:z_i=a_i\}$ contains at least one witness. The concrete next construction target is a family of such antichains for which every pair $(E,H)$ has low coverage: many anchors must either lack a witness inside one side or retain a witness inside $E\cap H$. Call this a high fusion-resistance witness design. The phrase is project vocabulary, not a standard parameter; it must be defined by the exact pair-coverage condition above.

Attempt result: the weighted/random-partition line has been pushed to all uniform support sizes and diffuse weighted measures, and its exact boundary is now visible. The next route must work directly with witness antichains or arbitrary monotone functions. Merely replacing a majority measure by a nonweighted semi-filter is insufficient: one still needs a distribution over anchored filters for which every pair captures vanishing mass, or a direct all-filter lower bound. The known near-linear proof-DAG bound also warns that counting literal leaves alone caps the current argument at $N$.

Next test: use the existing exact toy sem-filter enumerator to search for structured anchored antichains (not just weighted thresholds) whose maximum pair coverage drops as the toy dimension grows. Test non-decomposable compositions and code-based coupling; every coordinatewise monotone aggregator of the local triple below is closed. Reject any candidate when a common pair or small closure proof covers all anchors. For each survivor, prove that its literal generators belong to the upward closure and count pair coverage exactly before attempting an asymptotic argument.

Source boundary: Cavalar and Oliveira define semi-filters as arbitrary upward-closed families and allow arbitrary subset pairs in the cover problem ([primary paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14117v1)). The three-color cover bound here is a project-derived argument, not a claim attributed to that paper.

## Idea 58 - Complementary-pair collapse of symmetric block amplification

Status: exact two-pair cover; the natural threshold amplification of a nonweighted local filter fails for every block count and threshold. Proposition 18.11 strengthens this to every coordinatewise monotone aggregator of the same local membership bits.

Take the three four-point semi-filters from Proposition 18.10, whose minimal winning pairs are respectively

    F0: 12, 34, 13, 24
    F1: 12, 34, 14, 23
    F2: 13, 24, 14, 23

For k independent blocks and anchor a in {0,1,2}^k, define membership by requiring at least q blocks W_j to belong to their local filter F_{a_j}, with any 1<=q<=k. This is a valid semi-filter family.

Two endpoint pairs divide its entire anchor family. Pair A uses {1,2} and {3,4} in every block. It covers exactly the anchors with at least q coordinates in {0,1}. Pair B uses {1,2,3} and {1,2,4} in every block. It covers exactly those with fewer than q coordinates in {0,1}. Pair A's intersection is empty in every block; pair B's intersection is {1,2}, which is a local winning set for F0,F1 but not F2. Thus every anchor is hit by one of the two pairs, and the family cover number is at most two for all k and q.

The finite script experiment_threshold_block_filter.py checks the two coverage identities on 73,812 anchor-threshold instances for k<=8, and checks all 13,971 instances from arbitrary monotone aggregators through k=4. The argument in the audit is exact for all k and all allowed aggregators.

Learning: nonweighted local filters do not automatically create a hard product family. Here, the two local endpoint pairs induce complementary membership profiles, so every monotone Boolean aggregation preserves the two-pair collapse. For future block constructions, compute endpoint membership and intersection membership as functions of the anchor label before doing any asymptotic probability estimate. In particular, search for complementary profiles before choosing a threshold or other aggregator.

Next test: pursue non-decomposable anchor coupling or different local witness types, where no fixed block statistic allows complementary endpoint pairs. Any candidate must include the actual anchor generators, and the first proof obligation is to exclude a constant-size pair cover before attempting a fractional packing.

## Idea 59 - Parity boxes kill coordinate-cylinder witness antichains

Status: exact four-pair cover under a simple density hypothesis on the promise set. This rejects the natural semi-filter generated by all codimension-r coordinate cylinders matching an anchor. It does not cover arbitrary antichains.

Construction tested: with truth-table universe $\{0,1\}^N$ and promise $U$, let $C(a,I)=\{z\in U:z_I=a_I\}$ for every $r$-coordinate set $I$, and let $\mathcal F_a^{(r)}$ contain every superset of at least one such cylinder. For $r\ge1$, each literal generator is in the filter: extend its coordinate to any $r$-set. If every half-parity subcube still contains a point of $U$, choose disjoint coordinate blocks $I,J$, each of size $r$. The four pairs

    E_p = {z in U : parity(z on I)=p}
    H_q = {z in U : parity(z on J)=q}

cover all anchors. For each anchor, choose p and q to equal its two block parities. The matching I- and J-cylinders put E_p and H_q in the filter. No r-coordinate cylinder can force both block parities, since it fixes only r coordinates while the blocks contain 2r coordinates total. A free coordinate in at least one block lets a high-promise completion flip that parity, so the endpoint intersection contains no certificate. The formal condition is $|U^c|<2^{N-r-1}$; then each opposite-parity half-cylinder has more points than the entire excluded set.

For the Gap-MCSP promise, $|U^c|\le2^{O(N^\beta\log N)}$ for fixed $\beta<1$. Thus the four-pair argument applies to all $r$ with $N-r-1$ larger than that exponent, including $r=O(N^\beta\log N)$. The proof and limits are recorded as Proposition 18.12.

Finite check: experiment_parity_certificate_cover.py removes one point from the 6-bit cube and verifies the four parity pairs against all 64 anchors for $r=2$. It passes. experiment_coordinate_certificate_toy.py exactly enumerates endpoint pairs on the 4-bit weight-two shell with anchors of weight at most one and finds a one-pair cover for r=1 and r=2; this shell does not meet the parity lemma's density premise and only shows the candidate can fail even sooner on a small promise.

Implementation correction learned during that toy calculation: the first scratch enumeration used a Python closure that captured the final anchor's generator list, falsely making all filters identical. I discarded that output, rebuilt each membership family before enumerating pairs, and obtained the one-pair result above. Do not reuse the initial count.

Learning: enlarging the anchor certificates from one literal slice to all low-codimension matching cylinders does not create cover resistance. Endpoints can encode two independent parity checks; four endpoint pairs then cover every anchor. Any useful witness antichain must be harder to certify than a union of coordinate cylinders, and must resist several simultaneous parity-box covers while still placing a witness inside every literal generator.

Next test: choose non-cylinder witnesses inside the literal generators, for example anchor-indexed code or design blocks, and analyze the exact pair-coverage predicate before assuming randomization helps. The design must survive the four parity endpoints as well as the complementary-profile attack from Idea 58; test a finite instance and prove all required generator memberships first.

## Idea 60 - The witness-overlap window

Status: two finite random-construction searches failed to produce a difficult selected family. They suggest a design constraint but do not establish an asymptotic theorem.

Construction tested: for each low-circuit anchor $a$ and coordinate $i$, choose a certificate $S_{a,i}$ contained in the literal slice $G_{a,i}=U\cap\{z:z_i=a_i\}$, and let $\mathcal F_a$ be the upward closure of these certificates. This guarantees $\mathcal F_a$ is above $a$.

Finite results:

- On the 4-bit weight-two universe with the five weight-at-most-one anchors, 300 random size-two certificates per literal slice gave exact cover size one in 291 trials and two in nine. This scratch experiment was run after correcting the closure bug recorded in Idea 59.
- The reproducible dense experiment [experiment_dense_witness_antichains.py](experiment_dense_witness_antichains.py) uses the 4-bit universe of weight-at-least-two strings, the same five anchors, and random half-subsets of each literal slice. Exact enumeration of every ordered endpoint pair gave cover size one in 18 of 20 trials and two in the remaining trials. The largest single-pair coverage was at least four of five filters in every trial.

These universes are tiny and do not establish a general upper bound. The working diagnosis is that two easy regimes are visible: certificates with little cross-anchor overlap can be divided into disjoint endpoint unions, while dense random certificates tend to make endpoint unions overlap enough that intersections retain witnesses. The candidate needs a structured intermediate overlap pattern. This is a hypothesis to test, not a theorem.

Project vocabulary: call this the witness-overlap window. For certificate families $\mathcal A_a$, track both point load
$d(u)=|\{(a,i):u\in S_{a,i}\}|$
and pairwise intersection profiles $|S_{a,i}\cap S_{b,j}|$. A useful design must keep enough cross-anchor overlap to block disjoint endpoint splits but must avoid the kind of blanket overlap that makes $E\cap H$ contain a certificate for most anchors. The actual acceptance test remains exact: for every candidate pair $(E,H)$, count anchors with a witness in each side and no witness in their intersection.

Attempt result: naive random sparse samples and dense random subsets do not create a high-cover toy. The next search should construct incidence designs with controlled, nonuniform overlap, then use the exact cover solver before claiming any asymptotic signal. Include parity-box endpoints and complementary-profile pairs as adversarial checks.

Next test: choose a small block design or code-based incidence structure on high-circuit tables so that each anchor's certificates cover all its literal slices, then calculate the all-pair coverage exactly. Reject it if its certificates admit either a 2-color split by anchor labels or a dense-union intersection witness.

## Idea 61 - Property-B collapse for singleton minimal witnesses

Status: proved selected-family cover bound; all singleton-generated filters above anchors outside the promise set are coverable by $O(\log M)$ pairs.

If $\mathcal F_j=\{W\subseteq U:W\cap S_j\ne\emptyset\}$ for $|S_j|\ge2$, a uniformly random cut $U=E\sqcup H$ splits $S_j$ with probability $1-2^{1-|S_j|}\ge1/2$. On a split, $E,H\in\mathcal F_j$ and $E\cap H=\emptyset\notin\mathcal F_j$. Repeating $O(\log M)$ independent cuts covers any selected family of $M$ such filters by a union bound. Proposition 18.13 records the exact bound.

For an anchor $a\notin U$, a singleton witness set cannot put the hit filter above all coordinate literals: its one point would have to agree with $a$ on every coordinate and therefore equal $a$. So every singleton-witness anchored filter has at least two witnesses and falls under the random-cut theorem.

Learning: the hypergraph property-B route is too weak when filters ask only for one point from a witness set. A non-2-colorable hypergraph may force a monochromatic edge under every cut, but the cover only needs to split each selected edge, and $O(\log M)$ cuts always suffice. Any candidate based on hyperedges must require richer behavior than hitting a support.

Next test: keep minimal witness size at least two and design their overlaps so that neither random cuts nor the union of dense witness families gives a short cover. Use exact finite cover enumeration before investigating non-2-colorability or higher chromatic parameters; those alone do not address intersection membership.

## Idea 62 - Affine-slice witnesses still admit a universal toy pair

Status: failed finite construction. Random affine constraints inside each literal generator did not increase the cover number in the toy geometry.

Construction tested: on the 4-bit universe of weight-at-least-two strings, for each of the five weight-at-most-one anchors and each coordinate, choose a nonempty affine slice defined by the matching literal and one additional random parity equation. Generate the anchored semi-filter by upward closure from these witness sets, then enumerate all ordered pairs of endpoints.

Result: all 20 deterministic-seed trials had exact cover number one. In the first trial, one covering pair was

    E = {0110, 0111, 1001, 1011}
    H = {0101, 1001, 1100, 1101}
    E intersection H = {1001}

The shared point was not itself a witness, while each endpoint contained at least one affine witness for every anchor. The reproducible exhaustive check is experiment_affine_witness_antichains.py.

Learning: adding random parity equations to each certificate independently does not guarantee anchor-level resistance. A shared intersection can be too small to contain a witness while each side still contains one for every anchor. This is another finite rejection only; the five-anchor promise is too small to imply a general cover theorem.

Next test: search for a deliberately coordinated affine design rather than independent local equations. For each proposed design, compute the complete endpoint-pair incidence table and inspect a maximum-coverage pair. Require a proof that the design keeps every endpoint pair from realizing a common certificate split across all anchors.

## Idea 63 - Disjoint-witness cuts and the pairwise-intersecting frontier

Status: proved logarithmic-in-family cover bound with an exponential dependence on witness width.

Suppose each selected semi-filter $\mathcal F_a$ has two disjoint minimal members $S_a,T_a$, each of size at most $t$. A random cut $U=E\sqcup H$ places all of $S_a$ on one side and all of $T_a$ on the other with probability at least $4^{-t}$. Then both endpoints belong to $\mathcal F_a$ and their intersection is empty. Repeating $\lceil4^t(\ln(M+1)+1)\rceil$ cuts covers $M$ such filters. Proposition 18.14 gives the exact proof.

Together with the singleton result in Idea 61, this closes any bounded-size witness strategy where every filter has a disjoint pair of minimal witnesses. The remaining bounded-width case is an intersecting antichain of minimal witnesses for many anchors. It can still be nonprincipal because pairwise intersections may be nonempty while the total intersection is empty.

Learning: ordinary hypergraph non-2-colorability is not the right target by itself. A cover pair requires entire witnesses on both sides and no witness in the intersection. Random-cut bounds settle the disjoint-witness case, so a useful hypergraph construction must be pairwise intersecting and must control how many witness sets a common intersection can contain.

First exact test: in the 4-bit weight-two shell with the four weight-one anchors, choose one 2-point certificate in each literal slice, require the four certificates for an anchor to be pairwise intersecting with empty total intersection, and enumerate all endpoint pairs. Each anchor has three valid witness configurations, giving 3^4=81 selected families. Every one has a one-pair cover. The reproducible check is experiment_intersecting_witness_toy.py. This is a finite no-go for that toy pattern, not a theorem about larger intersecting designs.

Next test: move to larger universes or larger witness sets and search for pairwise-intersecting anchored antichains with cover number above two. First compute a maximum-coverage pair; use projective planes or block designs only when their anchor literal constraints are explicit.

## Idea 64 - Fusion susceptibility and approximate principality

Status: exact identity proved; inverse-quadratic peak-defect conjecture supported only by exhaustive checks through five points.

For a finite semi-filter $\mathcal F$, let $q_{\mathcal F}(p)$ be the acceptance probability under a p-biased random subset and define

$$
\Delta_{\mathcal F}(p)=q_{\mathcal F}(p)^2-q_{\mathcal F}(p^2),\qquad
\Psi(\mathcal F)=\max_{p\in[0,1]}\Delta_{\mathcal F}(p).
$$

The exact identity in Proposition 18.15 says $\Delta_{\mathcal F}(p)$ is the probability that two accepted random endpoints have an unaccepted intersection. At every interior bias it is positive exactly when $\mathcal F$ is nonprincipal. Thus the fusion-cover failure has a measurable size: the question is not only whether a witness survives intersection, but how often it survives under a specified endpoint distribution.

The acceptance profile also gives an algebraic test for principality. A principal filter generated by a $k$-point core has $q(p)=p^k$. Conversely, if a monotone semi-filter has $q(p)=p^k$, the coefficient of its lowest nonzero power counts its $k$-point minimal members, so it has exactly one and is principal. Therefore principal filters are exactly the semi-filters whose acceptance polynomial is a monomial. A nonprincipal filter can be viewed as a perturbation away from this exact multiplicative profile; $\Delta$ measures that perturbation under the squaring map $p\mapsto p^2$.

Exhaustive antichain enumeration in [experiment_fusion_defect_profiles.py](experiment_fusion_defect_profiles.py) gives the following smallest grid-maxima (grid step $0.005$):

| Universe size $N$ | All semi-filters | Nonprincipal | Smallest sampled $\Psi$ | Example minimal witnesses |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 2 | 4 | 1 | 0.125000 | $\{0\},\{1\}$ |
| 3 | 18 | 11 | 0.0438941 | $\{0,1\},\{0,2\}$ |
| 4 | 166 | 151 | 0.0222473 | two 3-sets sharing 2 points |
| 5 | 7,579 | 7,548 | 0.0134218 | two 4-sets sharing 3 points |

The displayed extremizers have two minimal witnesses $C\cup\{x\}$ and $C\cup\{y\}$ with $|C|=N-2$. Their exact defect is $2p^{2N-2}(1-p)^2$, maximized at $p=(N-1)/N$ with value $2(N-1)^{2N-2}/N^{2N}\sim2e^{-2}/N^2$.

**Conjecture:** every nonprincipal semi-filter on $N$ points has $\Psi(\mathcal F)\ge c/N^2$ for an absolute constant $c>0$. The two-witness family shows this scale would be sharp. No proof or counterexample is known in this project.

Why this may explain repeated failures: most constructions made either very little distinction between endpoint acceptance and intersection acceptance, or allowed a random cut to expose distinct witnesses immediately. $\Delta$ measures that exact tension. Qualitative nonprincipality is too weak for a cover lower bound; the profile must be quantitatively tiny at every useful bias, and peaks for different anchors must not align. If the conjecture holds, a Lipschitz grid argument gives an $O(N^5\log M)$ random-pair cover for any $M$ nonprincipal filters on an explicit $N$-point universe. That is polynomial in $N$ but may be exponential in the SAT input length when the universe is succinctly represented. The real challenge would then be to exploit that representation gap or leave the fusion-cover route.

Learning: ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“many approaches failedÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â is not evidence by itself that P versus NP is inaccessible. These experiments reveal a recurring mathematical mechanism inside this one route: intersection closure is an approximate-principality problem, while useful lower bounds need a quantitative anti-principality bound uniform over all endpoint distributions. This language describes the filter route only; it does not explain every failed P-versus-NP approach in the project.

Next attempt: treat the inverse-quadratic statement as secondary. The OR-face theorem in Idea 65 gives every individual filter a filter-specific product bias with constant defect, so the uniform conjecture matters only if a common scalar bias can be shared across anchors. Continue it only as part of that cross-anchor alignment question.

## Idea 65 - The OR-face theorem and the true cross-anchor bottleneck

Status: proved finite combinatorial theorem; checked against every nonprincipal four-point semi-filter.

Every nonprincipal semi-filter has a two-dimensional restriction equal to OR. Let $\mathcal A$ be its minimal-witness antichain, choose two distinct members $A,B$ minimizing $|A\cup B|$, choose $i\in A\setminus B$ and $j\in B\setminus A$, and put $Z=(A\cup B)\setminus\{i,j\}$. The two endpoints $Z\cup\{i\}$ and $Z\cup\{j\}$ are accepted. If $Z$ were accepted, some minimal witness $D\subseteq Z$ would give a distinct pair $D,A$ with strictly smaller union, a contradiction. So the four values on this face are $0,1,1,1$. Proposition 18.17 contains the full proof.

Equivalent form: a finite semi-filter is principal iff every two-coordinate face is a constant, a projection, or an AND, never OR. The coordinate-dependent fusion identity then gives a distribution with exact defect $1/8$: fix $Z$ in, fix every other coordinate out, and independently include $i,j$ with probability $1/2$. The deterministic endpoints $(Z\cup\{i\},Z\cup\{j\})$ themselves cover that filter.

The coordinate-dependent version is substantially stronger for individual filters than the uniform-bias profile in Idea 64. For two near-identical large witnesses, the uniform defect shrinks like $N^{-2}$ because the common core is randomly lost; fixing the core at probability one restores defect $1/8$. The exhaustive product-bias grid on all 151 nonprincipal four-point filters also found minimum sampled peak $1/8$; the theorem proves the exact lower bound in all finite dimensions. The reproducible checks are in [experiment_product_bias_fusion.py](experiment_product_bias_fusion.py).

Why the project still has a hard problem: the OR-face context $Z$ and tip pair $\{i,j\}$ depend on the filter. A single pair covers all filters exposing the same face, but up to $\binom N2 2^{N-2}$ faces can occur. Thus individual non-principality is easy to witness; the hard task is the cross-anchor geometry of these witnesses. A candidate lower-bound family must act like a large code of incompatible OR faces so each endpoint pair misses many anchors. Conversely, a short list that hits every anchor's OR face would collapse the cover route. This pinpoints the shared structure every new construction should test.

This also separates two questions that had been blended: the inverse-quadratic conjecture in Idea 64 concerns one *uniform* bias shared across all coordinates; the OR-face theorem gives a constant defect with a filter-specific coordinate vector. The first may still help if anchors share a common scalar bias. The second says a per-filter positive defect is automatic and therefore cannot by itself yield a family cover bound.

Next attempt: compute the canonical minimum-union OR face for every anchor in the exact Gap-MCSP toy and larger structured instances. Build the anchor-to-face incidence table; measure face collisions, Hamming distance between contexts, and whether a small set of endpoint pairs hits all faces. Then attempt a proof of either a polynomial face cover for anchored filters or a large packing of faces satisfying the literal-generator constraints. Do not count distinct faces alone as a lower bound, since one pair may cover filters through multiple faces.

First anchored test: [experiment_anchor_or_faces.py](experiment_anchor_or_faces.py) uses the five-anchor, six-point literal-cylinder toy. For certificate codimensions $r=1,2$, it finds 36 and 15 distinct OR faces, but the best OR-face pair covers only 3/5 and 2/5 anchors, while an unrestricted pair covers all five in both cases. The maximizing pair contains a compatible OR-face certificate for every anchor, but the anchors use different faces. This is a useful correction: face incidence is a lower-dimensional certificate system, not a complete encoding of arbitrary fusion pairs. A general endpoint pair may hold many distinct local faces at once, and can also use broader multi-coordinate witnesses.

Revised next test: given an arbitrary pair $(E,H)$ and every filter it covers, enumerate all minimal witnesses contained in $E$ and $H$. Study the bipartite incidence relation between these endpoint witnesses and each filter's OR-face antichain; search for a bounded-complexity descriptor that includes the multi-coordinate pair cases. Any proposed packing lower bound must survive the actual maximizing pair from the toy.

## Idea 66 - Failure calculus: record the first unpaid proof obligation

Status: research discipline / synthesis language; not a theorem.

The repeated failed attempts are correlated: many arise from the same missing transfer, hidden quantifier, or representation cost. Treat each candidate as a chain of four obligations:

1. **Object:** define the language/filter/fiber exactly, with input length, promise, and quantifier order.
2. **Witness:** prove the proposed certificate or combinatorial structure exists for every required instance.
3. **Transfer:** account for encoding length, runtime exponent, uniformity, and model changes in the reduction to SAT, circuit lower bounds, or P versus NP.
4. **Contradiction:** identify the exact theorem or separation that the transferred statement violates.

For every failed idea, mark the earliest broken obligation and preserve the strongest valid conditional statement. Examples across the project include: a promising semi-filter construction whose pair cover collapses at the witness stage; a self-reference whose generated object exceeds its own clock at transfer; a counting argument that proves existence but supplies no NP verifier at object/witness; and a restricted-model lower bound that does not transfer to general circuits. Repeated failures at the same stage should change the next experiment: do not vary the construction while leaving the same unpaid transfer debt untouched.

This is how to learn from failures without treating repeated dead ends as proof of impossibility. The ledger's new concrete vocabulary is now: **fiber/avoidance** for the shared search spine; **selector debt and clock dilation** for resource-transfer losses; **witness-overlap window** for antichain designs; and **fusion susceptibility** for acceptance lost under intersection. Use one term only where its definition applies, and keep every conjecture distinct from a theorem.

## Idea 67 - Shared-context OR faces collapse to graph coloring

Status: exact theorem for a natural face family; this construction fails as a large-cover route.

Take a fixed core $C$ and a graph $G=(V,E)$. For each edge $uv$, let $\mathcal F_{uv}$ be generated by the two witnesses $C\cup\{u\}$ and $C\cup\{v\}$. A fusion pair covers this edge-filter exactly when its endpoints both contain $C$ and split $u,v$ across the two sides. Thus each pair is a cut of $V$ and covers the graph edges crossing that cut. A list of $m$ cuts gives every vertex an $m$-bit signature; covering every edge is equivalent to these signatures being a proper coloring. Therefore the exact cover number is $\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$ (Proposition 18.18).

The check [experiment_or_face_graph_coding.py](experiment_or_face_graph_coding.py) verifies the identity for all 1,094 nonempty graphs on up to five vertices. The construction fails as a lower-bound route because even a high-chromatic graph needs only logarithmically many pairs. Multiple cuts combine in parallel through binary labels, defeating the attempt to make local face conflicts accumulate.

Learning: a shared core makes fusion-pair cover complexity collapse to ordinary graph coloring, whose chromatic information is compressed into $O(\log |V|)$ bits. Varying the contexts is necessary, but the literal-cylinder toy also shows that mere variation is insufficient: one pair can contain OR faces for several anchors at once. The next candidate must couple contexts and multi-coordinate witnesses so that no short list of cuts or witness-pair signatures works.

Next attempt: extend the graph model to filters with anchor-dependent cores $C_a$ and multiple tip sets. Determine whether the resulting cover parameter is a known coloring/boxicity/fractional-chromatic invariant, and test the exact endpoint-pair cover before treating it as a lower-bound lead. A useful construction must force a superlinear number of pairs in the projectÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s input parameter after encoding costs.

## Idea 68 - Co-singleton pairs give an exact quadratic cover code

Status: exact theorem for unrestricted semi-filters; the project-specific anchor embedding is open.

On an $N$-point universe $U$, index one semi-filter by every unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ and generate it from the two witnesses $U\setminus\{i\}$ and $U\setminus\{j\}$. A fusion pair covering this filter must have endpoints that omit exactly $i$ and $j$ on opposite sides: each endpoint must contain a generating co-singleton, while their intersection must contain neither. Thus the endpoint pair identifies one unique index pair. The full family has exact cover number $\binom N2$ (Proposition 18.19).

The reproducible exhaustive check [experiment_cosingleton_pair_filters.py](experiment_cosingleton_pair_filters.py) tests every endpoint pair for $N=2$ through $8$ and finds maximum pair coverage one. Unlike the shared-core graph family, these filters use varying cores $U\setminus\{i,j\}$, so binary cut codes cannot reuse one pair across edges. This is a concrete superlinear cover lower bound in the unrestricted semi-filter problem.

The exact gap to P versus NP is substantial: these filters are not known to lie above the projectÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s coordinate-literal generators. Indeed, a co-singleton witness is generally too large to fit inside those literal slices. Simply adding the literal generators can make the co-singleton witnesses redundant or restore an easy pair. Any embedding must define each anchored filter, prove every literal generator is accepted, and then show every endpoint pair still covers only a small number of anchors. Without those steps, this is a combinatorial construction, not a separation.

The direct toy check confirms the first obstacle. On the five-anchor, six-point literal-cylinder toy, all 30 anchor/co-singleton combinations are already accepted by the canonical filters for both certificate codimensions $r=1,2$. Adding those witnesses therefore does not change the filters at all. The test is included in [experiment_anchor_or_faces.py](experiment_anchor_or_faces.py).

Next attempt: search for a relative co-singleton construction on a carefully chosen block system where the blocked objects are literal slices or intersections of slices. Test whether a pair of special witnesses can be made minimal while every required literal generator remains accepted through separate witnesses. Enumerate the exact cover number on small truth-table shells before attempting the asymptotic anchored proof.

## Idea 69 - Complementary block cylinders meet the anchor condition but parity covers them

Status: exact anchor validity; full-cylinder and bounded-puncture variants have an exact two-pair cover whenever both blocks exceed the excluded-set logarithm; toys agree.

For each low anchor $a$, partition input coordinates into nonempty blocks $I,J$. Let $S_a$ be the high-table truth tables matching $a$ on all coordinates in $I$, and $T_a$ those matching on $J$. Generate $\mathcal F_a$ from $S_a,T_a$. Each literal generator is accepted: if coordinate $k\in I$, then $S_a$ is contained in the matching literal slice; if $k\in J$, use $T_a$. Since the two blocks cover all coordinates, $S_a\cap T_a$ contains only the anchor table, which is outside the high-complexity universe. This is a valid anchored nonprincipal filter construction whenever both cylinders are nonempty.

The exact toy experiment [experiment_two_block_anchor_filters.py](experiment_two_block_anchor_filters.py) uses the weight-two shell. For four input bits, five anchors, and every assignment of one of the three $2+2$ partitions to each anchor, it exhausts all endpoint pairs: six assignments have cover one and 237 have cover two. For five input bits, six anchors, and 12 seeded assignments of a $2+3$ partition, three have cover one and nine cover two. Every certificate cylinder is checked nonempty and contained in the required literal slices.

Learning: meeting the anchor condition is possible with only two generators per filter, but full cylinders have a stronger two-pair collapse. Proposition 18.20 uses two-bit labels on row and column patterns; it applies whenever $L+t<\min(2^{|I|-1},2^{|J|-1})$, where $L$ is the number of excluded tables and $t$ is the number of points punctured from each witness. Since $L=2^{O(N^\beta\log N)}$ in the project promise, this rules out full cylinders and any fixed number of punctures when both blocks exceed $O(N^\beta\log N)$, even if they are unequal. The experiment [experiment_punctured_cylinder_anchor_filters.py](experiment_punctured_cylinder_anchor_filters.py) adds finite evidence: 500 fixed and 500 anchor-dependent choices on the six-bit weight-two shell all had exact cover number one or two.

Next attempt: focus on the two cases left by Proposition 18.20: one block of size $O(N^\beta\log N)$, or sparse witness subsets that omit every opposite-label half-row/half-column. Measure witness cardinality, density in each cylinder, and the exact endpoint cover together. The construction must be sparse enough to evade the two-bit code but wide enough to evade the $4^t\log M$ random-cut bound.

## Idea 70 - Random sparse block witnesses still collapse in the eight-bit toy

Status: 300 exact random families checked; no cover number above two. This is finite evidence only.

To test the sparse exception in Idea 69, take the eight-bit weight-two universe ($|U|=28$), nine anchors of weight at most one, and a fixed $4+4$ coordinate partition. For each anchor, independently sample a size-$t$ subset from each matching block cylinder, for $t=2,3,4$, and generate the filter from those two witnesses. The witnesses remain nonempty, disjoint, and inside the literal generators assigned to their coordinate blocks.

[experiment_sparse_block_certificates.py](experiment_sparse_block_certificates.py) enumerates all $3^9$ witness orientations per family, which is exact for a two-minimum filter. In each of 100 trials per $t$, the cover number was one or two; a single pair covered at least eight of nine anchors in every trial. The script confirms arbitrary endpoint pairs cannot do better than the orientation enumeration: for every covered anchor, its two minimal witnesses must be split between endpoints; replacing endpoints by unions of those witnesses only shrinks the intersection, so it preserves rejection.

Learning: independent sparse sampling does not exploit the remaining window in this toy. The common pair can combine one certificate orientation across most anchors; random witnesses did not create the cross-anchor incompatibility required for a larger cover. The next test should coordinate certificate subsets across anchors to frustrate every shared orientation, while avoiding overlap patterns that create a universal pair.

The follow-up [experiment_variable_partition_sparse_witnesses.py](experiment_variable_partition_sparse_witnesses.py) added 210 exact trials on a dense 8-bit universe with anchor-dependent partitions. Every unrestricted cover was one pair, although literal-slice-only covers needed two to five. The arbitrary endpoint pair is the failure mechanism: it unions sparse witnesses from all anchors and its intersection preserves none of them. This closes random sparse incidence sampling on the current toy; another random sweep is not justified.

## Idea 71 - Active coordinate rectangles bound two-witness filters

**Status: proved upper bound; random construction route still fails.** Proposition 18.23 gives a direct coordinate description for any anchored semi-filter with exactly two minimal witnesses. Assign each input coordinate to a witness whose set lies in the matching anchor literal slice, obtaining a partition $I_a\sqcup J_a$. Let $X_a\subseteq J_a$ be the coordinates where the first witness can disagree with the anchor, and $Y_a\subseteq I_a$ those where the second can disagree. Every pair in $Y_a\times X_a$ gives a literal endpoint pair that covers the filter. If every point in the promise is at Hamming distance at least $\Delta$ from every anchor, then both active sides have size at least $\Delta$, and random coordinate pairs give a family cover of size

$$
O\!\left(\frac{N^2}{\Delta^2}\log(M+1)\right).
$$

For the project Gap-MCSP thresholds, single-point circuit patching gives $\Delta=\Omega(N^\beta/\log N)$ and $\log M=O(N^\beta)$, hence $O(N^{2-\beta}\log^2N)$ pairs for every two-minimum anchored family. This crosses below a target $N^{1+\varepsilon}$ when $\beta>1-\varepsilon$ with a fixed exponent gap. It does not close small $\beta$ or filters with three or more minimal witnesses.

This is a coordinate-cross rectangle: each filter contributes $Y_a\times X_a$, and a literal-pair cover must hit these rectangles with the corresponding anchor signs. Rectangle hitting and biclique covers are established adjacent subjects; the project-specific point is the reduction from two-minimum anchored filters. More importantly, a large hitting number for these canonical pairs is only necessary evidence for a hard filter family. In the dense 8-bit toy, 210 random variable-partition sparse families all had unrestricted exact cover one, while literal-slice-only covers needed two to five pairs. Arbitrary endpoints fused the signatures that the literal-pair diagnostic kept separate. See Proposition 18.23 and [experiment_variable_partition_sparse_witnesses.py](experiment_variable_partition_sparse_witnesses.py).

Learning: the two-witness route has a concrete ceiling set by coordinate-pair incidence and, in the actual promise, by anchor-to-promise Hamming distance. Further random sampling inside cylinders is not informative: it repeatedly gives arbitrary one-pair covers. A real lower-bound attempt must either create a structured family whose arbitrary endpoints cannot fuse its coordinate rectangles, or use at least three minimal witnesses so the two-witness reduction no longer applies. Any toy must distinguish the full endpoint cover from the literal-pair cover.

Next attempt: construct a three-minimum anchored family with an exact small-universe cover calculation, requiring every witness point to satisfy the Gap-MCSP distance lower bound and every literal generator to be accepted. First test whether one arbitrary pair covers all filters by encoding witness orientations; only then scale a promising pattern or prove a rectangle/packing lower bound against arbitrary endpoints.

## Idea 72 - Affine point pencils satisfy the literal promise but still fuse

**Status: anchored finite construction found; tested instances collapse to one pair.** In the affine plane $AG(2,q)$, take a sparse set $Y$ of anchor points and universe $U=AG(2,q)\setminus Y$. For anchor $p\in Y$, generate its semi-filter by the $q+1$ affine lines through $p$, restricted to $U$. Encode coordinates by one-hot bits for every affine form $\ell$ and field value $c$. If $c=\ell(p)$, the matching literal slice is the line $\ell=c$ through $p$; if $c\ne\ell(p)$, the matching-zero slice contains the line $\ell=\ell(p)$ through $p$. Thus every literal generator is accepted, and all $q+1$ line witnesses are nonempty in the tested cap sets.

The exact search [experiment_affine_pencil_anchor_filters.py](experiment_affine_pencil_anchor_filters.py) searches witness orientations and stops on the first full-cover pair. For $AG(2,3)$ with three parabola anchors, it finds one after 19 of $13^3=2{,}197$ possible assignments. For $AG(2,5)$ it finds one after 604 of $31^4=923{,}521$ assignments with four anchors, and after 1,197 of $31^5=28{,}629{,}151$ assignments with five anchors. It directly verifies all 36, 120, and 150 anchor-literal conditions respectively. The five-anchor instance uses every x-level and its one-pair witness has a nonempty three-point intersection that contains no line generator.

For the four-anchor $q=5$ instance, an exact search finds a one-pair witness early; it is a pair of unions of selected affine lines, not the grid construction from Proposition 18.24. The five-anchor instance shows the same flexible fusion even though the x-projection is already complete. Thus blocking the simple two-direction grid is insufficient. In the $q=3$ sample another orientation gives the same one-pair result.

Learning: incidence geometry can satisfy the anchor condition with many minimal witnesses, but line unions can fuse all filters even when the x-projection is complete. Projection completeness blocks only the simplest grid cover; a surviving set must resist arbitrary pairs of line covers. The affine-plane toy is not the high-circuit Gap-MCSP universe.

This route is now closed in every fixed affine dimension by Proposition 18.25: a coordinate-hyperplane blocker system gives at most $d+1$ pairs over the actual dense promise. Do not spend more search on enlarging line-pencil anchor sets or on projection completeness for this generator family.

## Idea 73 - The affine grid collapse survives the actual dense promise

**Status: proved construction-specific one-pair collapse.** Proposition 18.24 lifts Idea 72 from a finite affine plane to the Gap-MCSP high-complexity universe. Read two $k$-bit blocks of each truth table as a point of $\mathbb F_{2^k}^2$. Use anchors encoding a grid $X\times Y$, with $X,Y$ omitting the all-zero and all-one labels. For each anchor, generate its filter from every required bit literal plus the fibers of all affine lines through its projected point. The common endpoints are $E=\{z:\pi_x(z)\in X\}$ and $H=\{z:\pi_y(z)\in Y\}$.

The intersection consists of tables whose projection lies in the anchor grid. No line fiber is trapped there because the grid contains no complete affine line. No literal is trapped there either: for a bit in a projection block, choose an omitted zero/all-one label with the same bit; for a filler bit, fix that bit and project outside the grid. If the excluded low-circuit tables number fewer than $2^{N-2k-1}$, every such partial assignment has a high-complexity completion. Thus the intersection contains no generator and the same pair covers all filters.

With $k=c\log_2N$, the grid has $(2^k-2)^2=N^{2c+o(1)}$ anchors, all encodable by circuits of size $O(\log^2N)$. For any fixed magnification exponent $1+\varepsilon$, choose $c>(1+\varepsilon)/2$; still $k=O(\log N)$, and the family has more than $N^{1+\varepsilon}$ anchored filters while its cover number remains one. This is an exact closure of the affine-grid proposal at the project's parameters, not a P-vs-NP consequence. The finite checker [experiment_affine_grid_literal_collapse.py](experiment_affine_grid_literal_collapse.py) verifies the endpoint and generator conditions for $q=4$ with four anchors.

Learning: adding all literal generators does not rescue an incidence construction if one pair of coarse projections makes their intersection small in the projection space. High-complexity density then works against the construction by supplying an escaping witness for every generator. A surviving direction must prevent every small projection grid from separating the generator family, or make some generator concentrate entirely inside every candidate grid while keeping filters proper.

The higher-dimensional extension in Proposition 18.25 shows that merely making the projected anchors complete cannot rescue line pencils: blocker pairs can use complementary coordinate hyperplanes and cover every anchor in $d+1$ rounds. The next attempt should change the generator geometry so that an endpoint cannot exclude a hyperplane blocker while retaining one full witness through each covered anchor.

## Idea 74 - Coordinate blockers close affine line pencils in every dimension

**Status: proved construction-specific $d+1$-pair cover; finite $AG(3,4)$ verification.** For line-pencil filters projected to $\mathbb F_q^d$, let endpoint $E_t$ exclude one level in each of the first $d-1$ coordinate directions and let $H_t$ exclude one level in the last direction. Each anchor avoids all $d$ blockers for at least one of $d+1$ level choices, so $E_t$ retains its $e_d$ line and $H_t$ its $e_1$ line. Their intersection contains no full line through that anchor: any nonzero direction varies in a blocked coordinate. Density then keeps every line witness and every required literal nonempty outside the intersection. Proposition 18.25 gives the exact argument, including the $dk+1$ completion budget.

Learning: the plane's three-cross trick was a dimension-two case of a general dual-space principle. A small set of blocker normals can span all line directions while each endpoint separately leaves a nonzero kernel direction. More projected dimensions do not create a harder family; the cover grows only linearly with dimension. For fixed $d$, this is constant, and for $d=O(\log N)$ it is still far below the magnification scale. The affine pencil family should now be treated as closed.

New working term: the **blocker-rank budget** is the number of independent projected directions an endpoint pair must block to push the common witness-direction kernel below the dimension of a generator, while each endpoint keeps one full generator. For affine lines, the common kernel must lose one dimension; for affine $r$-flats it must lose $d-r+1$ independent directions. The $d-r+2$ level choices then cover every anchor. This term is exact for the hyperplane-complement constructions here, not a characterization of arbitrary endpoint sets. A surviving incidence design must evade low-rank blockers and also prevent unions of anchor-specific witnesses from rebuilding a broad pair.

Next attempt: test a different incidence object whose witnesses are not complete affine lines or flats. A plausible target is a nonlinear incidence system with large blocking number under coordinate hyperplanes, but compute the unrestricted arbitrary-endpoint cover and every literal condition before scaling it.

## Idea 75 - Sparse minimal witnesses can raise a toy cover, but only to two

**Status: exact finite result and exhaustive assignment audit; no scalable lower bound.** Let $U$ be the six 4-bit strings of weight two and take the five anchors of weight at most one. For each anchor, include all four matching literal slices and add one anchor-specific 2-point generator. Each added witness is inclusion-minimal because every literal generator has size at least three. Searching all 4,096 ordered endpoint pairs gives exact cover number one or two.

The seeded experiment [experiment_literal_plus_sparse_witnesses.py](experiment_literal_plus_sparse_witnesses.py) tested 100 families for each combination of one, two, or three added witnesses per anchor and witness size two or three. With one added witness, 12/100 size-two families and 4/100 size-three families needed two pairs. With two added witnesses, only 3/100 and 1/100 did; with three, all tested families collapsed to one pair. In each cover-two case a first pair covers four of five anchors and the second covers the remaining anchor. The intersection may have one or two points, and the anchor-specific witnesses are chosen so none lies inside it.

The stronger [experiment_exhaustive_sparse_witness_assignments.py](experiment_exhaustive_sparse_witness_assignments.py) checks all $15^5=759{,}375$ choices of exactly one 2-point witness per anchor. It finds 685,272 one-pair families and 74,103 two-pair families. For every assignment, some pair covers at least four anchors; the code certifies this by checking common endpoint-pair bitsets for each four-anchor subset. Each individual anchor filter has a pair cover, so two pairs suffice for the whole family. A hand extension to the 5-bit weight-two universe with six anchors also has exact cover two, after all 1,048,576 ordered endpoint pairs are checked (`experiment_sparse_witness_extension_n5.py`).

Learning: arbitrary sparse witnesses can break a specific common pair, so the all-one-pair toy results for literal-only filters are not a blanket theorem. But on this shell, the anchor literals still supply a pair that handles at least four anchors, and one more pair repairs the single miss. Adding more random witnesses usually increases endpoint flexibility and restores the one-pair cover. The next construction must make *every* pair miss a growing fraction of anchors, rather than merely poison one pair.

Call this exact finite property the **four-of-five concentration**: for every assignment of one 2-point witness to each of these five anchored filters, some arbitrary endpoint pair covers at least four filters. It is a verified property of this toy family only. It explains the two-pair ceiling and gives a concrete obstruction to extrapolation: finding one witness assignment that defeats a pair is insufficient if another pair covers all but one anchor.

Next attempt: seek a structured witness assignment on a growing weight-two or constant-weight shell that defeats the four-of-five mechanism. Build a candidate using an explicit incidence or code rule, then search arbitrary endpoint pairs; do not use random samples as evidence of a growing cover. If the exact maximum pair coverage remains $M-O(1)$ and the cover remains two, change the universe or the literal geometry.

## Idea 76 - Complementary blockers close affine flat pencils

**Status: proved construction-specific cover $d-r+2$; finite plane-pencil check.** Proposition 18.26 extends the line-pencil blocker argument to every proper affine $r$-flat pencil in $\mathbb F_q^d$. Write $m=d-r$. One endpoint excludes one blocker hyperplane in each of $m$ coordinate directions; the other excludes a hyperplane in one additional independent direction. Their common kernel has dimension $r-1$, so no $r$-flat through a covered anchor survives in the endpoint intersection. Each endpoint separately retains an $r$-flat through that anchor. Cycling through $m+2$ distinct blocker-level tuples covers every anchor, and the same $dk+1$-bit completion argument rejects every flat and literal generator on the dense promise.

The finite check [experiment_affine_plane_pencils_AG3_F4.py](experiment_affine_plane_pencils_AG3_F4.py) covers all 64 anchors in $AG(3,4)$ with 21 affine planes and eight literals per filter, using three pairs. This is an exact construction-specific closure, not a general theorem about non-affine incidence systems. The lesson is that higher-dimensional flats make the blocker budget depend on codimension $d-r$, not dimension; neither more anchor points nor complete coordinate projections rescue affine flats.

Next attempt: move to nonlinear incidence objects, where a small collection of coordinate hyperplanes may fail to hit every generator while each endpoint still contains one. Define and test an explicit finite family first. Alternatively, pursue a structured growing-shell witness family only if it avoids the exact two-pair ceiling found for one extra pair on the small weight-two shells.

## Idea 77 - More anchors and stronger one-pair misses still admit a two-pair repair

**Status: exact finite tests on three shells; no growing lower bound.** The one-extra-witness construction was moved from the six-point universe to $U=\{x\in\{0,1\}^5:|x|=3\}$ with all 16 anchors of weight at most two. Every filter contains its five matching literal generators and one anchor-specific 2-point minimal witness. Across 80 seeded assignments, exact enumeration of all 1,048,576 endpoint pairs found 17 one-pair families and 63 two-pair families. In the latter, the best pair covers 14 or 15 anchors.

To reduce the first-order pair coverage, [experiment_sparse_witness_minimax_weight3.py](experiment_sparse_witness_minimax_weight3.py) used 30,000 sampled endpoint pairs to guide a minimax search over witness assignments. Sampling only selected the candidate; the final test was exact over all ordered endpoint pairs. The resulting family still had exact cover two, even though no pair covered more than 13 of 16 anchors. The missing three anchors can be repaired by another pair.

A possible universal explanation was also checked exactly. [experiment_two_pair_blocker_certificate_weight3.py](experiment_two_pair_blocker_certificate_weight3.py) enumerated all 1,024 endpoint subsets and found only 11 endpoints accepted by every anchor filter using literals alone; no pair of these endpoints has an intersection rejected by all literal generators. So the observed two-pair covers cannot be explained by a fixed pair of globally literal-valid endpoints that automatically avoids every possible 2-point witness. The successful endpoint pairs exploit the particular anchor witness assignment.

A structured extension on the 15-point 6-bit weight-two shell has seven anchors and exactly 2,147,483,648 endpoints but 1,073,741,824 ordered endpoint pairs. Chunked exhaustive verification in [experiment_shell_n6_sparse_witness_exact.py](experiment_shell_n6_sparse_witness_exact.py) again found exact cover two; its best pair covers five of seven anchors. Across 120 random-greedy and 24 minimax-greedy witness assignments, the best exact result was still two pairs, with one family reaching a four-of-six maximum pair cap.

Learning: increasing the anchor count and reducing maximum pair coverage does not force a large cover. The remaining escape is a complementary repair: one pair covers a large subset and another covers its misses. The next objective must eliminate every pair of attainable coverage masks whose union is all anchors, rather than merely minimize the largest mask.

## Idea 78 - SAT counterexample-guided search for a three-pair toy family

**Status: interrupted exact finite search; no positive instance or impossibility proof.** The one-witness-per-anchor weight-three toy has 16 anchor variables, each choosing one of 45 possible two-point generators. Given a candidate assignment, `experiment_cegis_sparse_witness_cover3.py` enumerates all 1,048,576 endpoint pairs and searches for two pair-coverage masks whose union is all 16 anchors. Each such pair-of-pairs yields a sound SAT clause: at least one anchor must choose a witness that makes both endpoint pairs fail there. The solver accumulated clauses and repeated.

The last verified output on 24 September had passed 190 candidate iterations and added 2,972 clauses; candidates still had two-pair covers. The run was stopped on 25 September before completion, with no newly persisted candidate or final solver status. This is a search checkpoint, not a lower bound or impossibility proof. Reopen only if a specific logical conjecture needs this finite toy as a falsification test; if resumed, save checkpoints and any candidate immediately. Inclusion-direction audit: every 2-point choice is genuinely minimal here because every literal generator has at least four points; if a 2-point witness lies inside a literal slice, the smaller witness dominates that larger generator in the upward filter.

New working phrase: a **complementary repair pair** is a second fusion pair whose anchor-coverage mask contains the misses of the first. The SAT search attacks this repair directly. This is more precise than the earlier maximum-coverage objective, which can be large even when the cover number is three or larger, and can be small enough for a two-pair cover.

## Idea 79 - Fusion spectra expose the real cover obstruction

**Status: exact finite reformulation plus a small nonlinear incidence pilot; no scalable lower bound.** For an endpoint subset $S$, write its acceptance signature as $\sigma(S)=\{a:S\in F_a\}$. The **fusion profile** of an ordered endpoint pair $(E,H)$ is

$$\Phi(E,H)=\sigma(E)\cap\sigma(H)\setminus\sigma(E\cap H).$$

The **fusion spectrum** is the family of all nonempty attainable profiles. The endpoint-pair cover number is exactly the set-cover number of this spectrum on the anchor set. A two-pair cover exists precisely when two attainable profiles have union equal to all anchors. This explains why maximizing the size of one profile is the wrong objective: it says nothing about whether a second profile repairs its complement.

The standard fractional set-cover dual gives a compact lower-bound test. Assign nonnegative weights $w_a$ to anchors and require $\sum_{a\in C}w_a\le1$ for every attainable profile $C$. Then every integral endpoint-pair cover has size at least $\sum_a w_a$. This language isolates the exact certificate a proposed construction needs: a high-value feasible dual weighting, or a combinatorial obstruction to covering by a few profiles. A profile-size cap alone is weaker.

The exact pilot [experiment_projective_fano_semifilter.py](experiment_projective_fano_semifilter.py) uses the seven points of $PG(2,2)$ as anchors, with each filter generated by its matching binary coordinate slices and all incident projective lines. It checks all 128 endpoint subsets and all 16,384 ordered endpoint pairs. There are 60 nonempty fusion profiles; the largest covers four of seven anchors; the exact cover number is three. An independent direct check confirms that no one or two profiles cover all seven and that three do. With coordinate slices alone the exact cover number is two, so adding line generators raises it to three: enlarging the filters need not monotonically enlarge the pair-cover profiles, because acceptance can also appear in the endpoint intersection.

The larger [experiment_projective_pg2_3_semifilter.py](experiment_projective_pg2_3_semifilter.py) checks all 8,192 subsets of $PG(2,3)$ and all 67,108,864 ordered endpoint pairs, using the analogous three coordinate-value slices and line-incidence generators. The exact cover number is two for line-only, coordinate-only, and combined filters. The maximum profile covers nine of 13 anchors. The separate exact comparison [experiment_incidence_coloring_vs_fusion.py](experiment_incidence_coloring_vs_fusion.py) finds matching fusion-cover and weak-coloring numbers on four plane systems: $PG(2,2)$ gives 3, $PG(2,3)$ gives 2, $AG(2,2)$ gives 4, and $AG(2,3)$ gives 3. These matches motivated the coloring hypothesis below, but no asymptotic incidence lower bound follows.

A tempting explanation was that line-incidence fusion cover equals the weak chromatic number of the underlying hypergraph. It matches the four small planes above, but [experiment_hypergraph_coloring_fusion_counterexample.py](experiment_hypergraph_coloring_fusion_counterexample.py) refutes the general identity. On five vertices with triples $012,124,023,123,024$, coloring vertex 2 one color and the other vertices another gives weak chromatic number two. Every anchor is individually coverable, yet exact enumeration gives fusion cover three, with six attainable profiles and maximum profile size three. Ordinary coloring misses the paired endpoint/intersection condition; retain the fusion spectrum rather than substituting weak chromatic number.

The dual weak-coloring repair fails on the same toy. A two-coloring of its five hyperedges can make every anchor see both colors, but the two colored edge families each have the full five-vertex shadow. Their intersection therefore contains every generator edge, so the pair covers no anchor. Call this **overlap contamination**: witnesses chosen separately for the two endpoints can reappear inside their common intersection and erase the fusion profile.

For finite upward filters there is an exact witness-union normal form. Given any endpoint pair covering anchor set $C$, choose for each $a\in C$ one minimal generator $g_a\subseteq E$ and one $h_a\subseteq H$. Replace the endpoints by $E'=\bigcup_{a\in C}g_a$ and $H'=\bigcup_{a\in C}h_a$. These smaller endpoints still pass every covered anchor, while $E'\cap H'\subseteq E\cap H$; upward closure means an intersection rejected before shrinking remains rejected. Thus every endpoint-pair cover has a representative whose endpoints are unions of at most $|C|$ minimal witnesses per side. For a filter with $t_a$ minimal generators, the per-anchor witness choices are at most $1+t_a(t_a-1)$ (uncovered, or an ordered distinct witness pair); Proposition 18.21 is the two-witness special case. This makes the true search space an oriented witness-incidence system, but the number of orientations can still be enormous.

Numerical LP diagnostics sharpen the obstruction but do not rescue the route. For Fano, the fractional-cover optimum is exactly $19/10$: a rational dual weighting $(2,2,3,2,3,3,4)/10$ is feasible on every profile, and a matching primal fractional cover puts weights $(0.3,0.3,0.3,0.4,0.2,0.2,0.2)$ on 7-bit profile masks $(30,45,51,75,84,100,112)$. The integral cover is three, so the fractional LP has a real integrality gap and cannot certify the three-cover. For $PG(2,3)$ the numerical solver returns about 1.444/1.536 in line-only/combined modes; exact rational dual weights give feasible lower bounds $13/9$ and $106/69$. Any claimed asymptotic theorem needs a scale-growing dual certificate and a transfer argument.

Learning: the right object is the entire endpoint-fusion spectrum, including complementary pairs and its fractional covering value. Projective incidence can produce a cover-three exception at order two, but order three already has a two-pair repair. The strongest next move is to search for a family where every small collection of attainable profiles leaves an anchor uncovered and where the dual weight scales above the target threshold. Do not infer growth from one small projective plane or from maximum profile size.

## Idea 80 - Graph filters reduce to two-sided neighborhood-splittable independent sets

**Status: exact graph characterization and finite checks; embedding into the P-vs-NP promise remains open.** For a graph $G=(V,E)$, let anchor $v$ accept an endpoint $S\subseteq V$ iff $S$ contains an edge incident to $v$. A pair $(A,B)$ has fusion profile $C$ exactly when $C$ is an independent set and there are disjoint sets $X,Y\subseteq V\setminus C$ such that every $v\in C$ has a neighbor in both $X$ and $Y$.

Proof: if $v$ is covered, it belongs to $I=A\cap B$ and $I$ contains no edge incident to $v$. Hence $C$ is independent. Its witnesses in $A$ and $B$ must lie in the disjoint exclusive parts $X=A\setminus B$ and $Y=B\setminus A$. Conversely, given such $C,X,Y$, take $A=C\cup X$ and $B=C\cup Y$. Every $v\in C$ has an incident edge in each endpoint, while $A\cap B=C$ has none through $v$. Thus the exact cover number is the minimum number of independent sets with this two-sided neighborhood-splitting property needed to cover $V$.

This gives $\chi(G)\le\tau(G)$, because every profile is independent. If minimum degree is at least two, singleton profiles exist, so $\tau(G)$ is finite and at most $|V|$. The exact check [experiment_graph_vertex_filter_chromatic.py](experiment_graph_vertex_filter_chromatic.py) finds $\tau=\chi=5$ for $K_5$, $3$ for $C_5$, and $2$ for $K_{2,3}$. The six-cycle is more revealing: $\chi(C_6)=2$ but $\tau(C_6)=3$. Its two bipartition classes cannot each be one profile, because their opposite-side neighborhoods form an odd cycle of pair-splitting constraints. The additional cost is exactly the neighborhood-splitting obstruction missing from ordinary coloring.

Potential route: use graphs whose neighborhood hypergraphs require many colors to split, then lift their vertices to anchor codes over a much smaller witness universe. The current graph model has $|V|$ anchors and $|U|=|V|$, so $\tau\le |U|$ and misses the superlinear magnification target. A coded lift with $M\gg |U|$ could overcome that ceiling only if every literal-generator route is controlled; endpoints can currently accept an anchor through a literal without carrying its proposed graph token. This is the main unpaid obligation, not a solved construction.

The direct small lift [experiment_literal_overlay_graph_filters.py](experiment_literal_overlay_graph_filters.py) exposes that obligation exactly. It maps $C_6$ anchors into the 10-point 5-bit weight-three shell, adds the graph-edge 2-point witnesses, and restores all five matching literals per anchor. Across 25 injections, every exact cover is one pair after checking all 1,048,576 endpoint pairs each time. In the canonical injection, literal generators alone cover four of the six anchors with the winning pair; graph witnesses repair the remaining two. Thus the edge-witness independence argument does not survive even a small literal overlay. A viable lift must prevent such mixed literal/edge profiles.

The larger coded test [experiment_graph_code_lift_weight3.py](experiment_graph_code_lift_weight3.py) uses all 16 anchors of the 5-bit weight-three shell, a graph with a $K_4$ core and minimum degree two, and random distinct 2-point codewords on the ten universe points. Across 30 assignments, exact enumeration of all 1,048,576 endpoint pairs gives 28 one-pair covers and two two-pair covers; none needs three pairs. In the canonical assignment, the literal-only family already has a two-pair cover and a literal-only profile of size 15/16. The winning combined pair uses literals on 15 anchors and one graph-edge witness on the last anchor. This isolates the failure: the coordinate-literal profile leaves a single repair target that one special witness can fill.

The stronger distance-three anchor test [experiment_graph_code_lift_code_anchors.py](experiment_graph_code_lift_code_anchors.py) uses eight codewords from a punctured simplex code on six coordinates and a ten-point weight-two universe. It exhaustively checks every endpoint pair for 100 assignments of graph tokens; all 100 have cover one. More revealingly, in the first assignment the literal-only subfamily alone has a cover-one pair. Adding graph witnesses poisons three anchors in that particular literal pair's intersection, but a different endpoint pair restores all eight: its witnesses are mixed, with some anchors using a literal on one side and a graph edge on the other. Minimum distance protects the anchor code from collisions; it does not prevent coordinate-slice witnesses from jointly covering the code. This closes the naive distance-code graph lift, not every possible noncanonical construction.

## Idea 81 - Checkerboard fusion splits every full-product coordinate-slice family in two

**Status: exact general theorem plus exhaustive small checks; no P-vs-NP lower bound.** Let $U=[q]^n$ with $q\ge2$ and $n\ge2$.
