2. **Advice:** a length-dependent string is supplied to a uniform machine. A fixed high-K pad can act as polynomial advice in the preceding reduction, but this does not answer arbitrary membership questions about other strings.
3. **Membership oracle:** the machine can query whether any chosen string belongs to a designated high-complexity set. This is a stronger interface because it supplies a semantic compressibility test on demand.

This was tested as a possible shortcut: perhaps the known power of Kolmogorov-random oracles could be imported into the high-K promise-slice approach. It cannot be imported by simply ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œfeeding inÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â a high-K string. Allender et al. prove, for resource-bounded measures, results including $EXP=NP^{R_{Kt}}$ and $PSPACE=ZPP^{R_{Ks}}\subseteq P^{R_K}$ ([ECCC TR02-028](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/eccc-reports/2002/TR02-028/)). The oracle supplies answers about arbitrary queries; a promise algorithm receives no such answers. Our padding lemma transfers the promise solver in the opposite direction to a randomized SAT solver, yielding $NP\subseteq BPP$, not an oracle simulation.

A second surprise concerns the choice of universal machine. Milovanov constructs a universal plain decompressor $U$ for which $H\notin P^{R_{C_U}}$, where $R_{C_U}=\{x:C_U(x)\geq|x|\}$; the paper records prior work with another universal decompressor for which $H\in P^{R_{C_U}}$ ([arXiv:2605.16261](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16261)). The exact cutoff $C_U(x)\geq|x|$ has no growing gap, so an additive-constant change in universal-machine complexity can change oracle answers at the boundary. More generally, the bare predicate $K(z)\geq\delta|z|$ can change for objects within $O(1)$ of its boundary. But a reduction that produces the stronger bound $K(z)\geq(\delta+\epsilon)|z|$ stays within the $\delta$ promise under an additive machine change of at most $c$ bits whenever $|z|\geq c/\epsilon$. State the margin and prove the robustness actually needed.

**Failed derandomization test: polynomial-size pad lists.** Could we replace random padding in Idea 137 by a deterministic polynomial-size list of candidates and call $A$ on each? Not if all calls must be inside the high-K promise. Let $\varphi_n$ be a simple satisfiable formula of length $\Theta(n)$ with $K(\varphi_n)=O(\log n)$. For a fixed computable generator $g$, every candidate $z_{n,i}=g(n,i)$ indexed by one of $poly(n)$ list positions has $K(z_{n,i})\leq K(n,i)+O(1)=O(\log n)$, because $i$ takes only $O(\log n)$ bits. Yet $|z_{n,i}|\geq\Theta(n)$, so each candidate is outside every promise $K(z)\geq\delta|z|$ for fixed $\delta>0$ once $n$ is large. A list may contain a high-K string as a nonuniform object, but then its selection or description is not supplied by the fixed polynomial-time generator. Therefore ordinary small-seed derandomization cannot keep all promise calls valid. This closes one tempting upgrade of $NP\subseteq BPP$ to P, not all possible derandomization routes.

There is a further consequence chain for our promise slice. If its proposed P solver existed, then by Idea 137 $NP\subseteq BPP$. Hu, Lu, and Oliveira prove $MINnKT\in BPP$ iff $NP\subseteq BPP$ for their nondeterministic time-bounded Kolmogorov estimation problem ([ECCC TR25-203](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/203/)). Thus the promise solver would also imply $MINnKT\in BPP$, by composition of two class containments; this is not a direct reduction from padded SAT to $MINnKT$. Also, $NP\subseteq BPP$ rules out one-way functions: given a candidate image $y=f(x)$, the relation ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œthere is a preimage extending prefix $p$ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â is in NP, and a BPP decision procedure plus bit-by-bit self-reduction finds a preimage with high probability. Therefore existence of a one-way function would conditionally rule out the high-K promise solver. This still assumes a cryptographic object whose existence is unproved.

**Learning / model update.** Attach an access triple $(\mathcal K,\mathsf{access},\mu)$ to every use of algorithmic randomness: complexity notion, access mode (promise, advice, or oracle), and threshold margin. The recurring mistake is to treat ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œcontains many bits of informationÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â as equivalent to ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œan algorithm can query whether a candidate contains those bits.ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â Counting gives abundance, random padding gives a BPP reduction, and an oracle gives a separate source of semantic information. None yields a deterministic uniform SAT solver or a separation by itself.

**Next proof test.** For any proposed high-complexity hard slice, formalize the exact promise language and audit whether an alleged diagonalizer ever needs to test promise membership. If it does, charge that operation explicitly; it may be an uncomputable oracle hidden in the argument. Then show whether the threshold has enough slack to survive universal-machine changes. If the construction needs zero-slack oracle answers, it is definition-sensitive and cannot yet support a machine-independent P-vs-NP conclusion.

**Sources:** [Allender et al., *Power from Random Strings*, ECCC TR02-028](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/eccc-reports/2002/TR02-028/); [Milovanov, *Limit on the Computational Power of C-Random Strings*, arXiv:2605.16261](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16261); [Hu, Lu, and Oliveira, *Hardness of Computing Nondeterministic Kolmogorov Complexity*, ECCC TR25-203](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/203/).

## Idea 139 - The fixed-clock randomness frontier (25 September 2026)

**Status:** a direct coNP separation target plus a quantitative clock lower bound derived from a known immunity proof; no P-vs-NP separation proved.

Fix an integer $q\ge2$, the polynomial time bound $t(n)=n^q$, and a universal machine, and define

$$
R_t=\{x:K^t(x)\geq |x|-1\},
$$

where $K^t(x)$ is the minimum length of a program printing $x$ in at most $t(|x|)$ steps. This is distinct from Levin's $Kt(x)=\min(|p|+\log T)$, which charges runtime differently. For fixed polynomial $t$, the complement of $R_t$ is in NP: guess a program of length at most $|x|-2$ and simulate it for $t(|x|)$ steps. Counting gives at least one member of $R_t$ at each length. Therefore a proof that $R_t\notin P$ for even one fixed $q$ would establish $P\ne NP$.

**Literature result and reconstructed argument.** Hirahara proves that $R_t$ is P-immune for every super-polynomial time bound $t(n)=n^{\omega(1)}$ ([*Unexpected Hardness Results for Kolmogorov Complexity Under Uniform Reductions*, ECCC TR20-050](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2020/050/download/)). P-immunity means there is no infinite P language contained in $R_t$, a stronger statement than $R_t\notin P$. The core proof is short enough to expose the precise clock barrier.

Assume an infinite P subset $S\subseteq R_t$ has decider $M$ running in time $n^a$. At infinitely many lengths $n$, choose a member $r_n\in S$ and split it as $r_n=u_nv_n$, with $|u_n|=n-m$ and $m=C\log n$. Hard-code $u_n$ in a program; enumerate all suffixes $v\in\{0,1\}^m$ and run $M(u_nv)$ until one is accepted. At least $v_n$ is accepted, so the procedure halts and outputs some $y_n\in S$. Its description length is

$$
K(y_n)\leq n-m+O(\log n)<n-1
$$

for $C$ large enough. The runtime is $2^m n^{a+O(1)}=n^{a+C+O(1)}$. If $t$ is super-polynomial, this runtime eventually fits within $t(n)$, making $K^t(y_n)<n-1$, contrary to $y_n\in R_t$.

**Fresh quantitative deduction.** With a fixed polynomial clock $t(n)=n^q$ for integer $q\ge2$, the same proof only rules out a decider whose exponent obeys $a+C_0<q$, where $C_0$ absorbs the suffix search and universal-machine simulation overhead. Thus any P decider for $R_{n^q}$ must, if one exists, have exponent at least $q-O(1)$. This is a genuine clock-sensitive lower bound, but it does not exclude P: a decider with exponent $2q$ is consistent with it. Choosing $q$ after seeing the decider does not solve this, because the target language changes with $q$ and its P-decider exponent may also change with $q$.

**Attempted bridge via SAT and why it stops.** Since $R_{n^q}\in coNP$, under $P=NP$ it would be decidable in P. Encoding the bounded program simulation by Cook-Levin and applying a fixed SAT algorithm of exponent $d$ gives a polynomial-time bound roughly $n^{O(dq)}$ (the tableau itself has size polynomial in $n^q$). This is compatible with the lower bound $n^{q-O(1)}$. P=NP provides a fixed exponent for SAT but no exponent-preserving or sublinear-exponent bound in the clock parameter $q$, so no contradiction follows.

Hirahara also connects non-trivial SAT algorithms to immunity of Levin-$Kt$-random strings. In particular, Williams-style satisfiability algorithms imply immunity against P-uniform ACC$^0$ families, and the paper characterizes the relevant immunity by a non-trivial SAT search algorithm for a circuit class (Theorems 3.10ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Å“3.11). This is a useful bridge between SAT search and resource-bounded randomness. It does not directly yield a P-vs-NP separation: Levin-$Kt$-random strings are not known to be in coNP, while the coNP-friendly fixed-clock set is exactly where the known P-immunity proof loses its force.

**Learning.** There is a sharp resource window:

- Fixed polynomial output clock: low complexity has an NP witness; the high-complexity set is in coNP, making it a valid P-vs-NP target, but no P lower bound is known.
- Super-polynomial output clock: an enumeration argument gives P-immunity, but low complexity no longer has polynomial-size, polynomial-time NP verification.
- Levin $Kt$: runtime is charged logarithmically, enabling links to circuit SAT algorithms and immunity, but the resulting random set is not known to be coNP.

A successful proof must cross one boundary without losing the other property: preserve an NP/coNP verification structure while obtaining immunity against all fixed polynomial algorithms.

**Next proof test.** Try to strengthen the quantitative bound for $R_{n^q}$ into a contradiction under the assumption of a P decider, rather than a degree lower bound. Any attempted self-reference must control the function $a(q)$ giving the decider's exponent for the changing language $R_{n^q}$. Alternatively, find a structural property of this particular language that gives a nontrivial SAT search algorithm or immunity without increasing its output clock beyond polynomial. Keep the argument separate from the already closed simple-padding derandomization route.

**Source:** [Hirahara, *Unexpected Hardness Results for Kolmogorov Complexity Under Uniform Reductions*, ECCC TR20-050](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2020/050/download/), especially Theorem 1.1, Theorem 3.9, and Theorems 3.10-3.11.

## Idea 140 - Hitting lists, selector time, and the randomness clock (25 September 2026)

**Status:** proved conditional list-to-degree lemma plus a clock lower bound for generating a list; no P-vs-NP separation.

Korten and Santhanam's *How to Construct Random Strings* (CCC 2025) is a direct connection between explicit construction, range avoidance, pseudorandomness, and time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Under their strong hardness assumptions, they build short-seed generators fooling uniform algorithms with an NP oracle. Since strings with $K^{T(n)}(x)\geq n-1$ form a dense coNP set, the generator's range contains such a string. They concatenate candidates so the construction need not recognize which one is incompressible. The resulting deterministic construction is conditional and has polynomial running time, but the theorem does not bound that time below the clock $T$ used in the incompressibility claim. In one stated regime it gives $K^{n^k}(x)\geq n/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ for all lengths under the stated strong assumption; a different theorem obtains a near-maximal bound on infinitely many lengths under assumptions for every recursion depth.

**List-selector lemma.** Fix $q$ and write $R_q=\{x:K^{|x|^q}(x)\geq |x|-1\}$. Suppose a uniform deterministic algorithm outputs, in time $n^g$, a list $L_n$ of at most $n^b$ length-$n$ strings, and $L_n\cap R_q\ne\varnothing$ for infinitely many $n$. If a P decider $D$ for $R_q$ ran in time $n^a$, enumerate $L_n$, run $D$ on each entry, and output the first accepted string; if there is no accepted entry, output $0^n$. At every length where the list hits $R_q$, this succeeds and takes time $n^{\max(g,a+b)+O(1)}$. The output has a description of length $O(\log n)$ (encode $n$ and run the fixed generator and selector). If $q>\max(g,a+b)+O(1)$, the description prints the output within $n^q$ steps, contradicting its membership in $R_q$. Thus such a list forces a degree lower bound against P deciders. For a fixed q this only excludes low enough decider exponents; the exponent of a hypothetical decider is not controlled.

**Why the list itself cannot beat its clock.** If a polynomial-size list is enumerated in time $T'(n)$, any entry is described by the fixed enumerator, $n$, and an index of $O(\log n)$ bits. With ordinary universal-machine simulation overhead, when $T'(n)\log T'(n)=o(T(n))$, every listed entry has $K^{T(n)}=O(\log n)$. It follows that no such faster list can contain a member of the set $K^{T(n)}(x)\geq n-1$. This is the same simple description obstruction noted in the paper for producing one hard string in $o(T/\log T)$ time. It explains why $P=NP$ does not turn the paper's list into a contradiction: even if coNP membership lets us select the good entry, construction plus recognition has no established sub-$T$ bound.

**Relativization warning.** The paper proves that a polynomial-time NP-oracle construction of strings with $K^{\operatorname{poly}(n)}(x)\geq n-1$ is equivalent to a polynomial-time NP-oracle construction of exponentially hard truth tables (Theorem 46). It also rules out a specific relativizing black-box reduction between range-avoidance exponents separated by more than one (Theorem 48). This does not rule out non-black-box or nonrelativizing constructions, but it blocks treating ordinary hardness-to-randomness as a free exponent upgrade. The paper's exact statements and their scope are at [CCC 2025, Sections 4-5](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol339-ccc2025/html/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.35/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.35.html).

**Learning / next attempt.** Treat construction, candidate count, recognition, and selection as separate clocks: $(T_{\rm list},|L|,T_{\rm test},T_{\rm select},T_K)$. Close ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œconstruct a short list and select its incompressible memberÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â as a generic subclock route. The remaining creative options are to exploit a structural property of the particular P decider to search its accepted extensions faster than enumeration, control the degrees of one uniform family of fixed-clock deciders, or use a direct lower-bound invariant that does not require explicitly generating a $K^T$ string. Relate any multi-block information argument to the chain-rule debt: the revised time-bounded chain-rule characterization already in New Model Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â§6 shows that sublinear chain-rule error carries a circuit-lower-bound and a promise-gap meta-complexity premise; it is not an unconditional source of compression.

**Sources:** Korten and Santhanam, [*How to Construct Random Strings*, CCC 2025](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.35), [full text](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol339-ccc2025/html/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.35/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.35.html), especially Theorems 16, 23, 46, and 48; compare Hirahara, [ECCC TR20-050](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2020/050/download/), and Kabanets-Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089, Revision 1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/).

## Idea 141 - The suffix-search exponent is a coding-convention cost (25 September 2026)

**Status:** proved sharpening of Idea 139's degree bound under explicit machine conventions; it still does not exclude a P decider of the clock's own degree or higher.

The earlier estimate used a suffix of $m=C\log n$ bits, costing $2^m=n^C$ trials. That is safe but not tight. The required suffix length pays for the program's output-length encoding, and that cost differs between plain and prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity.

**Plain-program version.** Fix a plain universal machine whose program is given with an end marker, so it can inspect the program length. Choose a fixed constant $m$ larger than the interpreter header plus two bits. A description consists of a fixed search routine followed by a prefix $u$ of length $n-m$; the routine infers $n$ from the total input length, enumerates all $2^m$ suffixes, and runs the assumed P decider $M$ until it finds an accepted extension. For the prefix $u$ of a member of an infinite $S\subseteq R_{n^q}$, some extension is accepted. The description has length $n-m+O(1)\le n-2$, while its runtime on an efficient universal simulator is $O(n^a\log n)$ if $M$ runs in $n^a$. Thus any integer exponent $q>a$ contradicts membership in $R_{n^q}$. Under this plain-K convention, an infinite P subset cannot have a decider of degree below $q$.

**Prefix-free-program version.** A prefix-free description cannot use an unmarked raw prefix at every possible output length. Encode $n$ first with an Elias-delta code of length $h(n)=\log n+2\log\log n+O(1)$, then include $u$ of length $n-m(n)$, where $m(n)=h(n)+O(1)$ is large enough that the total description is at most $n-2$. The machine enumerates $2^{m(n)}=O(n(\log n)^2)$ suffixes. Its runtime is $O(n^{a+1}\operatorname{polylog} n)$, so it fits in $n^q$ whenever $q\ge a+2$. Hence the generic prefix-free argument rules out decider degrees $a\le q-2$ and yields the sharper floor $a\ge q-1$.

The logarithmic term in the prefix-free case is structural for a code that must handle every length and every prefix: if the codeword for each of the $2^{n-m(n)}$ possible prefixes has length $n-m(n)+h(n)+O(1)$, Kraft's inequality charges total mass $\Theta(2^{-h(n)})$ at length $n$. The sum over lengths must converge, so one cannot take $h(n)=O(1)$ uniformly; a standard integer code with $h(n)=\log n+O(\log\log n)$ is sufficient. A code tailored to the length spectrum of one particular P language might do better, but constructing/decoding that spectrum within the same clock is unpaid work, not a free optimization.

There is a sharper prefix-free argument for the **full language** $R_{n^q}$, as opposed to an arbitrary infinite P subset $S\subseteq R_{n^q}$. Counting gives a member of $R_{n^q}$ at every length, so restrict to $n=2^k$. Encode $k$ with a self-delimiting code of length $h(k)=\log k+O(\log\log k)=O(\log\log n)$, rather than encoding $n$ itself. For a prefix $u$ of a member of $R_{n^q}$, set suffix length $m=h(k)+C$ to pay for this code and the fixed interpreter. A fixed prefix-free decompressor can parse the code for $k$, read exactly $n-m$ literal prefix bits, and search the $2^m=O(k\operatorname{polylog}k)=O(\log n\operatorname{polyloglog}n)$ suffixes using the assumed decider. If that decider has degree $a<q$, the program runs in $n^a\operatorname{polylog}n<n^q$ for large $n$, while its description has length at most $n-2$. Its accepted output would contradict membership in $R_{n^q}$. Therefore a P decider for the full target must have degree at least $q$, under the stated efficient universal-simulation convention.

This sparse-length trick does **not** prove P-immunity of $R_{n^q}$: an arbitrary infinite P subset can have members only at complicated lengths, so we cannot assume it contains a member at $n=2^k$. The all-length abundance is the extra premise that makes the encoded length cheaper.

**Learning.** For an arbitrary infinite P subset, the generic prefix-free proof still loses one degree because its occupied lengths may be sparse and hard to encode. For the full language $R_{n^q}$, nonemptiness at every length lets us use the computable subsequence $n=2^k$ and recover the plain-K floor $a\ge q$. This sharpens the decider-degree lower bound but leaves all deciders of degree $q$ or higher untouched. The next proof must beat that exact-clock boundary or use a different invariant; increasing a fixed $q$ does not control the hypothetical decider's degree.

**Source:** Hirahara's paper explicitly notes the plain/prefix-free distinction and uses an $O(\log n)$ encoding for $n$ in its immunity proof ([ECCC TR20-050](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2020/050/download/), proof of Theorem 3.9). The tightened bounds above are derived here; efficient universal simulation incurs at most the standard logarithmic overhead assumed in the proof model.

## Idea 142 - Black-box suffix search cannot beat exhaustive search (25 September 2026)

**Status:** proved query-complexity limit for the generic suffix-search template; it says nothing about algorithms that inspect the decider's code.

Fix a prefix $u$ and let the hidden suffix relation be $f(v)=M(uv)$ for $v\in\{0,1\}^m$, with the promise that at least one suffix is accepted. Consider the singleton family $f_z(v)=1$ iff $v=z$. A deterministic oracle algorithm that makes fewer than $2^m-1$ all-negative queries leaves at least two suffixes consistent with its transcript, so it cannot always output an accepted one. Thus the worst-case query complexity is $\Omega(2^m)$. For randomized algorithms, choose $z$ uniformly; with $r$ queries the success probability is at most $(r+1)/2^m$, so constant success probability still requires $\Omega(2^m)$ queries.

This makes the suffix-search cost in Idea 139 optimal within the black-box model. In the prefix-free proof, the code-length requirement gives $m=\log n+O(\log\log n)$, and therefore the query cost is $n\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. A generic random sample cannot improve it because the accepting suffix may be unique. The restriction matters: the actual decider for $R_q$ is a fixed program, not an arbitrary oracle. A non-black-box proof may exploit its semantic structure; the query lower bound does not rule that out.

**Learning / next test.** Close black-box acceleration of the accepted-suffix search. If we keep the fixed-clock branch, formulate a structural property that every correct decider for $R_q$ must have and show how that property gives a faster search. Otherwise switch to a different invariant that does not ask us to find a high-K output by interrogating membership one suffix at a time. This is a method filter, not evidence that such a structural property exists.

**Proof:** singleton-oracle adversary for deterministic algorithms; Yao's minimax principle for randomized algorithms. See the fixed-clock context in [Idea 139](ideas.md#idea-139---the-fixed-clock-randomness-frontier) and [New Model, Section 2.24](New%20Model.MD).

## Idea 143 - A liar formula needs a size-controlled fixed point (25 September 2026)

**Status:** the direct Cook-Levin self-reference attempt fails at an explicit encoding-size step; this is a diagnosis of one construction, not a theorem ruling out all diagonalization.

Try to turn a proposed polynomial-time SAT decider $A$ into a liar instance $x$ with $SAT(x)=1-A(x)$. For any ordinary input string $z$ of length $n$, a standard computation-tableau reduction can produce a CNF formula $F_A(z)$ satisfiable exactly when $A(z)$ rejects. If $A$ runs for $T(n)=n^d$ steps, a full space-time tableau has $\Theta(T(n)^2)$ local cells/constraints in the usual Turing-machine encoding. Writing the indexed CNF explicitly costs $O(T(n)^2\log T(n))=n^{2d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ bits in a standard encoding.

The desired diagonal step needs the input to $A$ to be the formula whose satisfiability encodes $A$'s answer on that very formula. At length level, the direct map therefore asks for a large fixed point of roughly $n\mapsto n^{2d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. For every fixed $d\ge1$, this grows beyond $n$; padding the input only changes the next tableau size to a still larger power. Iterating the construction multiplies the length exponent again. The recursion theorem for program indices does not supply this missing bound: it gives behavioral self-reference, not a fixed point of the required size in the ordinary CNF encoding.

There is a second failure mode if we avoid the tableau by running $A$ while constructing the anti-answer. Let $\top$ and $\bot$ be fixed satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas and define $F_A(z)=\bot$ when $A(z)=1$, and $F_A(z)=\top$ when $A(z)=0$. This is polynomial-time computable if $A$ is, and $SAT(F_A(z))=1-A(z)$. But if $A$ is correct, $F_A(\top)=\bot$ and $F_A(\bot)=\top$: the map has a 2-cycle and no fixed point. The contradiction would require an input $z=F_A(z)$; ordinary recursion-theorem self-reference does not guarantee such a syntactic fixed point for a map that negates the answer. So the route fails even before formula size becomes relevant when $A$ is executed during construction.

**Exact unpaid step.** A successful self-reference proof must address both sides of the tradeoff: either encode enough of $A$'s behavior in the final ordinary SAT instance without the tableau's superlinear size growth, or establish a fixed point for a semantic construction that uses $A$ without simply mapping satisfiable formulas to contradictions and vice versa. Storing a circuit that *succinctly describes* the tableau changes the decision problem to succinct SAT; the assumed solver for ordinary SAT does not apply to that new input. A size-controlled encoding alone is insufficient if the induced map has no admissible fixed point.

**What this rules out and what it leaves open.** It rules out the direct full-tableau construction as a size-closing argument and the constant-formula anti-answer map as a source of guaranteed fixed points. It does not rule out all self-referential constructions, arithmetization, Williams-style nonrelativizing arguments, or a fixed point over a smaller witness object. The useful filter is to prove both the fixed-point existence and the size recurrence before invoking self-reference; a recursion theorem alone supplies neither for this SAT map.

**Literature calibration.** Ko's original study of time-bounded program-size problems establishes oracle dependence for certain variations, consistent with the need for a nonrelativizing ingredient in nearby randomness-based approaches ([SIAM J. Comput. 20(5), 1991](https://doi.org/10.1137/0220059)). This is not a claim that Ko's theorem settles the exact fixed-clock language $R_{n^q}$ used in Idea 139.

**Next test.** Try to identify a semantic object smaller than the full computation tableauÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Âsuch as a bounded witness interface or a self-reducible consistency conditionÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Âwhose polynomial-size encoding can be checked by ordinary SAT and whose correctness still forces $A$ to err. Before pursuing one, state its length, verifier time, and the SAT solver's time on the resulting instance. See [New Model, Section 2.25](New%20Model.MD) and [audit Section 105](P_VS_NP_PROJECT_AUDIT_2026-08-24.md).

## Idea 144 - Sparse output lengths remove the prefix-free degree tax for the full target (25 September 2026)

**Status:** proved sharpening of the fixed-clock decider-degree bound; still no P-vs-NP separation.

Fix integer $q\ge2$ and assume $D$ decides $R_{n^q}=\{x:K^{n^q}(x)\ge n-1\}$ in time $n^a$. Counting gives $R_{n^q}\cap\{0,1\}^n\ne\varnothing$ for every $n$. This all-length fact lets a prefix-free compressor choose only lengths $n=2^k$, so it needs to encode $k$ rather than $n$.

Let $e(k)$ be an Elias-delta code, with $h(k)=|e(k)|=\log k+O(\log\log k)$. Fix a prefix-free machine $V$ whose valid descriptions have form $e(k)u$, where $|u|=2^k-m(k)$ and $m(k)=h(k)+C$ for a fixed constant $C$ covering the universal-simulation prefix and two extra bits. On input $e(k)u$, $V$ computes $n=2^k$, enumerates all $m(k)$-bit suffixes $v$, runs $D(uv)$, and outputs the first accepted string. Its domain is prefix-free: the $e(k)$ codes are prefix-free across distinct $k$, and for each fixed $k$ all $u$ have one fixed length. For each sufficiently large $k$, choose $u$ as the prefix of any member of $R_{n^q}$ at length $n=2^k$; the search then halts.

The universal-machine description has length $n-m(k)+h(k)+O(1)\le n-2$. The number of suffix trials is $2^{m(k)}=O(k\operatorname{polylog}k)=O(\log n\operatorname{polyloglog}n)$. With standard efficient universal simulation, the total runtime, including writing the $n$-bit output, is $O(n+n^a\operatorname{polylog}n)=o(n^q)$ when $a<q$ and $q\ge2$. The accepted output is therefore in $R_{n^q}$ but has a description of length below $n-1$ within its defining clock, a contradiction. Thus any P decider for the full $R_{n^q}$ must have degree at least $q$, whether the underlying measure is plain or prefix-free K (with the corresponding code construction).

This argument is narrower than P-immunity. It cannot replace ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œthe full language has a member at every lengthÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â with ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œan arbitrary infinite P subset has a member at every simple length.ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â Such a subset may be supported only on a sparse, non-obviously-encodable set of lengths. The result still leaves a hypothetical decider of degree $q$ or greater, so it is a degree lower bound rather than a separation.

**Proof check / remaining edge.** Confirmed the three costs separately: self-delimiting code length $h(k)$, suffix enumeration $2^{h(k)+C}=\operatorname{poly}(k)$, and D's per-query time $n^a$. Since $k=\log n$, their product adds only polylogarithmic factors to $n^a$. The strict contradiction requires $a<q$; this does not eliminate $a=q$.

See the corrected statements in [New Model, Section 2.22](New%20Model.MD) and [audit Sections 101 and 103](P_VS_NP_PROJECT_AUDIT_2026-08-24.md).

## Idea 145 - Prefix-free coding leaves an unbounded search factor at the exact clock boundary (25 September 2026)

**Status:** proved obstruction for the black-box, one-prefix exhaustive-suffix template; no impossibility result for a decider whose code can be exploited.

Take any computable unbounded sequence of target lengths $n_j$ and a prefix-free code $e(j)$ for its indices, with length $h_j$. Consider the compression scheme that stores a prefix $u$ of length $n_j-m_j$ and then searches all $m_j$-bit suffixes using a decider for the full $R_{n^q}$. To make the universal prefix-free description at least two bits shorter than the output, the suffix budget must satisfy $m_j\ge h_j+C$ for a fixed constant $C$ covering compiler overhead and the two-bit gap. Thus the exhaustive search has at least $2^{h_j+C}$ candidates.

Kraft's inequality gives $\sum_j2^{-h_j}\le1$. In particular, $h_j$ tends to infinity along the indexed sequence: only finitely many codewords can have length at most any fixed constant. Therefore the suffix count is unbounded on every infinite computable sparse subsequence too. A singleton-oracle adversary shows that an algorithm with only yes/no membership access may need to query every candidate before finding the unique accepted suffix. If each query is allowed to use $\Theta(n_j^q)$ time, this template has no uniform $O(n_j^q)$ runtime bound. Making the output lengths sparser reduces the factor to a slower-growing unbounded quantity, but does not make it constant.

This does **not** show that the actual decider for $R_{n^q}$ requires that much time on these related inputs. It only says that correctness and the clock bound, treated as a black box, cannot close the equality case by exhaustive suffix search. A source-level proof would need a structural property of this particular decider that permits batched/shared computation, or a different compression invariant. It also does not rule out a different prefix-free coding layout unless that layout still pays the Kraft mass for the possible prefixes and finds a hit only by black-box search.

**Learning:** the sparse-length trick removes the *polynomial-degree* tax, but Kraft prevents it from removing every unbounded factor. At $a=q$, the remaining obstacle is now precisely a shared-computation/non-black-box question, not a better choice of computable sparse lengths. This sharpens the open task in [Idea 144](ideas.md#idea-144---sparse-output-lengths-remove-the-prefix-free-degree-tax-for-the-full-target) and [New Model, Section 2.26](New%20Model.MD).

## Idea 146 - Under P=NP, dense fixed-clock randomness has a total search problem (25 September 2026)

**Status:** formal conditional implication and a degree lower bound on its selector; no separation.

Fix integer $q\ge2$. Since $R_q=\{x:K^{|x|^q}(x)\ge |x|-1\}$ is in coNP, under $P=NP$ it has a P decider $D_q$. Counting guarantees that for every $n$ there is some accepted $n$-bit string. Define the prefix-extension language

$$
E_q=\{(1^n,u): |u|\le n\text{ and }\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{n-|u|}\;D_q(uz)=1\}.
$$

This is in NP: the suffix $z$ is a polynomial-size witness, and $D_q$ checks the completed string in polynomial time. Under $P=NP$, $E_q$ is in P. Starting from the empty prefix, ask whether an accepted completion remains after appending $0$; append $0$ if yes and $1$ otherwise. The invariant is that the current prefix has an accepted completion, so after $n$ steps this produces $x_n\in R_q$. Thus P=NP plus $R_q\in P$ implies a deterministic polynomial-time selector $G_q(1^n)=x_n\in R_q$ for every $n$. This is the ordinary FNP-to-FP consequence written for the exact dense target, with the extension predicate made explicit.

The selector's exponent cannot be ignored. Let $\widetilde T_G(n)$ be the running time on the fixed reference universal machine of the program consisting of $G_q$ and a self-delimiting encoding of $n$, including simulation and output costs. Then $K^{\widetilde T_G(n)}(x_n)=O(\log n)$. If $\widetilde T_G(n)\le n^q$ for infinitely many sufficiently large $n$, then $x_n\notin R_q$, contradiction. Hence this reference-machine program eventually exceeds the exact $n^q$ clock. In particular, a polynomial implementation with exponent below $q$ cannot serve as the selector; an implementation of degree $q$ with a large enough multiplicative constant is not ruled out. This recovers the exponent barrier from a search-to-decision viewpoint. P=NP guarantees a polynomial selector but says nothing that bounds its degree below $q$, so the implication does not close the separation.

**Why recent coding results do not erase this cost.** Hu, Lu, and Oliveira's 2026 ICALP result characterizes nontrivial coding for Levin $Kt$ by $EXP\ne BPP$; Kabanets and Kolokolova characterize a sublinear-error chain rule for $K^t$ using an exponential-time circuit lower bound together with a promise-gap meta-complexity algorithm. Neither theorem provides a degree-preserving selector for the fixed-clock set $R_q$. Keep $K^t$ (a hard output-time cap), $Kt$ (program length plus log runtime), and probabilistic variants distinct. See [Hu-Lu-Oliveira, ICALP 2026 / ECCC TR25-211](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/211/) and [Kabanets-Kolokolova, ECCC TR25-089, Revision 1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/).

**SAT-solver accounting (direct-tableau implementation):** if a SAT algorithm runs in time $N^d$, the direct rectangular Cook-Levin encoding gives a selector in time $n^{4qd^2+1+o(1)}$. This is a valid bound for that implementation, but it is not the best generic encoding bound. The correction and sharper accounting are recorded in Idea 154.

**Next proof target:** find a batch or exponent-preserving search theorem for this special extension predicate, or exploit structure of $D_q$ beyond its polynomial-time correctness. A contradiction would require a selector bound strictly below $q$ for some fixed $q$; ordinary FNP-to-FP closure does not provide that inequality. See Idea 154 for the quasilinear generic SAT-reduction accounting found here.

## Idea 147 - Infinitely-often pseudodeterminism hides a majority-projection step (25 September 2026)

**Status:** a verified conditional implication and a failed shortcut; no separation.

The dense-property theorem of Chen, Lu, Oliveira, Ren, and Santhanam applies to every dense P language. Fix $q\ge2$ and assume $P=NP$. The fixed-clock set

$$
R_q=\{x:K^{|x|^q}(x)\ge |x|-1\}
$$

is then in P (it is in coNP unconditionally), and counting gives $|R_q\cap\{0,1\}^n|\ge 2^{n-1}$ for each $n$. Their theorem therefore supplies a randomized polynomial-time machine $B$ and strings $x_n\in R_q$ such that, for every $n$, $B(1^n)$ outputs only $x_n$ or $\bot$ except with probability at most $2^{-n}$, while on infinitely many lengths it outputs $x_n$ with probability at least $1-2^{-n}$.

This looks like a way to turn $P=NP$ into a short deterministic description of an incompressible string, but the derandomization step is not automatic. For each bit position $i$, define $p_{n,i}$ to be the probability that $B(1^n)$ emits an $n$-bit output whose $i$th bit is 1. On every good length, $p_{n,i}$ is at least $1-2^{-n}$ when $x_n[i]=1$, and at most $2^{-n}$ when $x_n[i]=0$. Thus the PP predicate

$$
M_B=\{(1^n,i):p_{n,i}\ge 1/2\}
$$

recovers all bits of $x_n$ on every good length. But the theorem gives no probability gap on the other lengths. It therefore places this threshold predicate in PP, not necessarily in BPP. The implication $P=NP\Rightarrow BPP=P$ applies to total bounded-error predicates; it does not by itself decide this unpromised majority threshold. This is the precise break in the tempting "dense pseudo-constructor + P=NP" route.

As a conditional strengthening, if $PP=P$, then querying $M_B$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ gives a deterministic polynomial-time generator that outputs $x_n$ on infinitely many lengths. Its degree is still uncontrolled: the fixed-clock compression argument only rules out a reference-machine running-time exponent below $q$. So even the stronger collapse yields no P-vs-NP proof without a clock bound.

The theorem does give a genuine conditional randomness gap. On infinitely many $n$, the strings $x_n$ have randomized time-bounded description length $O(\log n)$ and polynomial randomized output time, while their deterministic $K^{n^q}$ complexity is at least $n-1$. The random seed cannot simply be fixed and charged as a short description: $B$ may use polynomially many random bits, so that seed may itself be much longer than $\log n$. Since randomized and deterministic K are different measures, this is not a contradiction.

**Learning / next proof target:** track which quantifier the proposed selector must resolve. Prefix extension is existential (an NP predicate) and is handled by the direct search-to-decision argument in Idea 146. Extracting the output of an infinitely-often randomized constructor asks for a majority over its random tapes (a PP predicate), with no all-length promise gap. A useful new lemma would have to turn this particular majority question into an NP-searchable certificate, prove a gap on every length, or avoid selecting the canonical output. Any such lemma must also preserve a clock below $n^q$ to force a contradiction.

Source: Chen et al., [Polynomial-Time Pseudodeterministic Construction of Primes, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15140), which proves the dense-property theorem and explicitly distinguishes its all-length "canonical-or-$\bot$" guarantee from success on only infinitely many lengths.

## Idea 148 - The majority gap survives a relativized P=NP collapse (25 September 2026)

**Status:** verified oracle barrier for relativizing arguments; it does not settle the unrelativized implication or P vs NP.

Aaronson, Ingram, and Kretschmer's Theorem 10 constructs an oracle $A$ such that

$$
P^A=NP^A\ne BQP^A=P^{\#P^A}.
$$

This implies $PP^A\ne P^A$, not merely that some quantum class remains stronger. The standard identity $P^{\#P^A}=P^{PP^A}$ holds relative to every oracle: a polynomial-time machine can compute a polynomial-bit #P count by binary-searching its value with PP threshold queries, and a PP query itself reduces to a #P threshold. If $PP^A=P^A$, then $P^{PP^A}=P^A$, contradicting the displayed theorem. Also $BPP^A=P^A$ in this world, since $BPP^A\subseteq PH^A=P^A$ when $P^A=NP^A$.

So there is an oracle world in which deterministic decision, NP search, and bounded-error randomness collapse to P, while majority/counting power remains strictly higher. Applied to Idea 147, this means the passage from an infinitely-often pseudo-constructor to a deterministic selector cannot follow just from relativizing consequences of $P=NP$ and $BPP=P$: the missing bit-extraction predicate is a PP threshold. The oracle result does not prove that the concrete predicate $M_B$ for $R_q$ is outside P in the ordinary world, and it does not rule out a nonrelativizing proof exploiting the actual decider or constructor. It does show that generic collapse reasoning cannot pay the majority-projection debt.

**Learning / proof target:** any attempt to extract the canonical output under $P=NP$ must identify a feature that fails to relativize: e.g. a source-specific algebraic or uniformity property of $B$, or a special certificate collapsing this particular PP threshold to NP/P. Generic self-reduction controls existential projections only. Record this as a class-interface barrier, not as evidence for either answer to P vs NP.

Source: Aaronson, Ingram, and Kretschmer, [The Acrobatics of BQP, CCC 2022, Theorem 10](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2022.20).

## Idea 149 - Search for a successful random tape instead of decoding a majority (25 September 2026)

**Status:** valid conditional selector construction; it avoids the PP bottleneck but does not beat the fixed-clock exponent.

The majority predicate in Ideas 147-148 is needed only to recover the *canonical* output bit by bit. A P-vs-NP contradiction needs any member of $R_q$. Fix $q\ge2$ and assume $P=NP$. Then $R_q\in P$ with some decider $D_q$. Apply the dense-property theorem to get randomized polynomial-time $B$ and $x_n\in R_q$ on infinitely many good lengths.

Let $r(n)$ be the polynomial number of random bits used by $B$ on input $1^n$. Define the seed-verification relation

$$
W_q(1^n,s)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B(1^n;s)\text{ outputs an }n\text{-bit }y\text{ and }D_q(y)=1.
$$

For fixed $q$ under the collapse assumption, $W_q$ is decidable in deterministic polynomial time: simulate $B$ on the supplied tape and run $D_q$. The prefix-extension relation

$$
F_q(1^n,p)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists s\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\text{ extending }p\text{ with }W_q(1^n,s)=1
$$

is therefore in NP and, under $P=NP$, in P. Greedy self-reduction over the $r(n)$ seed bits finds a successful tape whenever one exists. On every good length, $Pr[B(1^n)=x_n]\ge1-2^{-n}$, so at least one such tape exists and the output is a member of $R_q$. The resulting deterministic polynomial-time transducer outputs some member of $R_q$ on infinitely many lengths, without deciding any PP majority predicate.

The gain is real but limited: canonical-output extraction was an unnecessary goal. It does not improve the known runtime inequality. The transducer's polynomial degree comes from deciding $F_q$ and may be at least $q$; the compression contradiction needs a reference-machine description-and-output time below $n^q$. The generic P=NP-to-FP search theorem already constructs a member at every length, also with an uncontrolled degree (Idea 146). The seed route is useful only if the structured verifier $W_q$ admits a faster-than-generic existential search with a proved exponent below $q$. A SAT implementation with ordinary tableau reductions must account for the seed length, the verifier runtime (including $D_q$), tableau size, SAT-decider exponent, and the number of prefix queries; no such sub-$q$ bound has been obtained.

**Learning / next proof target:** keep the majority oracle issue scoped correctly: it blocks *canonical bit extraction*, not every way to exploit a pseudodeterministic constructor. For the any-member target, formulate and attack an exponent-preserving search theorem for the special seed relation $F_q$, or abandon the constructor and improve the direct prefix-extension selector. Do not count existence of a successful tape as a clock improvement.

## Idea 150 - Near-certain success still needs many black-box seed queries (25 September 2026)

**Status:** exact query-complexity lemma; it limits generic derandomization but not code-aware search.

Fix an input length $n$ and a random-tape length $r$. Suppose a membership oracle $f:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}$ accepts at least a $1-2^{-n}$ fraction of all tapes. The number of rejected tapes is at most

$$
b=\left\lfloor 2^{r-n}\right\rfloor.
$$

The deterministic worst-case query complexity of outputting an accepted tape is exactly $b$ (with zero queries if $b=0$). For the upper bound, query $b$ distinct tapes: if one is accepted, return it; if all $b$ are rejected, the promise says every unqueried tape is accepted. For the lower bound, let a deterministic strategy make $t<b$ queries, answer no to each, and let $z$ be its output. Define the rejected set to contain those queried tapes and also $z$ if it was not queried. This uses at most $t+1\le b$ rejects, so it satisfies the density promise while making the strategy fail. By contrast, one uniformly random query succeeds with probability at least $1-2^{-n}$.

Apply this to Idea 149 by letting $f(s)=1$ iff $B(1^n;s)$ outputs an $n$-bit string accepted by $D_q$. On every good length, the pseudodeterministic theorem guarantees acceptance density at least $1-2^{-n}$. Density alone gives a generic deterministic query bound of $2^{r(n)-n}$ when $r(n)\ge n$ (and zero queries suffice when $r(n)<n$). It is polynomial when $\max\{0,r(n)-n\}=O(\log n)$ and super-polynomial when $r(n)-n=\omega(\log n)$. Thus if the random-tape length exceeds $n$ by a super-logarithmic amount, density alone cannot give a deterministic polynomial-query black-box selector.

This is not a lower bound on the actual seed relation's deterministic running time. The algorithm knows the code of $B$ and $D_q$, and under $P=NP$ can query the existential prefix predicate $F_q$ from Idea 149; that stronger, code-aware interface is outside this oracle model. The lemma isolates the needed improvement: prove a structural shortcut for $F_q/W_q$, or reduce the random-bit budget to $n+O(\log n)$ and separately fit candidate verification below the $n^q$ clock. It does not rule out either route.

**Literature boundary:** Chattopadhyay, Dahiya, and Mahajan prove that for *total* search problems, deterministic query complexity is at most the cube of pseudo-deterministic query complexity (MFCS 2023, Theorem 3.2). They also discuss PromiseFIND1, where canonical-output pseudo-determinism is much harder than randomized any-witness search. That framework does not contradict this lemma: the present bound is for ordinary deterministic membership queries under a dense-set promise, and one random query is a randomized any-witness algorithm, not a pseudo-deterministic canonical-output algorithm. The dense constructor is also only successful on infinitely many lengths, not a solver for a total search relation. Keep total-search pseudo-determinism, promise search, randomized search, and deterministic search as separate interfaces.

Source: Chattopadhyay, Dahiya, and Mahajan, [Query Complexity of Search Problems](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2023.34), Theorem 3.2 and discussion of PromiseFIND1.


## Idea 151 - One advice bit selects the good branch but does not derandomize it (25 September 2026)

**Status:** exact conditional search implication; no new clock bound or separation.

Corollary 3.2 of Chen et al. gives a polynomial-time randomized algorithm with a sequence of one-bit advice values \(\alpha_n\): on each advised input it outputs a canonical string \(x_n\) with probability at least \(1-2^{-n}\), and \(x_n\) belongs to the dense easy property \(Q\) on infinitely many lengths. The advice selects the successful branch. The corollary does not give a polynomial-time procedure for computing \(\alpha_n\), nor does it promise that the selected output belongs to \(Q\) at every length.

For \(Q=R_q\), assume \(P=NP\), so \(R_q\) has a polynomial-time decider \(D_q\). We can eliminate the advice bit if the goal is only any valid output: quantify over both \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}\) and a random tape \(s\), simulate the advised machine deterministically on \((1^n,\alpha;s)\), and accept when it emits an \(n\)-bit \(y\) with \(D_q(y)=1\). This is an NP witness relation. Under \(P=NP\), its prefix-extension predicate is in P. First query the empty-prefix predicate; output a fixed default if no witness exists, and otherwise greedily find \((\alpha,s,y)\) on every length where such a witness exists. The corollary supplies such a witness on infinitely many lengths. This recovers an infinitely-often deterministic polynomial-time selector without being given the advice sequence. The direct selector in Idea 146 is stronger on coverage, because it finds a member of R_q at every length under the same assumption.

This does not improve Idea 149: the selector's polynomial degree is uncontrolled, while the compression contradiction needs reference-machine runtime below \(n^q\). The one advice bit is not an obstacle for existential any-witness search; trying both values removes it. Canonical-output decoding is different. For a fixed output bit, it thresholds the probability at \(1/2\). The gap is guaranteed along the selected advice sequence, but need not hold for every pair \((n,\alpha)\). The resulting question is promise-majority, not automatically a total BPP language to which \(P=NP\Rightarrow BPP=P\) applies. The relativized boundary in Idea 148 warns against inferring a generic PP collapse.

**Learning:** separate advice length from the cost of using advice. Finite existential branching absorbs the one-bit label, but does not decode the canonical randomized output or bound the selector below the fixed clock. The remaining target is a source-specific, exponent-preserving search theorem.

Source: Chen et al., [Polynomial-Time Pseudodeterministic Construction of Primes, Corollary 3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15140).


## Idea 152 - The exponent debt is a quantifier-order barrier (25 September 2026)

**Status:** rigorous diagnosis of the diagonalization gap; no P-vs-NP separation.

Enumerate nondeterministic machines with explicit polynomial clocks as \(N_i\), and deterministic machines with explicit polynomial clocks as \(D_j\). Let \(E(i,j,x)\) say that these two clocked machines agree on input \(x\). This is a computable predicate because both runs halt within their stated clocks. Then, up to the routine encoding of machine-clock pairs,

$$
P=NP\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall i\ \exists j\ \forall x\ E(i,j,x).
$$

Its negation is

$$
\exists i\ \forall j\ \exists x\ \neg E(i,j,x).
$$

Thus a separation proof must identify one polynomially clocked nondeterministic machine that differs from every deterministic polynomial-time machine, with the counterexample allowed to depend on the candidate decider. Beating every machine of one fixed exponent is insufficient: that establishes only that some language is outside \(\mathrm{DTIME}(n^c)\), not outside their union P.

Hartmanis and Stearns time hierarchy gives, for every fixed \(c\), a language \(L_c\in\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{c+1})\setminus\mathrm{DTIME}(n^c)\) (since \(n^c\log n=o(n^{c+1})\)). This proves unconditionally that P has no common fixed polynomial exponent. Under \(P=NP\), each such \(L_c\) is also in NP. Therefore even the collapse \(P=NP\) cannot mean that all NP languages share one deterministic exponent. A generic search-to-decision theorem with one exponent bound independent of the verifier's clock cannot be the missing step.

This explains the quantifier failure in the naive diagonal plan. Simulating the first \(k\) candidate deciders can be done with a polynomial clock whose degree depends on the largest exponent among those \(k\) machines. Letting \(k\) grow to cover every decider removes the fixed polynomial bound; freezing \(k\) leaves infinitely many untested candidates. Ordinary time hierarchy does not bridge this gap, because its diagonal language remains in deterministic polynomial time at a higher degree.

For the project target, Idea 144 gives an even sharper synchronization: if the full \(R_q=\{x:K^{n^q}(x)\ge n-1\}\) language has a polynomial decider of degree \(a\), then \(a\ge q\). The required degree rises with the clock parameter, so increasing \(q\) cannot outrun the generic selector obtained from \(P=NP\); that selector's degree is unconstrained and may rise with \(q\). A proof would need a target-specific argument that yields a contradiction across all degrees, not a uniform-degree collapse that time hierarchy already forbids.

The all-machine presentation above is syntactically \(\Pi^0_3\). A second, equivalent presentation uses SAT completeness: \(P=NP\) iff some clocked deterministic machine \(D_j\) decides SAT on every formula, \(\exists j\,\forall\varphi [D_j(\varphi)=SAT(\varphi)]\). Since SAT is decidable by exhaustive search, this gives a \(\Sigma^0_2\) form for \(P=NP\) and a \(\Pi^0_2\) form for its negation. These are quantifier descriptions, not independence results; neither form settles what ZFC proves.

Source for the hierarchy step: Hartmanis and Stearns, [On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms, Transactions of the AMS 117 (1965)](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1965-0170805-7).


## Idea 153 - Odd liar cycles are valid, but direct tableaux do not close (25 September 2026)

**Status:** exact contradiction schema; no construction of the required cycle.

Let \(A\) be a correct SAT decider. If ordinary CNFs \(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_{k-1}\), cyclically indexed, satisfied \(\operatorname{SAT}(\phi_i)=1-A(\phi_{i+1})\) for odd \(k\), then correctness gives \(b_i=1-b_{i+1}\), hence \(b_0=1-b_0\). This is a valid backward proof target: construct an actual odd-negation cycle of ordinary formulas.

The constant anti-answer map from Idea 143 instead creates a two-cycle (tautology, contradiction); alternating truth values are consistent. Adding a cyclic tag does not help: the state (tag,b) maps to (tag+1 mod k,1-b), whose period is 2k for odd k. More generally, every actual cycle of a map that flips SAT has even length, so finite closure alone cannot force an odd orbit. A recursion-theorem fixed point for a program index does not supply a fixed CNF string.

The direct attempt to encode each computation \(A(\phi_{i+1})\) as a full rectangular Cook-Levin tableau makes \(|\phi_i|=\Theta(T(|\phi_{i+1}|)^2)\), where \(T(m)\) is the decider's clock. Each edge expands the formula, so this particular cycle construction does not close. This quadratic estimate is specific to the direct rectangular tableau: generic nondeterministic time T computations have classical reductions to 3SAT of size T polylog(T), as summarized in Jahanjou, Miles, and Viola, Section 1.2. Even with that sharper reduction, if T(m)=m^d for d>1, the next formula has size m^{d+o(1)}, so the ordinary cycle still grows. This is no lower bound against a code-aware or otherwise non-generic fixed-point construction. Succinct encodings are succinct-SAT instances, outside an ordinary SAT decider's guarantee.

**Learning:** separate the odd semantic cycle, construction of ordinary CNFs realizing it, and the fixed NP-clock cost of constructing/verifying them. The parity contradiction is proved; size-controlled cycle closure is unpaid. This filters the direct tableau liar, not all self-reference arguments. See [Idea 143](ideas.md#idea-143---a-liar-formula-needs-a-size-controlled-fixed-point).

## Idea 154 - Quasilinear reductions shrink the generic selector loss, but do not close it (25 September 2026)

**Status:** corrected generic upper-bound accounting; no degree-preserving selector and no separation.

The previous SAT accounting treated a rectangular time-by-space tableau, of size roughly T squared, as though it were the strongest available Cook-Levin reduction. Classical machine-simulation reductions instead convert nondeterministic time T to a 3SAT formula of size T polylog(T). Jahanjou, Miles, and Viola summarize this as established prior work and cite the two-tape and oblivious-simulation lineage; their paper's own local-reduction theorem adds a separate clause-locality property. For this selector calculation, only the ordinary formula-size bound is needed.

Fix q >= 2 and suppose a deterministic SAT algorithm runs in N^d time. The complement of R_q has a nondeterministic verifier running in n^q polylog(n) time (the polylog allowance absorbs clock and machine bookkeeping). The quasilinear reduction makes a formula of size n^{q+o(1)}, so the induced decider D_q for R_q runs in n^{qd+o(1)} time. The prefix-extension predicate E_q then has a verifier that guesses the suffix and runs D_q once, in n^{qd+o(1)} time. Applying the same reduction again gives an E_q SAT instance of size n^{qd+o(1)}; one SAT call decides each prefix-extension question in n^{qd^2+o(1)} time. Greedy construction uses exactly n-1 adaptive questions: the density bound |R_q at length n| >= 2^{n-1}+1 makes both first-bit halves nonempty, so fix the first bit to 0 and query the remaining positions. This yields a selector in n^{qd^2+1+o(1)} time.

For standard explicit SAT encodings, d >= 1 because the algorithm must read its input. Hence qd^2+1 >= q+1 > q. The corrected generic pipeline is substantially better than the direct-tableau estimate n^{4qd^2+1+o(1)}, but it still does not produce the sub-n^q selector that the fixed-clock compression contradiction requires. The n-1 adaptive calls are not a lower bound: the formula instances may share computation visible to a code-aware method. A successful next lemma would need to batch or share those related extension computations, exploit the actual SAT algorithm's internals, or replace bitwise witness extraction with a different compression argument. The standard quasilinear reduction alone does none of these.

**Query-model boundary.** Gharibian and Kamminga summarize that classical SAT search uses Theta(n) NP queries and that an o(n)-query white-box algorithm would violate ETH: enumerate all possible answer transcripts and verify the resulting candidate. This is useful evidence that generic query compression is unlikely under ETH, but it does not lower-bound the specific E_q prefix instances here. More importantly, ETH is false under the assumption P=NP being tested, so this conditional lower bound cannot close our contradiction route. Query count and the running-time exponent of implementing each query must remain separate.

**Learning:** separate two costs that the earlier ledger merged: the size of a verifier-to-SAT encoding and the number of adaptive decision calls needed to extract a witness. Improving the first from quadratic to quasilinear removes a large constant-factor exponent penalty; it does not erase the second. This sharpens the search target to structured batch search while preserving the warning from Idea 152 that P=NP supplies no uniform polynomial degree.

Source: Jahanjou, Miles, and Viola, [Local Reductions, Section 1.2](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2013/099/revision/3/download/), which states the classical quasilinear reduction from nondeterministic time T to 3SAT and its simulation lineage; Pippenger and Fischer, [Relations Among Complexity Measures](https://doi.org/10.1145/322123.322138), for oblivious simulation in O(T log T); Gharibian and Kamminga, [BQP, meet NP, Section 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03943), for the ETH-conditional classical query bound and its transcript-enumeration argument.

## Idea 155 - Near-certain high-K construction forces a long random tape

**Status:** counting lemma about the pseudodeterministic route; no separation.

Fix q and let R_q consist of strings x of length n with K_U^{n^q}(x) >= n-1 for a fixed universal machine U. Suppose a randomized machine B on input 1^n uses exactly r(n) random bits and, on infinitely many good lengths, outputs some member of R_q with probability at least 1-2^{-h(n)}. It need not output the same member on different tapes. Assume B's deterministic running time, including its random-bit use, is at most n^c, with q chosen strictly larger than c and the fixed U-simulation overhead.

Then on every sufficiently large good length,

$$
r(n) >= n+h(n)-O(log n).
$$

For the proof, choose k=n-C log n so that every k-bit string s can be described to U by a program of length at most k+O(log n)<n-1: the program stores n and s, pads s with zeros as needed, runs B(1^n), and prints its output. If any such padded tape caused B to output a member of R_q, this program would violate that member's K_U^{n^q} lower bound. Therefore all 2^k padded tapes are failures. The success guarantee allows at most 2^{r(n)-h(n)} failed tapes, so 2^k <= 2^{r(n)-h(n)}, giving the inequality. If r(n)<k, every tape is already describable below n-1 and the positive success probability is itself a contradiction, so the same conclusion follows.

For the Chen et al. dense-property constructor, h(n)=n on its infinitely many successful lengths. Thus, if that constructor could run within the R_q clock, it would need at least 2n-O(log n) random bits there. This closes a tempting shortcut: near-certain success does not force a short successful seed. It is consistent with polynomial randomness and yields no P-vs-NP separation. The remaining target is a randomness-efficient constructor whose complete fixed-tape runtime is below n^q. The degree lower bound for deterministic R_q deciders does not transfer to a randomized constructor whose seed itself has at least n bits of information; no lower bound on B's runtime follows from this lemma.

**Learning:** entropy in the output distribution is not a substitute for a short deterministic description of a successful tape. The huge good-tape set can avoid every tape with a sub-(n-1)-bit description, provided the seed space is large enough; the error budget then forces r(n) to be about twice the output length. A concrete conditional target is now visible: under P=NP, construct a machine for R_q that succeeds with error at most 2^{-n}, uses 2n-\omega(\log n) random bits, and whose fixed-tape runtime fits n^q. The lemma would turn that into a contradiction. The dense-property theorem alone gives only polynomial randomness and an uncontrolled runtime exponent, so it does not supply this target.

This lemma applies to any machine that outputs any R_q member with the stated success probability; canonical pseudodeterminism is not needed. It depends on the fixed universal-machine convention and on the constructor running below the n^q clock. It is a route diagnosis, not evidence that such a constructor exists with that runtime.

See Idea 149 and the dense-property theorem of Chen et al., [Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15140).


## Idea 156 - Randomness is the missing description budget in pseudodeterministic compression (25 September 2026)

**Status:** exact randomized-description lower bound; no deterministic compression or P-vs-NP separation.

Let R_q consist of the n-bit strings x with K_U^{n^q}(x) >= n-1. Suppose a randomized program M, with fixed code length L, takes 1^n, uses r(n) random bits, and outputs some x_n in R_q with probability at least 1-2^{-h(n)}, where h(n) >= 1. Assume every fixed-tape run, including universal-machine simulation overhead, fits the n^q clock. Then

$$
L + r(n) >= n + min(h(n), r(n)) - O(log n).
$$

Proof: encode n, the fixed code for M, and a k-bit tape prefix s, where k = max(0,n-L-C log n) for a sufficiently large constant C. Completing the tape by zeros gives a U-program shorter than n-1. If k is positive, every one of the 2^k padded tapes must fail. If r < k, even a full r-bit tape has a short description, contradicting positive success; hence any existing construction has r >= k. When h <= r, the error bound permits at most 2^{r-h} failed tapes, so 2^k <= 2^{r-h} and L+r >= n+h-O(log n). When h > r, the error allowance is below one tape, forcing all tapes to succeed, which contradicts k > 0; thus k=0 and L >= n-O(log n). Combining the cases gives L+r >= n+min(h,r)-O(log n).

This refines Idea 155 by accounting for the randomized program's own description length instead of treating its code as constant. For a fixed short program L=O(1), error 2^{-n} forces r >= 2n-O(log n); success probability at least 1/2 forces r >= n-O(log n). The result explains how a randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov description can have an O(log n)-bit program while hiding linearly many bits in its uncharged random tape.

Chen et al.'s Theorem 1.1 gives a canonical output with error 2^{-n} on infinitely many lengths for every dense polynomial-time property, and Corollary 1.3 explicitly counts randomized program length while leaving random bits uncharged. If P=NP, R_q is such a dense easy property. However, the theorem's constructor has a polynomial exponent depending on the property decider; it does not show that its fixed-tape runtime fits the same n^q clock defining R_q. Thus this lemma is a resource-aligned constraint, not a way to apply the theorem inside the clock automatically.

**Learning:** randomized code length, random-tape length, and fixed-tape runtime are three separate resources. The paper's randomized-description corollary controls only the first and runtime at some polynomial degree. For a P-vs-NP proof, the needed new ingredient would have to align the constructor's clock with the K-clock or remove its randomness with a proved degree-preserving method. Merely calling the output pseudodeterministic does neither.

Source: Chen et al., [Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15140); comparison with the special fixed-code case in [Idea 155](ideas.md).

## Idea 157 - The dense-property theorem carries a degree tax tied to its decider (25 September 2026)

**Status:** source-level resource audit; it rules out a clock guarantee from this theorem as currently stated, not a proof that the theorem's constructor must run slowly.

Assume P=NP and fix q. Then R_q is dense and has a polynomial-time decider D_q. Let a_q be a polynomial exponent for that decider. The fixed-clock counting argument gives a_q >= q. Chen et al.'s dense-property theorem applies to R_q, but a close read of its proof does not supply a constructor inside the same n^q clock.

In the proof of Theorem 1.1, the authors choose tau so that A_Q runs in time n^(tau/3), then set lambda = c(tau+1)kappa and choose beta >= 100 lambda. Their recursive lengths obey n_(i+1) = n_i^beta. The reconstruction step is bounded by (d+n) M^(c rho); the proof also bounds d'_i by 2 n_i^c + n_i^tau and takes M=n_(i+1). Thus the displayed bound for this branch is on the order of n_i^(tau + beta*c*rho), before other polynomial overheads. Since tau is chosen from the exponent of A_Q and beta is chosen proportional to tau, the certified degree grows with the decider degree, which is already at least q. The theorem proves polynomial time for each fixed Q, but its stated analysis does not prove a runtime below n^q for Q=R_q.

This is an upper-bound audit, not a lower bound on the actual algorithm: the constructor might admit a faster implementation or a sharper analysis. The valid conclusion is narrower: the published dense-property theorem cannot be inserted into the fixed-clock contradiction with the needed clock inequality on the basis of its polynomial-time statement.

**Learning:** the randomness lemma from Idea 156 becomes useful only after clock alignment. Here the theorem's hardness-randomness bootstrapping explicitly scales its polynomial parameters with the property decider. Choosing q after measuring the constructor is circular because that changes R_q and its decider. A real advance would need a resource-preserving constructor for R_q with fixed-tape time below n^q, or a search/verification method that avoids running the full R_q decider at that cost.

Source: Chen et al., [Theorem 1.1, proof of the construction](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.15140v2), especially the parameter choice and reconstruction bounds in Section 3; see also [Idea 156](ideas.md).


## Idea 158 - Batch SAT checks improve query count, but the candidate list becomes the new barrier (25 September 2026)

**Status:** sharper conditional selector bound for a supplied list; no sub-clock generator.

Fix q and suppose SAT has a deterministic N^d-time decider. For each explicitly supplied n-bit string x_i, quasilinear Cook-Levin gives a 3CNF F_i of size n^(q+o(1)) that is satisfiable exactly when x_i has a description shorter than n-1 within the n^q clock; equivalently, x_i is outside R_q.

Suppose a list x_1,...,x_m is supplied with the promise that at least one item belongs to R_q. For an index block S, form the conjunction F_S of all F_i for i in S. Then F_S is satisfiable iff every candidate in S is outside R_q. Its size is O(|S| n^(q+o(1))). Query the whole list once; if F_[m] is unsatisfiable, it contains a high-K candidate. Split the list in half and query the conjunction for the left half. If that is unsatisfiable, keep the left half; otherwise the right half must contain a high-K candidate. Repeat. The balanced search uses O(log m) SAT calls.

At level j, the queried formula has size at most O((m/2^j)n^(q+o(1))). With an N^d SAT decider, the total time is a geometric sum bounded by O((m n^(q+o(1)))^d). For m=n, this is n^((q+1)d+o(1)). Compared with the generic prefix selector n^(qd^2+1+o(1)) from Idea 154, this improves the exponent whenever d>1 and matches it when d=1. It is a genuine refinement of the search pipeline, but (q+1)d >= q+1, so it still misses the n^q compression clock.

The list promise is the decisive limitation. Density alone cannot ensure that a polynomial-size list hits R_q: a set of more than half the hypercube may avoid any prescribed polynomial list. In fact, if one deterministic program enumerates m=poly(n) candidates in time n^c for c<q, then each x_i has K_U^{n^q}(x_i) <= |E|+O(log n+log m)=O(log n) for m=poly(n): its description is E, n, and the self-delimiting index i. The program runs within n^q, so for large n every listed string is outside R_q. A uniformly generated sub-clock candidate list therefore cannot contain the needed high-K output. A nonuniform list might hit, but its advice description is not free in the K argument.

**Learning:** batch SAT can trade n adaptive calls for O(log n) calls while preserving total formula volume, yielding an improved generic exponent. The compression obstacle has moved upstream: constructing a guaranteed high-K candidate list already requires either clock-exceeding computation or at least linear description information. The next target is a structured implicit list whose existence is guaranteed for this specific R_q and whose high-K member can be exposed without expanding the full list.

Source for the quasilinear formula-size premise: Jahanjou, Miles, and Viola, [Local Reductions, Section 1.2](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2013/099/revision/3/download/); selector comparison: [Idea 154](ideas.md).

## Idea 159 - The fixed-clock high-K set is a one-bit range-avoidance instance (25 September 2026)

**Status:** exact reduction to a standard total-search problem and a proof-complexity connection; the resource accounting still blocks a separation.

Fix q>=2 and define R_q at length n by K_U^{n^q}(y) >= n-1. There are 2^{n-1}-1 programs of length below n-1. Assign them to distinct inputs of an (n-1)-bit string, reserve the last input as a dummy, and construct a circuit

$$
C_{n,q}:\{0,1\}^{n-1}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}
$$

that simulates the indexed program for n^q steps, returning its n-bit output when it halts with that length and a fixed default string otherwise. Every n-bit string with a description shorter than n-1 is in Range(C_{n,q}); therefore every output outside the range belongs to R_q. Since the domain has half as many elements as the codomain, a missing output exists. This is an exact one-bit-stretch instance of circuit Range Avoidance.

The circuit can be generated uniformly with size O(n^q log n) by the Pippenger-Fischer/Koucky simulation (derived in Idea 161), rather than the earlier broad n^{O(q)} bound. General circuit Avoid is complete for APEPP, the total-search class associated with explicit constructions from counting/probabilistic existence. A candidate y is valid only if every circuit input misses it, so the solution check is coNP in the explicit circuit size.

**Implication under P=NP.** Then coNP=P, so validity of a proposed missing output is decidable in polynomial time in |C|. The total search can be solved in FP (equivalently, use the P=NP collapse to find a valid output bit by bit). The circuit has g=O(n^q log n) gates and a standard gate-list encoding of length S=O(g log g)=O(n^q(log n)^2). If a general Avoid solver takes S^d time, composition has an O(n^(qd)(log n)^(2d)) upper bound. That does not certify a run below the n^q clock, but it is not a lower bound on the solver for this structured family. The APEPP classification makes the universal verification visible without settling the special-instance runtime.

**Proof-complexity bridge.** Ren, Santhanam, and Wang's Theorem 6.6 characterizes, up to constant-stretch and their resource conventions, FNP algorithms for general Avoid by propositional proof systems that break every nonuniform proof-complexity generator. Their reduction explicitly maps a high time-bounded-K string search problem to a missing output of a short-program circuit. This is the same constructional spine as R_q, though their theorem uses a conditioned K variant and should not be quoted as an exact theorem about our fixed-clock definition. If we could prove that the validity language for this explicit uniform family is not in NP, then NP != coNP and hence P != NP; however, the general Avoid/proof-system equivalence does not transfer a lower bound from this one family to all circuits.

**Learning / next proof obligation.** Range avoidance is the right semantic object for "finding a string no short program outputs," and it exposes why the verifier is universal. But replacing SAT search with AVOID only changes the interface: under P=NP, a generic solver is polynomial in the explicit evaluator circuit, whose size is O(n^q log n) by Idea 161; the resulting generic upper bound still does not certify a subclock run. The promising proof target is now sharply stated: either obtain a sub-n^q solver for this special uniform avoidance family under P=NP, or prove its missing-output relation is not NP-verifiable. A proof must explain how it beats the circuit-description exponent or why this particular family resists NP certificates; merely invoking APEPP-completeness or the general proof-generator theorem does neither.

**Sources:** [Ren, Santhanam, and Wang, *On the Range Avoidance Problem for Circuits*, ECCC TR22-048](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2022/048/), especially the APEPP classification and Theorem 6.6; compare the project's fiber normal form in [New Model, Sections 2.2-2.3](New%20Model.MD).

## Idea 160 - Dual pigeonhole logic exposes proof-extraction debt (25 September 2026)

**Status:** literature-grounded conditional unprovability result; not an unconditional complexity separation and not a ZFC independence result.

The range-avoidance statement is the dual weak pigeonhole principle (dWPHP): for a polynomial-time map f:{0,1}^n->{0,1}^ell with ell>n, some y is missed by every input. Ordinary finite counting proves that such a y exists. The hard part is producing one feasibly and, in bounded arithmetic, proving the universal assertion with enough strength to extract a feasible witness.

Ilango, Li, and Williams make this proof-extraction gap exact. Cook's PV1 formalizes polynomial-time reasoning; Jerabek's APC1 extends it by dWPHP for PV functions and captures randomized polynomial-time reasoning. By the KPT witnessing theorem, a proof of the bounded dWPHP statement in a theory extending PV yields a constant-round Student-Teacher strategy: the student proposes a missing y, and a teacher who finds y in the range returns a preimage x as a counterexample. This is an AVOID algorithm with O(1) circuit-inversion oracle queries.

Their Corollary 23 says that, assuming JLS-secure indistinguishability obfuscation and coNP not in infinitely-often AM, dWPHP for circuit evaluation is not provable in TPV for every constructive output length ell(n)<=poly(n) with ell(n)>n. Consequently APC1 is a strict extension of PV1 under those assumptions. Their separate AVOID theorem says a deterministic polynomial-time AVOID algorithm for suitable polynomial-size circuits, under subexponentially secure iO, would imply coNP is contained in NP; that implication alone does not contradict P=NP, since P=NP already implies NP=coNP.

**What this says about foundations.** ZFC's finite pigeonhole proof establishes existence of a missing output, but it does not give a polynomial-time selector. Conditional nonprovability in PV1 is a statement about feasible proof extraction in a weak arithmetic theory; it is not evidence that the pigeonhole assertion is independent of ZFC. The KPT theorem identifies the missing resource precisely: a short proof of a universal-existential-universal claim would force a bounded-round candidate-and-counterexample strategy.

**Learning / next proof obligation.** Keep three questions separate: (i) is a missing output mathematically guaranteed? yes, by counting; (ii) can a weak theory prove that guarantee? conditionally, PV1 cannot; (iii) can a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm find it? the conditional lower bounds concern the general circuit problem. The constructed R_q family is one explicit instance, and these theorems do not by themselves give a lower bound for that family or an unconditional P-vs-NP proof. In particular, P=NP would make coNP a subset of AM, contradicting the bounded-arithmetic theorem's coNP not-in-i.o.AM premise. A new route would need either a proof-extraction lower bound tailored to the universal-program circuit or an unconditional way to turn the bounded arithmetic obstruction into an NP lower bound.

**Source:** Ilango, Li, and Williams, [*Indistinguishability Obfuscation, Range Avoidance, and Bounded Arithmetic*, ECCC TR23-038](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/038/), especially Theorems 18, 20-21 and Corollary 23; see also the project's existing [Audit Section 5.8](P_VS_NP_PROJECT_AUDIT_2026-08-24.md).

## Idea 161 - Uniform simulation tightens the range-circuit size to near the clock (25 September 2026)

**Status:** a sharper, source-checked circuit-size upper bound; the generic search bound does not certify a fit below the incompressibility clock.

Fix q>=2 and let T=n^q. There is a particularly clean index map for the short programs: every p of length j<n-1 corresponds to z=1^(n-2-j)0p in {0,1}^(n-1). This is a bijection from all programs of lengths 0 through n-2 onto all (n-1)-bit strings except 1^(n-1), which is the dummy index. Thus no exponential lookup table is needed; the decoder can be built with O(n^2) gates.

The remaining circuit simulates the fixed universal multitape machine U for T steps and returns its n-bit output, or a default if it does not halt with exactly n bits. Pippenger-Fischer, and the simpler construction of Koucky reproduced by Shalunov, give log-space-uniform circuits of size O(T log T) for t-time computations. Shalunov's proof constructs circuits that map an initial tape configuration to the full final configuration, so the statement applies to this multi-output evaluator; selecting the n output bits costs O(T) additional gates.
