## Idea 27 - Self-reference through fast consistency provers

Status: the literature supplies a precise proof-complexity framework and an open diagonalization target. The finite reflection construction exposes the cutoff/encoding cost, but it does not prove a lower bound for arbitrary proof systems.

A Cook-Reckhow propositional proof system is polynomially bounded exactly when NP=coNP. A fast consistency prover (FCP) is a consistent polynomial-time axiomatized theory S with polynomial-length S-proofs of every finite consistency statement Con_T(n), for each consistent polynomial-time theory T; KrajÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â­ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Âek and PudlÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¡k show that an FCP exists exactly when an optimal propositional proof system exists. NP=coNP implies an FCP, while the converse for this nonuniform, theory-by-theory polynomial bound is open. Joosten's ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“unlikely FCPÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â strengthens the definition with a uniform bound depending on the axiom-decision exponent, and its existence is equivalent to NP=coNP.

The unusual fixed-point mechanism in Joosten's paper uses ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´(x) ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¬Pr_S(h(x),ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬â„¢Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´(x)ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬â„¢Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â). If S is sound, ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´(n) is true and has no S-proof of length at most h(n). For recursively enumerable theories, a second theory T can be built from the theorems of S plus reflection axioms; this yields arbitrarily large finite-consistency proof lower bounds. The construction fails for polynomial-time theories because recognizing ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“is a theorem of SÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â is generally only recursively enumerable. The paper isolates Conjecture 7.1: for every sound polynomial-time theory S and every l, some sound polynomial-time T has S-proofs of Con_T(n) longer than n^l. Uniformizing this family of T's is the further obstacle to ruling out an FCP.

Our finite propositional version has the same size equation. Under P=NP, one can choose a Cook-Reckhow system whose proof of a tautology is essentially the formula itself: the verifier runs a polynomial-time TAUT decider. A self-referential tautology saying ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“there is no proof of this formula up to NÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â must explicitly range over N-bit candidate proofs, so its ordinary formula/circuit encoding has length at least on the order of N. Its guaranteed proof length is therefore not forced below N. A succinct circuit description can shrink the encoding, but then the proof assignment has exponential length relative to that description and the resulting problem is no longer ordinary NP. This is the representation cost, not a contradiction.

Primary sources: [Cook and Reckhow (1979), The Relative Efficiency of Propositional Proof Systems](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~sacook/homepage/cook_reckhow.pdf); [Joosten, Propositional Proof Systems and Fast Consistency Provers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431), especially Theorems 3.1 and 4.3 and Conjecture 7.1.

Reusable lesson: a self-reference result can give long proofs for a fixed system, but transferring it to a polynomial-time axiom theory requires a polynomial-time recognizable axiom set. The quantifier pattern matters too: ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“for every l there is a theory T_lÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â does not produce one T defeating a fast consistency prover. Track both the proof cutoff and the theory's axiom-decision exponent.

Next test: investigate whether a single polynomial-time theory can encode a growing sequence of these diagonal cutoffs without making its axiom checker superpolynomial. Any such construction must show how its uniform recognition exponent and its consistency-proof lower bound scale together.

## Idea 28 - P=NP-assisted bounded reflection, and the exponent ratio

Status: the per-k construction is a plausible conditional lower-bound route, not a proved theorem and not a P-vs-NP separation. Unary padding makes the bounded-proof witness polynomial in the axiom string length, but the direct speed-up transfers proof length to a consistency cutoff on the same padded scale. Idea 33 records the cancellation. The unresolved formal obligations and one-theory/uniform-degree gap remain.

Fix a sound polynomial-time theory S and an integer k. Let ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´_k(\bar n) be a fixed-point instance whose parameter n is written with a unary numeral of length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(n), and which asserts that it has no S-proof of length at most n^k. If S is sound, it has no such proof. The relation ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“there exists an S-proof of this specified sentence of length at most n^kÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â is in NP as a function of the unary-padded instance length: the witness has polynomial length n^k and S's proof checker runs in polynomial time. Under P=NP, it has a polynomial-time decider for each fixed k. If n were supplied only as a dyadic numeral of length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(log n), this NP argument would fail; the proof witness would be exponential in the formula input length.

Joosten's consistency target Con_T(\underline N) uses a dyadic numeral of length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(log N), while the fast-consistency bound is measured as a polynomial in the numeric cutoff N. The unary numeral above is a separate padding choice for the diagonal instance and for T's axiom candidates; it is not a claim that Joosten's Con_T(\underline N) is unary-coded.

The candidate T_k takes as axioms the S-theorems ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  that have an S-proof of length at most |ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â |^{k+1}, together with the local reflection instances Box_S ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢ ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â . These axioms are true if S is sound. For a candidate axiom of length L, bounded S-proof existence with cutoff L^{k+1} is in NP, so P=NP gives a polynomial-time axiom decider for each fixed k (with an exponent depending on k). The intended fixed-point speed-up would use a unary-padded ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´_k(\bar n): if S proves it within n^k symbols, its short S-proof makes it available to T_k, and the local reflection instances support the contradiction encoded by the fixed point. An adaptation of Joosten's Lemma 6.1 could then aim to force long S-proofs of Con_{T_k} at a cutoff proportional to the size of this padded instance. The formal proof of the lemma's two speed-up conditions, the exact padding constants, and their verification inside S remain open obligations for this sketch. The direct exponent accounting is summarized in Idea 33.

It does not give a contradiction. T_k depends on k, and the degree of its axiom-decision algorithm also grows with k: deciding a proof-existence question with an L^k-bit witness through a fixed SAT algorithm may take L^{O(k)} time. An FCP may use a different polynomial bound for each T_k, with exponent growing faster than k. Even a uniform FCP bound measured as a fixed polynomial in n^{DecExp(T)} scales with that growing decision exponent. Thus per-k lower bounds do not refute the existence of an FCP.

Trying to encode unbounded k into one axiom language also fails directly. If k is part of the input, the witness n^k is no longer polynomial in the input length, so P=NP does not decide the resulting axiomhood predicate. Padding the input until n^k becomes polynomial in its length also increases the formula and proof cutoff; after reparameterizing by the padded length, the lower-bound exponent is bounded by the fixed padding degree. The same resource is being spent twice: first to recognize a longer proof witness, then to claim a larger lower bound.

A sound FCP can be extended by any fixed true polynomial-time-checkable axiom, so in a hypothetical P=NP contradiction one could add the correctness statement for the chosen SAT decider to remove the concern that a weak base theory cannot formalize that machine. This repair still leaves the growing-degree/one-theory problem.

New target: first formalize the fixed-k speed-up lemma with separate variables for unary axiom-instance length n, dyadic consistency cutoff N, and proof bound h(n)=n^k. Then seek a single polynomial-time theory that defeats its own FCP proof-bound degree without putting an unbounded k into the axiom predicate. A circuit/PCP encoding is only useful if its certificate length stays polynomial in the actual padded input and its exponent does not grow with k.

Primary source for the FCP and decision-exponent framework: [Joosten, Propositional Proof Systems and Fast Consistency Provers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431), especially Section 7. For the underlying proof-system equivalence, see [Cook and Reckhow (1979)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~sacook/homepage/cook_reckhow.pdf).

## Idea 29 - A self-bootstrapping fast-consistency searcher

Status: an adaptive search could discover an unknown FCP polynomial degree, but making the theory depend on that search creates a circular class-membership argument. The encoding scale matters: the search may be polynomial in a numeric cutoff n while exponential in the bit length of a dyadic numeral for n.

Assume P=NP and a fast consistency prover S. For a fixed polynomial-time theory T, an algorithm can search increasing proof-length bounds s and use the P=NP decision procedure for ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“S has an S-proof of Con_T(\underline n) of length at most s.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â The proof-existence relation is NP when s is supplied in unary. If T is consistent, the FCP property guarantees that this search stops by some polynomial p_T(n), where n is the numeric cutoff. Its total runtime is polynomial in numeric n, with a T-dependent exponent; it need not be polynomial in the bit length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(log n) of the dyadic numeral. On an axiom instance padded to length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(n), this can be polynomial in the axiom-string length, but the exponent is still unknown.

Attempt: use Kleene's recursion theorem to define a theory T whose axiom checker runs this search for proofs of Con_T(n), measures the first proof length, and sets its own diagonal cutoff just above that measured length. Under the FCP assumption, the measured length would be polynomial, so the checker appears polynomial too. A fixed-point lower-bound lemma might then say S's proof is longer than the proof that the FCP searcher just found.

The circular step remains decisive. FCP applies only to theories already known to have polynomial-time axiom recognition. The proposed T is polynomial-time only if the FCP search terminates within a fixed polynomial in the actual axiom input length for this very T. The bound supplied by FCP is conditional on T already being in the class, and its degree is unknown. A fixed clock can make the checker polynomial, but an unknown FCP degree larger than that clock can evade the diagonal. For dyadic parameters, a polynomial in numeric n is exponential in the numeral length; unary padding makes it polynomial in the padded string length but does not remove the unknown-degree circularity. Recursion-theorem self-reference gives a program code but does not select the least fixed point ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“T is polynomial because FCP applies to T.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â

Learning carried forward: keep the numeric cutoff, its numeral length, the unary padding in an axiom instance, and the proof-search witness length as separate parameters. An assumption-conditional runtime bound cannot be used as the antecedent that licenses the assumption's own theorem. To make this work, prove T's axiom checker is polynomial independently of the FCP bound, or find a theorem that explicitly supports self-referential class-membership bootstrapping.

Next test: formalize the adaptive search with explicit input lengths for both dyadic and unary encodings. Try to make its axiom checker polynomial independently of the FCP bound; if its clock grows adaptively without a uniform cap, classify the theory as recursively enumerable rather than polynomial-time.

## Idea 30 - Exponent-transfer deficit as a design test

Status: new bookkeeping language distilled from the failed diagonals; no lower-bound theorem yet.

For a proposed diagonal construction, let d be the unknown polynomial exponent of the machine, proof generator, or axiom decider being challenged. Let D(d) be the exponent cost of encoding and verifying the diagonal object in the target language, including universal simulation, tableau size, witness length, and any padding. Define the contraction deficit

    ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ(d) = d - D(d).

This is only an audit quantity, not a standard complexity measure. A fixed-point diagonal that must simulate the challenged process within its own bound needs an actual positive deficit after all encoding and clock-conversion costs. If D(d)ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥d, no exponent choice closes the self-reference. If D(d)<d for an infinite range, a real construction may be possible, provided its witnesses remain polynomial in the ordinary input length and the machine family is uniform.

Examples from this ledger: Idea 22 has a tableau degree that grows with the unknown SAT-decider exponent; Idea 26 has a predictor clock t^{a} rather than a predictor running below t; Idea 28's bounded-proof axiom checker has degree growing with the chosen proof cutoff; Idea 29 cannot know the FCP exponent without already assuming the theory is polynomial-time. These all have nonpositive deficit under the direct encodings tested so far. Idea 20 has a related additive budget: its O(log T) chain-rule loss must fit strictly below the per-block complexity gain.

Design rule: every new diagonal proposal should write its transfer map D(d), the witness-size bound, and the verifier-time bound before using fixed-point language. A promising breakthrough candidate needs to explain what causes genuine contraction (or otherwise avoids the need for it) without switching to succinct-SAT/NEXP, nonuniform advice, or an unbounded proof theory.

Next test: apply ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ(d) first to any proposed PCP, interactive-proof, compressed-proof, or alternate-language construction. Look specifically for structure in the self-referential proof that permits a short certificate, since generic long proof strings have no guaranteed compression.

## Idea 31 - PCPs compress inspection, not the proof-length exponent (2026-09-24)

Status: the generic PCP-compression route is closed. PCPs reduce how many proof bits are inspected, but standard size bounds are polynomial in the full input length being certified. They do not by themselves turn a proof of length n^k into a certificate of length n^c for a fixed c independent of k.

The current 2026 algebraic PCP preprint gives a concrete check: for graph 3-colorability on an N-size input, it constructs a static proof of size poly(N), with O(log N) random bits and O(1) queries. Its completeness is perfect and its soundness rejects every false instance/proof with positive probability. Because there are only poly(N) random strings, enumerate them all and accept only if every run accepts. This yields a deterministic polynomial-time verifier with the same static proof and perfect soundness. So for static PCPs with logarithmic randomness, probabilistic soundness is not a barrier to deterministic verification; enumeration is already polynomial.

The scale is the barrier in our application. If the object being checked is an N=n^k-bit proof or tableau, a generic PCP has length poly(N)=n^{O(k)}. Enumerating its O(log N) random bits also costs poly(N)=n^{O(k)}. Constant query complexity reduces proof access, not the size of the proof string or the exponent measured against the smaller ambient parameter n. Under the P=NP hypothesis, each fixed-k bounded-proof predicate is already in P, but its decider and computation certificate may have a degree depending on k. PCP encoding preserves that dependence rather than eliminating it.

Interactive proofs are a distinct branch. Shamir's IP=PSPACE theorem uses a randomized polynomial-time verifier and an adaptive prover; a single transcript is not a static certificate that works for every verifier random string. Enumerating polynomially many random bits takes exponential time, and fixing one response transcript does not quantify over all prover responses. Thus IP=PSPACE does not by itself yield an NP-size proof of bounded non-provability with a fixed polynomial verifier degree.

Reusable lesson: track four separate quantitiesÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Âproof length, query count, random-bit count, and the length scale relative to which the polynomial is measured. A gain in query complexity is not a gain in proof length. Randomness can be removed by enumeration only for static proofs when the number of random bits is logarithmic in the relevant input size. Any future compressed-proof proposal must give a proof of size n^c with c independent of k, a deterministic sound verifier with a fixed polynomial exponent in n, and a completeness argument for the actual bounded-consistency statement. If its real input is the n^k-bit object, or its soundness depends on unenumerated randomness, it has not paid down the exponent-transfer deficit.

Primary sources: [Amireddy et al., A Simple Algebraic Proof of the PCP Theorem (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17429), which states the polynomial proof size, logarithmic randomness, constant queries, and perfect completeness for 3-colorability; [Shamir, IP=PSPACE (1992)](https://doi.org/10.1145/146585.146609); and [Joosten, Propositional Proof Systems and Fast Consistency Provers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431) for the bounded-consistency target.

Algebraic stress test: write the bounded-proof predicate as a circuit C_n(w), where |w|=N=n^k and C_n checks whether w is a valid short S-proof. An explicit circuit has size S=poly(N)=n^{O(k)}. A sum-check for the zero count over all w uses a number of rounds tied to the number of variables in an arithmetization of C_n (at least N and typically polynomial in S); the verifier and transcript therefore remain polynomial in S, not in n with a degree independent of k. Moreover, sum-check is interactive: the prover's later messages depend on random challenges. A single path transcript does not certify all challenge paths; writing down a full response strategy can be exponentially larger in the number of rounds. Converting the explicit circuit to a PCP again gives bounds polynomial in S. This closes the direct sum-check/PCP route; it does not rule out a specialized succinct certificate for the structured Con_T(n) language.

Next test: search for a special certificate for bounded non-provability that exploits the syntactic/algebraic structure of Con_T(n), rather than applying PCP or sum-check to an explicit long tableau. First derive its language and parameters; then reject it if the certificate remains n^{O(k)}, if the verifier's exponent grows with k, or if soundness depends on an interactive response strategy that cannot be encoded in polynomial size.

## Idea 32 - The succinctness tax and a NEXP boundary (2026-09-24)

Status: a conditional complexity boundary for generic proof compression; it does not rule out a certificate specialized to bounded consistency.

Succinct 3-colorability / succinct 3-SAT takes a small circuit describing an exponentially larger instance. Succinct 3-colorability is NEXP-complete. Suppose a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier accepted a polynomial-length certificate exactly for the succinctly described unsatisfiable instances. Then coNEXP would be contained in NP. Taking complements gives NEXP contained in coNP. Since NP is contained in NEXP, and coNP is contained in coNEXP, these inclusions force NP=coNP and then NEXP=NP. The same implication holds for any coNEXP-complete succinct-unsatisfiability language.

This does not prove such compression impossible: NEXP versus NP is open, and P=NP alone neither supplies nor forbids this additional collapse. It does quantify the price of a *generic* compressor. If a proposed PCP, algebraic fingerprint, or self-reference construction gives short, sound certificates for arbitrary succinct UNSAT, it has proved a major class collapse beyond the original P=NP hypothesis. If it is meant to avoid that consequence, it must use a property specific to the bounded-consistency statements and explain why that property does not extend to arbitrary succinct SAT.

Reusable lesson: every time an exponentially long proof or circuit is replaced by a small description, explicitly name the succinct language being certified. Ask whether the proposed certificate would also certify succinct 3-SAT unsatisfiability. If yes, the claim entails NEXP=NP; if no, isolate the structural feature that blocks the reduction. This is a stronger version of Idea 30's exponent-transfer audit: it checks the *class* paid for by compression, not just the polynomial degree.

Primary source: [Chen et al., Reducing NEXP-complete problems to DQBF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.06014), which states the NEXP-completeness of succinct 3-colorability and gives an explicit reduction; see also [Papadimitriou and Yannakakis (1986), A Note on Succinct Representations of Graphs](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(86)80009-2).

Next test: for any proposed special certificate for Con_T(n), formalize its input as either an explicit n-sized statement or a succinctly specified exponentially large relation. Then test whether the proof construction extends to arbitrary succinct 3-SAT. If it does, state the NEXP=NP consequence; if it does not, identify and use the exact restricted syntactic property.

## Idea 33 - Binary cutoff versus unary witness: padding cancels (2026-09-24)

Status: padding by itself does not create an exponent advantage. This is a parameter normalization from Joosten's exact conventions, not a theorem ruling out a specialized decider whose polynomial degree beats the witness exponent.

Joosten defines Pr_S(x,ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â ) using proofs of length at most x, writes the parameter with an efficient dyadic numeral \underline{x}, and defines Con_T(\underline{x}) accordingly. The formula has length ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(log x), but the FCP guarantee is a polynomial in the numeric cutoff x. A predicate asserting an S-proof of length x^k is not automatically NP in the dyadic formula length: its witness is exponentially long in log x. P=NP only applies after the actual input and witness are polynomially related.

Unary padding restores that relation. Let L(n) be the length of the unary-padded fixed-point instance ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´_n, and suppose its S-proof cutoff is h(n)=L(n)^c. The bounded-proof relation is then in NP as a function of L(n), so P=NP can make the corresponding axiomhood test polynomial-time for fixed c. But a direct Joosten-style speed-up must also put ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´_n, or a proof of it, into the T-derivation. A padding argument is not a contraction unless its cost vanishes after reparameterizing by the actual T-proof and consistency cutoffs.

Primary source: [Joosten, Propositional Proof Systems and Fast Consistency Provers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431), Definition 1.1 and Section 6 (especially the efficient dyadic numeral convention and the RE speed-up lemma).

## Idea 34 - Circuit abbreviations and the explicit-output boundary (2026-09-24)

Status: ordinary abbreviations do not yet break Idea 33's scale equation. Circuit syntax remains a possible research direction only if it yields a genuinely shorter proof of the relevant consistency implication.

Cook-Reckhow proof systems are polynomial-time maps from proof strings to tautology strings. A machine running in time poly(|ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬|) cannot output an explicit theorem longer than poly(|ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬|); Joosten's Lemma 2.5 even gives an equivalent proof system whose output tautology is no longer than its proof. Extended Frege and Circuit Frege permit extension variables or circuit-DAG lines and can share repeated subexpressions, but the proof and circuit descriptions are still measured by their encoded gate/symbol counts. Polynomial output compression can change exponents, so it must be charged explicitly; it does not produce an arbitrarily long explicit theorem from a logarithmic proof.

There are two distinct cases. If a circuit of size M is simply a DAG representation of a Boolean function on M inputs, its tautology predicate has an M-bit counterexample witness and is in coNP; circuit sharing by itself does not create an NEXP-sized assignment space. If a small generator describes an exponentially larger formula with exponentially many indexed variables or constraints, tautology can move to coNEXP, and a generic polynomial certificate for it triggers Idea 32's NEXP=NP consequence. Do not apply that collapse argument to ordinary circuit syntax without proving that the exponentially large universe is actually present.

Applied to the unary-padded fixed point, suppose a compressed code has length M and expands to a formula of length LÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¤M^e. If the P=NP bounded-proof decider runs in time L^{d_k} on explicit instances, running it on the compressed code after expansion costs M^{e d_k}; the lower-bound witness h=L^k becomes M^{e k}. The common expansion factor e cancels in the comparison, and the remaining question is whether the special bounded-proof decider has d_k<k by a useful margin or can avoid expansion altogether. For an unlikely-FCP-style uniform upper bound with degree q in n^{DecExp(T)}, the requirement is stronger: the diagonal exponent k must beat q times the theory's decision exponent d_k (after the shared e factor is cancelled). A generic SAT reduction gives d_k=O(k), which provides no such contraction. A proof system with ordinary explicit formula lines instead has MÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â°Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¥L, returning to Idea 33. If the code specifies exponentially many proof positions, analyze the succinct-language boundary in Idea 32.

Specific test on the numeral: a unary Peano numeral S^n(0) is a chain with n distinct nested subterms, so an ordinary DAG has ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(n) gates; extension variables do not share repeated subexpressions that are not present. The dyadic numeral is already ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(log n) symbols, but then an n^k proof witness is exponential in that input length. The two standard numeral encodings therefore reproduce Idea 33's tradeoff. A new compressed numeral operator would have to state how its value and bounded-proof predicate are verified within the claimed time.

Current primary sources: [Cook and Reckhow (1979)](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~sacook/homepage/cook_reckhow.pdf) define polynomial-time propositional proof systems; [Joosten (2006), Lemma 2.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431) gives an equivalent system with output length at most proof length; [KrajÃƒÆ’Ã†â€™Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â­ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Âek (2026), Extended Frege proofs, circuits and rewriting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13367) studies the relation between EF/CF proofs and circuit representations.

Next test: define one precise compressed syntax for ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â´_n and write its semantics, circuit size M(n), proof-checking time, axiom-decision time, and Con_T cutoff separately. Reject it if it expands in polynomial time to length L(n) with M(n) only polynomially related to L(n), or if verifying it requires the exponential universe that changes the language to a succinct NEXP-level problem.

## Idea 37 - Relative consistency, slow clocks, and selector proofs (2026-09-24)

Status: a literature-grounded route with a clear open gap. Recent proof theory makes the foundational version of the project more precise: the relevant resource is whether a theory can efficiently simulate its extension by a true sentence, and whether weak arithmetic can certify the relative consistency needed for that simulation.

Freund and Pakhomov show that PA has polynomial-size proofs of the finite consistency of PA extended by *slow* consistency, Con*(PA), while the analogous statement with ordinary Con(PA) is false by their Proposition 3.7. Their construction uses ordinal analysis and a slow enumeration tied to the fast-growing hierarchy. This is a useful warning: adding a strong-looking true reflection principle does not by itself force long finite-consistency proofs; the enumeration clock and proof system matter. PA's proof-theoretic strength does not make a slow axiom predicate polynomial-time.

Monroe's July 2026 revision studies polynomial simulation of S+ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â  by a sound arithmetic theory S with polynomial-time decidable axioms. Failure, part B: to use Monroe's certification theorem, one can add the true uniform simulation sentence for this fixed U as an axiom to S; then (S+Sim_U)+Con_S proves ÃƒÆ’Ã‚ÂÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â _x. But the resulting theory contains a sentence describing U and therefore x. Chaitin's incompleteness constant depends on the theory's description; it may grow with |x|. Applying the argument separately to each random x therefore gives no single fixed Chaitin bound that the chosen x exceeds. The construction needs one fixed theory to certify a uniform family of simulations for strings of unbounded complexity, while the FCP statement supplies only theory-by-theory bounds and certificates.

What survives: the P=NP proof search does produce a polynomial-time *per-input* selector when the input is an explicit derivation d of length n: it can search for the FCP proof at cutoff n and use that proof to derive that d is not a contradiction proof. However, turning these selected outputs into one correctness theorem inside a fixed theory again requires a uniform certificate for all inputs. This is the selector-proof distinction in Idea 37, now with the explicit obstruction identified: the selector's bound/certificate may depend on the target extension, and the target extension contains x.

Learning carried forward: keep three notions separateÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â(i) each cutoff has some short proof, (ii) a polynomial-time algorithm finds one when the cutoff is unary, and (iii) a fixed weak theory proves that the algorithm succeeds uniformly on binary-coded cutoffs. Neither P=NP nor an FCP currently supplies (iii) at the required scale. A viable Chaitin route must make the theory and its uniformity certificate independent of the random string while still forcing it to prove that string's randomness.

Sources: [Joosten, Definition 1.1 and Section 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431); [Monroe, Theorem 6.3 and Lemma 6.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27787); [Grobner, selector proofs and uniformity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00266).

Next test: try to construct one fixed, polynomial-time-recognizable selector theory whose proof outputs certify finite consistency for a parameterized family U_x, with code and exponent independent of x. Check whether the axiom encoding can express U_x without paying ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€¹Ã…â€œ(|x|) in the Chaitin constant, and whether the selector correctness proof is formalizable in EA/SÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…Â¡ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…Â¡ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¹ without assuming the very uniform simulation being derived.

## Idea 39 - Random extensions expose an uncertified-simulation gap (2026-09-24)

Status: verified corollary of known results; not a new theorem and not a complexity separation.

Let S be a sound fast consistency prover (FCP) extending EA and S_2^1. For every fixed consistent polynomial-time theory T, the FCP property gives some polynomial p_T such that S has proofs of Con_T(n) of size at most p_T(n). In particular, for each true Kolmogorov-randomness axiom x in R, the target U_x = S + (x in R) is consistent and polynomial-time axiomatized, so S externally polynomially simulates U_x.

Monroe's Theorem 6.9 already proves the certification barrier: for fixed sound S and any fixed sound computably axiomatized B extending EA, only finitely many x in R have B-proofs of any fixed-polynomial uniform simulation sentence for S versus U_x. Taking B = S, all but finitely many true random axioms therefore give an external polynomial simulation that S itself cannot certify. Taking B = S + Con_S gives the same conclusion for that stronger fixed theory. This is stronger and cleaner than the initial Chaitin-only derivation. A sound FCP of this kind is conditional: an optimal propositional proof system suffices, and NP = coNP is a stronger sufficient assumption; neither is known to hold.

Learning carried forward: the exact gap is between (a) for each fixed target, existence of a polynomial-length proof family, and (b) a fixed theory proving a uniform sentence that certifies that family. Monroe's theorem rules out (b) for almost every random extension while leaving (a) untouched. This is a consistency check on the definitions, not evidence for P != NP. Do not turn failure of internal certification into an external proof-size lower bound.

Sources: [Joosten, Theorem 3.1 and Sections 1, 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431); [Monroe, Theorems 6.3 and 6.9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27787).

## Idea 40 - Measure the index cost of external simulation

Status: precise research question; no lower bound or uniformization theorem yet.

For a fixed sound FCP S, define d_S(x) as the least exponent e for which there is a constant C_x with S-proofs of Con_{U_x}(n) of size at most C_x(n+1)^e for every n. FCP guarantees d_S(x) < infinity separately for each fixed x. It does not give one polynomial-time proof generator, one exponent for all x, or an S-proof of the uniform family statement.

The construction audit is explicit. Joosten fixes a target theory T and builds a separate proof system Q_T by adjoining to an optimal proof system P the propositional translations of the finite-consistency family for T. P's optimality supplies a polynomial proof-size simulation for this one fixed Q_T. Joosten's translation bound tracks the target axiom-decision exponent, but the simulation polynomial for Q_T has no stated bound in terms of the code of T. For U_x, the proof system itself changes with x, so the argument gives no computable estimate for d_S(x) from |x|. This is the gap between ordinary FCP and Joosten's stronger unlikely-FCP condition, whose uniform bound over all polynomial-time theories is equivalent to NP = coNP.

Learning carried forward: separately track target-description length |x|, axiom-decision exponent, polynomial degree d_S(x), leading constant C_x, and whether a weak theory proves correctness uniformly. A claimed contradiction must use a theorem connecting an external proof-size quantity to a complexity lower bound; Chaitin incompleteness alone constrains provability. Monroe's certification barrier also leaves d_S(x) unrestricted.

The first attempt to package all U_x into one Q_* fails: Q_* would have to output a tautology for every input x, but the finite-consistency formula for U_x is eventually false when x is not random. Testing a computable family of extensions that are all known consistent leads to Idea 42.

Sources: [Joosten, Definition 4.5 and Theorem 4.8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431); [Monroe, Theorem 6.9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27787).

## Idea 41 - Can a single sound proof system package all random extensions?

Status: attempted uniformization; blocked by soundness and the nondecidability of the randomness predicate.

A tempting move is to replace the separate Joosten systems Q_x used for each fixed target U_x by one system Q_* that, on input (x,n), outputs the propositional translation of Con_{U_x}(n). If Q_* were a sound proof system with polynomially sized descriptions uniform in |x|+n, optimality would yield a single simulation polynomial and might bound the degrees d_S(x) uniformly.

The construction fails at soundness: Con_{U_x}(n) is a tautology only when x in R (at least once n is large enough to detect any contradiction), while x in R is not decidable in polynomial time. Mapping nonrandom x to a default tautology requires recognizing nonrandomness, which is only semidecidable. Restricting the system's inputs to certified random x also fails because randomness has no finite certificate. Replacing true randomness by a bounded no-short-description test makes membership decidable only with a time bound that grows with the cutoff; the resulting target theory changes with n, so it no longer witnesses a single FCP simulation problem.

Learning carried forward: uniformizing a family of target-dependent reductions requires a single sound proof system, not merely a uniform formula generator. The truth of each output must be guaranteed for every input to that system. Future packaging attempts must identify a decidable index domain on which every target extension is known consistent, or find a different source of true hard information with efficiently recognizable indices.

Next test: Idea 42 replaces the random promise with a uniformly indexed, externally consistent tower. Reject the tower if its theory codes grow too quickly for one polynomial-time proof-system presentation.

Sources: [Joosten, Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 4.8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431); [Monroe, Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 6.9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27787).

## Idea 42 - Package a computable tower of true consistency axioms

Status: conditional packaging lead; uniform coding lemma and any P-versus-NP payoff remain unproved.

Assume an optimal propositional proof system P exists and take its sound FCP construction S = S_2^1 + RFN(P), extended by EA. Define a tower T_0 = S and T_{i+1} = T_i + Con_{T_i}. By external induction, every T_i is sound: if T_i is sound, Con_{T_i} is true, so adjoining it preserves soundness. Set U_i = S + Con_{T_i}; each U_i is consistent. Unlike the random-axiom family U_x, consistency is guaranteed for every index i by one metatheoretic induction.

Candidate uniformization: define one proof system Q_* extending P with the propositional translations of Con_{U_i}(n) for all i,n. Encode i in unary in the Q_* input. A uniform self-referential proof predicate for the tower should let the axiom checker for T_i recognize S-axioms and the earlier consistency sentences in time polynomial in i plus the candidate proof length; the resulting formula and translation sizes should then be polynomial in i+n. Since every U_i is consistent, every designated output of Q_* is a tautology, so Q_* is sound. Optimality of P would give one polynomial proof-size bound for all designated Q_* proofs. Reflection in S would then give S-proofs of Con_{U_i}(n) with a single polynomial bound in i+n. This is a conditional external uniform bound across the tower, stronger than applying FCP separately to each fixed i.

Envelope lemma (proved): suppose one fixed consistent polynomial-time theory T contains each U_i through proof translations that are polynomial in the unary index i and proof length, with uniformly generated EA proofs of the finite-consistency implications of size polynomial in i+n. If S is an EA-extending FCP, it has S-proofs of Con_T(q(i+n)) of size polynomial in q(i+n); EA proves Con_T(q(i+n)) -> Con_{U_i}(n). Appending that uniform implication proof gives S-proofs of Con_{U_i}(n) bounded by one polynomial in i+n. This turns per-target FCP into a uniform bound for any such family.

A candidate envelope for the tower is T_infinity = S + {Con_{T_i} : i is a natural number}. If the uniform fixed-point coding makes T_infinity polynomial-time axiomatized, metatheoretic induction makes it sound, and every U_i is a subtheory. FCP applied once to T_infinity then gives the common polynomial bound via the envelope lemma. This is not specific to the tower. Joosten already observes that an optimal proof system gives polynomially bounded proofs for every polynomial-time recognizable sequence of tautologies, which is the propositional counterpart of this packaging idea.

Proof obligations: implement the fixed-point proof predicate without expanding T_i's code exponentially; prove the tower and T_infinity axiom checkers are polynomial time with i encoded in unary; verify the translated finite-consistency formulas are tautologies for all i,n; and trace the resulting proof-size polynomial through RFN(P) or the envelope lemma. Do not claim a uniform proof-finding algorithm or an S-proof of its correctness: weak optimality gives short proofs, not necessarily an efficient translator or an internally certified family.

First-stage audit: U_0 = S + Con_S. Showing that S has no polynomial-size proofs of Con_{U_0}(n) is exactly the Pudlak finite-consistency conjecture in this setting, already enough to refute FCP. The higher tower adds value only if a varying-index lower bound is stronger than this fixed-stage conjecture. Monroe's certification theorem rules out an internal simulation certificate at U_0 but supplies no external proof-size lower bound.

Learning carried forward: replacing an uncomputable promise with a computable index domain can make one sound proof system possible, but it may still provide only conditional proof-length uniformity. The envelope lemma is a valid conditional consequence of FCP, not a P-versus-NP result. The candidate does not yet conflict with incompleteness and does not imply P = NP or P != NP. The literature check found no generalized external lower bound for this tower.

Next test: try a diagonal choice i = i(n) and determine whether the growing consistency rank forces a lower bound not reducible to the fixed U_0 Pudlak conjecture. If the proof only restates that conjecture, close the tower route as repackaging rather than a breakthrough.

Sources: [Joosten, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 4.8, and Observation 7.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05431); [Monroe, Theorems 6.3 and 6.7](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27787); [Freund-Pakhomov, Short Proofs for Slow Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.03251).

## Idea 43 - Build a recursive jump for tautology proof systems

Status: direct P-versus-NP target; the construction remains open and known oracle barriers block relativizing approaches.

A recursive jump operator J would take any code for a Cook-Reckhow proof system P and output a code for another sound proof system Q such that P does not polynomially simulate Q. If such a J exists for TAUT, then TAUT has no optimal proof system. Since NP = coNP implies a polynomially bounded, hence optimal, proof system, J would imply NP != coNP and therefore P != NP. This makes the target a precise alternative to trying to invent a hard tautology family for each proof system separately.

Egidy's 2026 ICALP paper gives a sharp barrier: there is an oracle relative to which PH is infinite, TAUT has no optimal proof systems, and TAUT has no recursive jump operators. Therefore a proof that non-optimality implies a recursive jump cannot relativize, even assuming PH is infinite. The oracle construction uses Kleene fixed points: a witness system evaluates the proposed jump on its own code, then oracle-controlled permissions let it either simulate the alleged stronger output or fall back to a baseline system while preserving soundness. The adjustable oracle is the resource that has no known unrelativized replacement.

Khaniki's 2024 candidate builds an interactive, sum-check-based implicit proof system [[IP,P]] from P. It simulates P, but proving strict improvement needs a hard tautology/proof-complexity generator. The paper's Theorem 5.11 gives equivalent finite-consistency lower-bound formulations of an efficient jump: one form asks for a single true finite theory T such that every finite S has no polynomial-size S-proofs of the finite consistency of T + Con_S. Another form restricts to S that prove T and asks for a Pudlak-style lower bound for Con_{S+Con_S}. Conjecture 5.1 remains that a partial recursive jump exists. This refines Idea 31: generic sum-check over an n^k-size proof keeps n^{O(k)} costs, while the interactive candidate also needs a way to certify all adaptive verifier challenges as a deterministic Cook-Reckhow system. IP=PSPACE alone does not provide that conversion.

Random-anchor stress test: take T to contain one fixed true axiom x in R. Chaitin's theorem can make x unprovable in a chosen fixed base, but Theorem 5.11 quantifies over every finite S (or every S proving T). Chaitin gives no lower bound on S-proofs of Con_{S+Con_S}(n), and an S that includes x in R defeats the intended non-provability premise. Also, setting S=T in the theorem's all-S-proving-T clause already requires the Pudlak lower bound for T+Con_T. So Idea 39 does not supply the jump condition; proving it needs new finite-consistency proof-size lower bounds, beyond Chaitin non-provability.

Learning carried forward: the missing object is not merely a self-referential sentence or a randomized protocol; it is a uniform construction that (i) outputs a sound Cook-Reckhow system for every valid input proof system and (ii) proves a super-polynomial separation from that input system. Oracle bits currently solve the soundness-control problem only relativistically. A fixed Chaitin sentence cannot replace the universal quantifier over theories in the finite-consistency characterization.

Audit result: T = Con_{S0} and every fixed consistency-tower stage still require the Pudlak-style lower bound when S is specialized to that candidate. A fixed randomness axiom supplies Chaitin non-provability in selected bases but not the required external finite-consistency proof-size bound. The substitutions expose the target but do not meet KhanikiÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s all-theory condition. Idea 44 is the next attempt to bridge that gap with moving, time-bounded incompressibility.

Sources: [Egidy, Recursive Jump Operators and Optimal Proof Systems, ICALP 2026](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol374/icalp2026/html/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.88/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.88.html); [Khaniki, Jump Operators, Interactive Proofs and Proof Complexity Generators, FOCS 2024](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS61266.2024.00044).

## Idea 44 - A moving Chaitin window for finite consistency

Status: a new scale-coupling test; no proof-size lower bound obtained. The motivation is to replace one fixed unprovable randomness axiom by a sequence of time-bounded incompressibility claims whose witness scale moves with the finite-consistency cutoff.

Candidate construction: for a description s of a string y, a time limit t, and threshold m, let H(s,t,m) assert that no program of length below m outputs y within t steps. Consider T = S + H(s,t,m). If H is false, a short program and its computation trace yield a concrete contradiction in T. Let B(s,t,m) be the length of this derivation. For N at least B, weak arithmetic can formalize Con_T(N) -> H(s,t,m); hence an S-proof of Con_T(N) gives an S-proof of H. The hoped-for next step is to turn such a proof into a program that outputs y within t, contradicting H when the proof is shorter than m.

Scale audit: when y is explicit and t is at least the time needed to print y, the literal-print program gives K^t(y) <= |y| + O(1), so a nonvacuous threshold has m <= |y| + O(1). The axiom code and a direct contradiction derivation then cost at least order |y|; a full one-tape computation tableau can cost O(t^2). Under this attempted extraction, the available information scale is at most linear in N; this is not itself a formal proof-length lower bound. If t is too small to print y, the time cutoff itself can make the assertion trivially true and supplies no useful information lower bound. If y is represented succinctly by s, its ordinary description is short, and the only possible separation is runtime: s must take longer than t to produce y. Then a proof cannot be converted into a t-time description merely by printing s. Moreover, a generic counterexample programÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s t-step trace may make B grow with t, erasing the hoped-for gap. No general succinct-trace theorem supplies the missing compression, and applying one to arbitrary computations would risk collapsing standard time and proof-complexity distinctions.

Concrete diagonal-generator test: for fixed c>0, simulate every program p of length below n-c for n steps and let y_n be the first n-bit string not output by any of them. Fewer than 2^{n-c} programs are simulated and each outputs at most one string, so y_n exists and K^n(y_n) >= n-c. A short generator can compute y_n, but only after about nÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â·2^n simulation steps. If y_n is written explicitly into H, the theory description and any proof referring to that axiom already carry ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©(n) bits; a counterexample computation can be recorded with an O(n^2) one-tape tableau, so the useful consistency cutoff is at least that large. This gives no super-polynomial proof-size separation. If y_n is replaced by its short generator to keep the theory description small, deciding the axiom requires the exponential search, so the theory is not polynomial-time axiomatized. The explicit diagonal is a valid source of moving time-bounded randomness, but it misses both the proof-size scale and uniformity requirements.
Learning carried forward: ChaitinÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s argument controls what a fixed sound theory can prove from the code length of a theorem; it does not automatically turn an external short proof of a moving bounded statement into a short description at the relevant runtime. Every candidate must simultaneously satisfy N >= B(s,t,m), proof length L(N) < m, and a uniform extraction of y from the proof in at most t steps. Explicit y makes m <= O(N); succinct y preserves information only if the proof-to-output runtime can beat t. This is a sharper version of the earlier lesson that non-provability and finite-consistency proof-size lower bounds are different resources.

Next test: try one highly structured slow computation whose long trace has a short arithmetic invariant, and check whether that invariant remains valid for every competing short compressor. State exact bounds B, N, L, m, and extraction time before claiming a separation. Stop the route if the argument needs succinct verification of arbitrary computations or only recovers a linear lower bound.

Literature check: MonroeÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s 2026 paper states that unconditional lower bounds S not-proves^{n^O(1)} Con_{S+phi}(n) are unknown for sound S extending S2^1, and that such a bound would rule out optimal proof systems. Its Higher Relative Consistency and Kolmogorov Hardness principles are conjectural; the proven direction is that a weak-base relative-consistency implication gives efficient simulation. This validates the gap being targeted, but does not establish the moving-window candidate.

Sources: [Monroe, Toward a Characterization of Simulation Between Arithmetic Theories, ECCC TR26-062 (revised July 2026)](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/062/); [Monroe, Hardness as an Information Constraint (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04257).

## Idea 45 - A self-referential tautology that denies its short proofs

Status: the fixed-point construction appears to give sound tautologies, but the size accounting only yields a polynomially compatible lower bound. No proof-system jump follows.

Candidate: if a polynomial-size syntactic fixed point can be built, define a propositional formula F_{P,n} whose assignments encode candidate P-proofs of length below n and whose truth condition says that the assigned string is not a P-proof of F_{P,n}. If P is sound, F_{P,n} must be a tautology: an assignment falsifying it would encode a valid P-proof of a nontautology. By construction P has no proof of F_{P,n} shorter than n. A candidate system Q would output F_{P,n} from the code of P and n. The exact self-referential encoding and its size are obligations, not established here. The direct ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©(n) count also assumes the formula really reads all n candidate bits; compressing or bypassing that read is the unresolved possibility being tested.

Stress test: the formula has to represent every candidate proof string of length n and run PÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s polynomial-time proof checker on it. The direct formula encoding reads n candidate bits and therefore costs ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©(n) symbols; its generic construction has polynomial size in n. A special checker invariant that bypasses those reads is exactly the open compression target. Even with a circuit representation, conversion to a standard formula preserves polynomial size but not a polylogarithmic one. Since QÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s proof must let its polynomial-time decoder print F_{P,n}, its proof length is polynomially related to |F_{P,n}|. Thus the lower bound n for P is still at most polynomial in QÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s proof size, exactly what p-simulation allows. Asking for a polylogarithmic-size output would require a succinct proof-string domain or exponentially succinct formula semantics; then the verifier no longer checks an ordinary Cook-Reckhow proof system in polynomial time. The fixed point secures semantic soundness but does not compress the diagonalized search. There is also an oracle filter: a transformation using only the input proof-system code and its verifier would relativize, while Egidy constructs an oracle world with no recursive jump. Therefore any successful variant must identify a genuinely non-relativizing ingredient.

Learning carried forward: self-reference can force ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“no short P-proofÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â once the output is known to be a tautology, but the tautology itself must encode the whole bounded search. Soundness is supplied by the assumption that P is a valid proof system; separation requires an output-size saving that the bounded search encoding consumes. This matches the oracle-jump obstacle in Idea 43: the hard part is an efficient, uniformly sound output whose proof is polynomially shorter in a way P cannot simulate.

Next test: attempt to replace explicit proof-string enumeration by a restricted arithmetic invariant of PÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s checker, then measure whether the invariant gives a formula of size o(n^ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Âµ) for every ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Âµ while retaining a standard polynomial-time Cook-Reckhow decoder. If it only compresses a general P-proof search, reject it as succinct semantics or a hidden complexity collapse.

Sources: [Khaniki, Jump Operators, Interactive Proofs and Proof Complexity Generators, FOCS 2024](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS61266.2024.00044); [Egidy, Recursive Jump Operators and Optimal Proof Systems, ICALP 2026](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol374/icalp2026/html/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.88/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.88.html).

## Idea 46 - Entropy amplification from demi-bits to hard tautologies

Status: a recent, literature-grounded conditional route with a proven amplification theorem; its necessary hardness premise remains unconstructed. This is a more precise bridge from average-case range hardness to the proof-system jump target in Idea 43.

New result audited: Li, Ren, and ZhongÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s September 19, 2026 preprint proves that a demi-bits generator against a well-behaved proof system contains many proof-complexity generators. In the constant-density case, if G:{0,1}^n -> {0,1}^{20n} is demi-bits-hard for P, a uniformly random projection onto 2n output coordinates is a PGC with constant probability. The proof uses PajorÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¾Ã‚Â¢s strengthening of SauerÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œShelah: a large hard-output set shatters a random coordinate set, so every projected target inherits a hard preimage. The projection itself adds no circuit complexity. The paper also gives a zero-error disperser/hash version for very weak hardness: if G is c n 2^n-weakly demi-bits-hard, with output length at least 2n, then a nonuniform PGC family secure against every uniform proof system follows (Corollary 4.9).

Conditional consequence checked: a single PGC family secure against every uniform proof system rules out a polynomially bounded CookÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œReckhow system. If NP=coNP, such a system exists and gives polynomial proofs for every tautology, including the out-of-range formulas of the PGC. Hence the barely-nontrivial demi-bits premise would imply NP!=coNP and therefore P!=NP. This is a genuine conditional route, not a proof: the preprint does not construct the required demi-bits generator unconditionally. Its ITCS predecessor shows demi-bits assumptions imply SearchNP-hard range avoidance, also a complexity-theoretic hardness premise.

Finite-consistency encoding attempt: fix a sound finite theory T and a cutoff k. Define G on seeds (p,z), where p is a k-bit candidate T-proof of contradiction and z is an r-bit label. If p is a valid contradiction proof, output the target string y_z=(z,1^{k+1}); otherwise output a default string. The output has k+r+1 bits versus k+r input bits. For every z, y_z is in Range(G) exactly when T has a contradiction proof within the cutoff. Thus, if T is consistent, each avoidance formula for y_z expresses Con_T(k). This is an exact polynomial-time encoding, but it fails the weak demi-bits threshold: there are only 2^r=2^{d-k} such nontrivial targets for seed length d=k+r, while Corollary 4.9 needs c d 2^d hard strings. The other non-range outputs are structurally obvious and have short proofs. Padding one consistency statement therefore cannot supply the required multiplicity. Exact-replica lemma: if every target label y in a set Y satisfies y not-in Range(G) iff Con_T(k), then |Y| <= 2^d for G:{0,1}^d -> {0,1}^N. If T has a contradiction proof below k, every avoidance statement is false, so every y in Y must belong to Range(G), whose size is at most 2^d. Thus the c d 2^d threshold requires many genuinely different hard statements, not multiple encodings of one Con_T(k).

Control tests: padded identity and any injective linear map fail immediately. For a full-rank linear map A, Gaussian elimination finds a separating parity check q for every y outside Im(A); the short certificate q lets an NP adversary prove all true avoidance statements. These maps achieve only the unavoidable 2^n hard false statements from their range, not the required extra true hard outputs.

Learning carried forward: the 2026 combinatorial theorem is a hardness amplifier, not a hardness source. It converts many hard outputs into a generator whose every output-avoidance statement is hard, but its premise already requires more than range-size counting. Our fixed-axiom and single-consistency ideas yield isolated or repeated statements; the near-trivial threshold needs at least c n 2^n hard outputs, including a large family of true statements that are not easy for any NP/poly adversary. Repetition by labels cannot pass the seed-count barrier, and linear algebra makes simple structured ranges easy to avoid.

Indexed-family test result: let z have a bits, let a candidate refutation p have k bits, and let q bits label repeated variants. A direct witness-triggered generator needs seeds (z,p,v) of length d=a+k+q and can designate at most 2^(a+q)=2^(d-k) target strings. The copies for fixed z all express the same Con_{T_z}(k); varying v consumes seed bits and does not add multiplicity beyond the seed count. More generally, every distinct designated target that must enter Range(G) when its encoded witness is supplied needs at least one distinct seed, so this proof-search mechanism cannot furnish more than 2^d such targets. This falls short of the c d 2^d threshold even before proving any of the true consistency statements hard against NP/poly. It is a construction-specific counting barrier, not a theorem that independent true hard instances cannot exist.

Learning carried forward: do not treat a large output alphabet as a source of many witnesses. For any proposed range encoding, distinguish targets whose truth follows from a shared witness predicate from independently true targets; count distinct seed preimages and charge all index, witness, and variant bits. Escaping the bound requires a different route to hard true nonrange statements, not relabeling proof searches.

Next test: Idea 47 tests direct self-referential proof diagonalization. Use a recursion-theorem fixed point so that a generator outputs y if a seed contains a short proof of y not-in Range(G). Check whether the resulting lower bound exceeds the seed length after accounting for output stretch and the proof system's polynomial proof bound.

Sources: [Li, Ren, and Zhong, Many Proof Complexity Generators Inside One Demi-Bits Generator (submitted September 19, 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23228); [Ren, Wang, and Zhong, Hardness of Range Avoidance and Proof Complexity Generators from Demi-Bits, ITCS 2026](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.111).

## Idea 47 - Self-referential proof-trigger diagonalization

Status: direct diagonal construction rules out short proofs for one tailored range-avoidance tautology; it does not reach superpolynomial proof length. Replacing the explicit short-proof seed by a P=NP proof-search call exposes a self-referential polynomial-exponent loop, not a completed contradiction.

Candidate: fix a Cook-Reckhow proof system P and a seed length d. By a recursion-theorem fixed point, define a generator G whose seed contains a candidate P-proof pi and whose output is a designated string y exactly when pi verifies the formula tau_y(G) asserting y not-in Range(G); all other seeds map to a default string. Choose the seed layout so pi has at most d-O(1) bits. The fixed point embeds G and y into the verifier being checked. If a valid pi existed, that same seed would put y in Range(G), making tau_y(G) false, contrary to soundness of P. Therefore y is outside the range, tau_y(G) is true, and P has no proof of it within the seed's proof-length budget.

Size audit: the argument excludes proofs only up to the number of bits that G can read from a seed, at most d-O(1). A polynomial-time generator has output length N bounded by poly(d), and a standard range-avoidance formula for its circuit has length M=poly(d) (including the fixed-point description overhead). The obtained lower bound is therefore at most linear in d and hence polynomial in M. For a proposed p-boundedness contradiction with proof bound M^e, the seed would need room for M^e proof bits while still satisfying N>d and M=poly(N); for e>0 this cannot be achieved by this direct construction. A succinct encoding of pi would require the generator to verify a potentially much longer proof from a short seed, which changes the verification model unless a separate polynomial-time decompression theorem is supplied.

Scope check: this can diagonalize against one fixed P with a P-dependent generator. It does not give one family secure against all uniform proof systems, and it does not contradict completeness of P: completeness supplies a proof of the true tau_y(G), but this construction only forces that proof to exceed the seed-sized cutoff. The step ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“unprovable within d bitsÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â must not be inflated into ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“superpolynomially hard.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â

Longer-proof variant under P=NP: try to avoid storing pi in the seed by having G decide whether a P-proof of tau_y(G) of length at most B exists, for B polynomial in the formula size. The decision predicate is in NP, so P=NP appears to make this check polynomial. The circular resource accounting remains: if G runs in time n^a, its explicit n-input circuit and the range-avoidance formula have size n^{O(a)}; checking proofs up to a polynomial B in that formula size via the assumed NP=P algorithm generally takes n^{O(a e b)}, where e is the proof-bound degree and b is the decision algorithm's polynomial exponent. That is polynomial in n for a fixed formula, but it changes the exponent of G, which then enlarges its own circuit and formula again. The direct argument supplies no finite uniform exponent closing this loop. A near-linear decision algorithm plus sufficiently tight formula encoding might change the inequality, but P=NP alone gives no such exponent bound. This pinpoints the required result: a self-reference-aware time/encoding estimate with a strict contraction, not merely ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“SAT is in P.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â

Learning carried forward: self-reference can turn a candidate proof into a contradiction only when the candidate proof is explicitly readable by the generator. The input/output length gap then caps the direct lower bound at the seed length. Any stronger diagonal route must identify a rigorously polynomial-time way to check a proof whose effective length is superpolynomial in the seed, or derive a new structural invariant that rules out proofs without reading them. Neither has been found here.

Next test: search the ledger's checker-invariant and proof-DAG compression ideas for an invariant that forbids a P-proof of tau_y(G) without placing that proof inside G's seed; in parallel, quantify whether any known proof-search or SAT encoding can make the longer-proof variant's exponent map a -> a' satisfy a'<a. Keep ordinary Cook-Reckhow soundness, completeness, and polynomial verifier time explicit; reject any proposal whose ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“compressed proofÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â merely hides an exponentially long proof or changes the verifier class.

Sources: [Kleene recursion theorem (self-reference mechanism)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/recursive-functions/); [Cook and Reckhow, The Relative Efficiency of Propositional Proof Systems](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3975(79)90036-5).

## Idea 48 - Make the range hit every feasible infinite NP set

Status: a strong-generator reformulation gives a cleaner target and rules out the indexed-consistency construction as a universal generator. The unconditional construction remains open.

Reframing from Krajicek: for a uniform polynomial-time generator g stretching n-bit inputs to n+1 bits, the conjecture that g is hard for every uniform propositional proof system is equivalent to Range(g) intersecting every infinite NP set; equivalently, the complement of Range(g) is NP-immune. This is a conjecture about one universal hitting generator, not a consequence of NP != coNP. Krajicek proves a restricted result under hypothesis H: there is one constant d such that every P language has circuits of size O(n^d). Under H, the truth-table gadget generator hits every feasibly infinite NP set, where feasible infinitude means that a polynomial-time procedure can produce arbitrarily large members. The paper lists P != NP as a consequence of H. The extension from feasible infinitude to arbitrary infinite NP sets remains open.

Stress test on Idea 46: fix one consistent T and cutoff k, and let r vary. The earlier uniform map has seed length d=k+r and designated targets y_{r,z}=(z,1^{k+1}) for every r-bit z. These targets are polynomial-time enumerable by output length, and each stays outside the corresponding Range(G_{k+r}). Their union is an infinite P set disjoint from the generator family's range, so this map cannot be a strong universal proof-complexity generator, regardless of whether its individual avoidance formulas are hard. It does not by itself rule out using G as a demi-bits source followed by a hash or projection, because the derived generator has a different range; the required weak-hardness premise is still missing.

New design constraint: a strong generator cannot publish an efficiently enumerable infinite list of its own missing strings. A successful construction must make the missing set NP-immune, so every infinite NP familyÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Âincluding every polynomial-time selector sequenceÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Âeventually hits the range. This suggests connecting time-bounded incompressibility and the project's first-missing-string constructions to universal hitting, but Idea 44's exhaustive first-missing construction has exponential generation cost. The remaining opportunity is a structured incompressibility measure whose long strings can be generated in polynomial time without yielding an NP witness sequence disjoint from the range.

Literature stress test: Krajicek also notes that known time-bounded Kolmogorov-complexity results suggest proving useful stretch bounds for this route may already require superpolynomial lower bounds for uniform or nonuniform computation. His Problem 5.2 asks whether every infinite NP set contains a string w with Kt(w)<|w|; the paper shows an affirmative answer would imply NP is a proper subclass of EXP, which by itself does not separate P from NP. Thus ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“choose the first string with high K^tÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â is not an independent escape hatch: absent a new selector or weak-arithmetic invariant, it relocates the lower-bound problem into the complexity of finding that string.

Learning carried forward: count hard targets only for demi-bits amplification; for a universal generator, also audit whether the targets form a feasible infinite NP set. More hard nonrange statements can actually demonstrate failure of universality when they are too explicitly indexed. Keep the quantifier order explicit: one g must hit every infinite NP set, while a separate g tailored to each proof system is weaker and does not establish a universal generator.

Next test: compare Idea 44's moving time-bounded complexity threshold with Krajicek's feasible-infinitude boundary. The first-missing string sequence is computable in exponential time, so it does not itself witness feasible infinitude; its membership in NP and the existence of a polynomial-time selector are both unproved. Test whether a structured slow computation can instead yield a polynomial-time selector or a PV-provable infinitude statement whose dWPHP non-witnessing can be derived from a mainstream assumption weaker than H. If not, mark the route as requiring a new explicit circuit lower bound; do not promote a result for feasibly infinite sets to all infinite NP sets.

Sources: [Krajicek, On the existence of strong proof complexity generators, Hypothesis H, Theorem 7.1, Problem 5.2, and Conjecture 1.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11642); [Li, Ren, and Zhong, demi-bits amplification, Corollary 4.9](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23228).

This gives disjointness for the modified generator, but changes the arbitrary target suffix and therefore does not inherit Krajicek's hitting theorem. Moving the identity tag into a restricted set of prefixes restores a language-readable tag only by triggering the lemma. A bijective relabeling that keeps every prefix eligible avoids this particular lemma, but the output prefix alone then does not identify which of the 2^c possible formula codes (or corresponding proof predicates) generated it. No impossibility is claimed for encodings that use a new argument to recover that identity.

Learning carried forward: at stretch one, the proof identity has a semantic alignment cost as well as a bit cost. The issue is not merely how many bits the output has; universal hitting depends on retaining an arbitrary target set's infinite-fiber prefix. Any next construction must show, in one encoding, both that the diagonal predicate can read the intended proof identity and that every infinite NP set still supplies an eligible output prefix.

Next test: search for a recursion-theorem fixed point in which the identity is recoverable from the entire prefix cylinder while every length-(c+1) cylinder remains eligible. If the fixed point necessarily reduces the eligible prefixes, close this branch and focus on Idea 49's non-effective choice of equivalent definitions.

## Idea 52 - Padding-aligned cylinder against a same-length formula tag

Status: closes the code-length issue for a restricted tagged generator, but does not extend to Krajicek's original generator, whose unrestricted suffix can carry the target tag.

Construction: for a length parameter c, let A_c consist of strings beginning with 0^(c+1)1^c, followed by arbitrary bits. The latter is not a valid formula code, so no normal output belongs to A_c; the default zero string also misses A_c. For the particular input formula ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦_c, the tail at q is false, while every other c+1-bit cylinder is syntactically empty and has short S^1_2 proofs, so the selected prefix is q and the output is qÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦_cz, still outside A_c. This verifies that identity-carrying output tags can make an easy infinite P set miss a restricted generator.

Why it does not transfer: Krajicek's g_T outputs w u_0, with u_0 an arbitrary seed suffix. On the seed ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦_c 1^c z it outputs q1^c z, which belongs to A_c. Learning carried forward: a padded self-consistent cylinder can solve the syntactic length equation, but tag-based disjointness depends on controlling every possible formula-length parse. The crucial advantage of the untagged generator is precisely that it preserves arbitrary suffixes. Any counterexample to it must force a true, unprovable tail for every possible equivalent definition, rather than merely reject one formula tag.

Multi-offset test (obstruction found): the natural NP language accepting a string when it contains some formula tag together with a T-proof of that tag's tail sentence can still contain an output of g_T via a tag unrelated to the formula parsed from the seed. Requiring the tag to match the hidden seed formula is not a membership condition on the output unless the encoding preserves that identity; requiring all possible tags to pass changes the infinitude argument and supplies no known infinite NP language. The missing property is recoverability of the specific input definition from the range string, which g_T deliberately does not preserve.

Literature status check: the 2025 published version of Krajicek's paper still states Problem 2.4 as open ([JSL article](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/66E7218F4395978787F616993A31D8B5/S0022481223000695a.pdf/proof_complexity_conjecture_and_the_incompleteness_theorem.pdf)). The 2024 strong-generator paper proves hitting for feasibly infinite NP sets under hypothesis H ([BSL article](https://doi.org/10.1017/bsl.2023.40)); its definition requires a polynomial-time selector producing arbitrarily large members, so padding an arbitrary infinite NP set does not supply the missing selector because it still does not find the base member in A.

Next test: try a uniform multi-length tag language that catches every offset at which an input formula can occur, while remaining NP and disjoint from the generator's full range. Reject it unless the membership verifier has a single polynomial bound and the language is proved infinite independently of a selector.

## Idea 54 - The identity-transport trilemma and the hole-resistance profile

Status: a synthesis of proved constraints from Ideas 50ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ53, useful as a design filter. It is not a P versus NP proof and does not rule out generators that transform the entire seed in a nontrivial way.

Identity-transport heuristic: the recent proof-tag diagonals need an output to retain enough information to identify which formula ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ generated a missing-proof choice. Three attempted transports have each paid a distinct cost. If ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ is discarded, an NP verifier for the proposed counterexample cannot ensure its proof claim matches the generator's ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ (Idea 50's unrelated-tag failure). If ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦ is carried as an output tag while arbitrary suffixes are preserved, the image tends to be a polynomial union of cylinders and the range becomes P (Idea 53). If only selected prefixes are permitted to encode ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦, a cylinder language can concentrate all its infinite mass on an excluded prefix, so the generic infinite-fiber argument breaks (Idea 51). These are established failures of those specific encodings, not an exhaustive theorem about every possible identity code.

New bookkeeping language: for a polynomial-time map G, call $H_G=\{0,1\}^*\setminus\operatorname{Range}(G)$ its hole set. Its hole-resistance profile records, for each NP verifier and polynomial resource bound, whether H_G contains an infinite language recognized by that verifier. Universal NP-hitting is exactly the statement that this profile is empty. A range-size deficit only proves that H_G is large at each length; the suffix-replay lemma shows how a polynomial cylinder cover makes its profile immediately nonempty (indeed H_G is then an infinite P language). This separates ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“many holesÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â from ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“holes no NP language can systematically select.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â The term is project vocabulary, not a standard complexity measure.

Design consequence to test: bijective suffix scrambling cannot improve a cylinder construction, because it preserves the full suffix image. Any useful new construction must either create a genuinely nontrivial suffix image or couple the header choice to the whole input; then its first proof obligation is to prevent an infinite NP subset of the holes. Test toy maps against that obligation before attempting diagonalization. Preserve the identity-transport costs above as a rejection checklist, not as a no-go theorem.

Next test: build a small family of suffix maps h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦} and classify when their range is still P by an explicit inverse/decider, then identify the first map in the family whose range complexity is not explained by a cylinder cover. Do not treat a hard inversion problem as evidence of NP-immunity; separately look for an NP subset of its complement.

## Idea 55 - Suffix scrambling does not buy range hardness for free

Status: simple variants tested analytically and rejected. This is a boundary result for suffix-only transforms, not an impossibility theorem for all generators.

Test family: on a formula cylinder ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦s, replace the copied suffix s by h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦}(s), retaining a header w_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦}. If each h_{n,ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â¦} is a bijection on suffixes of the same length, its image is still the full suffix cube even if computing h^{-1} is difficult; the output remains the same easy prefix cylinder. A length-dependent XOR mask is a concrete instance. If h is many-to-one but its image has a polynomial-time membership test, a polynomial union of branch images is again P. Appending parity or another P-computable checksum also fails: the image is described by a P-checkable relation, and its complement is an infinite P set. Thus invertibility hardness alone is irrelevant, while ordinary local redundancy produces publicly recognizable holes.

The unresolved transform must make the image membership hard enough that no infinite NP language can live in its complement. Merely making range membership NP-hard is insufficient: an NP-hard range can still have an infinite, easily recognized P subset in its complement. Under a cylinder decomposition into polynomially many branches, this obligation is already present for each branch image and cannot be supplied by the header bookkeeping.
