Both anchors admit preserving semi-filters under the two checkerboard pairs; at anchor $0000$, the exact stabilized closure has 679 members and five minimal members. This confirms that the failure persists after removing anchor points from the universe. A separate exhaustive universal-cover search [experiment_universal_cover_q2_n3_sparse_anchors.py](experiment_universal_cover_q2_n3_sparse_anchors.py) takes $A=\{000,111\}$ and the other six words as $U$. It checks all 2,080 one-pair candidates and finds none covers every semi-filter above both anchors; a two-pair cover is found after inspecting 690,071 candidate lists, so the exact universal cover is two on this sparse toy. Definition 19 of [Cavalar and Oliveira](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/033/download) supplies the required-slice condition; Proposition 21.1 in the project audit supplies the exact closure criterion for all semi-filters.

Learning: the fusion spectrum is a complete description only after the filter is fixed. For the universal cover problem, an endpoint pair is an adversarial closure rule: a semi-filter can add its intersection and thereby preserve the pair, unless later rules force the empty set. So a high profile cover for minimal filters gives no lower bound on $\rho$ by itself. All future finite experiments must distinguish (i) exact cover of a selected filter family, from (ii) universal cover of every semi-filter via preservation closure.

This has a useful logic translation. Treat each subset $S\subseteq U$ as a proposition ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“$S$ is in the filter.ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â Upward closure supplies implications $S\Rightarrow T$ whenever $S\subseteq T$. Each listed pair supplies the Horn rule $(E\land H)\Rightarrow(E\cap H)$. The anchor supplies the initial facts $B\cap U$ for each basis set containing it. The universal cover problem asks for the fewest Horn rules that make the empty-set proposition derivable from every anchor's initial facts. A lower bound asks for an anchor whose least fixed point remains consistent. This is an anchor-indexed Horn-refutation game; it links the fusion spectrum to the existing closure recurrence and proof-DAG analysis, while making clear why ordinary set-cover spectra omit the adversary's extension choices.

Every refutation also has a **disjoint seed**: the empty set can only be introduced by a rule whose endpoint intersection is already empty. All other pair rules can only relay nonempty intersections into larger endpoint sets until that seed becomes fireable. In the exact sparse-cube cover, the first pair has empty intersection and the second pair's nonempty intersection equals one endpoint of the seed. Thus universal cover lower bounds can be reframed as a seed-reachability problem: how many anchors can a short relay system deliver to any disjoint seed? This focuses the counting problem more tightly than counting arbitrary fusion profiles.

Next attempt: encode the universal cover as an anchor-dependent closure game. Given a proposed pair list, start from each anchor's forced slices and apply its intersection rules; find an anchor whose closure avoids $\emptyset$. Then exploit Gap-MCSP's large high-complexity cylinders to characterize which intersections can first empty out. The existing proof-DAG bound yields only a near-linear threshold, so the new ingredient must control how many anchors one rule can eliminate, not merely how many literal leaves a single anchor needs.

## Idea 83 - A directed-cycle relay is an exact universal-cover certificate

**Status: exact theorem on a two-anchor toy domain; no Gap-MCSP transfer yet.** It explains the observed $n-1$ rule count and tests the universal semi-filter quantifier directly.

Let $U_n=\{0,1\}^n\setminus\{0^n,1^n\}$ and take the two anchors $A_n=\{0^n,1^n\}$. At each anchor, force its $n$ matching coordinate slices. With indices modulo $n$, define

$$B_i=\{x\in U_n:x_i=0\text{ or }x_{i+1}=1\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.$$

For anchor $0^n$, the slice $x_i=0$ is contained in $B_i$; for anchor $1^n$, the slice $x_{i+1}=1$ is contained in $B_i$. Thus every semi-filter above either anchor contains every $B_i$.

Use the first pair $(B_1,B_2)$, then the relay pairs $(K_{j-1},B_j)$ for $j=3,\ldots,n$, where $K_j=\bigcap_{i=1}^j B_i$. Each rule forces its endpoint intersection into the preservation closure. The clauses say $x_i\le x_{i+1}$ around a directed cycle, so their common solutions are exactly $0^n$ and $1^n$. Both are removed from $U_n$, hence $K_n=\emptyset$. This gives a universal cover of size $n-1$.

The lower bound is tight. If $m$ pair rules derive $\emptyset$ for one anchor, trace the derivation as a connected acyclic proof DAG. With at most $m$ rule nodes and at most two antecedents per rule, it has at most $m+1$ initial-generator leaves. Their intersection must be empty. At anchor $0^n$, fewer than $n$ distinct coordinate-zero slices have a nonempty intersection inside $U_n$: set the fixed bits to zero and one unfixed bit to one. Therefore there must be at least $n$ leaves and $m\ge n-1$. The exact universal cover number is $n-1$.

**Prior-art correction:** the relay or cyclic-computation viewpoint is not a new framework. Cavalar and Oliveira's Theorem 30 characterizes cover complexity exactly by cyclic intersection complexity, and their Section 2.5 already gives a fixed-rule closure system as a cyclic monotone Boolean circuit. Our firing process is an instance of that framework. The project contribution here is the explicit punctured-cube certificate and matching leaf argument; we have not established that this exact toy value is new in the literature. See [Cavalar and Oliveira (2025), ÃƒÆ’Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â§2.5 and Theorem 30](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14117).

The finite checker [experiment_cycle_relay_cover.py](experiment_cycle_relay_cover.py) verifies the closure sequence for $n=2,\ldots,12$. The generic exact SAT model also finds covers of sizes $2,3,4,5,6$ at dimensions $3,4,5,6,7$ respectively; at $n=6$, four rules are UNSAT and five are SAT. The all-$n$ proof above makes the long $n=7,m=5$ UNSAT search unnecessary.

**What the earlier failures were missing:** profile covers of a fixed filter ignore the relay rules; a single pair need not kill a semi-filter if its nonempty intersection can be added. Here the list of pairs acts as a short proof program: intersections are intermediate states, and the final rule fires only after a cycle of local constraints accumulates. The witness geometry is an implication cycle, not a coloring or a static profile cover. At the same time, this construction exactly saturates the leaf bound. It gives linear cover complexity and therefore cannot by itself cross the project's superlinear magnification threshold.

**Next transfer test:** replace the two extreme anchors by the low-circuit anchor family and ask whether one shared relay system can force a full-coordinate contradiction for every anchor. For an endpoint $X$, record which matching basis slices it contains; for a derived intersection $K$, record the anchor set whose closure has derived it. Then track how one rule both (i) routes anchor sets through the exact recurrence of Proposition 21.4 and (ii) shortens the remaining coordinate assignments. A useful theorem must charge more than the $N$ literal leaves already counted in Proposition 21.7, likely through a lower bound on rule sharing across many anchors. First search for a Gap-MCSP analogue of the directed-cycle clause family; if each relay is accepted by every low anchor and the final intersection is empty on $U$, this is already a valid universal cover and an upper-bound breakthrough for the proxy. Otherwise identify precisely which anchors fail to enter the cycle and whether their activation patterns force more than linear many rules.

## Idea 84 - Anchor activation signatures create a sharing cost

**Status: exact SAT results through n=5; a general linear cover is now explicit.** To test whether the two-anchor cycle's linear count is an artifact of having only two anchors, change the promise geometry to

$$A_{n,1}=\{a\in\{0,1\}^n:\operatorname{wt}(a)\le1\},\qquad
U_{n,1}=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\operatorname{wt}(x)\ge2\}.$$

Run the exact unrolled least-fixed-point SAT encoding in [experiment_relay_cover_boolean_cube.py](experiment_relay_cover_boolean_cube.py) with the full anchor list. Each candidate endpoint is an arbitrary subset of $U$; the encoding checks every anchor and every possible firing order, and a SAT model is independently verified on the finite support family.

Results so far:

* $n=3$: one rule is UNSAT and two rules are SAT, so the exact cover is two.
* $n=4$: three rules are UNSAT; four rules are SAT and the full closure verifier [experiment_weight_one_anchor_cover4.py](experiment_weight_one_anchor_cover4.py) verifies all five anchors. Thus the exact cover is four, one above the $n-1$ leaf lower bound for a single anchor.
* $n=5$: four rules are UNSAT, and a five-rule PySAT/CaDiCaL run with endpoint-swap, rule-order, and all coordinate-permutation symmetry breaking returned UNSAT. A six-rule model is SAT; [experiment_weight_one_anchor_cover5_six_rules.py](experiment_weight_one_anchor_cover5_six_rules.py) verifies it for all six anchors by exact support-set closure. The symmetry actions preserve this instance, and the lex-leader encoding was exhaustively checked on all two-bit pairs. Thus the SAT search gives computed exact value $\rho=6$ for this toy; the run did not save a separately checkable DRAT proof.

There is a general fallback upper bound that works for every $n\ge3$. For each coordinate pair $i<j$, let $C_{ij}=\{x\in U:x_i=0\text{ or }x_j=0\}$. Every anchor of weight at most one has a matching zero-slice contained in each $C_{ij}$. Intersect all $\binom n2$ such clauses in a relay chain: their common solutions have weight at most one and hence none lie in $U$. The first rule intersects two clauses, and each later rule intersects the accumulated set with one new clause, using $\binom n2-1$ rules. [experiment_weight_one_pairwise_relay.py](experiment_weight_one_pairwise_relay.py) verifies this universal closure certificate for $n=3,\ldots,10$. This upper bound was sharpened substantially at $n=5$ by the six-rule SAT witness.

The $n=4$ witness has different closure schedules for different anchors. Its first-round fired-rule sets are $\{0,2\}$ for anchors $0000,0010$, $\{2\}$ for $0001,0100$, and $\{0\}$ for $1000$. These activation signatures then route through different relay orders, all reaching the disjoint seed. The common directed-cycle construction fails here for a precise reason: its clause $x_i=0\lor x_{i+1}=1$ has no forced matching slice at the unit anchor with $x_i=1,x_{i+1}=0$. A shared static cycle cannot serve all anchors; the SAT witness instead branches through anchor-dependent rule activation.

This suggests a useful state encoding alongside leaf count, not a new general complexity measure. For a pair list $\Lambda=\{(E_j,H_j)\}$, define its initial activation signature at anchor $a$ by

$$\sigma_\Lambda(a)=\{j:\exists G,G'\in\mathcal G_a\text{ with }G\subseteq E_j,\ G'\subseteq H_j\},$$

where $\mathcal G_a$ is the forced basis-slice family. A later rule fires when its two endpoints are supported by initial slices or intersections of already-fired rules. Thus $\sigma_\Lambda(a)$ is the input mask for a monotone AND-OR relay network on the rule indices. This is the same basic closure-to-cyclic-circuit translation already present in Cavalar and Oliveira, Section 2.5; the potentially new work is analyzing the activation profiles forced by this particular family of anchors. A proof-DAG leaf argument sees only the number of leaves for one anchor; it does not by itself bound the sharing of one rule network across all anchors.

**Why the path remains open:** this toy has only $n+1$ anchors and its cover is already $O(n)$; the general bound and its limitations are recorded in Idea 85. The exact $n=3,4,5$ values are $2,4,6$, but no general exact formula is proved. This family cannot supply the required superlinear lower bound. The useful surviving question is whether anchor-signature complexity can be lower-bounded for the actual Gap-MCSP promise rather than this threshold toy.

## Idea 85 - Prefix threshold states give a linear universal refutation

**Status: exact general upper construction and closure verification; no P-vs-NP transfer.** The low-weight anchor toy has a compact dynamic program that works for every anchor at once. Let $Z_i=\{x\in U:x_i=0\}$ and $O_i=\{x\in U:x_i=1\}$, with $U=\{x:\operatorname{wt}(x)\ge2\}$. Define

$$A_i=\bigcap_{j=1}^i Z_j,\qquad F_i=\{x\in U:\operatorname{wt}(x_1,\ldots,x_i)\le1\}.$$

Start with $A_2=Z_1\cap Z_2$ (one rule) and $F_2=Z_1\cup Z_2$ (a free upward superset). For $i=3,\ldots,n$, derive

$$A_i=A_{i-1}\cap Z_i\quad(i<n),\qquad
F_i=F_{i-1}\cap(Z_i\cup A_{i-1}).$$

The $A$ chain costs $n-2$ rules and the $F$ chain costs $n-2$, for $2n-4$ rules total. For any anchor $a$ of weight at most one, $F_2$ contains a matching zero-slice. At step $i$, the second endpoint $Z_i\cup A_{i-1}$ contains a forced slice: it contains $Z_i$ if $a_i=0$; if $a_i=1$, all earlier bits of $a$ are zero, so the already-derived $A_{i-1}$ is in the filter. Inductively the rule fires and adds $F_i$. Finally $F_n=\varnothing$ on $U$. This is a universal semi-filter proof because it uses only forced generators, upward closure, and listed intersections.

The independent checker [experiment_weight_one_linear_exact_certificate.py](experiment_weight_one_linear_exact_certificate.py) verifies the exact support-set preservation closure for every anchor for $n=3,\ldots,12$. Combined with the one-anchor proof-DAG lower bound $\rho\ge n-2$, this proves

$$n-2\le \rho(A_{n,1},U_{n,1})\le2n-4,$$

so this whole family has $\Theta(n)$ cover complexity and cannot be a superlinear route. SAT search gives exact values $2,4,6$ for $n=3,4,5$, matching the upper construction in those cases. The $n=5$ UNSAT result is solver-derived and has no saved proof trace; the six-rule upper certificate is independently checkable by the script.

This recurrence is a threshold-function computation, not a new general circuit model. Under the coordinate complement $y_i=1-x_i$, its target is the monotone threshold $\operatorname{wt}(y)\ge n-1$, the dual of threshold two. Classical monotone-threshold work already gives the corresponding linear acyclic gate scale (including the $2n-4$ gate-type bound for threshold two and its dual); see [Sergeev's threshold-circuit paper](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/dm1547). The open distinction here is cyclic relay complexity: an acyclic gate lower bound does not automatically lower-bound cyclic covers, and the exact match at three dimensions is finite evidence only.

The same construction works for every $0\le k\le n-2$. Let $S_{i,j}=\{x\in U:\operatorname{wt}(x_1,\ldots,x_i)=j\}$ for $j\le k$. For each valid branch of

$$S_{i,j}=(S_{i-1,j}\cap Z_i)\cup(S_{i-1,j-1}\cap O_i),$$

include one pair rule for that branch; the union is available by upward closure. Every anchor $a$ of weight at most $k$ follows the state $S_{i,\operatorname{wt}(a_1,\ldots,a_i)}$, and its final state is empty on $U$. The rule count is

$$R(n,k)=\sum_{i=2}^n\bigl(\min(i-1,k)+1+\min(i,k)\bigr)\le(2k+1)(n-1).$$

For anchor $0^n$, fewer than $n-k$ zero-slice leaves leave at least $k+1$ coordinates free, whose all-one assignment lies in $U$; the proof-DAG bound therefore gives $\rho\ge n-k-1$. So each fixed-threshold family also has $\Theta(n)$ cover complexity. [experiment_threshold_anchor_linear_cover.py](experiment_threshold_anchor_linear_cover.py) verifies the full support closure for every $k\le n-2$ at dimensions $2\le n\le8$. This generalization further identifies the failure mode: bounded prefix weight admits a small state machine, regardless of the number of anchors.

**Learning:** a large anchor family alone does not force expensive shared closure. If the anchors occupy a low-complexity boundary such as Hamming weight at most one, a two-state prefix summary is enough to route each anchor to the same empty target. Future constructions need to block compact state summaries or prove that their anchor-signature transition system has high width; counting anchors or invoking the ordinary one-anchor leaf bound will not do that.

## Idea 86 - Cofactor recursion spends the promise gap exponentially fast

**Status: exact recurrence obstruction for the naive recursive route; no general no-go theorem.** The project audit's one-split rectangle fact suggests recursively deciding Gap-MCSP on cofactors. Write $a$ for the low circuit-size threshold and $b$ for the high threshold, with $b>2a+O(1)$. Restricting a circuit to one variable cannot increase its size, so a low parent has two low cofactors at threshold $a$. In the other direction, a multiplexer combines circuits for the two cofactors at cost at most $C_0+C_1+3$. Therefore, if a parent has size at least $b$, at least one cofactor has size at least $b' = \lfloor(b-3)/2\rfloor$. On the parent promise, the conjunction of child promise separators for gap $(a,b')$ is correct: low parents give two low children, while high parents have at least one high child (the other may be in the gap).

This is a valid recursive circuit construction, but it consumes the gap. After $d$ cofactor levels the input truth tables have length $M_d=N/2^d$, while the high threshold is approximately $b_d=b/2^d$ (up to additive selector overhead). Thus the scale ratio $M_d/b_d$ stays approximately invariant at $N/b$. The gap itself closes after $d_{gap}\approx\log_2(b/a)$ levels. At that point, the remaining table length is about $aN/b$. For the magnification parameters $a=2^{\beta n}/(cn)$ and $b=2^{\beta n}$, $b/a=cn$ permits only $O(\log n)$ levels, while $N/b=N^{1-\beta}$ is still exponentially large. By contrast, the elementary DNF upper bound makes every table of length $M$ low only once $M=O(a)$, requiring

$$d\ge\log_2(N/a)=(1-\beta)n+O(\log n).$$

For every fixed $\beta<1$, this is linear in $n$, far deeper than the $O(\log n)$ gap budget. Even the sharper generic truth-table circuit bound $O(M/\log M)$ still requires $\Omega(n)$ levels. So this recursive cofactor idea reaches a smaller, still-hard gap instance; it does not bottom out in a trivial case.

The possible new ingredient is clear: find a decomposition whose circuit-combination cost grows submultiplicatively across many cofactors, or handle the intermediate cofactor region without deciding total MCSP. A plain rectangle/projection argument cannot do either. This is an exact diagnosis of this recursion's failure, not a barrier to all recursive or nonrelativizing arguments.

## Idea 87 - Sorting networks collapse every symmetric threshold toy

**Status: general construction, with exact closure verification through n=8; no Gap-MCSP transfer.** The prefix-count dynamic program in Idea 85 costs O(kn) rules when the threshold k grows. A different construction removes that dependence on k. Take the n zero-slice sets Z_i as Boolean inputs to Batcher's bitonic sorting network, padded to p=2^ceil(log2 n) wires with empty sets. Each comparator on endpoint sets (E,H) has outputs E intersection H and E union H: the intersection is one pair rule, while the union is available for free by upward closure. Sort in descending order. The wire at zero-based position n-k-1 is the predicate that at least n-k inputs are 1, hence the set of tables with at most k one-bits. On U={x:wt(x)>k}, this set is empty. Every anchor with wt(a)<=k supplies at least n-k matching zero-slices, so its closure follows the comparator computation to the empty set.

If p=2^r, the bitonic network uses p*r*(r+1)/4 comparators, so for every 0<=k<=n-2,

$$n-k-1\le \rho(A_{n,k},U_{n,k})\le \frac{p r(r+1)}4=O(n\log^2 n).$$

The lower bound is the single-anchor proof-DAG leaf argument from Idea 85. The verifier [experiment_threshold_sorting_cover.py](experiment_threshold_sorting_cover.py) independently checks the full support closure for every threshold at n=2,...,8; all checks pass. This closes the entire symmetric threshold family as a source of n^(1+epsilon) cover lower bounds, even when k grows with n. The sorting network itself is classical; the project-specific statement is its transfer to a universal semi-filter closure certificate.

**Learning:** the previous prefix-state failure was not just a convenient low-weight recurrence. Symmetric threshold predicates admit a sorting computation with near-linear polylogarithmic relay cost for every threshold. For a new anchor family, test whether a small monotone circuit or comparator network computes membership from its forced slices before investing in lower-bound experiments.

## Idea 88 - The missing charge is cross-anchor relay reuse

**Status: exact language and a candidate lower-bound target; the reuse inequality is open.** The repeated failures can be expressed in one anchor-conditioned proof-flow language. For a proposed list Lambda={(E_j,H_j)}, write K_j=E_j intersection H_j. A **carrier** is a subset X of the high-table universe U. Its **trigger set** S_X is the set of low anchors whose forced-slice closure derives X. Initially,

$$S_X^0=\{a:\exists i,\ B_{i,a_i}\subseteq X\},$$

and each relay updates support by

$$S_{K_j}\supseteq S_{E_j}\cap S_{H_j}.$$

Upward closure transfers support from K_j to every carrier containing K_j. The list is a universal refutation exactly when every low anchor reaches the empty carrier. This is a compact working vocabulary for Proposition 21.4's exact support recurrence, not a claim of a new general formalism.

For a fixed anchor a, tracing an empty derivation gives a proof DAG whose generator leaves fix a set Q of truth-table coordinates. The cylinder {y:y_Q=a_Q} contains no high-circuit table, so |Q|>=N-log2(M_2)-O(1)=N-o(N). This explains the strongest current lower bound and its ceiling: counting leaves charges a separate near-full-coordinate certificate for one anchor, but a relay node can be reused in proof DAGs for many anchors. The uncovered quantity is therefore **reuse bandwidth**: how many distinct anchors can share one relay node or sub-DAG while still allowing their different leaf cylinders to end at empty?

The first version of a fanout-versus-refinement conjecture was too crude. Exact closure traces for the saved n=4 four-rule and n=5 six-rule threshold covers show that **every listed rule fires for every anchor**. Thus raw rule-support cardinality can be maximal even in an easy instance and cannot serve as the missing charge. The open quantity must measure contextual reuse: how many distinct anchor-dependent leaf patterns can be routed through one shared relay sub-DAG without retaining a common high-table witness? A possible proof language is a cylinder-intersection hypergraph with anchor-tagged proof alternatives: vertices are low anchors, each tag is a leaf-coordinate pattern, and a relay joins two support regions while its carrier records which high completions remain possible. A scale-growing bound on these distinct contexts, rather than on rule fanout, could beat the N-leaf ceiling.

**Why this is not yet a theorem:** arbitrary endpoint sets can encode complicated unions of literal slices, intermediate carriers can be shared, and minimal proof DAGs for different anchors need not align. A proposed potential must be valid for every endpoint choice and account for these overlaps; ordinary profile covers, graph coloring, anchor count, raw rule fanout, and per-anchor certificate size do not do this. The next finite audit should log, for each carrier, its trigger set, anchor-specific minimal leaf patterns, and whether those proof alternatives share actual antecedent sub-DAGs. The exact n=4 and n=5 covers are counterexamples to any candidate based only on how many anchors trigger each rule. Then compare a refined potential on the live sparse-witness CEGIS candidates. Reject a candidate if it is not monotone under the exact support recurrence.

**Failure map to consult before each new experiment:** (1) distinguish all-semi-filter closure from coverage of selected filters; (2) keep the mandatory literal slices in the target instance; (3) optimize against the full endpoint-fusion spectrum, including mixed witnesses; (4) remember endpoints are arbitrary, uncharged subsets, so a lower bound must survive adversarial endpoint choices rather than only structured witnesses; (5) measure anchor-dependent proof contexts, not only one-anchor leaves or raw rule fanout; (6) check whether the anchor predicate has a compact monotone state machine or comparator network; and (7) for recursive decompositions, track both promise gap and remaining input length. These checks summarize why many apparently different constructions collapsed and should screen subsequent ideas.

## Idea 89 - Track proof-context antichains, not just anchor support

**Status: exact finite recurrence, independently cross-checked on the saved n=4 and n=5 covers; no asymptotic lower bound.** For a carrier $X$ and anchor $a$, define $\mathcal C_X(a)$ to be the inclusion-minimal sets of literal-coordinate indices that suffice as leaves to derive $X$. Its initial contexts are $\{\{i\}:B_{i,a_i}\subseteq X\}$. For rule $j=(E_j,H_j)$ with $K_j=E_j\cap H_j$, every carrier $X\supseteq K_j$ receives contexts

$$\min_{\subseteq}\{Q\cup R:Q\in\mathcal C_{E_j}(a),\ R\in\mathcal C_{H_j}(a)\},$$

where $\min_{\subseteq}$ keeps only inclusion-minimal coordinate sets. Iterating this recurrence to its least fixed point exactly records which carriers are derivable from each selected subset of an anchor's generators. For any $Q\subseteq[N]$, carrier $X$ is derivable using only the generators indexed by $Q$ iff some context in $\mathcal C_X(a)$ is a subset of $Q$. This is an antichain-valued version of the existing support recurrence: union of leaf sets is the product operation, and antichain minimization removes dominated proofs.

The verifier [experiment_relay_proof_contexts.py](experiment_relay_proof_contexts.py) checks that equivalence directly for every one of the $2^n$ subsets of literal generators, every relevant carrier, and every anchor in both saved universal covers. For n=4, the four-rule certificate has four minimal empty contexts at $0000$ and one at each unit anchor, all of size three. For n=5, the six-rule certificate has five minimal empty contexts at $00000$ and one at each unit anchor, all of size four. Every rule's carrier is supported at every anchor, yet each rule has only 7-10 anchor-context instances in these examples. This confirms that rule fanout and proof-context structure are different observables.

This language may expose the true sharing cost: a small rule list can have full anchor support, but it must route anchor-specific near-full coordinate certificates through the same fixed endpoint network. The unresolved question is whether the context antichains for the actual low-circuit anchor set require many more relay rules than their support masks suggest. The antichains can themselves be exponentially large, so the recurrence is a proof-analysis tool, not an efficient algorithm. First extend the exact minimization to the sparse-witness CEGIS candidates and look for a context-potential that is subadditive under rule composition and grows beyond the current $N-o(N)$ leaf bound.

## Idea 90 - Scramble the literal basis with a fast invertible linear map

**Status: the smallest exact toy closes this route; the high-dimensional version remains untested.** The prior checkerboard failures depend on the mandatory coordinate slices. A possible way to change their geometry while preserving circuit hardness is to encode each truth-table vector $y\in\{0,1\}^N$ as $T(y)$ for an invertible linear map $T$ computed by a small Boolean circuit. The new mandatory generators are ordinary coordinate slices of $T(y)$, whose preimages are parity hyperplanes in the original truth-table bits. Any separator for the transformed promise composes with $T$ to give a separator for the original promise with additive overhead equal to the size of $T$; an inverse circuit is not needed for this direction. A random sparse/butterfly linear circuit might make the low-circuit anchors less aligned with Hamming thresholds or low-dimensional incidence designs.

The exact test [experiment_linear_basis_scramble_toy.py](experiment_linear_basis_scramble_toy.py) enumerates every one of the 168 matrices in $GL(3,2)$ for the promise with anchors of weight at most one and universe points of weight at least two. Under the transformed coordinate slices, 72 bases have an exact one-pair universal cover. For each of the other 96 bases, the script exhaustively checks all 256 candidate pair rules and all 65,536 ordered two-rule lists; every one has a two-rule universal closure cover. Thus no invertible linear basis change raises this toy's cover number above two. This does not imply a general two-pair theorem, and a random dense matrix would also fail the required fast-circuit overhead at scale $N$.

The literature gives a useful cost warning. Ben-Hamou's [2025 analysis of random elementary transvections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08185) gives $O(N^2\log N)$ mixing steps for the standard walk on $GL(N,2)$, with one row-addition per step. Replaying that walk as a linear circuit costs the same order of XOR gates, too large for a near-linear magnification target. The paper's alternative row-resampling chain mixes in $\Theta(N\log N)$ updates, but a dense row replacement can itself cost $\Theta(N)$ XORs. The unresolved design problem is a genuinely fast ($N^{1+o(1)}$-size) invertible transform whose action on the low-circuit anchor family has enough pseudorandomness to help against every endpoint list.

**Learning:** changing the coordinate system does not by itself defeat the low-weight relay; the closure can adapt its arbitrary endpoints to the new basis. If revisiting basis scrambling, choose the transform and high-dimensional anchor family together, require a fast forward circuit, and attack arbitrary mixed endpoints in small dimensions before claiming any randomized-geometry effect.

## Idea 91 - A scrambled simplex reaches five relay rules in dimension four

**Status: exhaustive orbit classification with solver-derived lower bounds; every SAT upper witness is exact-closure verified, but UNSAT traces are not saved.** For 4-bit low-weight-one anchors $A=\{0,e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\}$, the high universe is exactly their complement. Invertible linear basis changes produce simplex anchor sets $\{0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$. The all-basis script [experiment_linear_basis_scramble_n4_orbits.py](experiment_linear_basis_scramble_n4_orbits.py) enumerates all 840 unordered bases of $\mathbb F_2^4$ and quotients by the 384 coordinate-permutation/bit-flip automorphisms, leaving 14 orbits. Arbitrary-endpoint PySAT searches give first satisfiable rule counts 2 for one orbit, 3 for three, 4 for nine, and 5 for one. The unsatisfiable smaller counts are solver-derived and have no DRAT/LRAT proof traces, so this is a strong finite computation rather than a paper proof.

The exceptional orbit representative has anchors $\{0,3,5,9,14\}$. The five-rule endpoint list is stored in [experiment_basis_exception_contexts.py](experiment_basis_exception_contexts.py), found by [experiment_relay_cover_pysat.py](experiment_relay_cover_pysat.py), and checked against direct closure for every subset of the four forced generators. Its closure routes all five anchors through four nonempty relay intersections to one disjoint seed. For each anchor the only minimal empty context fixes all four coordinates, and every rule fires for every anchor. The orbit script also computes the local cylinder-certificate profile: this is the only class where all five anchors need all four coordinates before their cylinder lies wholly inside the low set; every other class has at least one anchor with a three-coordinate certificate. This correlation may explain the extra rule, but no implication is proved. Thus a linear basis change can raise this toy's computed cover from four to five, but the gain is constant and does not establish a scalable lower bound.

A fixed-seed sample of 20 matrices had first-satisfiable counts 2 for two, 3 for six, and 4 for twelve. That sample missed the exceptional orbit. This is a useful warning: random sampling alone did not find the strongest class; orbit reduction exposed it. Next seek a structural invariant behind the exceptional affine-simplex geometry and a proof of the four-rule UNSAT result before attempting larger dimensions.

## Idea 92 - Relay proofs as a shared compiler for high-free transversals

**Status: exact necessary condition and a finite diagnostic match on three saved covers; the proposed selector-complexity lower bound is unproved.** Fix an anchor $a$ and an empty-carrier proof whose literal leaves use coordinates $Q$. For every high point $x\in U$, $Q$ must contain some coordinate where $a$ and $x$ differ. Otherwise $x$ lies in every selected matching slice; because all endpoints and their intersections are subsets of $U$ and the only operation is intersection followed by upward closure, induction puts $x$ in every carrier derived from those leaves, including the alleged empty carrier. Therefore every root context is a transversal of

$$\mathcal H_a=\{\{i:a_i\ne x_i\}:x\in U\}.$$

Equivalently, the common coordinate cylinder fixed by $Q$ at $a$ must be high-free. This is a set-theoretic statement, stronger in form than merely saying $|Q|\ge N-o(N)$: it identifies each proof context with an explicit hitting set. A derivation-minimal context need not be an inclusion-minimal transversal in general, because a smaller high-free coordinate set may fail to be expressible by the fixed relay rules.

The new diagnostic [experiment_anchor_transversal_audit.py](experiment_anchor_transversal_audit.py) enumerates the minimal high-free transversals and the exact root-context antichain of each saved cover. In all three currently audited certificates they coincide anchor by anchor: the exceptional scrambled simplex (five anchors, five rules), the native $n=4$ weight-one cover (five anchors, four rules), and the native $n=5$ weight-one cover (six anchors, six rules). For the all-zero anchor, the context/transversal counts are respectively 1, 4, and 5; every unit anchor has one. Every listed context is checked against every point of $U$. This is a finite and perhaps useful pattern, not a theorem that optimal covers must realize all minimal transversals.

The selector must remember the *sign* of every selected coordinate: the actual leaves are $(i,a_i)$ for $i\in Q$, not just the unsigned set $Q$. For a low anchor in Gap-MCSP, $Q=[N]$ is always a high-free certificate, but that fact alone does not give a fixed rule list able to route all anchor-specific sign patterns to empty. The five-bit radius-two family is easier because its lex selector is ÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€¦Ã¢â‚¬Å“take the first $n-2$ zero coordinatesÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¢ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬Å¡Ã‚Â¬Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â; Idea 93 verifies that a five-rule network can implement it at $n=5$.

The project-local algebra for this is the **relay proof polynomial**. Represent an antichain of coordinate sets as the minimal true monomials of a monotone Boolean function. Define $P\oplus R=\min_{\subseteq}(P\cup R)$ for alternative proofs and $P\otimes R=\min_{\subseteq}\{p\cup r:p\in P,r\in R\}$ for combining two premises. The zero is the empty antichain, the one is $\{\varnothing\}$, and coordinate $i$ is $\{\{i\}\}$. For carrier $X$ and anchor $a$, its exact least-fixed-point equation is

$$C_X(a)=\bigoplus_{i:B_{i,a_i}\subseteq X}\{\{i\}\}\;\oplus\!\bigoplus_{j:K_j\subseteq X}\big(C_{E_j}(a)\otimes C_{H_j}(a)\big),$$

where $K_j=E_j\cap H_j$. This is the existing context recurrence written as an idempotent semiring: alternatives add, paired premises multiply, and absorption removes dominated contexts. The empty-carrier polynomial's monomials must all be high-free transversals. The representation is exact but may have exponentially many monomials, so this alone does not make the computation efficient.

The lower-bound target is no longer just certificate length (the old one-anchor argument) or rule fanout (all rules can fire at every anchor); it is the cost for one shared relay program to select valid transversals across a large anchor family. A candidate invariant could measure selector complexity, but raw antichain size is already suspect. The geometry-only checker [experiment_sparse_ball_transversal_profiles.py](experiment_sparse_ball_transversal_profiles.py) computes the antichains for the same six seeded GL(5,2) images used by the now-interrupted arbitrary-endpoint SAT search. In this tiny sample each anchor has only 1-6 minimal transversals, except the native all-zero anchor with 10; minimum certificate sizes range from 3 to 5.

The restricted-generator test [experiment_sparse_ball_canonical_selector.py](experiment_sparse_ball_canonical_selector.py) gives a stronger warning. For each n=5 radius-two anchor, it retains only the first three zero-coordinate slices in the fixed coordinate order and asks for a five-rule cover. With coordinate symmetry disabled because this selector breaks it, PySAT finds a cover; the exact closure verifier succeeds using only those selected generators at every anchor. The saved endpoint list is [experiment_sparse_ball_canonical_selector_witness.py](experiment_sparse_ball_canonical_selector_witness.py). Under the full generator family, its proof-context antichains still contain all minimal high-free transversals, but exactly one root context per anchor is usable from the selected triple. So counting every available proof context would overcharge the actual universal-cover requirement. The right question is how hard it is for one shared relay list to realize *some* high-free selector for every anchor. The lexicographic selector is simple for this toy; for the Gap-MCSP anchor family, one would need a rigorous lower bound against every possible selector encoded by arbitrary endpoints. No P-vs-NP consequence has been obtained.

## Idea 93 - A five-state cyclic separator for the radius-two ball

**Status: exact-closure-verified n=5 upper witness; solver-derived minima for n=3,4,5; n=6 searches interrupted.** Take $A=\{a\in\{0,1\}^5:\operatorname{wt}(a)\le2\}$ and $U=\{x:\operatorname{wt}(x)\ge3\}$. The valid $S_5$-symmetry-broken search [experiment_sparse_ball_native_symmetry.py](experiment_sparse_ball_native_symmetry.py) returns no cover through four rules and a five-rule cover. The endpoint sets are saved in [experiment_sparse_ball_native_n5_witness.py](experiment_sparse_ball_native_n5_witness.py), with the full direct-closure trace in [sparse_ball_native_n5_m5.txt](sparse_ball_native_n5_m5.txt). Every one of the 16 anchors derives the empty set, checked independently by support closure. Solver statuses for one through four rules have no portable proof trace, so the minimum is solver-derived; the five-rule upper witness is exact.

The context audit now checks this witness for every subset of the five forced generators. If an anchor has weight $r\le2$, its minimal high-free coordinate certificates are exactly the $(5-2)=3$-subsets of its zero coordinates: fixing such a $Q$ leaves at most $2$ possible ones, while any smaller set leaves a high completion. The witness derives every one of these certificates, with counts $\binom{5-r}{3}=10,4,1$ for anchor weights $0,1,2$. This extends the earlier matching on weight-one toys, but it is a property of these witnesses, not a necessity for arbitrary covers: universality only requires at least one root context per anchor.

The saved endpoint list compiles to five cyclic rule flags. [experiment_sparse_ball_native_equations.py](experiment_sparse_ball_native_equations.py) records each endpoint's initial literal support and its fixed inclusion dependencies. The sole disjoint rule fires on exactly the 16 low anchors when evaluated over the whole cube; the other four rules may also fire on some weight-three inputs, but the disjoint rule rejects all of them. Thus the cover is a compact cyclic monotone separator for this finite threshold promise.

There is a short case proof of completeness for the saved endpoint list. Write $z_i=1$ when anchor bit $i$ is zero. The endpoint supports/inclusions listed by the script imply: rule 1 fires initially when $z_1z_2=1$; rule 2 fires initially when $(z_1\vee z_2)z_4=1$; rule 4 fires initially when $z_0(z_1\vee z_2\vee z_4)=1$, and can also receive rule 2's intersection; rule 0 can receive rule 1's intersection on its left and rule 2's on its right; the disjoint rule 3 can receive rule 4's intersection on its left and requires $z_3$ or rule 0 or rule 1 on its right. If $z_3=1$, split into $z_0=1$ (rule 4 fires directly, since at least one of $z_1,z_2,z_4$ is also 1), $z_0=0,z_4=1$ (rule 2 then rule 4), or $z_0=z_4=0$ (then $z_1=z_2=1$, so rules 1,0,2,4 fire in succession). If $z_3=0,z_0=1$, at least two of $z_1,z_2,z_4$ are 1, so rule 4 fires; rule 1 fires if $z_1=z_2=1$, and otherwise rule 2 then rule 0 fires. If $z_3=z_0=0$, low weight forces $z_1=z_2=z_4=1$, so rules 1,2,4 fire. Each case fires rule 3. Soundness on every high point follows from point preservation: all matching slices contain that point, and intersections preserve it, so no disjoint pair can fire. This proves the five-rule upper bound without relying on the SAT model's internal closure check.

Single-rule ablation in [experiment_sparse_ball_native_equations.py](experiment_sparse_ball_native_equations.py) finds that removing rule 0 uncovers anchors 10, 12, 17; removing rule 1 uncovers 9, 17, 24; removing rule 2 uncovers 1, 3, 5, 9, 10, 12, 17. Removing either rule 3 or rule 4 destroys the entire cover. Thus the disjoint seed depends on a mandatory relay through rule 4, while the first three rules patch distinct anchor cases. This describes this witness only; it does not prove every five-rule cover has the same architecture.

The observed solver-derived first-SAT counts for the radius-two balls are $1,2,5$ at dimensions $3,4,5$. At $n=5$, the canonical-selector search finds a second five-rule cover that succeeds when each anchor is initially allowed only its lexicographically first three zero slices. For $n=6$, the valid $S_6$-symmetry-reduced search returned UNSAT at five rules, giving solver-derived $\rho\ge6$ by harmless padding of smaller lists; no proof trace was saved. The six-rule and related canonical-selector/first-seed searches were stopped on 25 September without a newly persisted result. These tiny values are too little to infer a growth law and do not beat the known $O(n\log^2 n)$ sorting-network upper bound asymptotically. The general equivalence between set-fusion cover complexity and cyclic circuit complexity is established in Cavalar and Oliveira's [2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14117); the project contribution here is the explicit endpoint witnesses, selector restriction, and case proof, not a new cyclic-circuit framework. Even a linear cover family would not by itself imply a P-vs-NP separation.

**Learning:** the useful object is the anchor-dependent least fixed point of the rule flags, not just an acyclic monotone formula for a single threshold. A tempting lower-bound shortcut would count all minimal transversals, since the current witness realizes all of them. That shortcut is invalid until one proves arbitrary covers must realize many contexts. Preserve this distinction when interpreting the n=6 search.

## Idea 94 - A failure anatomy for shared-certificate lower bounds

**Status: exact semantic decomposition established for this cover model; the proposed selector-realization invariant is open.** The repeated failures are not random. They occur at distinct layers that earlier arguments often collapsed into one:

1. **Certificate geometry.** For each anchor $a$, a root proof must expose literal leaves whose coordinates hit every high-point disagreement set. This is necessary and gives the one-anchor $N-o(N)$ leaf lower bound in the Gap-MCSP setting, but $Q=[N]$ is already a valid high-free certificate for every anchor. Certificate existence or length alone cannot explain cross-anchor difficulty.
2. **Selector choice.** A universal cover needs only one usable transversal per anchor. Counting all minimal transversals or all derivations overcharges it: the n=5 canonical-selector cover works from one preselected minimum transversal at each of its 16 anchors.
3. **Shared realization.** The chosen signed leaves $(i,a_i)$ must be routed by one fixed endpoint network. This is the unpaid obligation. Raw rule fanout does not measure it: in the saved n=4 four-rule and n=5 six-rule weight-one covers, every rule fires at every low anchor. The radius-two n=5 witness shows the other possibility: its nonfinal rules spill onto some weight-three anchors, while its sole disjoint rule still fires exactly on the low ball. A valid potential must capture which anchor-dependent leaf choices can share intermediate carrier proofs and how those proofs' false-positive sets are filtered at the disjoint rule.
4. **Transfer.** Even a growing toy cover number matters only if it survives in an explicit low-circuit/high-circuit promise at the required scale and yields the desired circuit lower bound. The symmetric Hamming-threshold examples fail this check: sorting networks give an $O(n\log^2 n)$ universal upper bound.

The exact support semantics make the missing layer visible. For fixed endpoints $(E_j,H_j)$, put $K_j=E_j\cap H_j$ and let $S_t(X)$ be the anchors for which carrier $X$ is derivable after $t$ closure rounds. Then

$$S_0(X)=\{a:\exists i,\ B_{i,a_i}\subseteq X\},\qquad
S_{t+1}(X)=S_t(X)\cup\bigcup_{j:K_j\subseteq X}\big(S_t(E_j)\cap S_t(H_j)\big).$$

The least fixed point at $X=\varnothing$ must contain every anchor. For each individual anchor, its root antichain $\mathcal C_{\varnothing}(a)$ is contained in the family of high-free transversals of $\mathcal H_a=\{\{i:a_i\ne x_i\}:x\in U\}$. What is not captured by either equation alone is a lower bound on how many fixed rules are required to realize at least one such context for every anchor. This restates the target precisely; it is not yet a new lower-bound theorem.

The project's new working term is **selector realization debt**: the minimum size of a shared relay program needed to choose and combine one sound, anchor-specific signed transversal for each member of a promise family, when endpoint sets are arbitrary and all mixed derivations are allowed. The phrase is a research label, not a standard measure or a claim that the quantity differs from the original cover complexity. To become useful it needs a dual certificate or a structural theorem that lower-bounds it without enumerating the exponentially large root antichains.

### What the failures say about the foundations

The self-reference and proof-system experiments repeatedly spend their budget on the quantifiers. A diagonal statement can exclude the outputs or proofs visible to its seed, but after the diagonal formula, verifier, or proof cutoff is encoded, the time exponent and description length change. The saved attempts found no contraction that beats this growth. Changing the ambient formal language does not remove that accounting: it helps only if it yields a theorem whose encoding and uniform verifier stay within the needed resource bounds. Likewise, an unprovability result for one theory or one proof system is not a separation of P from NP unless the quantifiers cover every relevant algorithm/proof system and the implication back to P-vs-NP is proved.

The broad literature barriers explain why familiar proof shapes keep hitting walls, but they are not impossibility theorems for the problem. Baker, Gill, and Solovay constructed oracles on both sides of P-versus-NP, so a proof whose reasoning survives arbitrary oracle access cannot settle the question ([original paper](https://doi.org/10.1137/0204037)). Razborov and Rudich show, under cryptographic pseudorandom-function assumptions, why large, efficiently recognizable circuit-lower-bound properties cannot prove the desired general circuit lower bounds ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcss.1997.1494)). Aaronson and Wigderson identify the further algebrization barrier and argue that P-vs-NP needs non-algebrizing methods ([paper](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/eccc-reports/2008/TR08-005/Paper.pdf)). These results diagnose technique classes; they do not say every combinatorial or self-referential idea is blocked.

Our current relay-cover route has a known, particularly relevant constraint: Cavalar and Oliveira characterize cover complexity through cyclic Boolean circuits ([2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14117)). So translating the carrier process into cyclic-circuit language is an audit and simplification, not itself a novel resolution. The creative opportunity is to exploit the *specific promise anchors and signed-slice generators* to prove a lower bound on selector realization that does not collapse to known cyclic-circuit upper bounds or a barrier-prone generic property.

### Next falsifiable target

For the radius-two family, compare the unrestricted six-rule search with the n=6 fixed-selector search already running. If the restricted model succeeds, inspect whether its chosen selector is implementable by a simple recurrence; if it fails, that only rules out this one lexicographic selector, not all selectors. Then derive the per-rule Boolean support functions from the saved endpoints and check whether the shared network is merely a disguised threshold/sorting computation. Do not infer asymptotic growth from $n=5,6$. For a genuinely useful next family, require at the outset (i) a precise anchor language, (ii) all high-free signed transversals, (iii) arbitrary-endpoint closure, (iv) a selector-realization lower-bound target, and (v) a magnification transfer calculation.

## Idea 95 - Diagonalize against small relays without enumerating their free endpoints

**Status: the naive explicit diagonalization is blocked by a quantified description-length calculation; a faster implicit construction remains open.** A tempting use of the random-cover counting argument is to define an explicit target set that diagonalizes against every $m$-rule endpoint list. For a fixed generator family $\mathcal B$, the universal fusion construction depends only on the inclusion relations among $m$ rule pairs and the $b=|\mathcal B|$ generators. There are at most $O(m(b+m))$ such bits, so at most

$$2^{O(m(b+m))}$$

distinct target sets can be produced by $m$-rule lists. This explains why random target sets have high cover complexity, as in the random-graph result of Cavalar and Oliveira ([2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14117)). It does *not* by itself make the hard target explicit.

The direct diagonal algorithm would have to range over those incidence descriptions. For coordinate-slice bases, $b=2N$, so its straightforward running time is $2^{O(mN+m^2)}$. In Gap-MCSP magnification, the truth-table input length is $N=2^n$; even a constant $m$ gives an exponential-in-$N$ enumeration, while $m=N^\epsilon$ gives time $2^{N^{1+\epsilon}}$. These are costs of this enumeration method, not lower bounds against every possible diagonal algorithm. They show exactly why the random-instance count does not produce a uniform NP predicate or a low-description explicit family by itself.

There is a precise obstruction to compressing *all raw endpoint profiles* generically. In the full cube $U=\{0,1\}^N$, for each $S\subseteq[N]$ of size $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$ define $E_S=\bigcup_{i\in S}B_{i,0}$. Then $B_{j,0}\subseteq E_S$ exactly when $j\in S$, while no $B_{j,1}$ is contained in $E_S$. Distinct equal-size $S,T$ give incomparable $E_S,E_T$. Thus an ordered list of $2m$ distinct such endpoints realizes at least $(\binom{N}{\lfloor N/2\rfloor})_{2m}=2^{\Omega(mN)}$ distinct full incidence profiles whenever $m$ is at most a fixed fraction of that binomial coefficient. The $ÃƒÆ’Ã…Â½Ãƒâ€šÃ‚Â©(mN)$ raw profile information is real, not just an inefficient data format. A useful compression must therefore quotient profiles that induce the same target, or exploit the special Gap-MCSP promise; it cannot simply losslessly encode every arbitrary endpoint profile in fewer bits.

The new research target is an **implicit endpoint diagonal**: exploit the semantic constraints on relay endpoints to defeat all incidence types without listing them, while keeping the resulting target's verifier within the complexity class needed for magnification. The first falsification tests are to derive whether a candidate universal evaluator can quantify over endpoint types in polynomial space/time, and whether this merely raises the target from NP to a higher alternation class. Do not claim an explicit lower bound unless the full quantifier and runtime accounting closes. This is a fresh route to investigate, not a proposed solution.

## Idea 96 - Self-indexing diagonalization and the padding recursion

**Status: a natural self-indexing construction exposes a circular encoding cost; the uncompressed version does not reach the magnification scale.** Let $b=|\mathcal B|$ and consider all $m$-rule relay outcomes. Their universal descriptions use $O(m(b+m))$ endpoint/basis inclusion bits. A first attempt is to append a tag $z$ naming one such incidence type $\tau$, and on the tag-$\tau$ slice define a target opposite to the set universally generated by $\tau$. If the tag has room for every type, each $m$-rule cover is contradicted on its own tag slice. The target can be evaluated by simulating the universal generator from $\tau$ and the basis-membership pattern, so this looks like a way to turn nonconstructive counting into a uniform diagonal.

The self-indexing exposes a circularity. If the tag coordinates are *not* included in the generator basis, then the target may vary with the tag while every generated set is tag-invariant; it is outside the representable family for a trivial, non-transferable reason. If the tag coordinates *are* ordinary basis coordinates, they add two literal slices per bit. A cover may now use those slices, so its full incidence type must also describe relations with the tag generators. Under the naive raw incidence-matrix encoding, the tag length would have to satisfy

$$L=2m(b+2L)+4m^2,$$

where $2m(b+2L)$ bits record endpoint-to-generator incidences and $4m^2$ record endpoint-to-endpoint incidences. The right side already contains $4mL$, so no nonnegative finite $L$ solves this raw self-indexing equation for $m\ge1$. This is a coding-accounting obstruction to this particular construction, not a theorem against compressed or implicit diagonals; an escape would need a proved compression of the relevant type patterns.

Even if one ignores that recursive closure and indexes only types over the original $b=2N$ slices, the raw code uses $L=O(mN+m^2)$ tag bits. The diagonal lower bound $m$ is then at most $O(\sqrt{M})$ in enlarged input length $M=N+L$ (and can be smaller when $N$ dominates), far short of the superlinear Gap-MCSP cover threshold recorded in the audit. Thus the attempt explains why a self-reference tag does not by itself create the needed hardness.

**Escape condition:** compress the relevant endpoint types relative to the actual promise, or prove that arbitrary tag-dependent endpoints can be normalized to a tag-independent normal form without increasing rule count. Either claim must be shown before spending more effort. A small-$b,m$ exhaustive model could test proposed normal forms, but finite success would not resolve the self-indexing recurrence.

## Idea 97 - Causality-corrected false-positive cancellation at disjoint seeds

**Status: exact first-seed decomposition and six exhaustively computed finite covers; no lower bound follows yet.** Let $D=\{j:E_j\cap H_j=\varnothing\}$ be the disjoint rules. For a fixed anchor $a$, let $C^{-}(a)$ be the least closure from its literal generators using only the non-disjoint rules. Assuming no literal generator is itself empty (true in the audited toys), the exact output criterion is

$$\varnothing\text{ is derivable from }a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists j\in D:\ E_j,H_j\in C^{-}(a).$$

For the reverse direction, an active disjoint pair immediately derives $\varnothing$. For the forward direction, take the first disjoint rule that fires in any derivation of $\varnothing$; before it fires, only non-disjoint rules have been used, so its endpoints are already in $C^{-}(a)$. This excludes the circular contamination that appears if one measures endpoint supports only after the full least fixed point. Consequently the low set is exactly covered by at most $|D|$ first-seed intersections from the seedless closure, and none of those intersections contains a high anchor. This gives an exact first-seed normal form at unchanged rule count: non-disjoint pairs form the relay core, and disjoint pairs are terminal outputs whose activation tests the core but whose intersections are never fed back into it. Let $\Sigma_X^\Gamma$ be the anchor support of carrier $X$ in the closure generated by the non-disjoint core $\Gamma$. On the promise $P=A\cup U$, its output condition is exactly

$$A=\left(\bigcup_{(E,H)\in\Delta}\Sigma_E^\Gamma\cap\Sigma_H^\Gamma\right)\cap P,
\qquad U\cap\bigcup_{(E,H)\in\Delta}(\Sigma_E^\Gamma\cap\Sigma_H^\Gamma)=\varnothing,$$

where $\Delta$ is the family of terminal disjoint seeds. Minimizing $|\Gamma|+|\Delta|$ over such pairs is equivalent to the original cover problem. This is an equivalent presentation of the same cover quantity, not a new measure.

This normal form sharpens the one-anchor resource accounting. If the full list has $m$ rules and $d=|D|$ disjoint seeds, then its relay core has $p=m-d$ non-disjoint rules. A first-seed proof for one low anchor uses at most those $p$ core rules and one terminal seed, hence at most $p+2$ literal leaves by the proof-DAG bound. The Gap-MCSP high-free-cylinder argument requires $N-o(N)$ leaves, giving $p\ge N-o(N)-2$ and therefore $m\ge N-o(N)-2+d$. This is a precise refinement, but still only near-linear when $d$ is small; if $d$ is large, the seed count itself contributes to the lower bound.

The diagnostic [experiment_disjoint_seed_error_profiles.py](experiment_disjoint_seed_error_profiles.py) computes both final supports and first-seed supports across six saved covers. For the five one-seed covers, the first seed covers every low anchor. A sixth five-rule n=5 radius-two cover has two disjoint seeds. Its *final* support masks misleadingly make each seed appear to cover all 16 low anchors because, after the first seed derives $\varnothing$, upward closure feeds that result into the other seed. When all disjoint rules are removed before measuring premises, seed 0 covers 14 low anchors and seed 3 covers 9; their union covers all 16 and their overlap is 7. Each first-seed intersection is still high-free.

| First seed | Rules in cover | Premise support sizes before any disjoint seed | High spill counts | Low anchors covered |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| n=4, weight one | 4 | 12, 6 | 7, 1 | 5/5 |
| n=5, weight one | 6 | 7, 13 | 1, 7 | 6/6 |
| n=4, scrambled simplex | 5 | 14, 7 | 9, 2 | 5/5 |
| n=5, radius two, native | 5 | 21, 22 | 5, 6 | 16/16 |
| n=5, radius two, canonical selector | 5 | 19, 23 | 3, 7 | 16/16 |
| n=5, radius two, multiple-seed cover, rule 0 | 5 | 18, 20 | 3, 5 | 14/16 |
| n=5, radius two, multiple-seed cover, rule 3 | 5 | 16, 16 | 5, 2 | 9/16 |

Each pair of first-premise supports has zero overlap on the high set. The new SAT constraint in [experiment_sparse_ball_seed_tradeoff.py](experiment_sparse_ball_seed_tradeoff.py) tests how many disjoint seeds can fit into an n=5, five-rule cover under valid S5 symmetry breaking: one and two seeds are SAT with directly verified covers; at least three is UNSAT by solver status, with no proof trace. The two-seed witness is saved in [experiment_sparse_ball_multiple_disjoint_witness.py](experiment_sparse_ball_multiple_disjoint_witness.py). This finite tradeoff shows why final fixed-point support masks need a first-seed filter: after one seed derives empty, upward closure may make another seed's endpoints appear active on every low anchor.

The companion [experiment_preseed_context_profiles.py](experiment_preseed_context_profiles.py) audits the leaf antichains with all disjoint rules removed. For every anchor, every subset of literal generators, and every listed carrier, its context recurrence agrees with direct closure; every combined first-seed context is checked against every high point. On the three n=5 radius-two witnesses, minimum first-seed context size is exactly 3. The number of minimal contexts per activated anchor ranges from 1 to 10 for the native single-seed cover, 1 to 10 for the canonical-selector cover, 1 to 8 for seed 0 of the two-seed cover, and 1 to 4 for seed 3. This is a causal context audit, not evidence that context multiplicity forces cover size.
This suggests a more precise target: lower-bound the number of non-disjoint relay rules needed to produce a small family of zero-error first-seed intersections that covers all low anchors. The exact finite data are not an asymptotic theorem. Any proof must optimize over all disjoint seeds, arbitrary endpoints, and mixed derivations; support sizes alone are insufficient. The perspective is related to the established cyclic-circuit characterization and is not claimed as a new general framework.

## Idea 98 - Selector grammars versus flat cylinder covers

**Status: the flat-cover lower-bound route is falsified as a measure of shared program size; the grammar viewpoint is an audit language, not a new invariant.** A proof context is a partial assignment to input coordinates. It denotes a subcube; it is *high-free* when that subcube contains no point of $U$. Every first-seed derivation supplies such a context for its anchor. Flattening all proof contexts therefore gives a cover of the low set by high-free subcubes, but forgets how a short relay network shares the construction of many contexts.

There is an exact benchmark on the Hamming-threshold toy. Let $A=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:|x|\le k\}$ and $U=\{x:|x|>k\}$. The minimum number of high-free subcubes needed to cover $A$ is exactly $\binom nk$. A high-free subcube containing a weight-$k$ point must fix all $n-k$ zero coordinates of that point to zero: otherwise its free coordinates can be set to one to create a point of weight at least $k+1$. Distinct weight-$k$ points consequently require distinct subcubes. Conversely, for every $k$-set $S$, the subcube fixing all coordinates outside $S$ to zero is high-free, and these $\binom nk$ subcubes cover all of $A$.

The relay witnesses compress this flat family. The exact n=4, $k=2$ two-rule cover in [weight_two_ball_n4_m2.txt](weight_two_ball_n4_m2.txt) has two terminal disjoint seeds. [experiment_sparse_ball_subcube_grammar.py](experiment_sparse_ball_subcube_grammar.py) reconstructs six distinct signed root contexts from those seeds; they are exactly the minimum six-cylinder cover, with four contexts generated per seed and overlap between the seeds. All eleven low anchors are covered. For n=5, $k=2$, the minimum flat cover has ten cylinders, while the native five-rule witness generates twelve signed root contexts and the canonical-selector and two-seed witnesses each generate fifteen. Every generated context is checked high-free. These are exhaustive finite context computations, not a growing lower bound.

More decisively, threshold functions have sorting-network relay constructions with $O(n\log^2 n)$ rules, while their flat cylinder-cover numbers can be exponential: at $n=64,k=32$, $\binom{64}{32}=1{,}832{,}624{,}140{,}942{,}590{,}534$ and the Batcher network has 672 comparator rules. The exact bitonic construction and its closure checks on small dimensions are in [experiment_threshold_sorting_cover.py](experiment_threshold_sorting_cover.py). Thus certificate packing, minimum cylinder cover, and proof-context count alone cannot yield a strong relay lower bound; they measure unshared descriptions and ignore circuit reuse. This explains another repeated failure: establishing that every anchor needs many certificate leaves does not charge the shared program for routing those certificates.

The useful language is a **selector grammar**: signed generator leaves, alternative derivations (OR), and context unions (AND), with terminal first-seed tests at the root. This grammar exposes the sharing that a flat cylinder cover erases. Its support equations are the existing monotone/cyclic-circuit view of relay covers; Cavalar and Oliveira give an exact cover-complexity/cyclic-construction characterization ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14117)). So the grammar name is not a novelty claim and its minimum size may simply re-express the cover measure. A real advance would need a dual bound on grammar size, robust to arbitrary endpoint choices, and then a transfer from the Gap-MCSP anchor family to circuit lower bounds.

**Next falsifiable tests:** (i) extract the signed-context grammar from a restarted n=6 search only if a specific structural prediction warrants it and compare its term compression with the flat $\binom 62=15$ cover; (ii) seek a structural lower bound on shared grammar size rather than on the number or width of its contexts; (iii) require that any proposed bound survive sorting-network and threshold simplifications before applying it to Gap-MCSP. No asymptotic result or P-vs-NP breakthrough follows yet.

## Idea 99 - Co-occurrence cuts and core-built selector bundles

**Status: exact overlap lemma plus a finite mechanism for the n=4 to n=5 threshold jump; no growing relay lower bound yet.** For any high universe $U$ and matching literal slices $B_g,B_h$, define them to co-occur when $B_g\cap B_h\cap U\ne\varnothing$. If a terminal first-seed pair has disjoint endpoints $E\cap H=\varnothing$, then it is impossible to have $B_g\subseteq E$ and $B_h\subseteq H$ for a co-occurring pair: their common high point would lie in both endpoints. Therefore the literal generators directly available on opposite sides of any terminal seed form an anticomplete pair in the generator co-occurrence graph. This is an exact restriction on base-only selector splits; it does not constrain contexts that the non-disjoint core has already bundled into compound carriers.

For the threshold promise $A=\{x:|x|\le k\}$, $U=\{x:|x|\ge k+1\}$, take the zero slices $Z_i=\{x\in U:x_i=0\}$. When $n\ge k+3$, every two distinct $Z_i,Z_j$ co-occur: set those two coordinates to zero and all others to one, obtaining weight $n-2\ge k+1$. Thus their co-occurrence graph is complete. At the boundary $(n,k)=(4,2)$, $U$ has at most one zero in every point, so the graph has no edges. The two-rule witness [weight_two_ball_n4_m2.txt](weight_two_ball_n4_m2.txt) exploits exactly this: seed 0 directly splits zero literals as $\{0,1\}|\{2,3\}$ and seed 1 as $\{0,2\}|\{1,3\}$. Their crossing pairs jointly realize all six two-zero top-layer selectors. The two cuts separate every coordinate pair.

At $(n,k)=(5,2)$, every pair of zero slices overlaps on a high point, so no disjoint seed can put even one directly contained zero slice on each side. Also, every high-free context compatible with a weight-two anchor must fix all three zero coordinates; the top-layer minimal context therefore cannot be produced from the two endpoints' base singleton leaves alone. The modified [experiment_sparse_ball_subcube_grammar.py](experiment_sparse_ball_subcube_grammar.py) confirms the full overlap graphs (0/6 edges at n=4, 10/10 at n=5), verifies direct closure for every low and high point, and records the top-layer split sizes. In all saved n=5 witnesses, each minimum-width split uses at least one context produced through the relay core; the base zero literals at each disjoint seed lie on at most one endpoint side. This gives a concrete explanation of why the elegant two-cut construction stops working at n=5.

The same diagnostic on the weight-at-most-one witnesses gives complete zero-slice overlap graphs at both n=4 and n=5 (6/6 and 10/10 edges). Their terminal-seed top-layer contexts also require a core-derived side; the saved relay sizes are four and six rules. Together these toys support a precise mechanism, not a growth law: once high points can realize any pair of zero coordinates, a terminal seed cannot split those literals directly, so its shared core must first package them into compound contexts.

The possible next theorem would charge the core for generating compound selector blocks that can be combined at a disjoint seed without sharing a high witness. But threshold functions have small counting circuits, so a lower bound on the number of such blocks is defeated by circuit reuse just as the flat-cover bound is. To matter for P versus NP, a co-occurrence invariant must bound shared core size for the Gap-MCSP promise and survive arbitrary endpoints. The finite cut example is a mechanism diagnosis, not evidence of an asymptotic hardness gap.

## Idea 100 - Separating-code construction for the one-zero high layer

**Status: exact logarithmic construction for an easy threshold toy; checked on dimensions 2 through 12; not a P-vs-NP route by itself.** Let the high universe be $U_n=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:|x|\ge n-1\}$, so every high string has at most one zero. Let $d=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ and assign distinct binary codewords $c(i)\in\{0,1\}^d$ to the $n$ coordinates. For each code bit $t$, set

$$E_t=\bigcup_{i:c(i)_t=0}B_{i,0},\qquad H_t=\bigcup_{i:c(i)_t=1}B_{i,0},$$

where $B_{i,0}=\{x\in U_n:x_i=0\}$. Every pair $(E_t,H_t)$ is disjoint: a high string has at most one zero coordinate and so cannot belong to both sides. If a low anchor has weight at most $n-2$, it has at least two zero coordinates $i\ne j$. Their codewords differ on some bit $t$, so its matching zero-slice generators activate both $E_t$ and $H_t$, and that seed derives $\emptyset$. A high point activates at most one side of every seed. Hence these $d$ terminal rules give an exact universal cover.

Within the restricted construction class where each terminal endpoint is a union of zero slices and activation uses the base generators directly, this is optimal: the coordinate codewords must be pairwise distinct to separate every pair of zero positions, requiring $2^d\ge n$. This does **not** prove optimality against arbitrary relay endpoints; the full-endpoint PySAT search gives solver-derived UNSAT for every smaller rule count at n=3 through 10, matching the constructed upper bounds $2,2,3,3,3,3,4,4$. These UNSAT checks have no proof traces. The large-n runs use the new near-full column symmetry: sort the endpoint-membership columns of the $n$ single-zero high points. This is a complete canonicalization under $S_n$ for this promise, and its SAT statuses match the full-permutation symmetry encoding through n=7 in [experiment_near_full_symmetry_crosscheck.py](experiment_near_full_symmetry_crosscheck.py).

The new [experiment_near_full_cube_cut_cover.py](experiment_near_full_cube_cut_cover.py) independently checks full closure on every low and high point for n=2 through 12, with only $n+1$ high points per instance. The companion [experiment_near_full_cube_minimum_search.py](experiment_near_full_cube_minimum_search.py) saves normalized SAT outputs in `near_full_cube_n*_m*_solver.txt`; [experiment_near_full_symmetry_crosscheck.py](experiment_near_full_symmetry_crosscheck.py) compares its column-sorted symmetry with full $S_n$ lex leaders through n=7. This construction explains the n=4 radius-two two-seed witness as a pair-separating code. It is a calibration result for Idea 99, not a hard family: recognizing weight at most $n-2$ is easy and the high universe is tiny. A harder extension would need to preserve disjointness while the high set allows multiple zero coordinates; direct cut endpoints fail as soon as high strings can contain zeros from both sides.

## Idea 101 - Endpoint-signature fooling bound from paired high witnesses

**Status: proved lower bound for the one-zero high universe, valid for arbitrary relay endpoints; only logarithmic and not transferred to Gap-MCSP.** Continue with $U_n=\{\mathbf1^n,u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$, where $u_i$ is the all-ones string with coordinate $i$ zero, and low anchors all strings of weight at most $n-2$. A relay with $m$ rules has $2m$ endpoint sets. Give each $u_i$ its endpoint-membership signature

$$v_i=\big(\mathbf1[u_i\in E_1],\mathbf1[u_i\in H_1],\ldots,\mathbf1[u_i\in E_m],\mathbf1[u_i\in H_m]\big)\in\{0,1\}^{2m}.$$

These signatures must all be distinct. Suppose $v_i=v_j$ for $i\ne j$. Consider the low anchor $a^{ij}$ with zeros exactly at $i,j$ and the high anchor $u_i$. For any carrier $X$ among an endpoint, a rule intersection, or $\emptyset$, membership of $u_i$ and $u_j$ agrees: endpoint membership agrees by assumption, and intersection membership is the AND of endpoint memberships. Every matching generator of $a^{ij}$ contained in $X$ then implies a matching generator of $u_i$ is contained in $X$: the zero slice at $i$ is $\{u_i\}$; if the zero slice at $j$, $\{u_j\}$, is contained in $X$, signature equality gives $u_i\in X$ as well; and for every coordinate $q\notin\{i,j\}$ both anchors have bit one and use the same one-slice. Thus the initially supported carriers for $a^{ij}$ are a subset of those for $u_i$. The least-fixed-point rule recurrence is monotone in its initial carrier set, so deriving $\emptyset$ for $a^{ij}$ would also derive it for high anchor $u_i$, a contradiction. Hence $n\le2^{2m}$ and

$$m\ge\left\lceil\tfrac12\log_2 n\right\rceil.$$

This argument allows arbitrary endpoint subsets and every mixed relay derivation; it is not a restriction to the cut construction. [experiment_near_full_cube_cut_cover.py](experiment_near_full_cube_cut_cover.py) checks that the constructed cut covers have $n$ distinct signatures for $n=2,\ldots,12$. The SAT searches in Idea 100 give solver-derived matching minima for n=3 through 6, but those are not proof certificates. The general bound is within a factor of two of the $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ upper construction.

The transfer test is severe for two separate reasons. First, in this toy each zero generator is a singleton high point, so endpoint membership of $u_i$ decides whether that entire generator is contained in an endpoint. Gap-MCSP's matching literal slices are large sets of high tables; equality of two point-membership signatures would not imply equality or domination of those slice-containment flags. Second, the low-anchor hybrids used in the toy are Hamming-near to the high witnesses, which the Gap-MCSP distance promise forbids. A new witness family must recover the generator-domination relation without singleton slices or nearby low points. There is also a scale ceiling: injectivity gives $m\ge\frac12\log_2|S|$ for witness family $S$, and $|S|\le2^N$ for truth tables of length $N$, so even the largest possible family gives only $m\ge N/2$; generally the bound is smaller. It cannot meet the current superlinear magnification target on its own. It is a genuine toy lower-bound lemma and a map of the missing transfer, not P-vs-NP progress.

## Idea 102 - Seed activation codes and the failure of seed independence

**Status: exact normal-form decoder and a two-seed counterexample to pairwise independence; no size lower bound yet.** I tried to turn cross-anchor context splits into a Bollobas-style set-pair bound. The first implementation accidentally bucketed contexts by size and erased which terminal seed produced them. After retaining seed identity, the zero-crossing result for one-seed witnesses was just soundness: every left proof context lies inside that seed's endpoint $E_r$, every right context inside $H_r$, and $E_r\cap H_r=\emptyset$. That observation gives no cross-anchor restriction beyond correctness.

Multiple seeds behave differently. In the saved n=5 two-seed witness, a left context generated for seed 0 and a right context for seed 3 share the high point $10101_2$; in the reverse direction a left context for seed 3 and right context for seed 0 share $01011_2$. Thus opposite-side supports can have a genuine two-cycle across seeds. Any argument that orders seeds by disjoint support, assumes cross-seed independence, or applies a same-seed cross-intersection theorem to all seed contexts is false.

There is an exact compact language for the first-seed normal form. Let $D$ be the set of disjoint rules and close the initial literal generators using only non-disjoint rules. For each anchor $x$, set

$$L(x)=\{r\in D:E_r\text{ is active in this core closure}\},\qquad R(x)=\{r\in D:H_r\text{ is active in this core closure}\}.$$

Then the relay accepts $x$ exactly when $L(x)\cap R(x)\ne\emptyset$. This follows because a disjoint rule derives $\emptyset$ as soon as both premises are active, while non-disjoint rules cannot derive $\emptyset$; once any disjoint rule fires it produces every listed carrier, so no later seed contributes a distinct first event. Call $(L(x),R(x))$ the **seed activation code**. The valid promise requires intersecting codes on all low anchors and disjoint codes on all high anchors.

The exhaustive diagnostic [experiment_seed_activation_codes.py](experiment_seed_activation_codes.py) verifies this decoder for six saved covers. Four of the one-seed covers have four distinct activation codes (one low code and three high codes); the basis-exception example has three codes. The n=5 two-seed witness has 12 distinct codes, with five low-code classes and seven high-code classes. The cross-context check is in [experiment_context_split_cross_compatibility.py](experiment_context_split_cross_compatibility.py); it reports the two reciprocal high-point crossings above.

This language makes the remaining obstacle clearer but does not pay it: low anchors may collapse to one activation code, and many high anchors may collapse to another. Counting seed codes or charging seed interaction alone therefore cannot lower-bound the core. The actual objects $L(x),R(x)$ are computed by a shared non-disjoint relay circuit over endpoint-specific literal-containment predicates. A useful next result must lower-bound the complexity of that map for a hard anchor promise, while allowing reciprocal cross-seed overlaps and arbitrary endpoints. Re-run the activation-code and seed-crossing audit on any n=6 witness; do not revive the discarded seed-independence or size-bucketed Bollobas argument.

## Idea 103 - Dominance cuts among initial carrier supports

**Status: exact necessary separation lemma; finite covers need only 5--8 carrier tests, so no useful lower bound yet.** For an anchor $x$, let $S_x$ be the set of all tracked carriers initially activated by its matching literal slices. If $x$ is low, $y$ is high, and $S_x\subseteq S_y$, monotonicity of the closure recurrence forces every carrier derived from $x$ to be derived from $y$. This contradicts low/high correctness. Therefore every low/high pair must have some tracked carrier $C$ active at $x$ and inactive at $y$.

Each carrier predicate $C$ consequently defines a directed cut rectangle

$$\{x\in A:C\in S_x\}\times\{y\in U:C\notin S_y\},$$

and the carrier rectangles must cover $A\times U$. A relay with $m$ rules tracks at most $3m+1$ distinct carriers (two endpoints per rule, one intersection per rule, and $\emptyset$). Thus a promise-specific lower bound on the minimum number of such carrier cuts would imply a relay lower bound, even before accounting for how the relay computes them.
