This is a necessary condition only; an arbitrary family of separating carrier predicates need not be realizable by a relay.

The exact diagnostic [experiment_support_dominance_cut_cover.py](experiment_support_dominance_cut_cover.py) computes the minimum carrier-predicate set cover of all low/high anchor pairs for six verified small witnesses. The values are 5, 5, 8, 6, 5, and 5 carriers for relay sizes 4, 6, 5, 5, 5, and 5, respectively. A single carrier separates between 18 and 121 of the 55 or 256 low/high pairs. More decisively, all six have the literal-slice noncontainment property: no distinct matching slice is contained in another. Under this condition the $2N$ literal slices themselves are coordinate tests that separate every distinct low/high pair: for $x\ne y$, choose a differing coordinate $i$ and use $B_{i,x_i}$. Thus the *relaxed* carrier-cut cover always has an $O(N)$ witness, regardless of how difficult the target language is. On the six toys its exact literal-cut minima are 4, 5, 8, 5, 5, and 5.

This same ceiling applies to the project's Gap-MCSP promise. Here the high universe is $Z_{n,\beta}=\{z:\operatorname{CC}(z)\ge s_2\}$, and the number of tables outside it is at most $2^{O(s_2\log(n+s_2))}=2^{O(N^\beta\log N)}=2^{o(N)}$ for fixed $\beta<1$. Every face fixing any two truth-table coordinates has $2^{N-2}$ points, so for sufficiently large $N$ it contains a point of $Z_{n,\beta}$. Consequently no distinct literal slice is contained in another, and the $2N$ literal-carrier cuts separate every anchor in $Y$ from every point in $Z$. This does not say those cuts form a valid relay; it proves that the pair-separation relaxation has a linear-size witness even on the hard promise.

This closes the dominance cut cover as a standalone route to a superlinear lower bound. It forgets the central constraint: a relay must make its chosen carriers work together through the actual rule recurrence, and the cheap coordinate cuts need not yield a valid cover. The concept overlaps a standard monotone-dominance fooling argument; it can remain a diagnostic for a proposed relay, but a new lower bound must charge computation or seed-compatible composition rather than pair separation alone. Do not spend further work optimizing this relaxation.

## Idea 104 - Transfer the core through branching programs

**Status: exact read-once simulation, but the lower-bound transfer has a linear ceiling.** For each endpoint $C$, define its base clause

$$\phi_C(x)=\bigvee_{i:B_{i,0}\subseteq C}[x_i=0]\ \vee\ \bigvee_{i:B_{i,1}\subseteq C}[x_i=1].$$

The initial active/inactive state of all $2m$ endpoints is precisely the vector $(\phi_{E_1}(x),\phi_{H_1}(x),\ldots,\phi_{E_m}(x),\phi_{H_m}(x))$. Once that premise-state vector is known, the fixed-point closure and terminal-seed test are a fixed Boolean function $g_R$ of the vector; all endpoint incidence and rule structure is hardwired into $g_R$. Therefore the relay's acceptance function factors exactly as $g_R(\phi_{E_1}(x),\phi_{H_1}(x),\ldots)$. A read-once oblivious branching program can scan the $N$ bits, maintain the $2m$ clause-satisfaction flags, and label each final state by $g_R$. Its width is at most $2^{2m}$ and its size is $O(N2^{2m})$, even with arbitrary endpoint profiles.

This is a precise representation change, but it does not advance the magnification target. Known general branching-program lower bounds for total MCSP are polynomial, giving at most $m=\Omega(\log N)$ through this simulation; read-once co-nondeterministic lower bounds reach $2^{\widetilde\Omega(N)}$, which could imply only $m=\widetilde\Omega(N)$ even if they applied to the same promise. They do not: both results concern total MCSP, whereas our branching program is only required to separate $Y$ from $Z$. The current proof-DAG bound $m\ge N-o(N)$ is stronger than what this route transfers, and even a promise-specific exponential read-once lower bound cannot force superlinear $m$ through a width $2^{O(m)}$ encoding on $N$ input bits.

Close this route as a source of the required superlinear cover lower bound. Keep the exact read-once simulation as an audit tool for candidate covers; reopen only if it reveals a smaller semantic state encoding or connects to a model whose lower bound exceeds the linear state ceiling. Sources: [Cheraghchi et al., ICALP 2019](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2019.39), [Cheraghchi et al., STACS 2021](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2021.23).

## Idea 105 - Clause shadows and hidden carrier residue

**Status: exact density lemma; useful representation language, but it exposes why clause-state compression loses the hard part.** For each carrier $C\subseteq Z$, define its clause shadow

$$\operatorname{sh}(C)=\{(i,b):B_{i,b}\subseteq C\},\qquad B_{i,b}=\{z\in Z:z_i=b\}.$$

The anchor initially activates $C$ exactly when it satisfies the clause $\bigvee_{(i,b)\in\operatorname{sh}(C)}[x_i=b]$. Given a consistent literal set $S$, the smallest carrier with those mandatory slices is $C_S=\bigcup_{(i,b)\in S}B_{i,b}$. Write $M=2^N-|Z|$ for the number of tables outside the high universe. For any literal $\ell\notin S$, the assignments satisfying $\ell$ and falsifying every literal in $S$ form a face of size at least $2^{N-|S|-1}$. If

$$2^{N-|S|-1}>M,$$

that face contains a high table, so $B_\ell\nsubseteq C_S$. Hence $\operatorname{sh}(C_S)=S$. In the Gap-MCSP regime $M=2^{O(N^\beta\log N)}$, every consistent clause of width at most $N-O(N^\beta\log N)$ is realizable exactly as a carrier's initial test. The finite audit [experiment_clause_shadow_completeness.py](experiment_clause_shadow_completeness.py) enumerates all $3^n$ consistent literal sets on six saved witnesses; where the density inequality applies, every predicted clause profile is exact. The three sparse-ball toys violate the density hypothesis and show extra profiles already at width two.

The failure is equally informative: a clause shadow does **not** determine carrier interaction. In the n=4 dense toy, $\varnothing$ and a singleton high-point carrier have the same empty shadow, yet for $E=H=\{z\}$, the inclusion $E\cap H\subseteq C$ is false for the first consequent and true for the second. The script checks this residue witness. Thus the read-once flag vector captures all input-dependent initial activation, while arbitrary carrier residue can still encode the fixed intersection decoder. This explains why counting clause states or importing a clause lower bound stalls: it discards the uncharged set geometry that decides which relay rules fire.

The promising follow-up is a two-layer theory: (i) clause shadows, which are almost fully expressive under the dense promise, and (ii) residual intersection geometry, which is invisible to those shadows but controls closure. Any superlinear lower bound must couple both layers. A valid simplification would need a theorem that normalizes or charges the residuals while preserving all low-anchor derivations and high-anchor soundness; merely replacing $C$ by $C_{\operatorname{sh}(C)}$ is invalid.

## Idea 106 - Proof-context faces plus finite residue witnesses

**Status: exact full-closure-preserving normal form, proved and exhaustively checked on six witnesses; lower-bound value still unknown.** Let the $2m$ named endpoints be $C_1,\ldots,C_{2m}$ and rule $r$ have premise endpoints $a_r,b_r$. Write $M_r=C_{a_r}\cap C_{b_r}$. For a consistent partial assignment $P$, write $B_P=\{z\in Z:z\text{ extends }P\}$. Define context families $\mathcal D_j$ as the least fixed point generated by:

1. $\{(i,b)\}\in\mathcal D_j$ whenever $B_{i,b}\subseteq C_j$.
2. If $P\in\mathcal D_{a_r}$ and $Q\in\mathcal D_{b_r}$ are compatible and $M_r\subseteq C_j$, then $P\cup Q\in\mathcal D_j$.

Every face $B_P$ in $\mathcal D_j$ lies inside $C_j$. For each false inclusion $M_r\nsubseteq C_j$, choose one witness $z_{r,j}\in M_r\setminus C_j$; for each nonempty $M_r$, choose one point $z_r\in M_r$. Let $W$ be the set of these points, so $|W|\le 2m^2+m$. Replace each endpoint by

$$C'_j=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal D_j}B_P\ \cup\ \{z\in W:z\in C_j\}.$$

Then $C'_j\subseteq C_j$, and it has exactly the same literal-slice profile: every original literal generator appears as a singleton context, while shrinking cannot introduce a new contained slice. For every rule $r$ and endpoint $j$, the bit $[M_r\subseteq C_j]$ is preserved. A false bit keeps its selected witness; for a true bit, an intersection point in generated faces combines two compatible contexts and is therefore in $\mathcal D_j$, while any selected point witness is retained in $C'_j$ according to its original membership. The empty/nonempty bit of each rule intersection is preserved by shrinking plus the selected nonempty witness. Thus all initial endpoint flags and the entire rule-transition tensor are identical, so the relay accepts exactly the same anchors under full closure.

The finite checker [experiment_relay_context_normal_form.py](experiment_relay_context_normal_form.py) constructs this normal form and checks every rule-to-endpoint inclusion bit, every rule-pair nonemptiness bit, all endpoint activations, and empty-carrier acceptance on every input for six saved covers. It generates 77--260 contexts across those toy systems and uses only 5--9 point witnesses, below the general $2m^2+m$ bound. This replaces the vague 'hidden residue' with a precise split: proof-generated faces carry the input-sensitive behavior; at most quadratically many high points preserve static false inclusions.

This is an exact reduction of arbitrary endpoint sets to a context grammar plus finite witnesses, not a complexity lower bound. The number of generated contexts can still be exponential in $N$, and the point witnesses are uncharged arbitrary high tables. The next question is whether their interaction with the shared context grammar admits a scale-growing lower bound or an efficient universal realization. Do not claim the residue has been eliminated; it has been isolated into an explicit finite advice layer.

## Idea 107 - Dual-rail Horn circuits and the monotone-slice trap

**Status: exact circuit embedding and a negative transfer result; generic monotonicity does not improve the lower bound.** Replace each truth-table input bit $x_i$ by paired variables $y_{i,0},y_{i,1}$, restricted on real anchors to $y_{i,b}=[x_i=b]$. Every endpoint flag is a monotone clause $\phi_j(y)=\bigvee_{(i,b)\in\operatorname{sh}(C_j)}y_{i,b}$. With the first-seed normal form, the non-disjoint core obeys the monotone Horn recurrence

$$a_j^{(0)}=\phi_j(y),\qquad a_j^{(t+1)}=a_j^{(t)}\vee\bigvee_{r:\,M_r\subseteq C_j}\left(a_{a_r}^{(t)}\wedge a_{b_r}^{(t)}\right),$$

and acceptance is the OR of the terminal disjoint-seed tests. At most $2m$ rounds are needed because there are $2m$ endpoint flags. A fan-in-two unrolling has size $O(mN+m^3)$: endpoint clauses cost $O(mN)$ gates, while each round computes at most $m$ premise ANDs and $O(m^2)$ rule-to-endpoint OR incidences. [experiment_dualrail_horn_model.py](experiment_dualrail_horn_model.py) checks the paired-slice output on all anchors and monotonicity on every one of the $2^{2N}$ dual-rail inputs for six saved covers.

This exposes a barrier to using generic monotone-circuit theory. On the paired encoding, any De Morgan circuit of size $s$ can be converted to a monotone circuit of size $O(s)$ by replacing each positive/negative input literal with $y_{i,1}/y_{i,0}$; conversely substitute $x_i/\neg x_i$. Thus unrestricted monotone-circuit complexity on this paired slice is equivalent to ordinary circuit complexity up to constant/additive overhead. The relay is a much more structured Horn fixed point, so its rule grammar may still be exploitable, but monotonicity alone cannot do the work.

The pairing also sits inside the middle Hamming slice of $2N$ variables. A threshold wrapper turns the Horn circuit into a monotone middle-slice function without changing its value on the slice. Austrin--Risse prove SoS degree lower bounds for refuting small monotone circuits of slice functions, including a degree theorem for every slice function; that is a proof-system statement, not a circuit-size lower bound, so it does not transfer a relay lower bound by itself ([CCC 2023](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2023.31)). The known near-quadratic MCSP bounds against arbitrary-basis formulas and general branching programs also do not supply a general circuit lower bound ([Cheraghchi et al., ICALP 2019](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2019.39)). Close the generic monotone/slice route; pursue only bounds that exploit the relay's specific two-premise Horn recurrence and its realizable rule-to-endpoint incidence tensor.

## Idea 108 - Minimal context frontiers as high-free cube covers

**Status: exact antichain compression and seed-cover identity; finite-verified, with no scale-growing bound yet.** Order partial assignments by literal inclusion. If $P\subset Q$, then every anchor matching $Q$ also matches $P$, and $B_Q\subseteq B_P$. Thus $Q$ is dominated for both endpoint activation and the normalized carrier union. This dominance is preserved by every production: whenever $Q$ is compatible with $R$, so is $P$, and $P\cup R\subseteq Q\cup R$. Therefore the least proof-context grammar can be computed by retaining only inclusion-minimal contexts at each endpoint; the antichain recurrence is exact.

Under the first-seed normal form, remove disjoint rules from this context grammar. For a terminal seed $(a,b)$, every compatible pair $P\in\mathcal D_a$, $Q\in\mathcal D_b$ yields a context $P\cup Q$ whose high face is empty, because $B_P\subseteq E_a$, $B_Q\subseteq H_b$, and $E_a\cap H_b=\varnothing$. The accepted anchors are exactly the union of the input subcubes matching these terminal contexts. Hence any lower bound on the number/structure of high-free subcubes needed to cover the low set is a lower bound on the seed-frontier products $\sum_{(a,b)\text{ seed}}|\mathcal D_a||\mathcal D_b|$.

[experiment_relay_context_normal_form.py](experiment_relay_context_normal_form.py) independently computes the full context family and its minimal antichain for six covers, verifies identical anchor support and high-face union, then uses the antichain-normalized endpoints to recheck every rule relation and every anchor closure. Full context totals 77, 118, 197, 260, 200, and 189 shrink to 19, 31, 35, 41, 40, and 47 minimal contexts. [experiment_seed_context_frontier.py](experiment_seed_context_frontier.py) computes core-only frontiers and verifies their high-free terminal cubes cover exactly the accepted anchors: 4, 5, 5, 10, 10, and 12 minimal cubes, with all 16 or 32 inputs checked per instance.

This is a cleaner combinatorial object, but raw cube counts cannot force a superlinear relay bound: a target on $N$ bits has at most $2^N$ anchors, and a small shared grammar can generate exponentially many terms. Continue only with a lower bound on the *shared production grammar* or a stronger measure of its seed-frontier products; do not optimize antichain sizes on tiny toys as a proxy for the Gap-MCSP result.

## Idea 109 - Compile any circuit separator into a linear-size relay

**Status: general construction proved; parity instance exhaustively verified.** Let $Y,Z\subseteq\{0,1\}^N$ be disjoint and suppose a De Morgan circuit $C$ of size $s$ outputs 1 on $Y$ and 0 on $Z$. Convert $C$ to a monotone dual-rail circuit on $y_{i,0},y_{i,1}$, with $y_{i,b}=1$ exactly when $x_i=b$. For each monotone gate $g$, make a carrier

$$E_g=\{z\in Z:g(\iota(z))=1\}.$$

An AND gate $g=a\wedge b$ is represented by the relay rule $(E_a,E_b)$, since $E_a\cap E_b=E_g$. An OR gate $g=a\vee b$ is represented by $(E_a,Z)$ and $(E_b,Z)$, since the meet carriers $E_a,E_b$ are contained in $E_g$. The top carrier $Z$ is active for every anchor. A NOT gate in the original circuit swaps its two dual-rail signals. At most two monotone gates arise per original gate, and an AND costs one relay rule while an OR costs two, so adding a dummy output pair if needed gives at most $3s+1$ relay rules.

Completeness: for $x\in Y$, every matching literal carrier $B_{i,x_i}$ is initially active; induction through the dual-rail gates activates the output carrier. Since $C$ is 0 on all of $Z$, that output carrier is $\varnothing$, so the relay derives the empty carrier. Soundness: for a fixed $z\in Z$, every initially active gate carrier contains $z$, because the matching slice containing $z$ is contained in it. Rule activation preserves this invariant: active premises contain $z$, and every output carrier contains their intersection. The output carrier is empty, so no $z\in Z$ can activate it or trigger any disjoint seed. Thus every promise circuit separator gives a relay cover with $\rho(Y,Z)\le3s+1$ (up to constant gate-convention details).

The exact converse simulation from Idea 107 gives a Boolean circuit separator of size $O(mN+m^3)$ from an $m$-rule relay. Hence the relay measure is polynomially tied to general circuit separation on the same promise; the desired superlinear relay lower bound would itself give a superlinear general-circuit lower bound for Gap-MCSP. This is a genuine explanation for the ceiling faced by clause, context, and monotone-only arguments: the relay is expressive enough to encode arbitrary circuit computation using uncharged truth-set carriers.

The explicit test [experiment_dualrail_parity_relay.py](experiment_dualrail_parity_relay.py) compiles an $O(N)$ dual-rail parity circuit into relays with $8N-7$ rules for $N=2,\ldots,6$. Full closure matches odd parity on every input. The minimal terminal contexts are exactly the $2^{N-1}$ odd assignments, each a width-$N$ high-free cube, while the rule count is linear. This is a constructive counterexample to any lower bound based only on the number of high-free contexts. It does not solve the target problem; the remaining viable path must exploit a circuit lower-bound method for the specific Gap-MCSP promise or a feature the circuit compilation loses.

## Idea 110 - The globality floor and integration debt

**Status: one general query lower bound proved; new accounting language proposed; no circuit lower bound.** Let the truth-table input length be $N=2^n$. Write $\mathcal C_{<s_2}$ for the tables computed by circuits of size below $s_2$. Circuit counting gives

$$|\mathcal C_{<s_2}|\le 2^{O(s_2\log(s_2+n))}.$$

Choose $K$ such that $|\mathcal C_{<s_2}|\le 2^K$; circuit counting gives $K=O(s_2\log(s_2+n))$. Consider any deterministic adaptive algorithm that reads coordinates of a truth table and correctly distinguishes low tables $Y=\{f:\operatorname{CC}(f)\le s_1\}$ from high tables $Z=\{f:\operatorname{CC}(f)\ge s_2\}$. Run it on any $f\in Y$, and let $Q$ be the distinct coordinates queried on that path. Every table agreeing with $f$ on $Q$ follows the same path and receives the same output. There are $2^{N-|Q|}$ such completions. If

$$N-|Q|>K,$$

the completion cylinder is larger than all of $\mathcal C_{<s_2}$, so it contains a high table. The algorithm would give that high table the low answer, a contradiction. Therefore every such decision tree uses at least

$$N-K=N-O(s_2\log(s_2+n))$$

distinct queries on every low input. For the magnification regime $s_2=N^\beta$ with fixed $\beta<1$, this is $N-o(N)$. This is a promise-query lower bound, not a circuit-size lower bound: reading almost the whole input costs only $O(N)$ gates. It rules out deterministic approaches whose decisive information comes from $o(N)$ fixed or adaptive truth-table probes, but leaves the required superlinear *integration* cost completely open.

A second, related calculation is a patching-distance lemma. If $g$ is a size-$s_1$ circuit and $f$ differs from $g$ on $t$ of the $N$ rows, an equality test for a specified $n$-bit row costs $O(n)$ gates. OR the $t$ mismatch indicators and XOR with $g$ to obtain a circuit for $f$ of size at most $s_1+O(nt+n)$. Thus, when $s_2-s_1\gg n$, every high table is at Hamming distance $\Omega((s_2-s_1)/n)$ from every low circuit table. In the magnification parameters $s_1=\Theta(N^\beta/n)$, $s_2=N^\beta$, this distance fraction is only $\Omega(N^{\beta-1}/n)$. Combined with the $O(s_1\log(s_1+n))=O(N^\beta)$ description dimension of the low-circuit class, standard uniform-sampling bounds do not give a sublinear test. A union-bound hitting set for all low circuits uses $O((\log|\mathcal C_{s_1}|)/\delta)=O(N\log N)$ samples; a generic VC epsilon-net adds another $\log(1/\delta)$ factor and gives $O(N\log^2N)$. Both exceed the $N$ available rows: candidate-description entropy cancels the per-candidate distance gain. These are upper-bound calculations for generic sampling, not lower bounds against randomized algorithms; structured correlations among circuits could still beat them.

I will use a five-coordinate **resource vector** to diagnose representation-based proposals:

$$\mathsf R=(L,A,U,H,T),$$

where $L$ is description length of the proposed object, $A$ is the cost of the semantic operation actually needed (emptiness, intersection, inclusion, or verification), $U$ is the cost of constructing it uniformly from the instance, $H$ is the cost of sharing its work across anchors or witnesses, and $T$ is the exponent/magnification margin after reductions. A proposal has **unpaid debt** when it celebrates a small $L$ while leaving one of $A,U,H,T$ unrestricted. This is a project-specific audit language, not a new complexity measure or theorem.

It organizes the repeated failures without treating them as unrelated:

* SAT's factored fiber has $L=O(s)$ but emptiness still carries the hard operation $A$.
* Relay endpoints have tiny rule count but arbitrary semantic set content; circuit-to-relay compilation shows that a strong relay lower bound is already a general circuit lower bound. The endpoint-description and implication tensor costs must be made explicit before counting only rules.
* Context-frontier size can be exponential while a linear-size shared grammar generates it, so raw term count ignores $H$.
* The proof-DAG and query lower bounds reach $N-o(N)$, but magnification needs a superlinear circuit bound; the remaining debt is global integration beyond a full input scan.
* Self-reference and bounded-proof attempts repeatedly pay for target code length, verifier time, or clock dilation, so their $U$ or $T$ coordinate erases the intended gain.
* Monotone/slice and SoS transfers measure a restricted model or proof system, not the needed general-circuit size, so they fail at $T$.

The candidate escape is therefore sharpened: find a **nonlocal global invariant** of the full truth-table-versus-circuit-description relation that forces superlinear aggregation cost, while preserving the tiny low/high gap and remaining uniform. It must survive the locality stress test from Chen et al.'s analysis of hardness magnification and must not silently revert to generic circuit lower bounds. A plausible object to study is the complete disagreement matrix $D_f(c)=\{i:C_c(i)\ne f_i\}$ indexed by all candidate circuits $c$: the high promise says every allowed column has a nonempty disagreement set, while the low promise has one identically empty column. The open challenge is compressing this universal column test without enumerating circuits. No lower bound for that matrix or resulting P-vs-NP proof is claimed.

This has an exact **Skolem-selector** form. A table $f$ is high iff there exists a total selector $S:\mathcal C_{<s_2}\to[N]$ such that $C_c(S(c))\ne f_{S(c)}$ for every candidate circuit $c$. The lexicographically first disagreement gives a selector for every high table, so this equivalence itself is only a reformulation. The raw selector table has $|\mathcal C_{<s_2}|\log N=2^{O(s_2\log(s_2+n))}$ bits. A uniform circuit can compute the first mismatch by evaluating each candidate circuit across all $N$ rows, but the direct construction costs roughly $N$ times a universal-circuit evaluation. A short selector description is not enough: its *totality* and mismatch claim must be verified for every circuit code, or the original universal quantifier has merely been hidden. The new research target is a succinct selector plus a proof of totality whose construction, verification, and exponent survive all five coordinates of $\mathsf R$. PCP/IOP, coding, and cryptographic proof techniques are candidate sources, but no compact selector or useful verifier has been found.

Recent literature adds a conditional route relevant to the proof-complexity strand: Goldberg, Juvekar, and Kabanets (ECCC TR26-091, June 2026) combine subexponential indistinguishability obfuscation with a no-infinitely-often-subexponentially-optimal-proof-system assumption to obtain conditional NP-hardness for variants of implicit MCSP and full-support learning, using half-Levin reductions. The assumption itself already implies $\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}$ and hence $\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}$: if $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$, Cook--Reckhow gives a polynomially bounded proof system, which is p-optimal. So this conditional route is not an unconditional escape; its added contribution is hardness of meta-complexity/learning problems and a cryptographic construction. Its implicit-instance encoding and reduction notion also differ from ordinary truth-table Gap-MCSP. A technical idea worth retaining is the *witness non-recovery* mechanism: the reduction maps SAT witnesses forward but does not require recovering them from target witnesses. The paper also obtains a P-uniform hard-UNSAT sequence from the proof-system assumption, but the full reduction is nonconstructive at the reduction-code level because the assumption does not effectively choose the hard proof system. See [ECCC TR26-091](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/091/download/), [hardness magnification and locality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08297), and the [Gap-MCSP magnification theorem](https://www.theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v017a011/).

## Idea 111 - Exclusion sets have an Andreev completion floor

**Status:** theorem-level sharpening of Idea 110's selector analysis; it does not prove P != NP.

Let $N=2^n$ and let $\mathcal C_{<s}$ be the Boolean functions on $n$ bits computed by circuits of size below $s$. For a high table $f$ (so $\operatorname{CC}(f)\ge s$), define its selector image number

$$
\tau_s(f)=\min\{|Q|:Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall C\in\mathcal C_{<s}\ \exists x\in Q\ C(x)\ne f(x)\}.
$$

This is exactly the smallest image size of any Skolem counterexample selector $S:\mathcal C_{<s}\to\{0,1\}^n$ satisfying $C(S(C))\ne f(S(C))$. Equivalently, $f|_Q$ is a partial Boolean function that has no extension computed by a circuit below size $s$. In learning-theory language this is the zero-consistency version of a specifying/exclusion set. Angluin's exclusion dimension allows a specifying set to leave at most one consistent concept; adding one point where that final concept differs from $f$ makes it a zero-consistency certificate, so the two per-target quantities differ by at most one. This is established terminology, not a new invariant.

Andreev proved that, in a fixed complete nondegenerate bounded-fan-in basis, every partial Boolean function on $q$ points in $\{0,1\}^n$ has a total circuit completion of size $O(q/\log(q+1)+n)$. Therefore every high $f$ must satisfy

$$
\tau_s(f)=\Omega(s\log s)\quad\text{when }s\gg n.
$$

Otherwise the partial labeling $f|_Q$ would have a completion below size $s$. The constants depend on the gate basis. This is a distinct global certificate-size bound. Idea 110 separately lower-bounds the Hamming distance from one low table by $\Omega((s_2-s_1)/n)$; that distance estimate does not itself lower-bound $\tau_s(f)$. For $s=2^{\beta n}$ the new image floor is $\Omega(ns)$, but the two quantities measure different things.

The floor is tight for at least some high tables. There are at most $2^{O(s\log(s+n))}$ circuits of size below $s$. Fix any $Q$ with $q$ larger than the logarithm of this count. Since there are $2^q$ labelings on $Q$, some labeling is not the restriction of any low-circuit function. Any total completion $f$ of that labeling is high, and $Q$ excludes every low circuit. Thus, when $s\gg n$ and $s\log(s+n)=o(N)$,

$$
\min_{\operatorname{CC}(f)\ge s}\tau_s(f)=\Theta(s\log s).
$$

This is a best-case statement over high tables. It does not bound $\tau_s(f)$ from above for every high table; the trivial bound remains $N$. Nor does it give a constructive selector, a fast procedure for finding $Q$, or a verifier for the universal claim that no low circuit fits $f|_Q$.

**Verifier hardness audit.** Define partial MCSP as the language of pairs $(p,s)$ for which some size-$s$ circuit agrees with every defined entry of partial truth table $p$. Hirahara proved this problem NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time many-one reductions (FOCS 2022; [ECCC TR22-119](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2022/119/)). For a proposed selector image $Q$, validity is exactly that $(f|_Q,s-1)$ is a NO instance. Conversely, any partial instance $p$ can be mapped to a full extension $f$ (fill all stars with zero) and its domain $Q$; the proposed set is valid iff $p$ has no size-$(s-1)$ completion. Hence validating a supplied exclusion set is coNP-hard under randomized reductions in the general partial-table setting. This is a rigorous obstacle to a generic NP-style certificate verifier, not a proof that no structure-specific proof system can work.

**Why this changes the failure diagnosis.** The old $O(nt)$ point-repair argument treated each labeled row as a separate minterm and was too crude for partial tables. The optimal partial-function theorem compresses arbitrary partial behavior to roughly $q/\log q$ gates, forcing any exact high-side exclusion set to contain at least about $s\log s$ rows. But this is still only polynomial in $s$ and may be sublinear in the explicit truth-table length $N$. The computational bottleneck has moved from certificate existence to uniformly finding and certifying the exclusion set against every small circuit. Hirahara's partial-MCSP hardness makes the generic verification problem coNP-hard under randomized reductions, so the unresolved target must exploit structure linking $Q$ to the rest of $f$ or use a stronger proof system.

The exact formula toy in [experiment_formula_high_selector_toy.py](experiment_formula_high_selector_toy.py) was rerun. For three input bits, the minimum/maximum selector images across high De Morgan formulas were $4/4$, $4/6$, $5/6$, $6/8$, and $7/7$ rows at low cutoffs 1 through 5; tested promise gaps had minimum/median/maximum $4/4/4$ or $5/5/5$. For four input bits, exhaustive profiles at formula cutoffs 2 and 4 gave, respectively: 314 low and 65,222 high tables with selector minimum/median/maximum $4/4/6$; then 3,302 low and 62,234 high tables with $6/6/8$. The profile computation checks every high table in these finite formula classes.

I also added [experiment_circuit_high_selector_toy.py](experiment_circuit_high_selector_toy.py), which enumerates signal-set states so fanout and internal sharing are allowed. Through four gates, its n=3 circuit classes and selector profiles match the formula counts exactly; on n=4, circuit classes also match formula classes through four gates, with 998,524 distinct final signal-set states. This small test found no sharing advantage, so it has not tested the asymptotic obstruction or shown that shared circuits behave like formulas in general.

**Next test:** study the maximum, not just the minimum, of $\tau_s(f)$ over high tables in exact formula toys; then determine whether this one-sided exclusion-set problem has a compact, efficiently verifiable form for circuit classes. Keep certificate size, construction cost, and universal verification as three separate obligations.



## Idea 112 - Minimal selector shadows are critically unrealizable

**Status:** exact structural lemma plus a finite four-variable witness; no asymptotic lower bound.

Let $Q$ be a cardinality-minimum selector image for a high table $f$ against all circuits of size below $s$, and put $p=f|_Q$. For every row $x\in Q$, the smaller set $Q\setminus\{x\}$ cannot exclude every low circuit. Hence there is a circuit $C_x$ of size below $s$ that agrees with $f$ on every row in $Q\setminus\{x\}$. It must disagree at $x$, because $Q$ itself is an exclusion set. So the low-circuit restrictions to $Q$ contain every one-coordinate Hamming neighbor $p\oplus e_x$ but omit the center $p$. Call this a **punctured selector shadow**. The equivalent synthesis formula is unsatisfiable on all of $Q$, while deleting any one labeled example makes it satisfiable; it is a group-minimal unsatisfiable circuit-synthesis instance.

This gives a threshold sandwich. The partial circuit complexity of $p$ is at least $s$, since no smaller circuit agrees with all of $p$. Choose any one-row deletion witness $C_x$ and patch its output at the single point $x$ using an equality test on the $n$-bit row index. The added circuit costs $O(n)$ gates, so $p$ has a completion of size at most $s+O(n)$. Therefore

$$
s\leq \operatorname{CC}_{\partial}(p)\leq s+O(n).
$$

This sharpens the interpretation of a minimum selector image: it is not just a hitting set; it is a smallest support carrying a partial function exactly at the circuit-size threshold, with every one-row deletion dropping below that threshold. Moreover, the counting construction in Idea 111 can be pruned to an inclusion-minimal exclusion set. The Andreev lower bound still forces at least $\Omega(s\log s)$ rows, while counting gives $O(s\log s)$; so some high tables have critical shadows of size $\Theta(s\log s)$, although no efficient construction follows. The punctured-star property by itself does not certify that the center is absent: the circuit class could contain the center as well as all its neighbors. A separate refutation of the full synthesis instance is still needed, consistent with Idea 111's partial-MCSP verification hardness.

The finite profile in [experiment_formula_high_selector_toy.py](experiment_formula_high_selector_toy.py) finds an exact example for four input bits and formula cutoff $s=5$: $f=\mathtt{0x03c0}$ and $Q=\{0,2,4,6,8,10,12,14\}$. No formula with at most four AND/OR gates matches the eight labeled rows; for each of the eight rows, a low formula matches all the other seven. The first formula completion of this partial table has five gates, and the exact enumeration finds one such completion at the minimum. Thus its partial formula complexity is exactly $s$ in this toy. The result is finite and formula-specific.

**New research route:** encode the partial-circuit consistency problem for such punctured shadows and study its refutations. The deletion witnesses form a boundary layer around the missing target. Search for an algebraic interpolation, polynomial-calculus, or other proof-complexity invariant that certifies the missing center using the boundary witnesses plus structural facts about circuit size. Any proposed invariant must survive the general partial-MCSP* NP-hardness barrier; it cannot infer inconsistency from the star alone.

## Idea 113 - Trace holes can have coding geometry

**Status:** exact finite discovery for four-input De Morgan formulas, cross-checked against the shared-circuit function class through four gates; no asymptotic consequence and no P-vs-NP breakthrough.

For a low class $\mathcal C_{<s}$ and a row set $Q$, define its **trace** and **hole set** by

$$
T_s(Q)=\{C|_Q:C\in\mathcal C_{<s}\},\qquad H_s(Q)=\{0,1\}^Q\setminus T_s(Q).
$$

A partial labeling $p$ is threshold-critical on $Q$ exactly when $p\in H_s(Q)$ and every one-bit neighbor $p\oplus e_x$ lies in $T_s(Q)$. This is the trace-language form of Idea 112's punctured selector shadow. If the holes have minimum Hamming distance at least two, then every hole has all private one-row deletion witnesses. This only proves minimality relative to subsets of that particular $Q$; a total extension may still have a different, smaller selector elsewhere.

The exact experiment [experiment_critical_selector_trace_geometry.py](experiment_critical_selector_trace_geometry.py) scans all $3,302$ four-input De Morgan formula functions with at most four AND/OR gates and all $\binom{16}{8}=12,870$ row sets. The smallest possible hole set has size eight and occurs for 74 row sets. Ten of those 74 hole sets are affine cosets of a binary $[8,3,4]$ linear code with weight enumerator $1+6z^4+z^8$: after translating one hole to zero, the eight differences are an XOR-closed three-dimensional subspace with weights $0,4,4,4,4,4,4,8$. I am not assigning this code a named family. The other 64 best row sets also have eight holes but not this exact code geometry. The code pattern is real in this toy, but not universal even among its best row sets.

One especially simple instance uses the even-parity inputs

$$Q=\{0,3,5,6,9,10,12,15\}$$

and partial labeling $p=\mathtt{0x81}$ in this row order. Its hole set is

$$H_5(Q)=\{\mathtt{18},\mathtt{24},\mathtt{42},\mathtt{7e},\mathtt{81},\mathtt{bd},\mathtt{db},\mathtt{e7}\}.$$

Relative to $p=\mathtt{81}$, this is the affine coset $p+\langle\mathtt{99},\mathtt{a5},\mathtt{c3}\rangle_{\mathbb F_2}$. Its differences have weights $0$, six copies of $4$, and $8$, so the target's eight immediate neighbors all occur in the low-formula trace. Explicit formulas of at most three gates witness every one-row deletion: the row-0 deletion has witness $x_0x_1x_2$; deleting rows 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12 has witnesses respectively $(x_0x_1)\lor(\neg x_2\neg x_3)$, $(x_0x_2)\lor(\neg x_1\neg x_3)$, $(\neg x_0\neg x_3)\lor(x_1x_2)$, $(x_0x_3)\lor(\neg x_1\neg x_2)$, $(\neg x_0\neg x_2)\lor(x_1x_3)$, and $(\neg x_0\neg x_1)\lor(x_2x_3)$; the row-15 deletion has witness $\neg x_0\neg x_1\neg x_2$. Each displayed product has two AND gates, and each two-product disjunction has three gates.

This partial table has a total extension $f=\mathtt{0x8181}$, with ones on input indices $0,7,8,15$. It is the five-gate function $(\neg x_0\neg x_1\neg x_2)\lor(x_0x_1x_2)$, independent of $x_3$. Exhaustive trace and selector enumeration verifies formula complexity exactly five and $\tau_5(f)=8$. The separate shared-circuit enumerator has exactly the same four-input function class through four gates, so the lower bound and selector image hold for circuits with arbitrary fanout in this finite model as well. Each of the eight missing partial labelings on this $Q$ has 16 distinct exact five-gate total completions. This is a finite example where a code-shaped omitted trace supports a globally maximum selector, not just a locally minimal sample.

The failure audit matters too. The earlier selected maximum-selector table $\mathtt{0x03c0}$ on its even-row set realizes 206 of 256 restrictions, so its target is one of 50 holes, not an isolated hole. Also, 592 best-trace partial labelings pass the one-row-deletion test, and each has at least one total extension with selector size six; only 16 of these partials admit any extension with selector size eight. The table $\mathtt{0x8181}$ is among those 16. Thus local punctured minimality and global selector minimality are separate obligations.

**Next question:** can an explicit, scalable row set make the low-circuit trace omit a recognizable error-correcting code coset while a designated total function has no smaller alternative selector? A proof must explain the omitted patterns for every low circuit, and the selector lower bound must range over all row sets, not only subsets of the chosen code sample. Random or counting existence, code distance alone, and this finite formula toy do not meet those obligations.

**Scaling falsification:** the direct five-input lift did not preserve the critical-hole pattern. For all five-input De Morgan formulas of at most five AND/OR gates (147,136 functions), the 16 even-parity rows have 28,584 realized patterns and 36,952 holes, but zero holes whose every one-bit neighbor is realized. Four variants adding one odd row also had zero critical holes. A seeded sample of 10 row sets at each size $q=12,13,14,15,16,17$ found zero critical holes; a separate seeded 24-set sample at $q=17$ also found zero. Greedy addition maximizing the number of distinct formula traces reached 22,848 patterns on 17 rows, still with no critical hole. This is evidence against the naive five-input lift, not an exhaustive no-go theorem: these are selected row families, and the trace-count greedy algorithm is not globally optimal.

## Idea 114 - Polarity budgets and disagreement packings generate critical formula selectors

**Status:** exact all-$m$ theorem for one De Morgan formula family; no general circuit lower bound or P-vs-NP consequence.

For $m\ge3$, let $F_m(a,y)=1$ iff $y=0^m$ or $y=1^m$, with the extra bit $a$ ignored. In formulas with signed literals and binary AND/OR gates, its exact size is $2m-1$: both endpoint transitions force both literal polarities of each $y_i$, hence at least $2m$ leaves, and the two endpoint minterms attain that count. The sample

$$Q_m=\{(1,y):|y|\le1\}\cup\{(0,y):|y|\ge m-1\}$$

also forces the same polarities, so its target trace is absent from all formulas of at most $2m-2$ gates. At the same time, each of its $2m+2$ endpoint-neighborhood vectors indexes a low formula differing from $F_m$ on only that vector's two-row $a$-fiber. Those supports are pairwise disjoint. Every selector image must hit all of them, and $Q_m$ attains the lower bound, giving

$$\tau^{\mathrm{formula}}_{2m-1}(F_m)=2m+2.$$

The symbolic proof is recorded in [New Model.MD](New%20Model.MD) and Section 74 of the audit. [experiment_antipodal_formula_selector.py](experiment_antipodal_formula_selector.py) verifies the exact finite formula classes for $m=3$ and $m=4$ (3,302 and 662,176 low functions). The $m=4$ case is the scale-matched five-input example with target `0xC0000003` and exact selector size 10. This explains why the earlier five-input test at a fixed five-gate cutoff was not decisive against the scaled construction.

**Why it matters:** it identifies a proof-level source of punctured trace boundaries: opposing monotonicity obligations force literal polarity, while disjoint near-miss supports force selector size. This is a cleaner structural account than relying on code geometry in a single finite trace.

**Why it is not a breakthrough:** the argument depends on formula leaves. A shared circuit can reuse gates; the polarity occurrence count does not charge one gate per leaf. The lower bound is linear, the family is specially constructed, and no standard class separation follows. The particular identity's literature novelty is unverified; do not call it new mathematics without a targeted literature review.

There is also a decisive scale mismatch: the family has $n=m+1$ input bits, truth-table length $N=2^{m+1}$, and target size $s=2m-1=\Theta(\log N)$. Its selector size $2m+2$ is also only $\Theta(\log N)$. Magnification needs circuit lower bounds at a scale such as $N^\beta$ for fixed $\beta>0$. Thus even proving the matching circuit theorem for every $m$ would not by itself approach P vs NP.

**Finite circuit extension:** [experiment_circuit_selector_antipodal.py](experiment_circuit_selector_antipodal.py) encodes arbitrary-fanout circuits with free signed inputs/constants and AND/OR/NOT gates. For $m=3,4$, Z3 finds no circuit through $2m-2$ gates and finds a matching circuit at $2m-1$; SAT witnesses are independently evaluated. The $m=5$ Z3 partial-sample search timed out, so I wrote the independent one-hot CNF encoding [experiment_sat_circuit_selector_antipodal.py](experiment_sat_circuit_selector_antipodal.py). It reproduces the $m=3,4$ results and returns UNSAT at eight gates for $m=5$ with both CaDiCaL and Glucose. The disjoint formula witnesses give the selector lower bound; the endpoint-minterm formula gives the upper bound. Thus the finite circuit selector sizes are solver-derived as 8, 10, and 12 for $m=3,4,5$, and the target circuit sizes are 5, 7, and 9. These UNSAT results have no independently checked proof traces, and no general circuit theorem follows.

The next case $m=6$ was tested at ten gates. CaDiCaL exhausted a five-million-conflict budget without deciding it; the Glucose run was interrupted after the scale mismatch was identified. There is no $m=6$ conclusion. An inconclusive budget result is not evidence either way. The finite sequence is only a conjecture filter, not progress toward a magnification-scale lower bound.

**Next test:** derive a symbolic gate-based lower bound for the antipodal sample or find a small shared-circuit counterexample, without extending the dimension sweep absent a predicted payoff. Determine exactly which parts of the polarity argument survive fanout. If the only invariant is linear, record the obstruction and redirect effort to constructions already at a magnification-relevant scale.

## Idea 115 - Resource-bounded witness descriptions characterize the search gap

**Status:** exact equivalence with $P=NP$ for SAT; a proof target and diagnostic, not a separation.

Fix a universal machine $U$. For a Boolean formula $\varphi$, define

$$K_{\mathrm{SAT}}^t(\varphi)=\min\{|p|: U(p,\varphi)\text{ halts within }t(|\varphi|)\text{ steps and outputs }w\text{ with }\varphi(w)=1\},$$

and let the value be $\infty$ if no program qualifies. Then

$$P=NP\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists c,d\ \forall\varphi\in\mathrm{SAT},\ K_{\mathrm{SAT}}^{|\varphi|^d}(\varphi)\le c.$$

**Proof.** If $P=NP$, SAT has a polynomial-time decider. Fixing variables one at a time and asking whether a satisfying completion remains yields one polynomial-time witness finder. Its fixed program code has some constant length $c$, and its running time is bounded by $n^d$ for a fixed $d$. Conversely, assume such $c,d$ exist. On input $\varphi$, simulate every program of length at most $c$ for $|\varphi|^d$ steps; accept if one outputs an assignment that directly verifies against $\varphi$. There are only $2^{O(c)}$ such programs, a constant independent of $|\varphi|$. This is a polynomial-time SAT decider. Unsatisfiable inputs have no valid output from any simulated program. Thus SAT is in P, hence $P=NP$. Negating the statement gives the exact target: for every fixed pair $c,d$, some satisfiable $\varphi$ defeats all $c$-bit witness programs within the $|\varphi|^d$ clock.

**Fundamental correction to plain-K arguments.** The lexicographically first satisfying assignment is computable from $\varphi$ by exhaustive search. Therefore its ordinary conditional Kolmogorov complexity is at most a machine-dependent constant, even if the computation takes exponential time. Counting/randomness of witnesses cannot establish that *every* satisfying assignment has large plain $K(w\mid\varphi)$: at least one canonical witness always has a fixed short description. The only relevant version here is time-bounded conditional complexity, with the polynomial clock retained in the statement.

**Why this may help.** This puts the witness search/check gap into an exact logical form and filters self-reference ideas: a successful proof must defeat every short program at every fixed polynomial clock, for a satisfiable formula, while paying the formula's encoding and simulation costs. If encoding an $n^d$-step computation produces a formula of length about $n^d$, the candidate's own clock on that new formula is about $n^{d^2}$; the proposed diagonal has not closed. Any route must break this loop with a genuine structural theorem, not an unbounded-K argument or a clock hidden in a succinct representation.

**What it does not do.** The equivalence simply rewrites $P=NP$ as a bounded-description statement. It supplies no formulas with the required lower bound. Nor does it prove such formulas can be generated uniformly; a nonconstructive existence statement for every $c,d$ would still need a valid proof that all short programs fail on the selected formula. Treat it as a proof target and an error detector, not new complexity-theoretic evidence.

**Next proof task:** attempt one fixed-point SAT construction against all programs of length at most $c$ and clock $n^d$. Keep separate the seed length, the encoded computation tableau length, the final formula length, and the clock the alleged searcher receives on that final length. Either obtain a closed inequality that works for arbitrary $d$, or record exactly why this diagonal family cannot prove the criterion.

## Idea 116 - The finite-substrate one-wayness premise is the unresolved theorem

**Status:** valid conditional implication isolated; the advertised unconditional hardness step is unsupported by the cited finite arithmetic checks.

A June 2026 preprint describes the map $a_P(j)=g^j\bmod P$ as easy to compute and its inverse, discrete logarithm, as the one-way ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œscale-descent residue.ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â Its Theorem 5 correctly proves the standard implication: if a polynomial-time computable one-way family exists, then $P\ne NP$, because $P=NP$ would let one decide and self-reduce the NP relation $f(x)=y$ to find a preimage. The source marks the posted version as not peer-reviewed ([preprint](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202606.1781)).

The proof debt is the premise. The text asserts that no polynomial-time classical algorithm inverts the exponentiation map, calls discrete logarithm infeasible, and then treats this as derived from the finite-substrate framework. But its algebraic closure arguments establish only that exponentiation is computable and the discrete logarithm is the inverse operation. They do not establish that this inverse takes superpolynomial time. Testing finite fields or observing runtime growth on finite parameter samples cannot prove the universal asymptotic lower bound. Under standard complexity assumptions, the result is conditional on discrete-log hardness (or one-way functions); that premise already implies the desired separation.

There is a second, independent transfer gap. The paper bounds its carrier family by $\ell\le\tfrac12\log_2\Omega$ while treating $\Omega$ as a fixed finite totality, then says textbook asymptotic classes are recovered by dropping finitude. A fixed maximum input length yields only finitely many instances, for which any finite decision or inverse table can be hardcoded. Standard $P$ and $NP$ quantify over unbounded lengths with one uniform machine. A proof must define an unbounded, uniformly encoded family of carriers and preserve polynomial costs across it; the finite carrier calculations alone do not supply this bridge.

**Reusable logic check:** a representation change can alter resource costs only if its encoding and simulation overheads are accounted for. The preprint defines admissible representations to simulate standard machines with polynomial overhead, so such a representation definition cannot itself certify that a standard inverse has no polynomial-time algorithm. Any foundational proof must supply the missing lower bound in the committed classical bit model, rather than rename the unproved inverse cost as a horizon or residue.

**Next proof task:** for any proposed algebraic or logical ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œone-way residue,ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â separate (i) the elementary forward/inverse identities, (ii) the claimed uniform lower bound in input bit length, and (iii) the reduction from that bound to SAT search. Do not treat finite arithmetic verification as evidence for item (ii).

## Idea 117 - Backward implication audit and the hierarchy quantifier gap

**Status:** exact logical map and a falsification of the naive hierarchy-diagonal route; no separation.

Start from the two possible answers rather than from a technique. By Cook--Levin, $P=NP$ iff $SAT\in P$. Under this assumption, a SAT decider gives a polynomial witness finder by deciding, one bit at a time, whether a satisfying extension exists. The same search-to-decision argument applies to polynomially balanced NP witness relations, gives $NP=coNP$, and rules out standard length-indexed one-way functions. These are consequences of the assumption, not contradictions with known mathematics.

Conversely, $P\ne NP$ is equivalent to $SAT\notin P$. In the bounded-description formulation of Idea 115, it says

$$\forall c,d\;\exists\varphi\in SAT\;\forall p\ (|p|\le c\Rightarrow p\text{ fails to output a verified witness within }|\varphi|^d).$$

This is an all-clocks lower bound. It is stronger in quantifier shape than the direct conclusion of an ordinary hierarchy theorem: for every fixed $k$, the nondeterministic time hierarchy yields some $L_k\in NTIME(n^{k+1})\subseteq NP$ outside $NTIME(n^k)$, but the separation target is $\exists L\in NP\;\forall k\;L\notin DTIME(n^k)$. The family $L_k$ can vary with $k$. Treating those separate witnesses as one hard language is an invalid quantifier exchange.

**Naive diagonal attempt and its failure point.** Try to encode the run of a candidate witness program on a seed formula, then make the formula satisfiable exactly when the program fails to find a witness. If an $n^d$-step run is written as an ordinary tableau, the formula may have length $M=\Theta(n^d)$; the candidate's promised clock on that final formula is then $M^d=\Theta(n^{d^2})$. The construction has not diagonalized against the actual clock it must defeat. This is a size/exponent accounting failure for this direct tableau construction, not a no-go theorem for fixed points, succinct encodings, or other diagonalizations. Any claimed escape must prove its uniform verifier and encoding bounds.

**Adjacent axes that must not be conflated.** $NP=coNP$ is equivalent to existence of a polynomially bounded Cook--Reckhow proof system for TAUT. $P=NP$ implies $NP=coNP$, but $P\ne NP$ alone does not establish $NP\ne coNP$ and therefore does not rule out such a proof system. Likewise, one-way functions imply $P\ne NP$, but the converse is not known. Incompleteness of a fixed formal theory is not a lower bound on SAT or on all proof systems unless a separate reduction proves it.

**Learning:** the key obstruction is not self-reference as a theme; it is the exact scope of the universal quantifiers and the cost of placing the diagonal statement inside its own input. A valid proof needs one theorem that bridges the gapÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Âeither a construction defeating all fixed polynomial clocks while staying in SAT, or a different lower bound with a proved transfer. A sequence of per-clock diagonal languages, a proof-system result on one formal system, or a finite model does not bridge it.

**Next proof task:** formalize a candidate fixed-point statement with separate variables for seed length, tableau/description length, final formula length, and the final clock. Derive the inequalities before choosing a coding trick. If they do not close for arbitrary $d$, record the precise obstruction and switch to a non-self-referential structural route. The model's Section 2.1 now contains the implication map; no solver sweep is justified by this idea.

## Idea 118 - Arithmetize ZFC and integrate the proof-system route

**Status:** formal synthesis of ZFC and proof-complexity implications; Ideas 27ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Å“45 already contain the detailed FCP and self-reference attempts. No proof, independence result, or separation.

Let $M_e$ be the deterministic machine with code $e$. Because SAT is decidable, the predicate ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ$M_e$ correctly decides SAT on $\varphi$ within $(|\varphi|+2)^k$ stepsÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â is computable: simulate the finite clock and compare the output with exhaustive SAT evaluation. Therefore

$$
P=NP\iff SAT\in P\iff \exists e,k\ \forall\varphi\; M_e^{(|\varphi|+2)^k}(\varphi)=SAT(\varphi).
$$

In the standard arithmetization this is a $\Sigma^0_2$ sentence with a computable matrix; its negation is $\Pi^0_2$. This is only a classification of quantifier form. It neither makes the statement easy nor shows that ZFC proves either side. Enumerating ZFC proofs will find a proof if one exists, but if the sentence is independent the enumeration simply continues forever. No finite timeout distinguishes those cases. Incompleteness does not imply that this particular arithmetic sentence is independent; that would require separate relative-consistency arguments for ZFC plus each alternative.

**Stronger proof-complexity route.** A Cook--Reckhow proof system for TAUT is a polynomial-time map whose range is exactly the tautologies. Standardly, $NP=coNP$ iff there is one such system with a polynomial proof-length bound. Thus proving

$$
\forall\Pi\;\forall k\;\exists\tau\in TAUT\;\forall\pi\;
(|\pi|\le(|\tau|+2)^k\Rightarrow\Pi(\pi)\ne\tau)
$$

would imply $NP\ne coNP$, hence $P\ne NP$. This is stronger than required, but it gives a concrete proof-theoretic target. Under $P=NP$, every fixed proof system is also automatizable relative to the shortest proof length: deciding whether a proof of length at most a unary budget exists is an NP problem, and a proof can be found by search-to-decision. That does not make proofs polynomial in the tautology length in every chosen system.

**Attempted diagonal and precise debt.** Fix a sound system $\Pi$ and polynomial bound. A sentence asserting that it has no proof below that bound is useful only if the sentence is proved to be a tautology and its encoded length does not raise the proof bound enough to defeat the argument. It must also address every candidate system and exponent to obtain $NP\ne coNP$. This is a possible proof engine to investigate, but ordinary GÃƒÆ’Ã‚Â¶del self-reference or incompleteness for one fixed theory does not discharge those obligations.
**Failed first diagonal:** writing a cutoff $L=n^k$ into a sentence can make its final length $N=\mathrm{poly}(L)$. The assumed proof-size guarantee then applies at $(N+2)^k$, potentially far above $L$. More fundamentally, ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œno short proof of $G$ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â does not imply $G$ is a tautology: soundness only says that a proof certifies truth. The construction needs an independent truth proof and a bound closed on the final formula.

This rejects the naive assertion only; it does not reject Idea 45's stronger fixed point, which uses soundness to prove the constructed formula is a tautology and excludes every proof represented by its assignment interface. Its unresolved cost is covering all short proofs while keeping the output proof system much shorter.

**Learning:** separate (1) standard truth in $\mathbb N$, (2) derivability in ZFC, (3) proof length in one propositional system, and (4) a lower bound uniform over all systems. The old project repeatedly conflated these levels. The arithmetic classification clarifies the first two; the proof-system characterization offers a route to the class separation. Neither yields a result until an actual uniform lower-bound lemma is proved.

**Next proof task:** with Idea 119 formalized, investigate whether any verifier-specific normal form can cover all short proofs with fewer bits. If not, shift to the already identified non-relativizing jump or a new external finite-consistency lower bound; do not repeat the per-$k$ or fixed-system construction without a strict size gain.

## Idea 119 - Coverage cost of a direct proof-system diagonal

**Status:** a proved limitation for the direct candidate-proof encoding used by Idea 45; not a lower bound for arbitrary proof systems and not a class separation.

Fix a sound Cook--Reckhow proof system $\Pi$, a formula $\tau$, and a proof cutoff $L$. A direct self-referential tautology uses assignments $a\in\{0,1\}^m$ as encodings $E(a)$ of candidate $\Pi$-proof strings, and arranges the fixed point so that

$$
\tau(a)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Pi(E(a))=\tau.
$$

**Soundness argument.** If some assignment falsified $\tau$, its encoded string would be a $\Pi$-proof of $\tau$. Soundness of $\Pi$ says every output of $\Pi$ is a tautology, contradicting the falsifying assignment. Hence $\tau$ is a tautology. The same equivalence shows that no $\Pi$-proof of $\tau$ lies in the image of $E$.

The last sentence is weaker than ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œ$\tau$ has no proof of length at most $L$.ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â To infer that stronger claim by this method, every candidate proof of length at most $L$ must be represented by some assignment, or one must prove a separate normalization theorem taking every such valid proof to the encoded image without increasing the relevant cutoff. There are $2^{L+1}-1$ binary strings of length at most $L$. If $E$ is onto this whole set, then

$$
2^m\ge 2^{L+1}-1,\qquad\text{so for }L\ge1,\quad m\ge L+1.
$$

In the explicit propositional encoding where these $m$ candidate bits are available as formula variables, the formula has size at least $\Omega(m)$: each bit must occur in the formula's proof-checking interface. Thus full coverage forces $|\tau|=\Omega(L)$. This is the exact interface cost in Idea 45. It is a method-specific statement; a checker-specific compression or canonical proof form could evade it, but that would be a new theorem to prove.

**Why this does not yield a proof-system jump.** The construction forces $\Pi$-proofs of $\tau$ to have length at least $L$, while the tautology itself has length at least $L$. If another proof system gives $\tau$ a proof $\rho$, its polynomial-time decoder must print $\tau$, so $|\tau|\le |\rho|^c$ for some fixed $c$. Consequently $L\le|\rho|^c$ in this construction, which is compatible with polynomial simulation. A recursive jump needs a superpolynomial gap between the old system's proof and the new system's proof, not just a lower bound measured in the number of bits the diagonal formula already contains.

**Proof.** The soundness and image-exclusion claims follow directly from the fixed-point equivalence. The coverage bound is cardinality: a domain of $2^m$ assignments cannot map onto $2^{L+1}-1$ candidate strings unless the displayed inequality holds. In the explicit encoding, the formula reads the candidate bits, so its syntax must include at least one occurrence for each represented bit. Finally, a Cook--Reckhow map runs in polynomial time in $|\rho|$ and must output the entire formula $\tau$, giving $|\tau|\le|\rho|^c$ for its fixed runtime exponent. Combining with $L\le O(|\tau|)$ shows the lower bound is polynomially compatible with simulation.

**Learning and next target.** This sharpens the earlier ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œthe formula reads $L$ proof bitsÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â observation into a coverage lemma: the obstacle is not merely self-reference; it is proving that all short proofs are covered by the falsifying-assignment interface. Search for either (i) an efficiently checkable normal form for all $\Pi$-proofs of a target that uses substantially fewer than $L$ bits, with a proof that every short proof normalizes into it, or (ii) a non-relativizing proof-system jump / finite-consistency lower bound that does not enumerate the full proof space. A normalization result strong enough to establish polynomially bounded proofs for all tautologies would already imply $NP=coNP$, so keep its logical strength explicit.

**Scope warning:** this closes the direct full-string diagonal as a source of a superpolynomial gap; it does not rule out all proof-complexity lower bounds or all fixed-point arguments. It also does not invalidate Idea 45's conditional tautology construction. It explains why that construction can be sound and still fail to separate proof systems.

## Idea 120 - Independence transfer must run in the right direction

**Status:** valid conditional obstruction to a ZFC proof of $P=NP$; the required independent consequence has not been established, and this route gives no proof of $P\ne NP$.

Let $A$ be $P=NP$, let $C$ be any arithmetic sentence, and let $T$ be ZFC. The elementary transfer rule is

$$
T\vdash A\to C\quad\text{and}\quad T\nvdash C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\nvdash A.
$$

If $C$ is independent of $T$, the second premise holds, so this can rule out a $T$-proof of $A$. But it does not show $T\vdash\neg A$, does not settle the truth of $A$ in the standard natural numbers, and does not imply that $A$ itself is independent: $T$ might still prove $\neg A$. This route concerns proof status, not a computational lower bound.

**Literature lead and audit.** Williamson's 2024 arXiv preprint *On P=NP Either False or Independent of ZFC* gives a concrete candidate $C$: a subset-sum statement obtained as a corollary of a set-version of Friedman's Jump Free Theorem $J$. The paper argues that $A\to C$ and derives $C$ from $J$, but its abstract explicitly **conjectures** that the translated theorem and $C$ are independent of ZFC; it does not establish this missing premise ([preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00468)). More basically, $J\to C$ is the wrong direction for transferring unprovability: from $T\nvdash J$ one cannot infer $T\nvdash C$. Such a transfer would need $C\to J$, an equivalence, or a model construction for $C$ itself. The paper's title should therefore not be read as a proved conditional resolution of P versus NP.

The formal conditional is useful: if the encoding is correct and one proves $C$ independent, then ZFC cannot prove $P=NP$. To certify the encoding, the subset-sum instance lengths and one uniform exponent $t$ must be checked against the standard bit model; merely solving each finite instance in some polynomial does not supply one uniform bound over all $p$. Even after those checks, the result would not prove $P\ne NP$.

**Implication-map update.** This adds a fourth layer to the project map: (i) truth in the standard model; (ii) derivability of $A$ or $\neg A$ in ZFC; (iii) provability of an auxiliary combinatorial consequence $C$; and (iv) polynomial-time complexity of the represented instances. The sound implications currently justified are $A\to C$ (claimed by the preprint, to be checked at encoding level), $J\to C$ (its stated corollary), and the proof-theoretic rule $(T\vdash A\to C\land T\nvdash C)\to T\nvdash A$. There is no established arrow from $J$'s independence to $C$'s independence, or from $T\nvdash A$ to $A$ being false.

**Learning.** Finding some independent sentence is not the hard part for this target. The hard part is preserving enough of the independent content through a reduction that also encodes the uniform SAT algorithm hypothesis. A weaker consequence can become provable even when its source theorem is independent. Proof-status arguments must track implication direction just as complexity arguments track reduction direction.

**Next proof task:** see Idea 121. The canonical encoding is ZFC-provable by a bounded-weight dynamic program. Continue the independence branch only if the paper's intended fixed noncanonical encodings, instance-size measure, and uniformity requirement are made explicit; otherwise close this route and return to the all-clocks SAT witness lower bound. Do not claim a P-vs-NP separation from it.

## Idea 121 - The canonical subset-sum corollary has a direct ZFC proof

**Status:** proved for the natural signed-integer encoding and the corollary's existential choice of witnesses; no P-vs-NP consequence. This shows that the paper's corollary is too weak to be independent for this encoding.

The 2024 preprint defines $F(\hat f_p)$ and $H(\hat f_p)$ by applying three bijections $\gamma_i:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ to values of a finite reflexive function, then conjectures that its subset-sum corollary is independent of ZFC. Fix the allowed canonical triple $\gamma_0=\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\gamma$ with

$$
\gamma(2j)=j,\qquad \gamma(2j+1)=-(j+1).
$$

For each $p\ge2$, choose $E_p=\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ and $D_p=E_p^k$. The family $S$ is full, so some $f_p\in S$ has domain exactly $D_p$. Reflexivity forces

$$
\operatorname{range}(f_p)\subseteq\operatorname{field}(D_p)=E_p.
$$

Consequently every integer in either explicit list $F(\hat f_p)$ or $H(\hat f_p)$ has absolute value at most $p$. There are at most $p^k$ entries in either list, even if multiplicities are retained. This choice uses fullness only; it does not use jump-freeness or the Jump Free Theorem.

Here is the uniform solver. On a list $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ with $n\le p^k$ and $|a_i|\le p$, set $B=\sum_i|a_i|\le p^{k+1}$, initialize $R_0=\{0\}$, and update

$$
R_i=R_{i-1}\cup\{s+a_i:s\in R_{i-1}\}.
$$

Then $0\in R_n$ exactly when some subset sums to zero; every $R_i$ is contained in $[-B,B]$. Each update scans $O(B)$ states, with $O(\mathrm{polylog}(p))$ bit overhead, giving $O(nB\,\mathrm{polylog}(p))=O(p^{2k+1}\,\mathrm{polylog}(p))$ bit operations. For a nonempty-subset definition of zero-sum, add a Boolean state recording whether an item has been selected; if the empty subset is allowed, the answer is trivially yes, so either convention is covered. For fixed $k\ge2$, this lies in $O(p^{3k})$ on a multitape Turing machine. Squaring this bound for a single-tape simulation and absorbing logarithmic factors gives $O(p^{6k})$, so one fixed $t=6$ works under either standard model. The algorithm takes the list as input and is independent of how the witness functions were selected.

Thus, with the canonical triple, the existential statement ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œthere is one fixed exponent and a sequence of $f_p$ for which the two subset-sum sequences have equivalent polynomial-time solvability at that boundÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â is provable in ZFC: choose the full-family witnesses above and run this solver on each list. This bypasses the claimed independence source. The phrase ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã…â€œthe only known proof uses the Jump Free TheoremÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‚Â is not an independence argument; a direct ZFC proof can exist even when the known proof presented in a paper uses an independent theorem.

**Scope and remaining ambiguity.** The result is for the canonical encoding. If the corollary is intended for arbitrary fixed bijections $\gamma_i$, a $p^k$-entry list may contain integers with superpolynomial bit length in $p$, and the P=NP hypothesis yields polynomial time in the *full binary input length*, not necessarily $O(p^{kt})$. A sufficient repair for the implication $P=NP\Rightarrow C$ is a uniform bound $N_p\le p^c$ on the total binary input length of both lists for some fixed $c$; then a polynomial-time subset-sum algorithm running in $N_p^d$ gives an $O(p^{cd})$ bound, which can be written as $O(p^{kt})$ for a fixed $t$. If the functions $\gamma_i$ are noncomputable, the instances may not even form an effective sequence unless lists are supplied as input. The paper's use of arbitrary bijections, its `$p^k$ is instance size' convention, and the uniform-generation quantifiers therefore need to be resolved before considering an arbitrary-$\gamma$ variant.

The predecessor paper [*Subset Sum Instances in ZFC Limbo*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.05385) makes the size convention explicit: it measures instance size by $p^k$ while the entries are integers whose bit lengths are not bounded there. Its definitions form $H_p$ by set unions, but also describe the $p^k$ values as a multiset. The proof's counts of at most $k^k$ negative terms and at most $t\log(p^k)$ small positive terms are counts of distinct values; they justify enumerating subsets if repeated values are collapsed as a set, but not automatically if copies are separate multiset items. This is a representation issue to clarify, not by itself a refutation: with explicit binary lists, polynomially many arithmetic operations on polynomial-size integers are polynomial in the full input length, although not necessarily $O(p^{kt})$ bit operations.

**Learning and next move.** The ambitious set-theoretic source can disappear under a small encoding choice: fullness lets us put the whole witness domain in $[p]^k$, reflexivity bounds every output, and bounded weights make the computational corollary elementary. This is a rigorous route-specific closure, not evidence for either answer to P versus NP. Do not pursue independence for the canonical corollary. If analyzing an arbitrary-$\gamma$ statement, first rewrite it as a closed sentence with all maps and size parameters quantified; then check whether a dynamic program or a simple reparameterization proves it in ZFC before attempting a model-theoretic independence proof.

## Idea 122 - Coupling derivatives are not computational distinguishability

**Status:** exact finite coupling lemma proved; identifies a model-completeness gap in the recent quantale/evidence preprint and a sharper metric for future work. No P-vs-NP consequence by itself.

Let $\Omega_0,\Omega_1$ be finite world spaces with distributions $\mu_0,\mu_1$, and let $T$ be any finite-valued observation. Write $P_b=T_*\mu_b$ for the induced law of the observation in phase $b$. Among all couplings $\Gamma$ of $\mu_0,\mu_1$,

$$
\min_{\Gamma}\Pr_{(X_0,X_1)\sim\Gamma}[T(X_0)\ne T(X_1)]
=\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1).
$$

**Proof.** For any coupling and any output value $z$, the mass of pairs with $T(X_0)=T(X_1)=z$ is at most $\min(P_0(z),P_1(z))$. Summing gives agreement probability at most $\sum_z\min(P_0(z),P_1(z))=1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)$, hence disagreement is at least total variation. For equality, maximally couple the two finite output laws: place mass $\min(P_0(z),P_1(z))$ on each diagonal pair $(z,z)$, then couple the residual laws, whose supports are disjoint. Lift this output coupling to the original worlds by sampling each endpoint from its phase law conditioned on its chosen output value. The lifted marginals are $\mu_0,\mu_1$ and its disagreement probability is exactly total variation. $ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â‚¬â€œÃ‚Â¡$

This exact identity exposes why a derivative computed under one fixed coupling is not, by itself, a measure of predictive power. If $\mu_0=\mu_1$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}$ and $T$ is the identity, the anti-diagonal coupling has disagreement $1$ even though $\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)=0$ and no predictor can distinguish the phases. An arbitrary coupling can therefore manufacture pair disagreement that carries no statistical information. A structure-compatible coupling is useful only if the proof also shows that its derivative bounds the relevant computational prediction advantage.

**Full-public-input consequence.** In the Goertzel preprint, the single-message promise makes every target bit $B_j$ a deterministic function of the public instance $Y$ on the sampler support. Thus the conditional laws $\mathcal{L}(Y\mid B_j=0)$ and $\mathcal{L}(Y\mid B_j=1)$ have disjoint supports and total variation $1$. Equivalently, every pair of opposite-message worlds has different public strings. A full-string observation separates every such pair. This does not provide a polynomial-time predictor: the separating set could be computationally hard. It does mean that a lower-bound argument whose zero-cost "neutral" atoms cover every readable public bit conflicts with pair-neutrality; if the atoms cover only a common skeleton, the proof still owes a compilation of ordinary algorithms reading the omitted bits into its allowed trace model.

The conflict has a quantitative finite form. Write $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_L)$. For any coupling $\Gamma_j$ supported on opposite target phases,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{L}\Pr_{\Gamma_j}[Y_i(X_0)\ne Y_i(X_1)]\ge1,
$$

because every coupled pair differs in at least one coordinate. Hence not all public-bit observations can have zero pairwise derivative under this coupling. A valid atomic classification must expose at least one charged public observation on every opposite-phase pair or prove how its model avoids full-input reads.

The missing bridge is explicit in the paper's definitions. Section 5.6 expands observers using its declared primitive-read interface, while Hypotheses 4.22 and D.33 assert that all target-relevant leaves normalize to neutral, safe-buffer, or gauge atoms. The paper states that observers see the full $Y$, but does not establish that every polynomial-time Turing machine on the full bit string has a trace in this vocabulary whose target-relevant public reads satisfy those classifications. A ban on a literal target-tag field does not establish such semantic completeness. The audit of the sampler hypotheses and this separate observer-model gap is recorded in Audit Sections 28 and 84 ([preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08814)).

**A local-to-global counterexample.** For any even $n\ge4$, let $J$ be the all-ones matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ and set $A=I+J$. Since $J^2=nJ=0$ and $2J=0$ over $\mathbb F_2$, $A^2=I$; hence $A$ is invertible. Take uniform $M\in\{0,1\}^n$ and publish $Y=AM$. Then

$$
M_i=\bigoplus_{r\ne i}Y_r.
$$

For every set $S$ of at most $n-2$ public coordinates, $Y_S$ leaves at least one bit of this parity unobserved, so $M_i$ remains uniform conditioned on $Y_S$. Yet all $n$ public bits recover every message bit by parity. This proves that bounded-coordinate or bounded-arity leakage checks do not imply hardness against a polynomial-time computation of the whole input. It is a finite algebraic counterexample to that inference, not a SAT construction or a complexity separation.

**Local 3CNF realization.** This algebraic example can be turned into an explicit SAT family. Sample uniform $M$, set $Y=AM$, and let $\Phi_Y$ be a Tseitin 3CNF encoding of the bounded-fan-in XOR network computing each equation $(AZ)_i=Y_i$. Each XOR gate has a constant-size 3CNF equivalence encoding, and there are $O(n^2)$ gates, so $|\Phi_Y|=O(n^2)$. Since $A$ is invertible, every satisfying assignment has the same $Z=A^{-1}Y=M$; with full gate-equivalence constraints, the Tseitin variables are also uniquely determined. The family is uniformly polynomial-time samplable and its unique message is recovered from the public right-hand sides by the parity map $A^{-1}$ in polynomial time. No public clause needs to assert a target variable $Z_i=b$ directly; each individual RHS bit is a parity of $n-1$ message bits, and any at-most-$n-2$ RHS coordinates leave each $M_i$ uniform. A simple gauge lift can be added using raw variables $X,G$ and local equations $Z=X\oplus G$; the message remains easy to decode from $Y$.

This is a direct stress test for the claimed proof architecture: bounded-arity SAT clauses, a rigid message across all witnesses, and even a hidden gauge orbit do not by themselves make the public message hard. If the no-public-tag condition rules out this construction only by forbidding every polynomial-time function of the full public syntax that recovers the message, that condition already contains the computational hardness burden that the lower-bound proof must establish.

**Correct computational norm.** For balanced phase distributions over public strings, the robust prediction quantity for a circuit class $\mathcal{C}$ is

$$
\operatorname{Adv}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y;B_j)
=\sup_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\left|\Pr[C(Y)=1\mid B_j=1]-\Pr[C(Y)=1\mid B_j=0]\right|.
$$

For unrestricted tests this equals total variation; for polynomial-size circuits it is computational indistinguishability. It automatically includes global parity circuits and the actual public encoding. Replacing the paper's atomic evidence budget with this norm does not solve the lower-bound task: proving it $o(1)$ for a fixed explicit uniform family would itself be a strong average-case hardness theorem. It is, however, the right quantity against which to compare an ordinary SAT self-reduction.

**Relevant current literature.** Kabanets and Kolokolova's revised 2026 ECCC paper characterizes a sublinear-error chain rule for time-bounded conditional Kolmogorov complexity by a conjunction of an exponential-time circuit lower bound ($E\not\subset io\,SIZE[2^{o(n)}]$) and polynomial-time solvability of a promise gap problem for $K^t$.
