The selector degree is not controlled by a membership-decider degree through generic search-to-decision, so this gives no contradiction. The 2026 theorem's n^epsilon bound is weaker than the selector's O(log n) code and does not improve the clock bound. The attractive coding transfer has therefore been pushed to its current limit without producing a separation.


## Idea 163 - The exponent floor scales with the clock (25 September 2026)

**Status:** the quantifier audit explains why increasing the fixed clock parameter does not turn the existing lower bound into P != NP. A conditional range-avoidance paper reinforces the need to track the constructor's actual exponent.

For each fixed q, R_q is in coNP. Under P=NP it has some P decider D_q, but its exponent may depend on q. The fixed-clock compression argument proves that any such decider has degree at least q. Conversely, if SAT has a P algorithm of degree d, a quasilinear Cook-Levin encoding of the n^q-step verifier gives a generic R_q decider with runtime n^(qd) polylog(n)^(O(1)). Thus the known lower and upper bounds both scale linearly in q. P contains languages of arbitrarily high fixed polynomial degree, so these statements can all hold together.

This is a quantifier barrier, not a proof barrier that can be removed by choosing a larger q. The invalid move is to inspect a decider for R_q, learn its degree a, and then switch to R_(a+1): that changes the language and does not contradict existence of the original decider. Putting q on the input does not solve it, because verifying a candidate description for n^q steps ceases to be polynomial time when q is unbounded. A separation needs one fixed R_q outside P (or another fixed NP language), not merely a family whose required degrees grow.

**Conditional construction check.** Korten and Santhanam's ECCC TR25-104 proves, under strong time-versus-NP-oracle/advice hypotheses, polynomial-time construction of strings with K^(n^k)(x) >= n - poly(log^[d](n)) for infinitely many n, and conditional algorithms for uniform Range Avoidance in specified circuit-size/stretch regimes. This is a close conceptual neighbor: the theorem turns resource lower-bound assumptions into explicit objects. Its stated complexity deficit is not the exact n-1 threshold defining R_q, the uniform-Avoid corollary has parameter conditions that must be checked against our evaluator, and the theorem does not bound the constructor's polynomial degree below k. The paper's general output-time observation gives a lower bound of order T/log T for constructing a K^T-hard string; for T=n^k, this forces near-n^k time on successful lengths. If a constructor outputs an R_q member at length n, its reference-machine simulation must exceed n^q for all sufficiently large such n; otherwise its O(log n)-bit description would contradict membership. This bound applies on successful lengths, not necessarily on other lengths. The conditional theorem therefore does not erase the degree floor.

**Constructor clock floor.** The paper observes that any algorithm outputting a K^T-hard string cannot run in o(T/log T): its own short description would reproduce that output within the K clock. Applying this with T=n^k to Theorem 12 shows that a constructor achieving the near-linear K^(n^k) guarantee must itself take at least n^k/polylog(n) time on its successful lengths. Thus the theorem's polynomial-time conclusion does not provide a constructor below the same clock.

**Range-avoidance transfer test.** Suppose a uniform circuit C_n maps r(n) bits to m(n) bits and its generation and evaluation fit the K clock T. Each range output has K^T at most r(n)+O(log n), using a program containing the input and a uniform evaluator. A constructor lower bound K^T(x)>=m(n)-Delta(n) proves x is outside the range only if m(n)-Delta(n)>r(n)+O(log n). Thus the stretch must beat both the complexity deficit and the encoding overhead. The Korten-Santhanam deficit poly(log^[d] n) does not yield this inequality for the one-bit stretch m=r+1 in the R_q evaluator. This identifies why conditional near-maximal K constructions do not solve our exact AVOID instance.

**Formal-logic note.** P vs NP is expressible as an arithmetic sentence in ZFC, but no one knows whether ZFC proves it, refutes it, or is independent for this sentence. Proof enumeration on both sides terminates only if ZFC decides the statement. Hence the hope that enough proof search must eventually succeed is not justified by decidability; it is a research heuristic, not a theorem.

**Learning:** maintain a per-target resource ledger (q, verifier clock, decider exponent, selector exponent, output deficit). Never infer a fixed-language lower bound from an exponent that grows across different languages. For conditional explicit-construction papers, record the exact parameter regime and polynomial degree before attempting a P-vs-NP transfer.

**Source:** Korten and Santhanam, [*How to Construct Random Strings*, ECCC TR25-104](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/104/), especially Theorem 12 and Section 4.4. See [New Model, Section 2.44](New%20Model.MD) and [Audit Section 125](P_VS_NP_PROJECT_AUDIT_2026-08-24.md).


### Idea 164 - Treat the multi-string time-bounded chain rule as a cryptographic stress test (25 September 2026)

**Status:** the implication tree is now explicit, but it does not yield an unconditional separation. It gives a rigorous conditional obstruction and a sharper witness target.

Write CR for the conditional multi-string chain rule with an error function (e(N)=o(N)): for every fixed (D>1), some fixed polynomial clock (p_D) and constants make

\[
K^t(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\mid y) \geq \sum_i K^{p_D(t)}(x_i\mid y,x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1}) - O(\ell\log t)-N/D
\]

hold for all sufficiently large admissible inputs. Kabanets and Kolokolova's exact characterization says this is equivalent to an exponential circuit lower-bound condition for E together with polynomial-time solvability of a gap version of conditional minimum time-bounded K.

**Collapse direction, checked from the proof.** If P=NP, then for each fixed C>1 the predicate

\[
A_C(x,y,1^t)=1 \iff \exists p\ (|p|\le |x|-|x|/C \text{ and } U^t(p,y)=x)
\]

is in NP and hence in P. For each fixed y, counting says at least half of n-bit x have plain conditional K(x|y)>n-O(1); since time-bounded K is no smaller, A_C rejects at least half of x for large n. Thus A_C is a P-computable natural property for conditional K^t with usefulness n-n/C. Kabanets-Kolokolova also cite Kannan's theorem for the needed E lower-bound condition under P=NP. Their characterization therefore gives P=NP => CR. Consequently, a proof that CR fails with a linear-in-N deficit on arbitrarily large instances would prove P!=NP.

**Cryptographic obstruction, derived from their construction.** Conversely, CR with e(N)=o(N) gives a P-computable natural property for K^t with usefulness n-n/D for every fixed D>1. Choose D=10. If standard cryptographic one-way functions existed, the standard OWF-to-PRG theorem gives a polynomial-time generator G from n^epsilon seed bits to n output bits for some epsilon<1. Set t to dominate G's runtime. Every G(z) has K^t(G(z))<=n^epsilon+O(1)<0.9n, so the natural property accepts every generator output, while rejecting at least half of uniform strings. That is a polynomial-time distinguisher, contradicting PRG security. Therefore CR implies that standard cryptographic OWFs do not exist. The paper's Appendix B proves an even more quantitative two-string statement for a much smaller error, delta=o(n^(1/3)); keep that separate from the broader multi-string e=o(N) implication.

This gives the implication ladder

\[
P=NP \Longrightarrow CR \Longrightarrow \text{no cryptographic OWFs}, \qquad \text{cryptographic OWFs} \Longrightarrow P\ne NP \text{ and } \neg CR.
\]

The final arrow to \(\neg CR\) is conditional on OWF existence, which remains unproved. CR is therefore a useful separator between the collapse world and standard cryptographic worlds, but it is not known to be equivalent to P=NP without the paper's separate NP-hardness assumption for the gap problem.

**Refined PRG construction: conditional witnesses under OWFs.** The seed-plus-output idea becomes a real conditional construction when the output is split into logarithmic-clock-size blocks. Fix a proposed chain rule with clock polynomial p, hidden coefficient a in O(ell log t), and error e(N,t)=o(N). Choose a fixed D>1 so that the PRG seed length N^alpha is below N-N/D by a constant fraction. Choose C>2D; for all sufficiently large N, e(N,t)Ã¢â€°Â¤N/C. Set t=N^k above the chain-rule and generator clocks, and partition an N-bit stretched PRG output into ellÃ¢â€°Ë†N/(c log t) blocks of bÃ¢â€°Ë†c log t bits.

Set S=floor((N-N/D+a ell log t+N/C)/ell). Choose c sufficiently large (and a block-compatible output length, truncating fewer than b bits if needed) so SÃ¢â€°Â¤b-2log ell-O(1). Define the deterministic test A(x)=1 iff some block x_i has K^{p(t)}(x_i|x_1...x_{i-1})Ã¢â€°Â¤S. This is polynomial time in t: enumerate fewer than 2^(S+1)=t^{O(c)} programs and simulate each for p(t) steps. For uniform x, plain-K counting gives probability O(1/ell) that any block has such a short conditional description, so A rejects almost all uniform strings. Since A is a polynomial-time distinguisher, PRG security forces it to reject almost all PRG outputs too. Pick any seed z for which A(G(z))=0. Then every block has conditional complexity >S, whence

\[
\sum_i K^{p(t)}(x_i|x_{<i}) > N-N/D+a\ell\log t+N/C.
\]

But the whole x=G(z) has K^t(x)Ã¢â€°Â¤N^alpha+O(log N)<N-N/D-ÃŽÂ©(N). After subtracting the proposed O(ell log t) and e(N,t)Ã¢â€°Â¤N/C, the claimed chain-rule lower bound would require K^t(x)>N-N/D, a contradiction. Thus, assuming a secure polynomial-stretch PRG (and hence OWFs), this procedure gives arbitrarily large, linearly violating tuples against every proposed polynomial clock and constants. Sampling seeds and retaining one for which A rejects is an expected-polynomial-time witness constructor; in fact the rejection probability tends to one. This is a conditional construction, not an unconditional separation.

The first naive version was incomplete because standard PRG security does not directly lower-bound conditional K: that predicate is coNP-style. The refinement makes the tested block only O(log t) bits long, so exhaustive bounded-program search becomes polynomial time and can serve as the distinguisher. This is the exact mechanism that closes the conditional construction.

**Exact witness obligation without crypto assumptions.** To refute CR unconditionally, for some fixed D>1 one must defeat every proposed polynomial p_D and hidden error constants at arbitrarily large N with a linear deficit after the O(ell log t) term. The PRG method achieves that only if OWFs exist. The remaining target is to produce the same low-joint/high-conditional tuple without assuming a secure generator, or to derive such a generator from a strictly weaker premise already implied by P!=NP. No such implication is known.

**Learning:** superconstant-string amplification does more than characterize the error term: after block size is reduced to O(log t), it converts PRG indistinguishability into an efficient search for a chain-rule witness. The earlier obstruction was a granularity mistake; local brute force is feasible at logarithmic block size even when global conditional-K testing is not. The unconditional gap is now isolated to obtaining this witness without an unproved cryptographic premise.

**Sources:** Kabanets and Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089, revision 1, Theorems 5.2, 7.1, 7.6 and B.1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/); Huang, Ilango, and Ren, [ECCC TR23-046](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/046/).



### Idea 165 - Separate the chain-rule consequences by hardness model (25 September 2026)

**Question.** Does CR -> no one-way functions, combined with the Grollmann-Selman theorem, force P=UP and then P=NP?

**Audit: the first bridge is invalid.** There are two distinct notions of one-wayness here.

* The Grollmann-Selman/Ko characterization uses a worst-case, deterministic notion: a polynomial-time honest injective function has no deterministic polynomial-time inverter that succeeds on every range input. Such functions exist iff P != UP.
* The chain-rule consequence in Kabanets-Kolokolova is cryptographic: no polynomial-time randomized inverter succeeds on a non-negligible fraction of uniformly random inputs for a length-indexed function family. The natural-property argument rules out secure PRGs, hence standard cryptographic OWFs.

A function may be invertible on almost every random input and still fail to have a deterministic polynomial-time inverter on every input. In particular, the chain-rule consequence does not establish that the Grollmann-Selman worst-case one-way functions do not exist, so it does not establish P=UP. This is a quantifier/model mismatch, not a missing application of the GS theorem.

**What CR does force.** The Kabanets-Kolokolova characterization gives CR -> E not-subset io-SIZE[2^{o(n)}] and CR -> the relevant conditional GapMcK^tP promise problem is in P. The first statement implies BPP=P by their hardness-versus-randomness theorem. Separately, the efficient natural property derived from CR breaks every secure polynomial-stretch PRG, so CR implies no standard cryptographic OWFs.

If, in addition, the exact GapMcK^tP promise problem solved by the characterization is NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions, then CR implies NP subseteq BPP; combine with BPP=P to get P=NP. Conversely P=NP implies CR by the paper's Kannan-based circuit lower bound plus its characterization. Thus CR iff P=NP is obtained under the stated gap-hardness assumption, not from the no-cryptographic-OWF consequence alone. Huang-Ilango-Ren establish relevant meta-complexity hardness under cryptographic assumptions in specified parameter regimes; do not erase those assumptions or parameter restrictions when citing it.

**Valiant-Vazirani's exact role.** P=UP gives UniqueSAT in P, so Valiant-Vazirani yields NP subseteq RP. This alone is not a known proof of P=NP. In the CR setting, however, we already have BPP=P and RP is a subset of BPP; therefore, if one could validly derive P=UP from CR, the two consequences together would indeed give P=NP. The problem is the unsupported CR -> P=UP arrow.

**Next proof target.** Work directly on the missing implication: either prove NP-hardness of the relevant GapMcK^tP promise problem without cryptographic assumptions, or find a direct reduction from SAT to that exact promise problem which preserves the time, description, and additive-gap parameters. The candidate reduction must output its instance in polynomial time without already finding a satisfying witness.

**Learning.** Every implication in the notebook now needs a hardness-type label: worst-case vs average-case; deterministic vs randomized inverter; single function vs length-indexed family; unconditional vs assumption-dependent. The word Ã¢â‚¬Å“one-wayÃ¢â‚¬Â alone is not a usable premise. The proof route's current bottleneck is an NP-hardness bridge, not more consequences of the natural property.

**Sources:** Kabanets and Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089 revision 1, Theorems 2.2, 4.1, 5.2, 6.2, 6.5, and Appendix A](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/); Grollmann and Selman, [*Complexity Measures for Public-Key Cryptosystems*](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0217018); Huang, Ilango, and Ren, [*NP-Hardness of Approximating Meta-Complexity: A Cryptographic Approach*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/046/download/).



### Idea 166 - Match the witness-encryption hardness promise to the chain-rule gap solver (25 September 2026)

**Conditional theorem, with the parameter match written out.** Kabanets-Kolokolova Theorem 6.4 (citing Huang-Ilango-Ren) assumes subexponentially secure witness encryption for NP. Under that assumption, the following promise problem is NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions: for \(|x|=n\) and \(|y|=\mathrm{poly}(n)\), distinguish
\[
K^{t_H(n)}(x\mid y)\le \sqrt n
\quad\text{from}\quad
K^{2^{n^2}}(x\mid y)\ge n-O(1),
\]
for a polynomial \(t_H\).

If CR held, Corollary 2.17 / Theorem 6.2 gives, for a fixed constant \(C>1\), a polynomial-time solver for a promise gap with yes side \(K^t(x\mid y)\le s\), no side \(K^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)>s+n/C\), and some polynomial \(\tau\). On a HIR instance, submit \(s=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) and unary \(t=t_H(n)\). A HIR yes instance meets the gap solver's yes promise. On a HIR no instance, \(\tau(t_H(n))\) is polynomial in \(n\), hence eventually less than \(2^{n^2}\). Since time-bounded K is nonincreasing in its clock,
\[
K^{\tau(t_H(n))}(x\mid y)\ge K^{2^{n^2}}(x\mid y)\ge n-O(1)>\lceil\sqrt n\rceil+n/C
\]
for all sufficiently large n. So the CR-derived solver decides the NP-hard HIR promise problem.

The reduction to the HIR promise problem is randomized, so this establishes \(NP\subseteq BPP\), not directly \(NP\subseteq P\). But CR also implies \(E\not\subset io\text{-}SIZE[2^{o(n)}]\), which gives \(BPP=P\) by hardness-versus-randomness. Thus
\[
\text{subexponentially secure witness encryption for NP} + CR
\Longrightarrow NP=P.
\]
The reverse \(P=NP\Rightarrow CR\) is unconditional. Therefore CR is equivalent to \(P=NP\) under this witness-encryption assumption. This is the fully checked conditional route; it is not an unconditional proof because the assumption is not known.

**Learning.** The comparison needs both clock monotonicity and the fact that the gap input carries unary \(t\): a polynomial HIR clock keeps the query polynomial size, while its \(\tau(t)\) no-clock remains far below the HIR \(2^{n^2}\) clock. The huge complexity separation is what lets the gap solver's linear additive promise absorb the \(\sqrt n\) yes threshold. Keep the randomized-reduction step visible: it yields BPP first, and the exponential circuit lower bound is what turns that into P.

**Sources:** Kabanets-Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089 revision 1, Corollary 2.17 and Theorems 6.2, 6.4, 6.5](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/); Huang-Ilango-Ren, [ECCC TR23-046, Theorem 3.1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/046/download/).



### Idea 167 - A direct SAT-to-gap reduction must hide the compressed description

The conditional HIR bridge suggests a structural audit for a proposed unconditional reduction \(R\) from SAT to \(\mathrm{GapMcK}^t\mathrm P\). Suppose \(R(\varphi;r)\) outputs \((x,y,1^s,1^t)\), where \(r\) is its random tape.

**Elementary obstruction.** If there is a fixed program \(q\), of length \(d\le s\), that on conditional input \(y\) outputs \(x\) within time \(t\) for every output of \(R\), then every output is a YES instance:
\[
K^t(x\mid y)\le d\le s.
\]
So \(R\) cannot map unsatisfiable formulas to promised NO instances. In particular, a construction where \(y\) contains the formula and the reduction's random seed, and \(x\) is efficiently reconstructed from them, collapses both cases to the low-complexity side. The same issue occurs if \(y\) lets a fixed polynomial-time computation reconstruct \(x\) and that computation fits the YES clock.

For a valid reduction, yes instances must have a short conditional description that is available when a witness exists, while no instances must remain incompressible even with the much larger \(\tau(t)\) clock. The reduction itself must still generate \((x,y)\) in polynomial time without knowing the witness. This is exactly the tension witness encryption addresses: ciphertext y can be generated without a witness, a satisfying witness can unlock a short description of x, and in the unsatisfiable case y hides the relation between x and the ciphertext. Merely putting \(\varphi\) in y makes the verifier accessible but also lets the short program exploit the formula in both cases; omitting all witness-related information leaves no known way to create the yes-side compression.

This is a no-go only for the explicit Ã¢â‚¬Å“conditional input already contains an efficient reconstruction of xÃ¢â‚¬Â template, not for all SAT reductions. It explains why a direct construction has to supply a new witness-locking mechanism or prove an unconditional complexity property of its output distribution. It also gives a quick rejection test for future ideas: write the actual \(q(y)\), its code length, and runtime before claiming a no-case K lower bound.

**Learning.** The hard part of a meta-complexity reduction is not producing a short description on YES instances alone. It is arranging an efficiently generated instance where the hidden witness changes whether the description exists, without making x reconstructible from y in the NO case. Any proposed Ã¢â‚¬Å“self-referenceÃ¢â‚¬Â or ZFC encoding still owes this operational hiding property in explicit form.

**Connection:** Idea 166 records the fully checked witness-encryption construction and its conditional CR iff P=NP consequence.



### Idea 168 - Exhaustive diagonalization and witness length collide

Test the obvious assumption-free construction against a SAT input \(\varphi\) of length \(m\).

To construct an \(n\)-bit string \(x\) that is outside the outputs of every program of length at most \(s\), the direct diagonal method enumerates \(2^{s+1}-1\) programs and simulates each for the relevant clock. If the clocks and simulation overhead are polynomial in \(m\), this takes \(2^{s+O(1)}\mathrm{poly}(m)\) time. For a polynomial-time reduction, this method requires \(s=O(\log m)\).

By contrast, the naive YES certificate program hardcodes a satisfying assignment for a general formula. Its description has length at least the witness encoding length up to interpreter overhead, ordinarily \(\Omega(m)\) for a Cook-Levin witness. Thus this template asks simultaneously for \(s=O(\log m)\) to carry out the exhaustive diagonalization and \(s=\Omega(m)\) to encode the witness. Padding the target \(x\) does not fix this: if \(n=\mathrm{poly}(m)\) and \(s\) is a constant fraction of n, enumerating \(2^s\) programs remains superpolynomial in m.

This is a barrier only for the direct Ã¢â‚¬Å“diagonalize against every short program, then put the SAT witness in a short programÃ¢â‚¬Â construction. It does not rule out more efficient diagonalization, smaller witness encodings for a special source problem, or a non-diagonal way to certify high K.

Randomly sampling x can avoid exhaustive enumeration on NO instances: conditional-K counting says a random x is usually incompressible relative to a fixed y. But in YES instances the reduction still has to arrange that a short program recovers that sampled x using a satisfying witness, even though the reduction generated x without knowing the witness. If y includes all randomness and the efficient reconstruction, x is short in both SAT cases. If y hides the seed, the witness must unlock it. This returns to the witness-locking obligation in Idea 167.

**Parameter ledger.** For source length m, a proposed direct reduction must explain all four items together: (i) target length n=poly(m), (ii) program cutoff s large enough for its YES description, (iii) construction of x in poly(m) time, and (iv) high K^{\tau(t)} on NO instances. The naive exhaustive method fails at (ii) versus (iii); random sampling handles (iv) probabilistically but leaves (ii) dependent on a witness lock.

**Learning.** Do not write Ã¢â‚¬Å“choose a random high-K stringÃ¢â‚¬Â as a complete reduction step: high complexity can be likely without being efficiently certifiable, and that randomness does not by itself create a witness-dependent short YES program.



### Idea 169 - Unique-witness rank coding trades description length for an unusable clock

A tempting repair to Idea 168 is: after Valiant-Vazirani isolation, encode the satisfying assignment by its rank among satisfying assignments. With a unique witness the rank is 1, so its code is constant size. But the program that receives \(\varphi\) and rank 1 must find the first satisfying assignment. The direct algorithm enumerates up to \(2^m\) assignments and checks each in polynomial time. Thus its output clock is exponential in the formula size.

In the \(\mathrm{GapMcK}^t\mathrm P\) reduction, \(t\) is supplied in unary. Setting \(t=2^{\Theta(m)}\) makes the reduction output length exponential, so it is not a polynomial-time reduction. Keeping \(t=\mathrm{poly}(m)\) means the rank program cannot complete the search. Isolation controls the *number* of witnesses; it does not provide an efficient way to locate the unique one.

More generally, storing a witness by its rank among all \(m\)-bit strings costs m bits. Storing its rank among the satisfying witnesses can be short when there is a unique witness, but computing that ranked witness is itself the hard search. Any rank-based compression must account separately for the bits needed to name the rank and the time needed to recover the corresponding witness.

**Checked consequence for this template.** Valiant-Vazirani plus a constant-size rank is not a replacement for witness encryption in the conditional-K reduction: it fixes the program-length budget only by spending an exponential computation clock.

**Learning.** In time-bounded Kolmogorov reductions, unique existence is not the same as efficient recoverability. Record both description size and decoder runtime; rank compression can improve one while destroying the other.



### Idea 170 - The conditional hardness reduction is a witness-locked random message

The HIR construction makes Idea 167 concrete. On a formula \(\varphi\), the reduction samples a uniformly random \(n\)-bit message \(m\) and encryption randomness \(r\), then outputs
\[
x=m,\qquad y=\operatorname{WE}(1^\lambda,\varphi,m;r).
\]
The output is computable in polynomial time without finding a satisfying assignment.

**Satisfiable case.** If \(w\) satisfies \(\varphi\), the decryption algorithm recovers m from \(y,\varphi,w\). A program for \(x\) given \(y\) stores \(\varphi\) and the fixed decryption code, and uses \(w\) as part of its description. The theorem chooses the message length n large enough relative to the formula size that this description is at most \(n^{1/c}\), and it runs within a polynomial clock \(t_1(n)\).

**Unsatisfiable case.** Define \(Low(y)=\{z\in\{0,1\}^n:K^{t_2(n)}(z\mid y)\le n-105\}\), where \(t_2(n)=2^{n^c}\). Enumerating every program up to length \(n-105\) and simulating for \(t_2(n)\) gives a list containing every low-complexity string. The list is computable within the subexponential security budget selected by the reduction. List-security of witness encryption says a uniform plaintext m is in this list with probability at most \(1/3\); hence with probability at least \(2/3\), \(K^{t_2(n)}(m\mid y)>n-105\).

The critical asymmetry is therefore not created by an exotic choice of x: x is an ordinary random message. The ciphertext y is efficiently sampled in both cases, but a satisfying witness supplies exactly the missing decoder information, while in the unsatisfiable case the ciphertext prevents short descriptions from identifying m. Witness encryption packages this lock; the security assumption pays for the NO-case lower bound.

**Assumption-free construction target.** Reproduce this distributional property for a SAT-derived y without assuming witness encryption or another primitive that already provides witness-gated hiding:
\[
\Pr[\text{short program recovers }m\mid \varphi\in SAT]\ge 1-\epsilon,
\quad
\Pr[K^{T}(m\mid y)\le n-\Delta\mid \varphi\notin SAT]\le\epsilon,
\]
for large \(\Delta\), with polynomial-time sampling and parameters matching the gap solver. Any proposal that simply makes y a public encoding of \(\varphi\) and r fails, since a fixed decoder then recovers m on unsatisfiable formulas too.

**Learning.** The hard subgoal is list-hiding in the NO case, not just decryption on YES instances. A valid replacement must defeat all short programs (equivalently, their enumerated candidate list) on random messages while preserving witness-based decoding.



### Idea 171 - Witness encryption is consistent with P = NP

Check whether the assumption used in Ideas 166 and 170 secretly already implies the desired separation. Under the standard witness-encryption definition, security is required only on NO instances; correctness requires decryption when a witness exists.

If \(P=NP\), an encryption algorithm can decide whether \(\varphi\in SAT\). On a satisfiable input, it outputs a tagged plaintext \((1,m)\). On an unsatisfiable input, it outputs \((0,r)\) for fresh uniform randomness r of the appropriate length, independent of m. Given a satisfying witness, the decryption algorithm returns m from the first branch. There is no correctness requirement on the no-witness branch. For unsatisfiable \(\varphi\), the ciphertext distributions for any two messages are identical, so semantic security is perfect, including against subexponential adversaries.

This is a valid conditional construction in a \(P=NP\) world: the encryption routine uses the assumed polynomial-time SAT decider. Therefore subexponentially secure witness encryption for NP does not itself imply \(P\ne NP\). The conditional theorem Ã¢â‚¬Å“WE + CR implies \(P=NP\)Ã¢â‚¬Â is not circular and cannot be converted into a separation by claiming the assumption already excludes the collapse.

**Learning.** An assumption can enable the NP-hardness reduction while remaining compatible with the collapse conclusion. Keep the theorem conditional; do not infer \(P\ne NP\) from witness encryption alone.



### Idea 172 - An algorithmic chain rule is stronger evidence, but its complexity notion does not match the HIR reduction

Hirahara and Nanashima's revised 2026 report gives an algorithmic proof of a time-bounded chain rule. Under their promise assumption \(GapK^t\text{-vs-}K\in pr\text{-}BPP\), an efficient randomized procedure, given each prefix \(x_{\le i}\), outputs bounds \(k_i\) which simultaneously satisfy, with high probability,
\[
k_i\ge q^{\tau(t)}(x_i\mid x_{<i}),\qquad
\sum_i k_i\le q^t(x)+m\,O(\log t).
\]
Here \(q^t\) is the information content of a time-bounded universal distribution. This is an *algorithmic witness to the accounting*: it outputs the individual per-coordinate budgets, rather than merely asserting that suitable budgets exist. The paper uses this to obtain polynomial-time universal inductive inference under its assumption.

The assumption and the KK/HIR promise must not be conflated. Hirahara--Nanashima's displayed gap is unconditional in its input (no side-information string y) and its NO condition is plain, unbounded \(K(x)>s+c\log(t|x|)\). KK/HIR instead use conditional \(K^t(x\mid y)\), and HIR's NO guarantee is \(K^{2^{n^2}}(x\mid y)\ge n-O(1)\), at a specified finite clock. These are two separate mismatches: conditional versus unconditional complexity, and unbounded versus clock-bounded lower bounds.

The clock direction makes the second mismatch decisive. \(K^T(x)\) is nonincreasing in T and \(K(x)=\inf_T K^T(x)\). Therefore a lower bound on \(K^T(x)\) at one enormous finite T does not imply the same lower bound on unbounded \(K(x)\): a shorter description might halt only after that clock. By contrast, a lower bound on plain \(K(x)\) would imply the same lower bound for every clocked \(K^T(x)\). HIR's list-security proof establishes the former kind of finite-clock statement, so it cannot be inserted into the newer \(GapK^t\text{-vs-}K\) promise by parameter substitution alone.

There is also no free way to erase the side information y from the HIR YES case. A conditional program for x can use y at zero description cost; an unconditional program has to describe or regenerate y, in addition to the formula and witness. That added description may exceed the YES cutoff. Any proposed bridge needs a bound on the actual code length and decoder time for y, not an appeal to the fact that the reduction sampled y efficiently.

**New proof target.** Audit a *variant-preserving reduction*: keep track of (1) whether K is conditional, (2) whether the lower bound is for K or K^T, (3) the exact clock encoding, and (4) whether the premise supplies deterministic K-complexity or randomized universal-distribution q-complexity. The 2026 algorithmic chain rule gives a constructive tool after its meta-complexity premise is met; it does not itself construct the SAT-to-gap bridge or imply P=NP.

The implication direction also matters. \(P=NP\) implies \(DistNP\subseteq AvgP\), which implies the paper's \(GapK^t\text{-vs-}K\in pr\text{-}BPP\) assumption, which in turn gives the inductive-inference theorem. So this route is compatible with \(P=NP\); its current theorem is an algorithmic consequence of an average-case/meta-complexity premise, not a way to refute the collapse. The paper does not prove the reverse implication from its gap assumption to \(P=NP\).

**Learning.** Algorithmic proof can be a real upgrade: the produced \(k_i\)'s might support adaptive compression arguments that an existential chain-rule inequality cannot. But it only advances the target if the complexity notion and side information survive the reduction unchanged. Do not merge \(K\), \(K^T\), conditional \(K^T(\cdot\mid y)\), or \(q^T\) into a generic Ã¢â‚¬Å“Kolmogorov complexity.Ã¢â‚¬Â

Source: Hirahara--Nanashima, [Complexity-Theoretic Universal Inductive Inference, ECCC TR25-092 revision 1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/092/revision/1/download/), especially Definitions 2.1/4.3 and Lemma 5.1; compare Kabanets--Kolokolova [TR25-089 revision 1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/) and Huang--Ilango--Ren [TR23-046](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/046/download/).



## Idea 173 - Reinterpret the range-avoidance output as a truth table

The fixed-clock construction in Idea 159 can be pushed into a conditional near-maximum circuit lower bound. The key parameter change is to call the output length \(N=2^m\), and regard the \(N\)-bit missing output as the truth table of a Boolean function on \(m=\log N\) inputs.

Fix a sufficiently large constant \(q\). Let \(C_{N,q}:\{0,1\}^{N-1}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\) enumerate all programs \(p\) with \(|p|<N-1\), simulate each for \(N^q\) steps, and return its \(N\)-bit output or a default string. Idea 161 gives a uniform circuit for this map with \(G=O(N^q\log N)\) gates. A standard gate-list encoding has length \(S=O(G\log G)=O(N^q(\log N)^2)\). A missing output \(y_N\) exists by counting, and every such output has \(K_U^{N^q}(y_N)\ge N-1\).

Assume \(P=NP\). The range-avoidance search problem is then in FP: for a prefix \(u\), the predicate Ã¢â‚¬Å“some missing output extends uÃ¢â‚¬Â is in \(\Sigma_2^P\), hence in P after the polynomial hierarchy collapses; ask this predicate one output bit at a time. On the explicit gate-list input \(C_{N,q}\), this produces \(y_N\) in \(\mathrm{poly}(S)=N^{O(q)}\) time. Define \(f_m\) to be the Boolean function whose truth table is \(y_{2^m}\). Given an \(m\)-bit input z, a deterministic algorithm can construct the gate list for \(C_{2^m,q}\), run the fixed range-avoidance algorithm, and read the bit indexed by z. Its running time is \(2^{O(m)}\), so the language/function family \(f_m\) is in E. The fact that this construction may take more than \(N^q\) steps is harmless here: E measures time in \(m=\log N\), not in the truth-table length N.

Now suppose \(f_m\) has a fan-in-two circuit D of size \(s\). A fixed program can store D, evaluate it on all \(N\) inputs, and print \(y_N\). For a fixed universal machine, its description length is at most \(a s\log s+O(\log N)\), and its running time is at most \(N^b\) for a fixed b when \(s\le N\). Choose \(q>b\) and then a sufficiently small constant c>0. If \(s\le cN/m\), then the program length is less than \(N-1\) for all sufficiently large m, and its runtime is at most \(N^q\). This would put \(y_N\) in Range(\(C_{N,q}\)), contradiction. Hence
$$
C(f_m)>c\,\frac{2^m}{m}
$$
for all sufficiently large m, after adjusting c for the chosen machine and circuit encoding. This is a near-maximum circuit lower bound for an E language.

**What the deduction establishes.** \(P=NP\) forces \(E\not\subset io\text{-}SIZE[2^{o(m)}]\), with a concrete near-maximum hard truth-table construction. Thus the exponential circuit-lower-bound conjunct in the KK chain-rule characterization is not an independent contradiction to \(P=NP\); the collapse hypothesis itself supplies it. The argument also explains why Idea 161's failure to beat the \(N^q\) clock does not block the E lower bound: the hard function's input length is only \(\log N\).

**Novelty calibration.** The broad implication Ã¢â‚¬Å“polynomial-time Range Avoidance yields exponential circuit lower bounds for EÃ¢â‚¬Â is established in the Range Avoidance literature; see the overview in ECCC TR24-076. This entry instantiates that principle with the project's fixed-clock universal-program family and makes the \(N=2^m\) reparameterization explicit. It is a conditional project derivation, not a claim of a new unconditional circuit-lower-bound theorem.

**Limit.** This is conditional on \(P=NP\), exactly as a Kannan-style implication should be. It does not establish the hypothesis. To get \(P\ne NP\) from this construction one would need an incompatible upper bound for every E function, or another argument showing the constructed truth tables cannot be in E. Neither follows from range avoidance.

The class location is the decisive direction check: this witness is in E, not NP. \(P=NP\) does not collapse E to P; the deterministic time hierarchy gives \(P\subsetneq E\). Therefore an E circuit lower bound of this strength is fully compatible with \(P=NP\).

**Proof audit:** the only algorithmic collapse used is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\Rightarrow\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{P}\), which makes the prefix-extension predicate decidable in P. The circuit family \(C_{N,q}\) and the simulation program must use the same universal-machine convention; q is chosen after fixing that convention. The construction uses poly(S) time only to show \(f\in E\); the contradiction with the range relies separately on the \(N^q\) clock.

**Sources:** project construction and simulation accounting in [Ideas 159 and 161](ideas.md); Chen, Hirahara, and Ren, [*Symmetric Exponential Time Requires Near-Maximum Circuit Size*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12912), for the Range-Avoidance-to-circuit-lower-bound framework; Kabanets--Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089 revision 1, Theorems 7.1 and 7.6](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/), for the role of the E lower-bound conjunct.

## Idea 174 - Cross-audit of the clock-degree barrier

This is a consistency check against the earlier fixed-clock analyses in Ideas 139, 161, and 163, not a new independent lead. Its specific purpose is to ensure that the conditional E-hardness construction in Idea 173 is not misread as a subclock selector.

This pushes Idea 173 back to its exact algorithmic bottleneck. Fix q and let \(C_{n,q}\) be the explicit circuit from Idea 159: it maps \(n-1\) bits to n bits and simulates each short program for \(n^q\) steps. Every missing output \(y_n\) has \(K_U^{n^q}(y_n)\ge n-1\). The circuit has \(G=O(n^q\log n)\) gates and standard gate-list length \(M(n,q)=O(n^q(\log n)^2)\).

Assume \(P=NP\). The decision predicate Ã¢â‚¬Å“there is a missing output extending prefix uÃ¢â‚¬Â is in \(\Sigma_2^P\), so it has a fixed polynomial-time decider after the hierarchy collapses. Let d be the degree of that decider in its explicit input length. Bit-by-bit search makes at most n calls, each on an instance of length \(O(M(n,q))\), and therefore has the generic upper bound
\[
T_{\mathrm{search}}(n,q)\le O(nM(n,q)^d)
=n^{qd+1}(\log n)^{2d}.
\]

This upper bound cannot contradict the \(n^q\)-step incompressibility clock: the exponent inequality needed for that argument, \(qd+1<q\), has no solution for \(d\ge1\). Even granting a direct functional selector with degree \(d'\ge1\) in M, its generic \(M^{d'}\) bound would require \(qd'<q\), also impossible. The degree d is fixed for the general AVOID decider; increasing q multiplies both the input-size exponent and the clock exponent, so it does not repair the inequality.

**Succinct-input test.** One might pass the short uniform code for \(C_{n,q}\) instead of its gate list. At the empty-prefix query, if \(n=2^m\), the missing-output quantifier ranges over n-bit y and the preimage quantifier over \((n-1)\)-bit x, both exponential in the short code length m; evaluating the represented circuit also takes exponential time in m. The resulting predicate is in \(\Sigma_2^{EXP}\) under this standard succinct encoding, not thereby in \(\Sigma_2^P\). \(P=NP\) collapses PH but supplies no algorithm for this exponentially succinct problem. Padding the query with \(1^n\) can put it back at the polynomial-hierarchy input scale, but for each fixed q the resulting language has its own P-decider degree, with no bound relating that degree to q. Padding all the way to \(n^q\) makes the input length match the incompressibility clock. Neither padding gives a free exponent gain.

This is an obstruction to the *generic search-to-decision analysis*, not a lower bound on the actual running time of every solver on this structured family. A family-specific algorithm could in principle have a much better bound than the general polynomial guarantee. The K argument does prove that a fixed program taking only n (with q fixed) cannot generate a missing \(y_n\) in \(o(n^q)\) time. A general AVOID solver instead receives the full gate list for \(C_{n,q}\); using it as a program for \(y_n\) requires first supplying or generating that explicit circuit, whose standard uniform construction takes \(O(n^q(\log n)^2)\) time. The K bound therefore does not directly lower-bound the solver's running time measured from receipt of the explicit circuit. Under \(P=NP\), polynomial-time solvability is compatible because Ã¢â‚¬Å“polynomial in circuit sizeÃ¢â‚¬Â may mean time at least \(n^q\) on this family.

**Logical lesson.** The collapse \(P=NP\) can turn a \(\Sigma_2^P\) existence predicate into a P decision procedure. The K-complexity witness constrains a uniform generator that starts from n, while the decision-to-search algorithm is measured on a much longer explicit circuit input. Keeping those input models separate removes the apparent contradiction. The constructive branch therefore yields the E circuit lower bound in Idea 173, but cannot by itself yield a contradiction.

**Remaining positive target.** To get a separation from this line, a proof would need a different implication that does not ask the missing-output constructor to run below its own incompressibility clock. The precise candidates are: (i) a new bridge from a proof-theoretic or semantic property of SAT to a circuit bound incompatible with \(P=NP\); or (ii) a diagonalization inside NP that handles all polynomial exponents with one fixed verifier. Merely strengthening the generic polynomial bound for AVOID cannot suffice.

**Sources:** the fixed-clock construction and circuit accounting are in [Ideas 159, 161, and 173](ideas.md). The Range Avoidance framework and its relation to explicit circuit lower bounds are developed by Chen, Hirahara, and Ren, [*Symmetric Exponential Time Requires Near-Maximum Circuit Size*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12912), and Kabanets--Kolokolova, [ECCC TR25-089 revision 1](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/089/revision/1/download/). The published state of exponential circuit lower bounds is summarized in [ECCC TR24-076](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2024/076/).

## Idea 175 - A source-hiding inequality for SAT-to-K-gap reductions

This extracts a quantitative necessary condition from Idea 167's witness-locking obstruction. Let a randomized reduction \(R\), on input \(\varphi\) of length m and random tape r of length \(\rho(m)\), output a gap instance \((x,y,1^s,1^t)\), with \(|x|=n\). Write \(T_R(m)\) for a polynomial bound on running R and printing x. Suppose the NO promise is
\[
K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)>s+\Delta(n).
\]

**Composition lemma.** Fix any conditional description q which, given y, outputs \(\langle\varphi,r\rangle\) within \(T_0\) steps. A fixed wrapper can run q, then run R on the recovered source and tape, and print x. Thus, whenever this composition fits within \(\tau(t)\),
\[
K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)\le |q|+O(1).
\]
Consequently every NO output must satisfy
\[
K_U^{T_0}(\langle\varphi,r\rangle\mid y)>s+\Delta(n)-O(1)
\]
for every \(T_0\) whose composition with R fits the NO clock. In particular, if \(y\) itself lets a fixed polynomial-time program recover \((\varphi,r)\), the output cannot be a promised NO instance once the recovery-plus-reduction clock fits.

There is also a source-length floor independent of y. A program can store \(\varphi,r\), ignore y, run R, and print x. If this fits the NO clock, then
\[
K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)\le m+\rho(m)+O(\log(m+\rho(m))).
\]
So a valid NO output requires \(m+\rho(m)+O(\log(m+\rho(m)))>s+\Delta(n)-O(1)\). This immediately rejects parameter choices where the source and random tape are shorter than the promised high-K threshold.

**Implication for the missing hardness bridge.** On the good random tapes for an unsatisfiable formula, the side information y must leave the source-and-randomness pair conditionally incompressible to roughly the full NO threshold, for every decoder whose work still fits the large NO clock. This is a precise information-hiding obligation. HIR's witness-encryption reduction supplies a conditional mechanism for making the *message* incompressible given y; that is not the same as proving a separate source-and-tape hiding theorem. The lemma does not imply a one-way function or rule out all unconditional reductions: the source code may already exceed the target threshold, and high conditional K alone is not a cryptographic inversion theorem.

**Next test.** For any proposed SAT-to-gap reduction, write its actual \(\rho(m)\), \(T_R(m)\), \(s\), \(\Delta(n)\), and \(\tau(t)\), then test whether y permits recovery of \((\varphi,r)\) inside the NO clock. A claimed reduction that omits this budget has not yet established the NO promise.

**Connection:** [Idea 167](ideas.md) gives the simpler special case where y directly reconstructs x. This lemma tracks the reduction's source and random tape, and makes the time composition explicit. The conditional HIR parameters are audited in [Idea 166](ideas.md).


## Idea 176 - NO-side incompressibility forces randomness when the output is longer than the source

Idea 175's source-code floor can be isolated as a direct reduction constraint. Let a randomized reduction \(R\), on a fixed source formula \(\varphi\) of length \(m\) and a fixed-length random tape \(r\in\{0,1\}^{\rho(m)}\), output \((x,y,1^s,1^t)\). Suppose the reduction runs in time \(T_R(m)\), and let the target NO cutoff be \(k(m)=s+\Delta(|x|)\), measured using the promised NO clock \(\tau(t)\).

A conditional program can ignore \(y\), store \(\varphi\) and \(r\), run \(R(\varphi;r)\), and print \(x\). Its description length is
\[
m+\rho(m)+O(\log(m+\rho(m))),
\]
and its running time is the reduction time plus fixed universal-machine simulation overhead. Whenever this fits within \(\tau(t)\), every tape therefore satisfies
\[
K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)\le m+\rho(m)+O(\log(m+\rho(m))).
\]
Consequently, if the NO requirement is \(K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)>k(m)\), a reduction cannot produce even one promised NO output unless its tape length clears this source-description floor. Up to the self-delimiting length overhead, this requires
\[
\rho(m)\ge k(m)-m-O(\log(m+\rho(m))).
\]

For a target with \(k=n-O(1)\), target length \(n\), and source length \(m=o(n)\), a valid reduction must use at least \(n-o(n)\) random bits, provided the NO clock covers the reduction wrapper. This is a necessary random-tape length budget, not a claim that randomness alone creates incompressibility.

A sharp special case is \(\rho(m)=0\): if the NO clock covers the deterministic reduction and \(k(m)-m=\omega(\log m)\), then every output has \(K_U^{\tau(t)}(x\mid y)\le m+O(\log m)<k(m)\) for sufficiently large m. Such a reduction cannot map even one NO source instance to the promised NO side. More generally, any randomized reduction whose tape is too short to clear the source-description floor fails on every tape, not merely with noticeable probability.

**HIR sanity check.** Huang--Ilango--Ren output \(x=M\), where \(M\) is sampled uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), and \(y=\mathrm{WE}(1^\lambda,\varphi,M;r)\). The reduction's tape therefore already contains the \(n\)-bit message, in addition to encryption coins. Its source-code floor is at least \(n+|\varphi|-O(\log n)\), consistent with (and not contradictory to) the NO guarantee \(K^{2^{n^2}}(M\mid y)\ge n-O(1)\). List-security supplies the substantive guarantee that \(y\) does not enable a short description of \(M\) on NO inputs. The source-and-tape lemma alone gives no new hardness consequence for HIR.

**Use.** This rejects proposed reductions that try to get a near-\(n\)-bit NO complexity gap from substantially fewer than \(n-m\) random bits while generating \(x\) within the NO clock. It does not distinguish a pseudorandom tape from genuine randomness, prove cryptographic hiding, or rule out reductions whose source and target lengths make the floor vacuous. Keep it as an early parameter filter, not as a candidate P-vs-NP separation.

**Source:** HIR, [ECCC TR23-046, revised paper](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2023/046/revision/1/download/), Theorem 3.1 and its SAT reduction.


### Idea 177 - The promise-cover transfer already includes arbitrary circuits

The route has an unrestricted bridge. Set the ground set to Gamma=Y union Z, the target to Y, the complement U to Z, and the generators to the 2N truth-table literals restricted to Gamma. This matches the finite set-system instance in Cavalar and Oliveira's fusion theorem. Their inequality rho(Y,B) <= D_cap(Y|B) means every fan-in-two De Morgan separator needs at least rho AND gates. The firing-rule compiler from a cover to a circuit is a different direction and is not needed for this implication.

This closes the concern that a solver might use another representation, sharing, or nonlocal computation. The open step is the lower bound itself: prove rho>N^(1+epsilon) for every sufficiently small fixed beta in the magnification regime. The current proof-DAG argument gives only N-o(N); its leaves count input coordinates and cannot by itself pass the N ceiling. Future attempts must charge reuse across anchors or another global resource and must allow arbitrary endpoint subsets.

See research/CURRENT_STATE.md, research/OPEN_OBLIGATIONS.md, and Cavalar and Oliveira, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14117. This is a route audit, not a new lower bound or a P-vs-NP proof.


### Idea 178 - The Hamming-ball threshold family collapses under one pair

The earlier audit incorrectly treated global intersection closure as part of the semi-filter definition. Cavalar and Oliveira define a semi-filter as a nonempty upward-closed family excluding the empty set; preservation is required only for the chosen pair list. Thus F_a={S subseteq U : mu_a(S)>1/4} is a valid semi-filter whenever its matching literal generators have mass above 1/4.

Let N=2^n, s2=N^beta, s1=s2/(c n), U={z:CC(z)>=s2}, and Y={a:CC(a)<=s1}. For each a, take mu_a uniform on the tables in U within Hamming distance d=K s2 of a. Circuit counting gives at most M2=2^(O(s2 log(n+s2))) excluded tables. For any fixed beta<=1/2, a sufficiently large universal K makes the Hamming ball volume, at least (N/d)^d, exceed M2 by a factor 2^(Omega(s2 log N)). Since d/N=o(1), every matching coordinate slice has mu_a-mass 1-o(1), hence exceeds 3/4. The number of low anchors is only 2^(O(s2)), while every support H_a has size 2^(Omega(s2 log N)).

Independently color every point of U red or blue. Hoeffding and a union bound over Y show that some partition U=E disjoint-union H gives both colors mass greater than 1/4 under every mu_a. Then E,H belong to every F_a, and E intersect H is empty, so the same pair violates all these selected filters. The full parameter and concentration proof is C-10.

**Result.** This rigorously defeats the proposed fractional dual supported on these local Hamming-ball threshold filters: one pair covers its entire support. It does not rule out a distribution over more varied, nonlocal semi-filters. The useful constraint is that any viable dual must survive an arbitrary balanced partition chosen after its measures are fixed.

**Correction.** The previous version of this idea claimed F_a was invalid because it was not intersection-closed. That was a definition error; the source only requires upward closure and exclusion of the empty set. The balanced-pair argument is the actual failure mechanism.
### Idea 179 - Extended Frege supplies a separate conditional route

Pich and Santhanam prove a conditional route to P != NP: non-polynomial-boundedness of Extended Frege, together with an S2^1-provable polynomial-time function witnessing an error for every incorrect polynomial-size SAT circuit, implies the separation. Their feasible-antichecker statement is a separate sufficient condition. The error-witness condition ranges over arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, so it does not assume a solver's internal representation. It does, however, move the hard step to EF non-p-boundedness and the exact S2^1 proof obligation.

Direction check under P=NP: given a circuit C on n-bit formula encodings, deciding whether there exists an n-bit formula on which C disagrees with SAT is in NP, because SAT would have a polynomial-time decider. The associated search problem can then be solved in FP by prefix self-reduction. Thus standard-model feasible error finding is compatible with P=NP; this observation alone does not yield the paper's formalized hypothesis. The route currently has no advantage over the Gap-MCSP route because EF non-p-boundedness is an additional major open statement. Source: Pich and Santhanam, https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08163.

## Idea 180 Ã¢â‚¬â€ The symmetric high-anchor count fails; interpolation gives a weaker bound

**Attempt and correction.** The low-anchor fusion trace gives $\rho(Y,\mathcal B)\ge N-\log M_2-1$. I tried to repeat the same count for high anchors, claiming that a coordinate subcube containing no low table has at most $M_1$ points. This is false: the subcube may contain gap and high tables. The claimed $\rho(Z)\ge N-\log M_1-1$ and $D\ge2N-o(N)$ conclusions are withdrawn.

**Valid replacement.** If the high-anchor trace fixes $q$ positions, any prescribed pattern on those positions has a DNF extension of size $O(qn)$. Therefore an empty subcube must have $q=\Omega(s_1/n)=\Omega(N^\beta/n^2)$, giving only a sublinear bound on $\rho(Z)$. Complement duality adds it to the OR side, but it does not improve the leading $N-o(N)$ bound.

**Lesson.** Ã¢â‚¬Å“Avoids the sparse setÃ¢â‚¬Â does not mean Ã¢â‚¬Å“consists of points from the sparse set.Ã¢â‚¬Â Counting the size of a subcube requires every point in it to belong to the counted class. The previous mistake is documented in Ã‚Â§2.62 of [New Model](New%20Model.MD) and the correction in Ã‚Â§2.64.

**Status.** Corrected elementary lemma, no magnification progress. See [C-13](research/CLAIM_LEDGER.md), [OPEN_OBLIGATIONS](research/OPEN_OBLIGATIONS.md), and [frontier reassessment](research/FRONTIER_REASSESSMENT_2026-09-25.md).

## Idea 181 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Anti-checker selection must adapt to the truth table

For $N=2^n$, fixed $0<\beta<1/10$, and any fixed query set $Q$ of size at most $2^{10\beta n}$, the number of functions zero on $Q$ is $2^{N-|Q|}$. The number of circuits of size at most $s_2=2^{\beta n}$ is only $2^{O(n2^{\beta n})}$. Since $2^{10\beta n}+n2^{\beta n}=o(N)$, at least one high-complexity truth table remains zero on $Q$. Thus the constant-zero circuit passes every fixed sample; see C-15 for the count.

OPS's anti-checker list must therefore be selected from the entire input truth table. The actual target is an adaptive multi-output circuit with access to all $N$ bits, which on high-complexity inputs selects sample points refuting all circuits of size $s_1=s_2/(10n)$. OPS show this map has size $N^{1+O(\beta)}$ if $NP\subseteq Circuit[poly]$. A lower bound on this adaptive selector may offer a distinct route, but the fixed-sample lemma supplies no lower bound against it. Static anti-checker-family attacks and adaptive-selector lower bounds are different problems.

**Lesson.** Input-dependent choice is the first place the adversary can evade the counting argument. Any proposed selector invariant must survive unrestricted dependence on every truth-table bit.
## Idea 182 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Self-referentially patch the selector output against a fixed small circuit

Fix a selector $A$ and a small circuit $D$. From $f_i$, evaluate $A(f_i)$ and overwrite every selected truth-table bit with $D$'s value there. The Hamming distance to $D$ strictly decreases whenever $CC(f_i)>s_2$, because the anti-checker property guarantees a disagreement in the selected set. Thus the process terminates within at most $N$ strict rounds at $f_*$ with $CC(f_*)\le s_2$ and $A(f_*)$ consistent with $D$.

For a start with $CC(f_0)>2s_2$, pointwise DNF patching shows $d_H(f_0,f_*)=\Omega(s_2/n)$. However the selector's batch has $t=2^{10\beta n}$ locations, much more than $s_2/n$, so this is compatible with one round. If only one mismatch is overwritten at a time, many rounds follow, but repeated use of a small circuit is not a contradiction. The terminal table can lie in the full interval $(s_1,s_2]$, so this does not yield a low-side MCSP instance.

**Result.** This self-reference has a clean descent invariant but no separation. Its exact failure is recorded as C-16: the only guaranteed endpoint is below the selector's high threshold, not below the MCSP low threshold.
## Idea 183 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Range-size lower bound for adaptive anti-checker selectors

Suppose a selector has only $q$ distinct output query sets, each containing at most $t$ points. Their union has at most $qt$ coordinates. If $qt<N-\log_2M_2$, with $M_2$ the number of tables of circuit size at most $s_2$, there is a high-complexity $f$ zero on every coordinate in that union. The constant-zero circuit then passes whichever query set the selector chooses. Thus a valid selector needs $q\ge(N-\log_2M_2)/t=(1-o(1))N^{1-10\beta}$ distinct outputs for the OPS parameters. Full proof: C-17.

**Lesson.** Adaptivity has a combinatorial information floor: the selector cannot range over only a small menu. At the C-17 scale $q<N$, one query address can copy $\lceil\log q\rceil$ input bits to realize that many outputs by wiring alone. For the stronger C-18 range, all $tn$ output-address bits can encode $2^{\Theta(tn)}$ samples, enough for the lower bound because $tn\gg s_2/n$. Neither construction ensures that an output is a valid anti-checker. The hard part is routing each table to a sample whose labels refute every small circuit.

## Idea 187 - Use minimax to separate anti-checker existence from synthesis

For a fixed hard table $f$, let the circuit player choose a circuit $D$ of size at most $s$ and the input player choose $x$, with payoff $1[D(x)\ne f(x)]$. If no input distribution forces error at least $1/2-\varepsilon$, minimax supplies a distribution over circuits whose expected error is below that threshold on every input. A sample of $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ such circuits has a majority that computes $f$ exactly, contradicting $CC(f)\gg ns/\varepsilon^2$. Therefore a max-min input distribution exists. Sampling $O(\log|\mathcal C_s|/\varepsilon^2)$ inputs then gives a short constant-error anti-checker by Hoeffding and a union bound.

**Result.** This reconstructs the Lipton-Young anti-checker theorem. The support is short, but depends on $f$; no selector follows. OPS's hard/low size ratio is the right $n$-factor parameter regime, up to constants. See C-21 and New Model Ã‚Â§2.71.

**Use.** Treat existence as closed. All further work must concern the complexity of producing a support from the explicit truth table.

## Idea 188 - Anti-checker synthesis is a total search problem with a coNP witness predicate

For explicit $f,Q$, anti-checking all size-$s$ circuits is a coNP predicate: a violating circuit witnesses failure. Finding a completion of a partial query list is in $\Sigma_2^P$. On high-complexity inputs, minimax makes the search total. Thus $P=NP$ would collapse $\Sigma_2^P$ and allow polynomial-time self-reduction to find a sample, but the resulting polynomial degree is uncontrolled. OPS's conditional $N^{1+O(\beta)}$ construction is much sharper.

**Lesson.** There is no contradiction in saying that P=NP makes witnesses findable and that the OPS near-linear construction remains the critical issue. The magnification threshold is quantitative. A lower bound for the selector at the matching exponents would itself imply $NP\not\subseteq P/poly$.

## Idea 189 - Random sparse hard tables have easy anti-checkers

Let $R$ be a uniformly random support of size $s_2$. Fix $Q_0$ hitting the 1-set of every size-$s_1$ circuit with density greater than one half; random sampling gives $|Q_0|=O(\log M_1)$. With probability $1-o(1)$, no size-$s_1$ circuit of density at most one half contains all of $R$, $R$ is disjoint from $Q_0$, and $1_R$ has complexity greater than $s_2$. Then $R\cup Q_0$ anti-checks every size-$s_1$ circuit: circuits missing a positive are caught in $R$; circuits containing all positives must be dense and are caught by $Q_0$ at a zero.

Sorting the full truth table outputs all positives and appends $Q_0$ in $O(Nn^3)$ size, within the OPS list length for small $\beta$. This handles a $1-o(1)$ fraction of weight-$s_2$ supports, not all high-complexity tables. The exceptional supports are those contained in sparse low-circuit sets. The result corrects the inference from C-18: exponential sample-range size can coexist with a near-linear selector on almost every sparse input.

## Idea 190 - Uniform distinguisher magnification is a separate route

Atserias and MÃƒÂ¼ller (2025) construct sparse distinguishers and prove a uniform magnification theorem: a near-linear lower bound for a suitable approximation of subexponential-threshold MCSP against P-uniform circuits implies $P\ne NP^{\oplus P}$. This is structurally different from OPS's nonuniform anti-checker selector and is worth tracking as a route around nonuniform synthesis.

It does not currently yield $P\ne NP$: the displayed class separation does not by itself show $NP\not\subseteq P$ or $P\ne NP$. The needed lower bound is still open, and even proving it would reach a different class separation. Keep this as a side route until a rigorous implication to the target is found.

## Idea 191 - Test sparse supports inside low-density regions by recovering their hull

The fixed dense-circuit hitting set from Idea 189 does not catch a low-density circuit region containing all positives. Test an axis-aligned subcube $A$ of size $a\approx s_2^{10}$ and choose $w=K s_2$ random positive points $R\subseteq A$. For large enough K, $\binom{a}{w}$ exceeds the number of size-$s_2$ circuits, so almost every $1_R$ still has complexity above $s_2$. It also exceeds the number of restrictions of size-$s_1$ circuits to A, so almost no low circuit matches the whole truth table on A. Random positives expose every free coordinate of A with high probability, so their coordinate hull recovers A. Outputting A then anti-checks all low circuits, in $O(Nn^3)$ circuit size. See C-24.

**Result.** A low-density containing region is not by itself a hard case. If positives reveal a small canonical hull, the selector can output the whole hull. The candidate hard family must hide the region from simple closure operations.

## Idea 192 - Relative-density split for a known support region

Let $A$ be known, with $|A|=a$, and let $R$ be a uniformly random $w$-subset of $A$. For a candidate family of $M$ low circuits, choose a fixed random-like list $Q_A$ of $m$ points in $A$. If $M\eta^m=o(1)$, $M(1-\eta)^w=o(1)$, and $wm/a=o(1)$, then there is a fixed $Q_A$ such that with high probability over $R$ every candidate circuit is anti-checked by $R\cup Q_A$. A circuit with density $\le1-\eta$ is unlikely to contain all positives; a denser one is hit by $Q_A$; the two lists are disjoint with high probability. Full proof and quantifiers: C-25.

**New distinction.** This removes the need for a global density threshold: densities are relative to whatever region contains the support. It also isolates the true open issue more sharply. Conditional on knowing a region, the combinatorics are easy. A lower bound needs either a region whose useful description is provably hard to recover from the truth table, or an argument that every selector must solve an equivalent hitting-set problem. The latter is currently unproved; do not infer it from the failure of the natural construction.

**Next stress test.** Try algebraic closures (affine span and cosets) and then more general matroid or code closures. If random positives reveal the region through a cheap closure and the full region anti-checks low circuits, that is another easy subdomain to exclude from candidate hard instances. This remains diagnostic rather than progress toward a worst-case lower bound.

## Idea 193 - Generalize the subcube hull to affine span

Take $A$ to be an affine subspace of dimension $d=\lfloor10\beta n\rfloor$, with $a=2^d\le t$, and choose $w=K s_2$ random positive points in $A$. For $K$ large enough, support counting makes $1_R$ have circuit complexity above $s_2$, and the restriction count makes it unlikely that any size-$s_1$ circuit agrees with $1_R$ throughout $A$. The random positives span $A$ affinely with probability $1-o(1)$, since otherwise they lie in one of at most $2^{d+1}$ affine hyperplanes, each containing at most half the region. Recover the span by Gaussian elimination, output all of $A$, and get an $O(Nn^3)$ selector on this promise family. See C-26.

**Lesson.** Coordinate hulls are not the only cheap closure. Linear-algebraic regions are also exposed by enough random positives. The current obstacle is not a lack of candidate structures to test; it is converting a hidden-region obstruction into a statement about every selector, or identifying a region class whose membership/recovery complexity gives a rigorous circuit lower bound. C-26 is another exclusion of easy distributions, not magnification progress.

## Idea 194 - Treat anti-checker synthesis as a version-space transversal

For sparse $f=1_R$, circuits rejecting any positive are already caught by querying $R$. Every remaining size-$s_1$ circuit accepts all of $R$ and has residual extension $E_D=D^{-1}(1)\setminus R$, a set of false positives. An additional zero-query set is valid exactly when it hits every such $E_D$ (C-27). Thus anti-checker existence is a transversal theorem for the extension family of the low-circuit version space.

C-21's minimax proof supplies a fractional transversal: a distribution on inputs gives constant mass to every residual error set; $O(\log|\mathcal C_{s_1}|)$ samples produce an integral transversal. C-25 is a direct region-aware way to build a transversal for two density classes. Neither tells us how a near-linear circuit finds the transversal from an arbitrary truth table.

**Next proof attempt.** Work on the primal/dual obstruction directly. A lower bound must show that any circuit producing such transversals across all high-complexity tables is superlinear at OPS parameters, or derive that bound from another established hard task. The minimax theorem only proves existence, and the region construction only proves one way to obtain a transversal. Keep this distinction explicit.

## Idea 195 - Use majority to constrain residual-extension overlap

Take an odd number $q$ of low circuits that all accept the sparse positive set $R$. If every zero input is accepted by at most $(q-1)/2$ of them, their majority computes $1_R$ exactly. So if $CC(1_R)>O(qs_1+q^2)$, every such subfamily has a point accepted by a majority of its circuits (C-28). At the OPS ratio $s_2/s_1=cn$, this applies to subfamilies of size up to a constant fraction of $n$.

**Attempt / limit.** This proves a local overlap obstruction, but does not make the global transversal small or computable. The majority point depends on the chosen subfamily. Bounded matching number alone is insufficient for a small transversal, and we have no general theorem converting this stronger overlap condition into one. The next step would need a way to choose a subfamily and compute its majority witness without exhaustive circuit enumeration.

## Idea 196 - Stress-test majority overlap against arbitrary set systems

Take a universe of $m$ points and every subset of size greater than $m/2$ as a hyperedge. Any $q$ selected edges have more than $qm/2$ incidences, so some point lies in a strict majority of them. But the transversal number is exactly $\lceil m/2\rceil$: any smaller set has a complement containing one of the edges. Thus even an all-subfamilies majority-point theorem does not imply a small hitting set for a general family.

**Lesson.** The majority consequence of circuit hardness is not enough by itself. A future selector proof must use additional structure specific to residual circuit error sets. Generic matching, majority-overlap, or Helly-style arguments cannot supply the missing quantitative synthesis theorem without stronger hypotheses.

## Idea 197 - Try partitioning the truth table into restrictions

Partition $\{0,1\}^n$ by $k$ input bits into $B=2^k$ blocks. If every restriction has circuit complexity at most $u$, a multiplexer combines them into a circuit of size $O(Bu+Bk)$. Thus $CC(f)>s_2$ guarantees only that some block has complexity roughly $s_2/B$.

To use minimax locally against size-$s_1$ circuits, a restriction on $n-k$ bits needs complexity on the order of $(n-k)s_1$. Since $s_2=\Theta(ns_1)$, the ratio allows only $B=O(1)$ blocks (up to fixed theorem constants); it does not support branching into polynomially many simpler subproblems. A constant number of restrictions may preserve a fixed-factor margin, but gives no asymptotic simplification of the selector task.

**Result.** The naive recursive restriction strategy does not produce a scalable reduction. It spends the same $n$-factor gap that made the original anti-checker theorem work. Revisit only if a restriction has an independently stronger complexity guarantee or the combination circuit can be made substantially cheaper than the block sum.

## Idea 198 - Split known regions at the sample budget

Combine full-region output with the relative-density lemma. For a fixed known $A$ and random support $R$ of enough entropy: if $|A|\le t$, output all of $A$; circuit counting says no size-$s_1$ circuit agrees throughout $A$ with high probability. If $|A|>t=s_2^{10}$, take $m,w=O(s_2)$ and apply C-25 with $\eta=1/2$; the overlap term $wm/|A|$ is negligible, and $R\cup Q_A$ anti-checks. Both outputs fit the sample budget and have $O(Nn^3)$ selector circuits for each fixed A. See C-29.

**Result / limit.** No troublesome region-size band remains when A is known. The selector circuit may hardwire A and its hitting set, so this is not a construction for hidden A. Any hard support example must hide the useful region from the input-dependent selector, or invalidate this two-case construction in some other way. We still have no proof that every selector needs to identify a region.

## Idea 199 - Recover bounded-degree algebraic regions from positives

Represent each point $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$ by its vector $\phi_d(x)$ of all squarefree monomials through fixed degree $d$. The points in the degree-$d$ algebraic closure of a sample $R$ are exactly those whose feature vectors lie in $\operatorname{span}(\phi_d(R))$: orthogonality gives the polynomials of degree at most $d$ vanishing on every sample point. If random positives span the feature space of a degree-$d$-closed region A, this recovers A.

If every nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial restriction to A has relative weight at least $\delta$, the failure probability is at most $2^L(1-\delta)^w$, with $L=\sum_{i\le d}\binom ni$. For fixed d and constant relative distance, this vanishes when $w=K s_2$. A bounded-degree polynomial graph is an example: its defining equations give degree closure, while restriction raises degree by only a constant factor and retains constant minimum weight. Support counting then makes random sparse tables high-complexity, and outputting the recovered region anti-checks low circuits. Full statement and proof: C-30.

**Lesson.** Cheap sample closures extend from geometric hulls to vanishing-ideal/feature-span recovery. Future hard supports should be tested against algebraic closure too. C-30 is a uniform construction on this structured promise family, not a general selector or separation.

## Idea 200 - Hamming balls falsify bounded-degree closure, then yield to max weight

Take a Hamming ball $A=B_k$ with $H_2(k/n)=\gamma$ for $\beta<\gamma<10\beta$, so $|A|<t=s_2^{10}$. With $w=K s_2$ random positives, support counting makes $1_R$ high-complexity and prevents low circuits from agreeing on all of A. Yet for any fixed feature degree $d$, A contains all weight-$\le d$ points, whose feature vectors span the entire degree-$d$ space. Thus bounded-degree closure of the sample is the whole cube and exceeds the output budget. See C-31.

This does not make a hard family: the boundary layer is a constant fraction of A, so R contains a point of weight k with high probability. The maximum weight among positives recovers k; output the entire ball. The example teaches that an algebraic-closure failure can be repaired by a simpler statistic. A candidate hard region must evade several observables at once, without assuming all selectors use any one of them.

## Idea 201 - Hide a product region behind a secret linear basis

Use $A=T^{-1}(B^m)$, where $B=\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_r\}$, $r$ is fixed, and $T$ is an unknown invertible linear map. Choose $r$ so $\beta<\gamma=\log_2(r+1)/r<10\beta$; then $A$ has enough support entropy for $w=K s_2$ random positives to be hard, but $|A|<t$. Fixed-degree algebraic closure is the whole cube, so that method fails.

The region is still recoverable from the truth table. A fast Walsh-Hadamard transform estimates all parity biases. For the uniform distribution on B, local bias is $(r+1-2|u|)/(r+1)$; in the product, the largest nonzero coefficients form one-block frequency sets. Threshold them, group vectors by their unique minimal dependencies, project sample points into those hidden blocks, and learn each block's allowed patterns. The reconstructed region is a valid anti-checker with high probability (C-32).

**Lesson.** Secret linear coordinates do not make a structured region hard if its Fourier spectrum has a gap and its high-frequency vectors carry a simple matroid. This gives a concrete synthesis attack to falsify future product-region candidates. It is still a structured distribution result, not a lower bound for arbitrary selectors.

## Idea 202 - Generalize spectral recovery by the Fourier peak matroid

For a fixed block alphabet $B\subseteq\mathbb F_2^r$, let S be the nonzero frequencies with maximum absolute Fourier coefficient under the uniform distribution on B. In a product $B^m$, all multi-block coefficients are at most $\alpha^2$, where $\alpha$ is the local maximum; the single-block copies of S are spectrally isolated. If S spans and its binary matroid is connected, the connected components of the global peak set recover the hidden blocks after any unknown invertible linear map. Then sample projections learn the local allowed patterns and recover the region. C-33 proves the criterion; C-32 is one concrete instance.

**Next attempt.** Examine alphabets for which S is disconnected or does not span, and determine whether secondary spectral levels recursively expose the missing directions. A flat or fragmented peak set could resist this selector, but that would only defeat this algorithm until a lower bound on every transversal is proved.

## Idea 203 - Charge the routing from a hard table to its anti-checker

**Reason for pivot.** The region-recovery line has generated many valid special-case selectors, but no theorem forcing an arbitrary selector to recover any such region. The highest unresolved node is the unrestricted Gap-MCSP lower bound itself, so the next target must apply to every selector.

**Universal fact (C-34).** A valid OPS anti-checker selector must depend on at least $N-t-\log_2 M_2-O(1)=N-o(N)$ truth-table positions. If it ignores a large set, set the read positions to zero, observe its fixed output list $Q$, then complete the table to be zero on $Q$ while choosing the remaining bits to have circuit complexity above $s_2$. The constant-zero circuit agrees on the list. Counting guarantees such a hard completion when more than $\log_2M_2$ bits remain free.

**Sharper gate count (C-38).** In a fan-in-two circuit with $E$ essential input variables and $L$ output ports, retain only paths from those inputs to outputs. If there are $S'$ retained gates and $c$ connected components, then $c\le L$ and edge connectivity gives at least $E+S'$ edges, while fan-in gives at most $2S'+L$. Thus $S'\ge E-L$, so the selector uses at least $N-t-\log_2M_2-tn-O(1)=N-o(N)$ gates. This replaces the earlier half-$N$ conversion. It still does not cross the superlinear threshold.

**Why it does not solve the target.** The graph count improves the universal fan-in-two lower bound to $N-o(N)$ gates, but this is still linear: $N-o(N)$ variables can be aggregated with $O(N)$ gates. This exposes the limit of pure dependency and connectivity arguments. The difficult part is *routing*: output a short list whose observed labels hit the residual error set of every circuit of size $s_1$ that survives earlier queries.

**Next proof target.** Establish a superlinear circuit lower bound for this routing function, or show that a proposed routing invariant implies the direct Gap-MCSP lower bound without circular assumptions. Start with adversarial selectors, not natural hull-recovery algorithms. Specifically test whether any low-gate circuit can use a compact global summary of all truth-table bits to choose a valid transversal; if it can, characterize what a lower-bound proof must rule out. Do not turn the near-total input-dependence lemma into a superlinear claim.

**Route comparison.** Direct Gap-MCSP lower bounds, feasible SAT-error witnesses plus Extended Frege, and self-referential NP diagonalization remain the three alternatives. The latter two still require a major open proof-system premise or a polynomial-size self-reference that current constructions lack. The direct lower bound is the shortest route but also the first genuinely hard unresolved statement.

## Idea 204 - Use conditional fibers to attack compact address sketches

**C-35 input.** A fixed $t$-point sample anti-checks a uniformly random table except with probability at most $M_1 2^{-t}$, and almost every random table is above $s_2$. This is not a worst-case selector: its failure set consists of large cylinders on which sampled labels imitate a small circuit, and every high-complexity member of those cylinders still needs handling.
