**C-36 theorem.** Suppose the address list factors through a rank-$k$ linear sketch $Af$ whose row space has minimum distance greater than $t$. For every sketch value $h$, deleting the queried coordinates leaves rank $k$. Hence there are exactly $2^{N-|Q_h|-k}$ tables with sketch $h$ and all queried labels zero. If this exceeds $M_2$, one is high complexity and the constant-zero circuit certifies failure. At OPS parameters, it does so for every $k=o(N)$; in particular it covers robust affine summaries no longer than the $tn=o(N)$ output address bits, even with an unlimited decoder.

**General fiber condition.** For any valid selector with address list $Q_f$, every fixed list $q$ and every trace $y$ realized by a size-$s_1$ circuit must satisfy $|\{f:Q_f=q, f|_q=y\}|\le M_2$. This is necessary for unrestricted selectors, but by itself it is only a geometric restatement of validity and gives no circuit lower bound.

**What is ruled out.** Robust linear sketches cannot be the missing compressed summary. Any surviving compact-summary route needs nonlinear query-label feedback: selected table bits must influence the addresses so that fixing both the sketch and a low-circuit trace leaves at most $M_2$ tables. It remains open whether small general circuits can do that.

**Adversarial dead ends.** A fixed sample or fixed menu fails whenever one can zero its coordinate union and retain more than $\log_2M_2$ free bits. A universal self-reference argument forcing agreement with the constant-zero circuit also fails: Ã¢â‚¬Å“query the first 1-bitÃ¢â‚¬Â has no nonzero all-zero self-consistent input. Future fixed-point arguments must enforce agreement with some low circuit while preserving high complexity, or handle all low traces at once.

**Status / next attack.** C-36 is an architecture-specific obstruction, not a superlinear lower bound or a new P-vs-NP implication. Try a general fiber-shrinkage theorem for bounded-fan-in address circuits, then test it against selectors that use queried labels in their address computation. If such a theorem implicitly yields O-1, state the equivalence rather than treating it as a bridge.

## Idea 205 - Use priority encoders as an adversarial selector baseline

**Construction (C-39).** A balanced priority encoder finds the first 1 in an $N$-bit truth table in $O(N)$ fan-in-two gates: each subtree stores a nonempty flag and the first-one index, and combining a height-$h$ node costs $O(h)$ gates. Run a second encoder on the complement to find the first 0. For every nonconstant table, these two queries disagree with the constant-zero and constant-one hypotheses.

**What this falsifies.** No proof can get a superlinear lower bound merely by forcing a selector to find one positive, one negative, or to avoid agreement with a fixed finite family of constant-size circuits. The selected labels can feed back into address computation at linear cost. The full anti-checker requirement is difficult because it must hit the disagreement set of every size-$s_1$ circuit simultaneously.

**Next direction.** Seek a quantitative obstruction for simultaneous witness routing over an exponentially large circuit family. One option is to lower-bound the circuit complexity of the address map using the geometry of all low-circuit traces, rather than the number of essential inputs or the behavior against selected constants. Any conjectured obstruction should first be tested on the two priority-encoder outputs.

## Idea 206 - Treat anti-checkers as constructive minimax certificates

**Reconstruction (C-40).** For a table $f$, let
\[
\Delta_s(f)=\max_{\mu}\min_{D\in\mathcal C_s}\Pr_{x\sim\mu}[D(x)\ne f(x)].
\]
If $CC(f)>Cns$, then $\Delta_s(f)\ge1/3$: otherwise minimax supplies a mixture of size-$s$ circuits with pointwise error below $1/3$, and a majority of $O(n)$ sampled circuits computes $f$ with size $O(ns)$. Sampling $O(s\log(s+n))$ points from the witnessing distribution yields a short anti-checker.

**New model.** The selector is a sparse hard-core distribution extractor for the circuit class. Existence is a game-theoretic theorem; computation is the open step. A rational LP candidate is separated by weighted circuit fitting (NP). Random rounding is an oracle-assisted randomized upper bound, while deterministic list validity is coNP and generic list search has an existential-universal ($\Sigma_2^P$) form. The margin itself is zero exactly on size-$s$ circuit tables and is bounded away from zero on the high side, so it does not lower the complexity of Gap-MCSP.

**Creative route to test.** Standard no-regret or multiplicative-weights constructions need a best-response oracle for weighted circuit fitting. Look for a *truth-table-driven* update rule that produces the same dual witness without optimizing over circuits. It must work on exceptional tables where fixed samples fail, and must not assume a preferred circuit representation. If every plausible update asks for a weighted best response, record that as a constructive minimax obstruction rather than renaming it as an algorithm.

**Status.** This sharpens the model and identifies the exact oracle hidden in the direct LP route. It is not a new lower bound. Keep the direct target O-1 primary; pursue constructive minimax only when a concrete oracle-free update can be stated.

## Idea 207 - A sparse hard table defeats every small fixed prior menu

**Theorem (C-41).** Let $w=Kns=\Theta(N^\beta)=o(N)$ and let $S=Cns$. For any fixed menu of $m$ distributions with $mw/N=o(1)$, choose a random support $R$ of size $w$. For each menu distribution, $\mathbb E[\mu_j(R)]=w/N$. Markov and a union bound give probability at least $1/2$ that every mass is at most $2mw/N=o(1)$. Circuit counting makes the fraction of supports with $CC(1_R)\le S$ be $o(1)$ for sufficiently large constant $K$. Hence some support is both high circuit complexity and nearly invisible to every prior in the menu. The constant-zero circuit has vanishing error under all those priors.

**What this rules out.** The table-conditioned minimax distribution cannot be replaced by any small menu fixed before seeing $f$. This is stronger than showing one fixed sample fails.

**What remains.** The selector can have exponentially many outputs and choose among them based on all $N$ table bits. C-41 does not constrain that input-dependent routing. The decisive challenge is to bound how a near-linear circuit adapts a prior to an adversarial sparse support.

## Idea 208 - Audit Ã¢â‚¬Å“new languageÃ¢â‚¬Â proofs at the resource bridge

**Literature trigger (C-42).** Isong's August 2026 Loop-theoretic manuscript proposes internal complexity classes using archival spaces and transitions. Its SSRN abstract states that the classical separation follows under an internal finite-transition capacity principle and explicit Loop-to-complexity bridge axioms.

**Logical test.** An internal lower bound does not imply $P\ne NP$ until the bridge maps every ordinary polynomial-time verifier/solver into the internal model and preserves polynomial resource bounds. The abstract advertises such axioms, but their exact statements and proof status need full-text inspection. SSRN blocked the PDF with a 403 during this check, so no claim of falsity or circularity is made.

**Use in our model.** Treat novel languages as candidate invariant-finding tools; place the resource-preserving translation theorem as an explicit DAG node. If it is an axiom, conditional conclusion only. If it is proved from the usual machine model, attack its quantifiers and size bounds. This route remains secondary until the full paper is accessible and the bridge is verified.

## Idea 209 - Quantifier collapse finds anti-checkers, but does not give near-linear circuits

For a high-complexity table $f$, a candidate anti-checker list $Q$ is validated by
\[
\forall D\in\mathcal C_s\;\exists q\in Q:\ D(q)\ne f(q).
\]
The list search is $\Sigma_2^P$: existentially choose $Q$, universally range over circuits, and evaluate the finite list in polynomial time. C-40 proves a suitable $Q$ exists. Therefore P=NP collapses PH and gives a polynomial-time search algorithm by prefix self-reduction on the explicit $N$-bit truth table.

The algorithm only has some polynomial exponent. This does not reach OPS's $N^{1+\epsilon}$ circuit scale; by contraposition, OPS gives a near-linear nonuniform selector for an appropriate small-$\beta$ choice under the stronger premise $NP\subseteq P/poly$. Learning: collapsing quantifiers settles logical existence-to-search but not the circuit-size exponent. A proof route must control the resource of the selector itself.

**Status.** Correct conditional route audit (C-44), no separation progress. See `research/CLAIM_LEDGER.md` and Q19.

## Idea 211 - View anti-checker synthesis as eliminating a residual version space

For each small circuit $D$, write $E_D(f)=\{x:D(x)\ne f(x)\}$. A list $Q$ is valid exactly when it hits every $E_D$. After seeing $Q$, the residual version space is $V_f(Q)=\{D:E_D(f)\cap Q=\emptyset\}$.

The simple loop Ã¢â‚¬Å“find a survivor, add one disagreementÃ¢â‚¬Â removes at least one circuit each round and therefore has only the useless worst-case bound $|\mathcal C_s|=2^{O(s\log s)}$. Yet C-40's dual margin gives a distribution with mass at least $\gamma$ on every $E_D$, so a random $O(\gamma^{-1}\log|\mathcal C_s|)$ sample is a short transversal. The constructive gap is deterministic extraction for a table-dependent distribution.

One possible potential chooses a coordinate on which a constant fraction of the surviving circuits disagree. Evaluating this potential seems to require weighted counts of circuits, but this is not shown necessary and no #P-hardness reduction has been proved. The next attack is to find a circuit-specific way to build the same short transversal without enumerating/counting all survivors. An abstract set-system example only shows a black-box counterexample loop may be exponentially slow, not that real circuit instances are.

**Status.** C-45 is a proved reformulation and potential calculation, not a circuit lower bound. It makes the missing step more explicit; O-1 remains the primary objective.

## Idea 213 - Use residual-circuit counts as the exact contraction potential

Let $Z_Q$ count size-$s$ circuit descriptions matching $f$ on the current list, and let $G_{Q,x}$ count those that disagree at a candidate new point $x$. C-40's dual margin gives
\[
\sum_x\mu_f(x)G_{Q,x}=\sum_{D\in V_f(Q)}\mu_f(E_D)\ge\gamma Z_Q,
\]
so some $x$ eliminates at least a $\gamma$ fraction of survivors. Choosing the maximum $G_{Q,x}$ repeatedly builds a valid list in $O(\gamma^{-1}\log|\mathcal C_s|)$ points. Since $Z_Q$ and $G_{Q,x}$ count polynomially described circuits satisfying polynomial-time checks, each is a #P function. This gives a deterministic $\mathrm{FP}^{\#P}$ selector with $O(N\log|\mathcal C_s|)$ oracle calls.

**What was learned.** The sample-size obstacle is fully removed even deterministically at the existential level; the implementation bottleneck is evaluating or approximating residual circuit mass. The #P route is a baseline, not a proof that all selectors must count. P=NP by itself does not evaluate #P functions.

**Initial next attack (superseded by C-48).** Seek a near-linear ordinary-circuit surrogate for $G_{Q,x}$ or $Z_Q$. C-48 shows that approximate scores suffice for the conditional OPS construction under $NP\subseteq P/poly$. A lower bound against the score implementation would still not constrain selectors using a different computation, so the primary target returns to the universal puncturing-certificate map. No score lower bound or necessity reduction is established.

## Idea 214 - Replace exact #P contraction scores by local approximate counts

For a current transcript $\tau=((q_i,f(q_i)))$, define $G_{\tau,x}$ as the number of size-$s$ circuit descriptions consistent with $\tau$ and disagreeing with $f(x)$. C-40's dual margin implies that some $x$ has $G_{\tau,x}\ge\gamma Z_\tau$, where $Z_\tau$ is the number of surviving descriptions. Exact scores give C-47.

The useful refinement is that only a constant-factor approximation to every nonzero $G_{\tau,x}$ is needed: the maximizer of approximate scores still removes a constant fraction. Stockmeyer puts local approximate counting in BPP$^{NP}$. Under $NP\subseteq P/poly$, the approximation circuit can be made correct on every transcript of a fixed length by amplifying and fixing coins across the finite input space. Since the transcript is $O(sn^2)=N^{\beta+o(1)}$ bits, score computation for all $N$ candidate coordinates and $O(s\log(s+n))$ rounds gives an $N^{1+O(\beta)}$ selector. This reconstructs the conditional OPS upper bound; it is not an unconditional selector or a lower bound.

**Learning.** C-47's #P oracle is not the essential conceptual obstruction. More importantly, no argument says arbitrary selectors must use these scores. Therefore C-48 closes the score-construction branch under the same strong assumption used by magnification, while leaving O-1 unchanged. Drop the conjecture that defeating approximate score circuits alone would prove the desired universal selector lower bound unless a reduction is found.

**Next step.** Attack the puncturing-certificate function directly: a selector maps $f$ to coordinates $Q$ with $f|_Q\notin\pi_Q(\mathcal C_s)$. Any proposed lower-bound invariant must cover all such maps and nonlinear feedback, not only greedy ones.

## Idea 212 - Stress-test circuit transversals with hard teaching-set constructions

The version space $V_f(Q)$ evolves exactly like a hypothesis class after labeled queries. C-45 shows why an arbitrary-counterexample loop can be long in a black-box model, but dual margin guarantees an ideal max-coverage query removes a constant fraction of survivors. C-46's one-point greedy lower bound is only $\Omega(\log|\mathcal C|)$, matching our $O(\log|\mathcal C_s|)$ query budget at constant margin; it does not refute the potential argument.

**Next research step.** The real target is the computational cost of identifying a point that removes a constant fraction of the current circuit survivors. Investigate whether this can be done without weighted circuit counting, or prove a circuit lower bound for every such routing algorithm. A teaching-set lower bound on query count is not enough, because C-45 already proves the desired logarithmic count existentially.

## Idea 210 - A KPT flattening theorem would have to remove witness dependence

PichÃ¢â‚¬â€œSanthanam's existential formulation for anti-checkers is $\forall\Sigma^b_2$. KPT extraction yields finitely many adaptive polynomial-time functions, with later outputs depending on prior challenge witnesses, including satisfying assignments. A generic attempt to make the output independent of those witnesses enumerates $2^n$ assignments; plugging in a conjectural SAT solver does not make its correctness $S^1_2$-provable.

The concrete missing lemma would be a polynomial-overhead composition theorem for these adaptive transcripts, or a witness-independent invariant producing one stable generator. It must avoid assuming the SAT circuit lower bound or EF conclusion. This route remains secondary because it also requires EF not p-bounded; no such flattening is known here.

## Idea 213 - The error-overlap graph as a circuit-specific organization

C-51 turns C-50 into a graph theorem: every triple of low-circuit functions has a pair that is simultaneously wrong with the high table on $\Omega(N^\beta/n)$ inputs, so a constant fraction of all pairs are heavy-overlap pairs. This is a genuine global structure, not merely a statement about one chosen tuple.

The first use was to seek a residual-set contraction. Pair-coordinate incidence gives a point that eliminates only an $\Omega(N^{-(1-\beta)/2}/\sqrt n)$ fraction of a residual family. The resulting query bound is worse than the existing minimax list, and exact point selection remains. The graph density alone does not encode a small transversal: the generic all-large-subsets example needs a large transversal, while an abstract common-core class can have many distinct hypotheses, maximal overlap, and an easy constant-size selector.

The useful next question is not whether more extremal graph facts can be derived. It is whether the circuit class has a representation-independent closure property that makes heavy pair intersections align at common coordinates or makes such coordinates computable without counting circuit descriptions. Any conjecture here must survive the common-core countermodel by explicitly using the full circuit class.

## Literature note - conditional implicit MCSP route (June 2026)

Goldberg, Juvekar, and Kabanets prove conditional NP-hardness for gap ImpMCSP and full-support PAC learning from subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation plus a proof-complexity assumption denying infinitely-often subexponentially optimal propositional proof systems. This is a potentially useful hard-instance-generation template: cryptographic samplers and proof-complexity non-optimality interact to produce implicit hard functions. It does not yield an unconditional result or the explicit truth-table Gap-MCSP lower bound required by OPS. The proof obligation for this project remains to remove the assumptions and preserve the explicit OPS parameters.

The adjacent 2025 paper by Goldberg and Kabanets proves unconditional NP-hardness of a semi-proper circuit-learning problem and connects certain CGL reductions to witness encryption. Its instances are sampler/distribution descriptions. Full support gives existence of a preimage for each label, not an efficient label-extraction procedure; materializing a table of arity n costs 2^n bits. A reduction from these implicit objects to explicit OPS tables would have to preserve source-input polynomial size and the circuit gap. This remains Q26, not an established route.

## Attempt audit - do not infer average distance from high majority moments

For a random low-circuit function, let $p_x$ be its error probability at coordinate $x$. A $k$-majority bound implies $\sum_x p_x^r\ge h/2^k$. I initially tested whether this forces a linear lower bound on $\sum_xp_x$, but this inference is invalid: for $r>1$, the standard power-mean inequality gives an upper bound on the first moment from the r-th moment. A vector with $p_x=1$ on $h$ coordinates and zero elsewhere is the immediate counterexample. The valid max-coordinate consequence is weak and already subsumed by C-40. This closes the proposed average-error route unless an additional anti-concentration fact about circuit functions is proved.


## Idea 215 - Compress the root of the version-space tree

At the OPS ratio, Delta_s1(f)>=3/10 follows from minimax: otherwise the majority of the smallest odd k>=9n samples from a distribution on size-s1 circuits computes f on all N points with (0.9+o(1))s2<s2 gates. Average the margin over uniform fixed-length low-circuit descriptions. Some coordinate has disagreement mass at least 3/10.

A sample of O(n) descriptions estimates all coordinate marginals to error 3/40. Hardwire the N integer frequencies and choose a coordinate of maximum empirical disagreement; its true error mass is at least 3/20. A tournament implements this in O(Nn) gates. This is a universal first-query contraction, proved in C-52.

**Learning.** The first point is not where the selector's extra cost must hide. For each residual version space the dual margin still gives a constant-error coordinate, but one global sample can miss rare survivors. Empirical emptiness therefore does not certify a complete anti-checker. Next pursue conditional reconstruction or a structural tail-elimination lemma; do not claim the sample limitation applies to arbitrary architectures. Full proof: [C-52 report](research/C52_FIRST_QUERY_AND_ADAPTIVE_SAMPLING.md).


## Idea 216 - Use relative range sampling for conditional greedy scores

C-52 used additive Hoeffding to estimate residual and disagreement masses, which gave a sample bound with $1/\rho^2$ at minimum residual mass $\rho$. Improve this with relative Chernoff bounds over the finite family of all transcript ranges. Set $\lambda=\gamma\rho/8$. Simultaneously approximate every range of mass at least $\lambda$ within relative error $1/4$, and ensure every smaller one has empirical frequency below $2\lambda$. The union bound over $O((k+1)(2N)^{k+1})$ ranges gives sample size $O((kn+\log(1/\eta))/(\gamma\rho))$.

For a residual of mass $r\ge\rho$, the dual margin supplies a disagreement event of mass at least $\gamma r$. Its empirical count is at least $3\gamma r/4$. Any event with true mass below $\gamma r/2$ has empirical count at most $5\gamma r/8$ (or below $\gamma r/4$ if it is under the cutoff), so the empirical maximizer still removes a $\gamma/2$ fraction. This holds simultaneously for every transcript, including an adaptive one.

**Adversarial limit.** With polynomial sample size, this can track down to inverse-polynomial mass, which permits only $O(n)$ constant-factor contractions before the residual falls below the tracked scale unless already empty. To guarantee the final nonempty survivor is represented, set $\rho=1/|\mathcal H|$, making the sample depend on the entire circuit-description count. The method remains global sampling, not a universal lower bound. The corrected detailed calculation is in [C-52/C-53 report](research/C52_FIRST_QUERY_AND_ADAPTIVE_SAMPLING.md).


## Idea 217 - Interpolation forces the sample guarantee to end at a live residual

A transcript of $q$ labeled points always has a DNF completion: OR the minterms for the positive labels. It uses $O(qn)$ gates. Thus for $q=O(n)$, a low circuit still survives because $s_1=2^{\beta n}/(10n)\gg n^2$.

C-53's relative global sample can preserve constant-fraction contraction down to inverse-polynomial mass $N^{-a}$, which takes $O(n)$ rounds. The first crossing is therefore a nonempty version space, by the DNF completion. A direct sample-score implementation fits $N^{1+a}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ gates for this prefix, but cannot certify the full anti-checker. The necessary list length is at least $\Omega(s_1/n)$, much longer than the guaranteed prefix.

**Learning / next attempt.** This is now a precise method boundary: avoid spending more effort optimizing the same global relative sample unless it reaches subexponential inverse mass. Look for a conditional sampler with resource independent of $1/\rho$, an exact circuit-specific continuation after the transcript becomes too long for DNF interpolation, or a potential that does not measure uniform residual mass. None is known here.


## Idea 218 - Extract a selector from the minimax proof

The anti-checker theorem is a total witness relation on high tables: every high $f$ has a short $Q$ such that no low circuit agrees with $f$ on all of $Q$. Its verifier is coNP because a low circuit is a counterexample. The minimax/greedy proof gives pointwise witnesses, but not a small circuit mapping every $f$ to one.

**Attack.** Formalize the exact proof in a weak arithmetic theory and test whether feasible witnessing (Herbrand/KPT extraction) yields a selector with manageable size. The greedy coordinate predicate asks for counts of low circuits consistent with a transcript; its direct implementation is #P-like. KPT-style extraction may instead produce adaptive responses to circuit counterexamples, whose flattening can be exponential. The existing C-43 audit is the adversarial baseline: do not call an adaptive list of existential witnesses a single selector.

**Fast falsification / limit.** A general quantifier principle cannot supply the needed near-linear bound from $\forall f\exists Q$ alone. The extracted functions must retain explicit resource bounds and handle every high table; if their counterexample oracle is a SAT/Gap-MCSP solver or their witness tree needs exponential expansion, the route has returned to O-1. This is a logic-first reframing, not a proof or evidence of P$\ne$NP.


## Idea 219 - Trace cylinders defeat output-counting lower bounds

For fixed $Q$, the anti-checker predicate depends only on the trace $f|_Q$. If that trace is not realized by any size-$s_1$ circuit, then all $2^{N-|Q|}$ extensions of the trace share the same valid anti-checker. Since the number of tables of circuit complexity at most $s_2$ is at most $2^{O(s_2\log(n+s_2))}$, at OPS list lengths and fixed $\beta<1/10$ almost all these extensions are still high-complexity.

Under a uniformly random truth table, a fixed list succeeds with probability exactly $1-|T_Q|/2^{|Q|}$, which is at least $1-|\mathcal C_{s_1}|/2^{|Q|}$. Yet the all-zero trace always lies in $T_Q$, and its cylinder contains high tables because $|Q|+\log M_2=o(N)$. So Ã¢â‚¬Å“works for almost every tableÃ¢â‚¬Â and Ã¢â‚¬Å“works for every high tableÃ¢â‚¬Â differ by a rare but unavoidable exception cylinder.

**Learning from the attack.** Counting possible lists or noting their short output length cannot by itself lower-bound a selector: a single valid list can cover a huge cylinder. What remains hard is which anti-realizable trace the input-dependent selector chooses. This rules out a broad information/entropy shortcut, while leaving the arbitrary routing problem untouched. See C-56.


## Idea 220 - Separate external teaching number from teacher circuit size

For a high target $f$ and the low-circuit class $\mathcal C_{s_1}$, define an external teaching set $Q$ by $f|_Q\notin\{D|_Q:D\in\mathcal C_{s_1}\}$. The proven length bounds are $\Omega(s_1/n)\le\operatorname{ETD}(f)\le O(s_1\log(s_1+n))$. The upper bound is existential greedy contraction from the 3/10 margin; the lower bound is C-49 point patching.

**Learning.** The list-length question is already within polynomial factors, while the goal's real resource is the circuit complexity of selecting a list as a function of the full truth table. NP-hardness of minimizing teaching sets for other concept classes does not transfer to this external, nonminimal, succinct-circuit setting without a reduction. Explore a reduction only if it addresses arbitrary valid lists, not just minimum ones.


## Idea 221 - VC dimension alone cannot give external witnesses

Counterexample: on a domain $X$ of size $m\ge3$, let $\mathcal C=\{X\setminus\{i\}:i\in X\}$. The class shatters every singleton but no pair (the 00 pattern is absent), so $\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal C)=1$. The outside target $f\equiv1$ agrees with some class member on every proper $Q$: choose an omitted point $i\notin Q$. Thus its minimum external teaching set has size $m$.

**Learning.** A generic VC/sample-compression theorem cannot replace the circuit-specific margin. The short anti-checker comes from majority closure and minimax; its construction remains the hard part.

## Idea 222 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Make selector hardness survive every valid output

A Kannan transfer is not merely a reduction to the predicate Ã¢â‚¬Å“is this list valid?Ã¢â‚¬Â The table generator must always produce high tables, and a polynomial-size decoder $B(x,Q,f_x|_Q)$ must recover the source answer for **every** valid selector list. Local patching fails as an output channel if the payload misses one valid base witness: that list and its labels remain valid after the patch (C-58). A decoder that also receives $x$ must be charged its circuit exponent; if the common list makes the selector output irrelevant, that decoder alone would compute the source language.

A common stronger gadget associates each source bit with a disjoint, efficiently recognizable region and a low circuit agreeing with the table outside that region. C-59 rules this out: two approximants plus a mux compute the allegedly high table in $2s_1+\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gates. Do not infer this approximant condition merely from Ã¢â‚¬Å“every list of length at most $t$ hits the regionÃ¢â‚¬Â; the hypergraph with edges $\{p,x_i\}$ falsifies that step.

**What could still work.** A nonlocal gadget might force information through correlations across many query labels without a separately localized low approximant for each bit. The smallest validating theorem is a high-promise, all-valid-output reduction from a fixed hard problem with controlled exponent blowup. For Kannan's $L_k$, include table-generation and decoder costs: if their exponents are $b_k,d_k$ and the table blowup is $m^{a_k}$, the effective exponent is $e_k=\max\{a_k(1+\epsilon),b_k,d_k\}$, so the construction must prove $k>e_k$.

**Status.** Constraint on reduction design, not a lower bound. Do not keep refining localized patch gadgets unless they evade the mux lemma and common-list trap.

## Idea 223 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Self-consistent low-circuit completion against a selector

For any proposed selector circuit $S$, its failure is witnessed by a high table $f$ and a low circuit $D$ satisfying $D(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in S(f)$. This exact form removes the reduction machinery: it asks whether the selector's own address list can be made consistent with one small circuit while the unqueried table bits are completed to remain high.

C-34 solves the restricted case where S leaves more than $t_n+\log_2 M_2+O(1)$ table bits unread: fix the read bits to zero, obtain a fixed list, then complete a high table agreeing with constant zero there. C-38 converts this to a linear gate bound. This cannot extend just by selecting a constant D: C-39's priority encoder finds both a zero and a one. For unrestricted S, every output address may depend on all table bits, so the completion equations are self-referential.

**Smallest theorem.** For every size-$N^{1+\delta}$ candidate S, prove existence of $f,D$ with $CC(f)>s_2$, $CC(D)\le s_1$, and $D|_{S(f)}=f|_{S(f)}$. This is the direct negation of a universal selector, not a proved lemma. A useful attack must make D depend on S without enumerating all circuits or silently fixing S's future addresses.

**Immediate falsification.** Test constructions with D constant (already defeated for the basic labels), or with Q fixed in advance (C-56's cylinder analysis shows why this does not reach all inputs). The general nonconstant self-consistent completion remains open.

## Idea 224 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Dual mass limits mandatory address regions

For a fixed high table f, C-52 gives one distribution nu on coordinates under which every size-s1 circuit disagrees with f on mass at least 3/10. Suppose every valid list of at most t queries must intersect P. If nu(P)=p<3/10, conditioning nu outside P leaves every low circuit an error mass at least (3/10-p)/(1-p). Sampling t points there hits every one of M1 low-circuit functions as soon as

$$
t(3/10-p)/(1-p)>ln(M1).
$$

So a mandatory region must have nu-mass at least (3/10-alpha)/(1-alpha), alpha=ln(M1)/t. With OPS t=N^(10 beta) and ln(M1)=O(N^beta), alpha=o(1). Four pairwise-disjoint mandatory regions would have total mass greater than one for sufficiently large n; hence there can be at most three.

**Use.** This proves that an all-valid-output reduction cannot encode many source bits by requiring every valid list to touch one separate disjoint region per bit. It is stronger than the patch-switch test because it does not assume a low circuit whose entire error set lies in each region.

**Limit.** The theorem says nothing about overlapping regions, multiple bits encoded by the address or label of points inside one region, or arbitrary correlations across the whole query list. It is a proved restriction on a gadget class, not a selector-circuit lower bound. Full proof is C-61 in the claim ledger.

**Fractional extension.** The same argument bounds the fractional packing number of mandatory regions by 10/3+o(1): if pointwise total packing weight is at most one, integrate against the dual distribution. So the simple region route remains blocked even with bounded overlap, not only disjoint blocks. High-overlap or list-correlation encodings remain open.
**Common-witness form.** More sharply, if the union of all source-dependent patches has dual mass below (3/10-alpha)/(1-alpha), one sampled list outside that union is valid for every encoded table with the same labeled trace. Hence a patch reduction cannot rely on raw support size alone; it must control the dual mass of the region that changes.

## Idea 225 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Output-only reductions need dual-mass separation

For two high tables f,g, let P be their difference set. If either table's dual-margin distribution assigns P mass below p*=(gamma-alpha)/(1-alpha), conditioning and sampling gives one valid labeled anti-checker list for both. Therefore an output-only decoder that must distinguish opposite source answers needs both directed dual distances nu_f(P), nu_g(P) at least p*.

This gives a semantic constraint on how a reduction can encode its answer: changing many raw bits is insufficient if those bits carry little dual mass. The limit is important: a decoder that also reads the source input x can use x when the same list appears, so its circuit cost must be included and the common-list fact alone does not refute the reduction.

## Idea 226 - Parity padding and shared dual-heavy changes

A tempting extension of C-62 is to append r switch bits z and replace a hard source answer L(x) by L(x) XOR parity(z), hoping every source-coordinate edge forces fresh table support. This inference fails without an independence condition: the map can switch between two tables A_x and B_x based only on parity(z), so every z-edge uses the same support P(A_x,B_x). The C-62 distance condition can be met by one shared dual-heavy perturbation.

This is not a complete selector reduction: the pair A_x,B_x must still be high, output-decodable for every valid list, and computable within the exponent budget. It does falsify an additive edge-sensitivity argument based only on C-62. A useful lower bound would need to rule out shared parity/masking across many source bits.
## Idea 227 - Self-indexed agreement fibers

The exact failure object for selector S and low circuit D is \(A_D^S=\{f:f|_{S(f)}=D|_{S(f)}\}\). A selector is valid on all high tables iff each A_D^S is contained in SIZE(s2). Thus prove S-1 by showing every small S has a low D whose fiber also contains a high table.

The first generalization fails: for the two-constant class, a linear priority selector queries both labels on every nonconstant table, leaving singleton agreement fibers. Therefore the missing fact must exploit the full circuit-size class, perhaps a closure-under-patching principle that forces a fiber to have a high completion despite S's address feedback. The fiber predicate itself has circuit size O(|S|+t(N+s1+n)); this cost is not a lower bound on S.

**Status.** Exact restatement and counterexample to class-generic versions; no asymptotic progress yet. See C-63.
## Idea 228 - Force the adversary to range over all low circuits

For fixed D, comparing the table to D and priority-encoding the first mismatch costs O(N) gates. For m fixed D_j, output one mismatch per table at O(mN) gates. Therefore a superlinear selector lower bound cannot come from one predetermined low circuit or a small hardwired menu. The witness pair (f,D) in C-63 must be chosen jointly against S, and the obstruction must use the full low-circuit family.

**Next possibility.** Investigate whether the many point-patched neighbors of a low function force a global conflict among the query lists S(f), or whether an arbitrary selector can route around all such local neighborhoods. Any proposed averaging argument must account for the fact that the same address can witness disagreement with many circuits.

**Status.** Fixed-menu shortcut ruled out; no full-class theorem.

## Idea 229 - Adaptive least-fixed-point closure potential

For a q-pair semantic list, C-67 gives an exact least fixed point on q consequence bits. Each rule needs supports on both endpoints; each initial support predicate is a clause of signed truth-table bits (C-68). A surviving anchor's canonical obstruction is the Q-dependent least preserving closure itself.

Define \(\delta_Q(w)\) as the minimum number of additional pairs needed to derive empty from the current partial list Q. It lies in \([0,N-1]\), and adding one pair changes it by at most one (C-69). This is a proved local potential. The actual research target is to bound the weighted decrease across low anchors uniformly after arbitrary partial Q, or to find a short global list. Raw incidence is insufficient because one pair can influence at least N anchors (C-09).

**Learning from the failed shortcut.** A fixed family of R filters can be covered in \(O(N\log R)\) pairs if its fractional cover has weight \(O(N)\), but the global problem ranges over all extensions. A new pair may add a nonempty intersection to the current closure rather than kill it, after which the adversary's closure changes. So one selected filter per anchor and static threshold families do not prove a global upper or lower bound.

**Finite check.** The exact recurrence agrees with explicit closure on 204,160 comparisons in experiment_fusion_closure_recurrence.py and recovers the sparse toy's two-pair cover. No asymptotic bound follows.

**Status.** Exact state model and local Lipschitz fact proved; the static-distribution marginal theorem is refuted by C-73; no P-vs-NP breakthrough.

## Idea 230 - Empty rules need a nonempty bootstrap

The high side two-wise shatters truth-table coordinates because every two-bit cylinder has \(2^{N-2}\) tables and only \(2^{o(N)}\) tables have circuit complexity at most \(s_2=N^\beta\). Hence an empty-intersection rule cannot have both sides supported directly by matching literal slices: the two slices either meet in a high table or are inconsistent with the anchor.

Unfolding a round-t contradiction into an AND/OR proof tree gives at most \(2^t\) literal leaves. Their intersection must exclude the high side, which requires \(N-\log_2M_2\) distinct coordinates. Thus \(t\ge\log_2N-o(\log N)\). This proves a parallel-depth floor and explains why a direct disjoint partition cannot solve the problem at the first round.

**Limit.** The floor is only logarithmic in rounds and does not yield a superlinear total number of pair rules. It must be joined to cross-anchor non-shareability; C-72 records the proof.

## Idea 231 - Shared-intersection potential after the static average fails

For every static distribution on low anchors, a minimum local certificate has \(N-o(N)\) literal leaves. Averaging over coordinate pairs finds one pair \((G_{k,b},G_{\ell,c})\) that saves one rule for at least \(1/4-o(1)\) of the weight. C-73 therefore refutes the plan to telescope tiny per-pair decreases of an additive anchor-distance potential.

The next object should charge an intermediate intersection state once, even when many anchor proofs reuse it. A lower bound would then need to show that the later intersections required to reach empty cannot be compressed into a small shared DAG. The simple candidate of charging each anchor separately has already failed; any replacement must be checked against the four-pattern pair sharing above and arbitrary semantic endpoints.

**Status.** New direction only; no global state-complexity inequality has been proved.

## Idea 232 - The closure system is a dual-rail separator program

C-74 translates each q-rule pair list into q recursive activation sets. Each activation set is the intersection of two unions, with each union containing fixed signed-literal half-cubes and prior activation sets selected by semantic containments. The least fixed point recognizes K_Q, a set disjoint from the high table set U. A successful cover must include all low anchors Y, so it computes a promise separator Y subseteq K_Q subseteq {0,1}^N minus U.

This makes the charged global object explicit: q distinct intersection states. The exact one-rule gain in C-73 is shared inside this program rather than charged separately to each anchor. A direct lower bound on q in this recursive model would solve the active O-2 subroute. Unrolling incurs q^2 AND gates, so ordinary circuit lower bounds do not transfer at the required exponent.

**Adversarial controls.** Preserve the C-73 two-literal sharing; catch the unlisted (A,B) shortcut in the failed catalogue gadget; allow the logarithmic depth from C-72. Do not count endpoint descriptions.

**Literature analogy.** AND-gate minimization in monotone circuits (Ã¢â‚¬Å“conjunctive complexityÃ¢â‚¬Â) may suggest proof techniques, but it does not match recursive least-fixed-point semantics with complementary dual rails and a promise separator. Related starting point: Amano and Maruoka (2006), https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-006-0073-0.

**Status.** Exact reformulation only. No superlinear lower bound or P-versus-NP breakthrough.

## Idea 233 - The closure proof gives a mismatch protocol, but its depth is too weak

C-75 constructs a deterministic protocol on a low truth table w and a high truth table z. Bob identifies a side of the current active rule with no support at z; Alice supplies a support true at w. Either this gives a differing coordinate or moves to a lower-rank state. At most q states are visited.

The direct lower bound fails because Alice can send a size-s1 circuit for w, after which Bob scans z. The communication cost is only N^(beta+o(1)), weaker than the existing local linear q bound. The useful lesson is to preserve state/DAG complexity; depth and bits erase the shared computation we need to charge.

**Status.** Proof correct; asymptotic route closed unless a state-complexity version is found.

## Idea 234 - Every low table needs a high-excluding seed-clause CNF

For a pair list Q, the vector sigma(w) of its 2q seed clauses is a sufficient statistic: the fixed containment network computes the same closure from equal seed vectors. Its output h_Q is monotone in those bits. Therefore no low codeword can be coordinatewise below a high codeword. For each low w, the conjunction of all nonconstant seed clauses true at w excludes every high table.

A satisfiable m-clause CNF on N coordinates has at least 2^(N-m) satisfying assignments, so each low w must satisfy at least N-log2(M2)=N-o(N) seed clauses. More strongly, the matched-literal hypergraph has transversal number at least that value. This is exact but only gives q>=N/2; C-03 already gives q>=N-o(N). A dictionary of 2N signed unit clauses can isolate every table, so the next lower bound must charge the monotone decoder's shared state cost.

**Status.** Necessary-condition lemma proved as C-76. No superlinear progress.


## Idea 235 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Ranked cyclic rectangle states

Represent each fusion state \(i\) by the rectangle \(R_i=\{w:x_i(w)=1\}\times\{z:x_i(z)=0\}\). A valid low/high input pair starts at an empty-consequence state and follows a support predecessor until a signed literal mismatch. The graph can have cycles, but activation rank on Alice's low input decreases on every valid transition. This makes the exact communication object a ranked loop game.

**What this clarifies:** C-O's cyclic intersection complexity is exactly the fusion cover measure; the old ordinary-DAG analogy incurs qÃ‚Â² AND-count or O(qÃ‚Â³) full binary-DAG costs. The key lower-bound target is now cyclic state non-shareability.

**What it does not prove:** no q-state lower bound follows merely from the path certificate; low-circuit descriptions only bound ordinary communication bits, and low/high promise separators may accept medium tables.

**Next test:** devise a bottleneck measure for transitions within a cyclic SCC and test it against the two-state cycle with opposite input-dependent ranks; retain per-anchor \(N-o(N)\), fractional \(O(N)\), and fixed-family \(O(N\log R)\) ceilings.

## Idea 236 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Pattern-sharing DAG for all low/high mismatches

Let \(\pi_I(Y)\) be the number of distinct low-table restrictions to dyadic interval I. A rect-DAG can branch on the low row, then use states \(R_{I,u}=Y_{I=u}\times\{z\in Z:z|_I\ne u\}\); each interval state branches to its two halves, and singleton intervals output a mismatch. This gives \(O(|Y|+\sum_I\pi_I(Y))\) states and shares all equal restriction patterns.

**Result:** valid universal DAG construction, but not near-linear using current bounds. It does not show every DAG needs these projection-pattern states.

**Learning:** interval comparison can share across circuit descriptions when the compared truth-table restriction agrees. The remaining cost is the number of distinct residual patterns, not the description length itself. Any use as a lower bound must prove a canonicalization theorem for arbitrary DAGs, which is not known.

## Idea 237 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Medium-band escape filter

For \(Y=\mathrm{SIZE}(s_1)\), \(M=\mathrm{SIZE}(s_2)\setminus Y\), \(Z=\mathrm{SIZE}(s_2)^c\), and a low anchor w, generate a filter over \(M\cup Z\) from M and every matching literal slice. For sufficiently small OPS \(\beta\), each slice contains a medium table: k-variable Boolean functions provide \(2^{\Theta(s_2)}\) size-\(\le s_2\) tables per prescribed coordinate value, exceeding the low-circuit count.

**Result:** every pair with endpoints contained in Z preserves this filter. A cover for the larger positive class cannot be re-used directly to cover Y.

**Learning:** promise-to-exact conversion has to account for the gap band explicitly. The lemma blocks endpoint reuse but does not prevent adding new pairs involving M and does not itself lower-bound \(\rho(Y)\).

See C-78/C-79 and [the DAG/Fusion bridge audit](research/DAG_FUSION_BRIDGE_2026-09-26.md).

## Idea 238 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Common block codes do not force many DAG states

Take all functions of k input bits, lifted to tables constant on the corresponding \(2^k\) blocks. With \(2^k=\Theta(s_1)\), this is an exponentially large low-table family. Yet against any high table, Bob finds a block on which z is mixed (otherwise z is also a low k-junta); Alice gives the low block value, and Bob selects an opposite coordinate. A rectangle-DAG implements this in \(O(N)\) states.

**Learning:** large code size and high per-anchor mismatch distance do not establish cross-instance non-shareability when the rows share an exposed structure. The remaining candidate is a lower bound for the cost of routing across the many incompatible partitions induced by arbitrary low circuits.

**Status:** exact counterexample to code-family counting as a lower-bound strategy; it does not address all low tables. See C-80 / O-82.



## Idea 239 - Row signatures have a diameter bound, but too few colors

If two low rows have the same membership signature across all rect-DAG nodes and differ on D, then 2^|D| must be at most the number of size-s2 tables. Otherwise a completion of their common restriction is high, and the same reachable leaf would need to output incompatible mismatches. Thus each signature class has diameter at most N^(beta+o(1)).

**Learning:** this is a valid non-shareability lemma. The C-80 block code gives only S=Omega(s1), because S nodes encode at most 2^S signatures. Any row-signature-only argument is capped by log|Y|=N^(beta+o(1))=o(N), far below the rect-DAG transfer scale.

## Idea 240 - Dual column signatures are low-excluding certificates

If two high columns share a full signature, their common agreement restriction cannot have any low completion. Otherwise the same reachable leaf for that low row would need to be a valid mismatch for both columns. Every pattern on O(s1/n) coordinates has a low completion by minterm interpolation, but large irregular restrictions may not.

**Learning:** the condition is exact, but small-cylinder extension gives no column packing or DAG lower bound. A stronger invariant must combine row and column residuals or charge transitions.

## Idea 241 - Use cyclic rank semantics honestly

The q fusion states form a terminating input-ranked cyclic witness game: each rule-support transition decreases first-activation rank on the low input. The static graph may cycle and has O(q^2+qN) support arcs. This is exactly D^circ_cap=rho, not a standard acyclic rect-DAG.

**Learning:** q states are a compact loop representation, but this is not a near-lossless reduction. Standard binary acyclic rank unrolling remains O(q^3). A better conversion must respect endpoint containment and rectangle semantics.


## Idea 242 - Every row-signature class has a common high-free core

For a whole row-signature class R and any fixed high z, feasible vertices and reachable leaves are identical for all (w,z), w in R. A common leaf must work for every row, so its coordinate belongs to the agreement core of R. This proves the common pattern on all coordinates fixed across R has no high completion, and counting forces the core to fix N-log|SIZE(s2)| coordinates.

**Learning:** the state class is contained in a very thin high-free cylinder. A rect-DAG with S vertices gives at most 2^S such cylinders, so S >= log C_cyl(Y,Z). But singleton cylinders cap the bound by log|Y|=o(N), and the promise cylinders may contain medium tables. Need a transition-sensitive cover lower bound.


## Idea 243 - Joint row/column classes have a common separating coordinate

Partition low rows and high columns by their full signatures over all rect-DAG nodes. Every product of one row class R and one column class C has identical feasible nodes and leaves. Thus one leaf is valid for every pair in R x C, forcing a coordinate fixed on all of R and all of C with opposite bits.

**Learning:** this couples the two one-sided signature certificates. The missing step is to show that circuit-induced class pairs cannot be organized with few shared states; the 2N signed-coordinate rectangle cover means leaf-cover counting alone will not suffice.

Signature counts themselves cannot reach the transfer target: at most o(N) from rows, N from columns, and N+o(N) from class pairs. The target is routing structure.


## Idea 244 - Do not merge away a mismatch-relevant prefix

A scan state labelled by all of Y x Z still has to solve pairs whose mismatch occurred in the prefix. If the next state searches only later coordinates, it can fail. The valid prefix-equality region is a union of pattern rectangles, so a single rectangle state cannot represent it without preserving the pattern.

**Learning:** the simple linear scan is not a valid Sokolov rect-DAG. This is a specific failed universal construction, not a general lower bound.


## Idea 245 - Linear sketches collide with a high completion

A rank-r linear sketch partitions all N-bit tables into fibers of size 2^(N-r). If r<N-log|SIZE(s2)|, each fiber is larger than the entire size-s2 class, so every low table shares its sketch with a high table.

**Learning:** fixed linear samples, parities, and linear fingerprints need N-o(N) bits for exact separation. This does not constrain nonlinear or adaptive shared computation.

## Idea 246 - Circuit-description input still needs residual restrictions

Alice can send a short circuit description, giving cheap communication. In a shared interval search, states indexed by u=G(d)|I are rectangles; the predicate that the interval has any mismatch is mixed in d,z and is not itself a rectangle. The known construction pays for all restriction profiles and is not near-linear.

**Learning:** syntax makes each row succinct but does not resolve rectangle factorization. This is an obstacle for the current construction, not an impossibility theorem for all DAGs.


## Idea 247 - Shared mismatch DAG equals a promise-separator circuit

A rect-DAG for low/high signed mismatch yields a Boolean circuit h that accepts all low tables and rejects all high tables. Build leaf literals from mismatch labels, then AND/OR/reuse gates from the rectangle-cover relation at internal nodes. Conversely, a circuit separator yields a full KW game whose DAG restricts to the promise.

**Learning:** the shared-DAG measure is equivalent to promise-separator circuit size. The DAG-to-active-promise-cover conversion costs O(L); the q-cover-to-DAG conversion costs O(q^3). Medium tables only obstruct upgrading to the separate full-domain exact cover, not the active promise cover.

## Idea 248 - Promise DAGs reverse to the active promise cover

There are two different fusion parameters. The active Gap-MCSP cover uses \(\Gamma=Y\sqcup Z\) and filters over Z; the exact full-domain cover includes medium tables M as well. A rect-DAG for mismatch on \(Y\times Z\) yields a separator circuit and therefore a cover for the active promise with O(L) pairs. A full-domain cover can be restricted to Z, proving \(\rho_{\rm prom}\le\rho_{\rm full}\).

**Learning:** C-79's escape filter only blocks lifting promise endpoints unchanged into the full-domain universe. It does not block the requested DAG-to-promise-cover conversion. The active inequality chain is \(\rho_{\rm prom}\le\mathrm{SepCirc}\asymp\mathrm{rectdag}\le O(\rho_{\rm prom}^3)\); q itself still needs a direct superlinear lower bound, since the acyclic forward conversion is cubic.
## Idea 249 - Localize cyclic fusion cost by SCCs

After deleting the redundant self-support loops, let the support graph have edge j -> i whenever T_j=E_j intersect H_j is contained in an endpoint of pair i. The SCC condensation is acyclic. For an SCC of size r, fix its already-computed external supports and iterate its r internal activation bits for at most r rounds; each round costs O(r^2) bounded-fanin support ORs plus O(r) ANDs. Seed clauses and external edges cost O(qN+q^2). Therefore the active promise separator has size O(qN+q^2+sum_C r_C^3)=O(q^2+q d^2), with d the largest SCC and q>=N-o(N).

**Learning:** rank-unrolling all q states globally hides the fact that only mutual recursion costs repeated layers. For an SCC C with r states and e internal side-support incidences, the compiler cost is O(r e+r^2); globally it is O(qN+q^2+sum_C(r_C e_C+r_C^2)). Acyclic covers and sparse SCCs compile with O(q^2) ordinary gates. The unresolved bottleneck is a large, dense SCC, not the mere presence of cycles. This does not prove such an SCC is necessary or hard to share. See C-91 and Q51.


## Idea 250 - Inclusion poset prunes transitive two-sided support

After removing self-support, organize the distinct carriers T_i by inclusion. For every carrier cover s<t, every rule at s supports every rule at t on both sides. Those cover edges imply activation along any strict inclusion chain. So a non-cover lower carrier can be removed from both side-support lists without changing the least fixed point. C-92 proves this for every seed assignment.

**Learning:** transitive nesting can make the raw graph dense without adding recursive power. This does not eliminate one-sided support or candidate distinctions among equal carriers.


## Idea 251 - Quotient duplicate carriers and keep a disjunctive menu

Rules with the same carrier T have identical recursive membership at the least fixed point: if one activates, every peer has it on both support sides and activates. Collapse their q state bits to one of p distinct carriers. The activation predicate of a duplicate group is still the OR of its q candidate conjunctions, so its alternatives remain distinct. C-93 proves exact lfp preservation and a carrier-SCC compiler bound O(qN+e_out+sum_C p_C(e_C+q_C)).

**Learning:** the recursive dimension and the number of two-sided alternatives are separate resources. Naively unioning the candidate endpoints changes OR_i(A_i AND B_i) into (OR_i A_i) AND (OR_i B_i), which adds invalid cross-pair combinations. A further compression must preserve that compatibility structure. No lower bound follows yet.


## Idea 252 - Cycles require one-sided escape supports

After deleting self-loops, pruning transitive two-sided supports, and quotienting equal carriers, every remaining support from a strict subcarrier is a shared Hasse-cover edge. Factor the common lower-cover signal K_t from all candidates at carrier t. Any other remaining support comes from a carrier u not contained in t and can lie on only one endpoint, because support on both endpoints would imply u subseteq t. The carrier cover graph is a DAG, so every dependency cycle must contain such a one-sided escape.

C-94 replaces the recurrence H_t=K_t OR D_t by the fixed-point-equivalent macro map G(x)=Up(D(x)). If s distinct carrier values appear as escape sources, G stabilizes after at most s+1 rounds. Its separator compiler costs O(qN+(s+1)(xi+kappa+q)), with xi escape side incidences and kappa Hasse covers.

**Learning:** the cyclic core is localized to candidate-specific endpoint extensions beyond the intersection carrier. The exact non-shareability problem now concerns the escape alternatives and their interaction with upward closure. The compiler bound is not a lower bound; neither s nor xi has been shown large.


## Idea 253 - The contradiction gate cannot be seed-only

At an empty-carrier rule, the two direct seed predicates are ORs of signed table literals. If their conjunction is satisfiable, select one true literal from each clause and fix at most two bits; the resulting \(2^{N-2}\)-sized subcube still satisfies both. Since the non-high class has fewer than \(2^{N-2}\) tables, this includes a high input, where the empty rule would activate directly. Thus a successful cover's empty-rule seed conjunctions are all unsatisfiable.

Every low anchor that activates an empty rule must therefore use an escape source in \(S_0\), the carriers on one-sided supports into empty rules. Their activation sets cover Y, but can overlap; this alone does not bound \(|S_0|\). The missing charge is how the other endpoint remains false across the high side. See C-95.

If both seed clauses are nonempty, their unsatisfiability forces complementary unit literals on one coordinate. That bit determines which endpoint needs an escape source. If a seed clause is empty, that endpoint always needs an escape. This gives a coordinate-indexed terminal-routing constraint for the next proof attempt.

## Idea 254 - Localize the terminal contradiction, then confront overlap

For each low anchor, choose an active empty-carrier rule and one true support from each side. The union of the selected predecessor ancestor cones and the terminal rule must contain at least (N-log2 M2)/2 states: their true seed clauses form a CNF with at most M2 models. The selected cones, but not necessarily the terminal rule's other incoming supports, are predecessor-closed.

**Learning:** this is a real local causal-cone theorem but does not improve the global linear floor q>=N-o(N). Many anchors can share the same cone, so the next invariant must charge cross-anchor reuse against high-side blocking. See C-96.

## Idea 255 - Circuit descriptions quotient away in standard DAG complexity

A first attempt to exploit short descriptions d failed for a precise reason: standard Boolean communication-game predicates allow arbitrary local computation. For any surjection G:D1->Y, a DAG on descriptions lifts from a DAG on tables, and a DAG on descriptions restricts to the image of a section. Thus both domains have exactly equal minimum rect-DAG size. The same holds for communication cost and protocol trees when local computation is free.

**Learning:** sending d explains the low communication cost, but not the graph-sharing cost. A small standard DAG is equivalent to a small Boolean separator circuit for the low/high promise. Universal-circuit evaluation only handles G(d)(k); a state that merges all scan prefixes is invalid because interval mismatch is not a rectangle. The pattern-profile construction is valid but not near-linear. This kills the naive universal scan, not all universal DAGs. A near-linear DAG would kill the rho lower-bound route by the reverse inequality; otherwise the desired theorem is a genuine separator/non-shareability lower bound. See C-97.

## Idea 256 - PRF truth tables conditionally force shared-DAG hardness

Under a one-bit PRF secure against nonuniform polynomial-size distinguishers and with per-key evaluation size lambda^d, take N=Theta(lambda^a) with a*beta > d. Restrict each PRF to N padded inputs. Each resulting table is in the low class because s1=N^beta/(cn) dominates lambda^d; a uniformly random truth table is high with probability 1-2^(-N+o(N)). Any N^C-size promise separator becomes a polynomial-size distinguisher making N queries.

**Learning:** conditional on PRFs, the description-vs-sharing objection has a sharp answer: descriptions alone do not help build a polynomial shared DAG, because such a DAG would solve range separation and break pseudorandomness. The general MCSP/PRF principle is already known; the project-specific result is the exact gap and transfer to rho_prom. This is only conditional and does not supply the unconditional theorem required for P vs NP. See C-98.

## Idea 257 - Audit the strength of conditional crypto routes

C-99 shows that C-98's nonuniform-secure PRF assumption already implies NP not subset P/poly. MCSP lies in NP; under NP subset P/poly it has polynomial-size circuits. At threshold s2 this circuit separates the project's low and high sets, and querying all N PRF outputs breaks security.

**Learning:** the conditional superpolynomial rho theorem is a valid quantitative benchmark, but the assumption already gives the class separation that OPS targets. It does not bypass the unconditional difficulty. Uniform PRF security alone is too weak to rule out arbitrary nonuniform separator circuits.

## Idea 258 - Batch OR supports before unrolling the escape closure

For r fixed OR clauses over one common m-bit state vector, split the inputs into blocks of about log r bits. Precompute every subset OR within each block and combine the relevant block outputs for each clause. This gives \(O(r(1+m/\min\{m,\log r\}))\) fan-in-two gates. Applying it to the C-94 seed clauses, escape lists, and up-closure downsets improves the general q-pair-to-standard-DAG compilation from \(O(q^3)\) to \(O(q^3/\log q)\), with a parameterized bound using p, s, xi, and kappa.

**Learning:** support routing contains redundant repeated OR work, so the compiler can be tightened. The gain is only logarithmic: escape fixed-point rounds and the full range-separation problem remain. This does not give a lower bound, and the proof target remains direct cyclic non-shareability or an unconditional promise-separator lower bound. See C-100 in the DAG/fusion bridge report.

## Idea 259 - Terminal-cone VC reformulation stops at the counting ceiling

A C-96 terminal cone gives an m-clause CNF with no high tables. Selecting one true literal per clause yields a coordinate cube of dimension at least N-m inside SIZE(s2). If Delta_box(s2) is the maximum such cube dimension, then m >= N-Delta_box(s2). Circuit counting gives Delta_box=O(s2 log(n+s2)), so this recovers only N-o(N). A localized subcube of the input domain gives Delta_box>=Omega(s2), but that lower bound does not help because the cone inequality needs an upper bound on Delta_box.

**Learning:** ordinary VC dimension allows the other table coordinates to vary and is weaker than the contained-cube parameter. C-80's block-constant family is not an axis-aligned table cube. The route does not charge overlap across different low anchors; return to cross-instance reuse. See C-101.

## Idea 260 - Every high table cuts one edge within a low table's fibers

For a low table w, view its two fibers as two cliques on the input domain. If a high table z were constant on each clique, then z would be a unary function of w and would itself be low. Thus some pair a,b has w(a)=w(b) but z(a)!=z(b). Each candidate edge is certified by a rectangle: Alice's side checks equal w-bits, Bob's side checks unequal z-bits.

**Learning:** the O(N^2) candidate rectangles give nondeterministic certificates, but not a deterministic shared DAG. A sequential router must remember which candidate pairs failed and cannot advance based on a joint test for free. This is a useful structural reformulation only if it can be linked to the ranked fusion states or if an arbitrary shared router can be lower-bounded. No such link is proved. See C-102.

## Idea 261 - Fiber search has an upper-bound transfer, not a lower-bound transfer

C-103: every fiber-search leaf refines into at most four rectangles and yields a signed-mismatch DAG, so rho_prom <= O(S_fib). C-105 rules out near-linear fiber DAGs via Omega(N^(2-beta)/log N) output labels. This auxiliary lower bound does not transfer through C-104's N^2 loss.

**Learning:** C-105 closes the small-fiber-DAG falsification branch by proving it impossible at fixed beta<1. The fiber relation is now an auxiliary output-label lower bound, not the target; keep the attack on cyclic fusion unless C-106's edge-set extraction can be proved.

## Idea 262 - The fiber search comparison is only polynomially equivalent

C-104 supplies a reverse construction: mismatch games on constants 0 and 1 produce z=1 and z=0 coordinates p,q; after retaining (p,q), a mismatch game on w or not-w gives a third point that completes a fiber witness. The graph needs O(N^2 S_mis) states, and the complement query requires restricting the row set to SIZE(s1-1). Through the q-to-DAG compiler this asks for a fiber lower bound above N^(5+3epsilon)/log N.

**Learning:** the relation is strong enough to test for a small universal DAG, but its output-index memory makes the reverse simulation too expensive for an efficient proof route. Keep the lower-bound attack on cyclic fusion or ordinary mismatch separators.


## Idea 263 - Force many fiber-DAG output labels inside every affine subcube

Let E be the fixed set of pair outputs on the leaves of a fiber-disagreement DAG. Choose affine subspace A of size a=Theta(s2 n), with low anchor w=1_A. If E[A] has fewer than a/8 edges, it has Omega(a) isolated vertices. Among their size-a/4 subsets S there are 2^(Omega(a)) truth tables z=1_(A\S), more than M2 when the constant in a is large enough, so at least one z is high. For that pair (w,z), no E-edge is a valid output. Therefore every such A must induce Omega(a) output edges. Averaging over random affine subspaces gives |E|=Omega(N^2/(s2 n))=Omega(N^(2-beta)/n).

**Learning:** this is a genuine superlinear leaf-label lower bound for the auxiliary fiber relation. C-104's N^2 loss makes the transferred mismatch bound vacuous, so it is not a P-vs-NP result. The next mathematical target is to derive fiber witnesses directly from the q-state fusion closure without remembering two arbitrary coordinates.


## Idea 264 - The fiber-output alphabet gives a conditional q lower bound, but exposes the missing map

C-105 shows that a fiber-disagreement DAG needs Omega(N^(2-beta)/log N) different coordinate-pair labels, so the hoped-for near-linear fiber DAG cannot exist for fixed beta<1. But this does not transfer through C-104's N^2 loss.

C-106 gives a precise conditional: if every q-pair closure induced a universal edge set E_Q of O(q log^d N) valid fiber outputs, then q=Omega(N^(2-beta)/(log N)^(d+1)). The path supplies one mismatch point in cell 01 or 10; a fiber output needs a second point in that same w-row, and an arbitrary agreement point may be in the other row. There is no proved extraction of E_Q. The next work should inspect seed supports and paired predecessor cones for a shared edge mechanism, not keep trying to build a small fiber DAG.



## Idea 265 - Prove the missing transfer needs global state

C-107 kills any pointwise lift whose encoded mismatches are all expected to be valid fiber outputs. A fiber output requires Alice's pattern u=(w(a),w(b)) in {00,11} and Bob's pattern v=(z(a),z(b)) in {01,10}. Those valid patterns form a product A x B, but the mismatch set of independent local encodings F(u),G(v) cannot be a nonempty subset of that product: equality on one outside row and column forces all codewords equal. A more elaborate DAG could still route around false mismatches.

**Learning:** pairwise parity failed for a structural reason, not a bad choice of encoding. A transfer from Q must use stateful routing across candidates to suppress invalid cross-patterns. This narrows O-96 to shared-history/non-shareability, but does not prove that such routing is large.


## Idea 266 - Random edge hitting is near-optimal for certificates, not for DAGs

C-108: a high z is at distance Theta(s2/n) from every unary postprocessing of low w, by the point-patching circuit bound. Therefore in one w-fiber z has a cut with both sides at least r=Theta(s2/n). A random graph of density p=Theta(n/r)=Theta(n^2/s2) hits every such cut for all low w; union-bounding over the 2^(O(s2)) low tables and their cuts works. It yields a fixed universal fiber output list of O(N^(2-beta)n^2) edges, while C-105 lower-bounds every such list by Omega(N^(2-beta)/n), a log^3 gap.

**Learning:** the missing resource is not finding a short list of possible answers; it is routing deterministically to a jointly accepted answer. The candidate-scan residual is a union of rectangles, so sharing only the current list index loses prior rejection context. The fiber relation's certificate-label complexity is nearly settled, but this does not transfer to the C-75 q-state target.

## Idea 267 - A universal certificate list is not a deterministic shared DAG

C-108 gives a fixed edge set of O(N^(2-beta)log^2N) that contains a valid fiber output for every low/high pair; C-105 lower-bounds any such list by Omega(N^(2-beta)/logN). Thus answer-label/certificate complexity is nearly settled for this auxiliary relation.

The list does not provide a deterministic route. At candidate edge i, Alice's endpoint-equality test and Bob's endpoint-inequality test are separate; after failure the remaining pairs form a nonrectangular union. Merging them into one suffix state can skip the only valid earlier edge. The exact-row DAG costs 2^(O(s2))|E|. Focus next on state routing for these structured edge subsets, while keeping the missing transfer to q explicit.

## Idea 268 - Charge edge selection, not only anchor sharing

C-109 proves that any tuple of r<=eta log N low tables has a joint fiber edge for every high z: if z were constant on fibers of their vector W, then z=h(W) would have a circuit of size r s1+O(r2^r)<s2. The pair a,b is common to all rows in the tuple but may change with z.

**Learning:** a small set of anchors is not a fooling family for fiber outputs. One shared state might serve those rows by routing to different edges for different high columns. A useful non-shareability lemma must charge the state/DAG work needed to select that varying edge. This does not yet connect to the cyclic fusion q-states.


## Idea 269 - Rectangular hulls are the actual price of forgetting protocol history

C-110 proves that a rect-DAG state must work on its full product rectangle. When transcript contexts merge, the state acquires cross-pairs \(A_i\times B_j\), not merely the input pairs that used to reach it. Its descendant output coordinates must separate the row and column projections. This exactly explains why scanning a common prefix and then forgetting which prefix it was cannot work with suffix-only outputs: the cross-prefix rectangle includes pairs that agree throughout the suffix.

The fusion support graph has the analogous property: for every rule state, the coordinates on reachable literal outputs separate its active-low rows from inactive-high columns, by the per-input activation-rank descent. This is a proved invariant but gives no q lower bound until descendant output sets or cross-context incompatibility are quantitatively charged.

**Next:** instantiate the product-hull test on circuit-description prefixes and actual low/high tables. The full-cube prefix example kills one router only; do not present it as a lower bound for Gap-MCSP.


## Idea 270 - Use high-complexity masks to test actual promise cross-pairs

C-111 builds a mask p on the within-block domain whose function and complement both have complexity \(>s_2+O(k)\); the counting gap \(B=\Theta(nN^{1-\beta})\gg s_2 n\) guarantees such a mask for \(\beta<1/2\). Splicing two distinct block-constant low tables across P={p=1} and its complement yields a high table. It matches the first low table on the suffix and has the second row's P-pattern. Therefore no prefix-first rect-DAG state can merge two exact pattern contexts if its descendants output only in the suffix.

The result answers O-98 for this router on actual Gap-MCSP inputs. It does not constrain adaptive DAGs: C-80's mixed-block search bypasses prefix storage in O(N) states for this same low family. The next challenge is to force incompatibility among different circuit partitions even when the DAG chooses its search order adaptively.


## Idea 271 - Randomly splice a well-separated code of low tables

C-112: for any K-table code with minimum Hamming distance d, a random coordinate split makes each ordered off-diagonal splice uniform among 2^d completions. If \(d>2\log K+\log|\mathrm{SIZE}(s_2)|\), one split makes all off-diagonal splices high. A constant-distance code inside C-80 has \(K=2^{\Omega(s_1)}\) and \(d=\Omega(N)\), so this works for every fixed \(\beta<1\).

For the prefix-first/suffix-only router, every pair of P-pattern contexts now has a high cross-pair that matches the first low row on the suffix. Hence the router needs \(2^{\Omega(s_1)}\) continuation states. C-80's O(N) mixed-block DAG remains an adaptive escape, so this does not lower-bound general DAG size or rho.


## Idea 272 - Adaptive partition diversity, not one bad split

C-112 proves a strong fixed-split obstruction; C-80's O(N) mixed-block DAG bypasses it adaptively. This is a useful falsification: a family can have every off-diagonal splice high across one split and still admit a small shared DAG because all low rows share a partition that exposes a mixed block.

A global lower bound needs low circuits with incompatible partitions and a proof that every adaptive rect-DAG must retain partition information, or it should return to direct cyclic-state lower bounds. Static cross-pair examples alone do not transfer to rho.


## Idea 273 - Essential-variable set intersection yields an adaptive router

C-113 handles all functions depending on at most k input variables, even though their supports vary over \(\binom nk\) choices. For low w choose a k-set S containing its essential variables; high z has at least k+1 essential variables. The sets [n]\\S and Ess(z) intersect. A count-state PLS on balanced intervals finds an intersecting direction with n^{O(1)} rect-DAG size; Bob picks a z-boundary edge in that direction, where w is constant, and the parties output a mismatch endpoint. Total size O(N log N+polylog N).

The lesson is that partition diversity is not enough: a compact cardinality invariant can guide adaptive sharing. To approach the full low-circuit class, find an analogous structural witness for circuits with many essential variables, where the complexity lies in how the function uses its support.

## Idea 274 - Reuse the count-intersection PLS beyond juntas

C-114 isolates a generic router. Given party-local subsets A_x,B_y of [n] with |A_x|+|B_y|>n on every pair, a balanced interval PLS finds an intersection in O(n^2) states with O(log n) communication per transition; the Sokolov conversion gives n^{O(1)} rect-DAG size. If every witness i admits a valid full rectangle A_i x B_i for its suffix task, suffixes can be shared once per i.

C-113 is the witness instance: the low side chooses irrelevant variables, the high side supplies essential variables, and the shared direction yields a hypercube edge mismatch. The attempt to apply this to all low circuits by using irrelevant variables fails on parity (size O(n), all variables essential). Next, seek a richer set system derived from low-circuit cofactors or gates and high-table variation; it must give a common witness for every promise pair, not just many witnesses for typical pairs.

## Idea 275 - Search within low-circuit gate-signature fibers

For a low circuit C, choose k=Theta(log s2) of its wire values, including the output (input wires may pad the selection), so \(s_1+O(k2^k)<s_2\). A high table z cannot be constant on every joint-signature cell: otherwise a k-bit lookup after C computes z below the high threshold. More strongly, the majority function on the cells is still a sub-\(s_2\) circuit, so z must have \(\Omega(s_2/n)\) minority points across the cells by sparse-point patching.

This gives a circuit-dependent fiber-disagreement witness even when w has every input variable essential. The route stalls at sharing: the cells vary with C, and the minority mass can sit in one cell. On \([N]^2\), the two candidate-set sizes do not meet the C-114 count-intersection invariant. A useful next theorem must route across these circuit-specific cells or charge the cross-pairs caused by merging them. Keep C-80 as the falsification family; shared block structure still permits O(N) search.

## Idea 276 - Use hard cofactors, then preserve the mismatch location

C-116 proves a fixed \(m=\Theta(n)\) prefix partition has a cofactor of complexity \(>4s_1\) for every high \(z\); otherwise the \(m\) restricted circuits mux to a full circuit below \(s_2\). Every low row remains size \(\le s_1\) after restriction. This creates an adaptive router to a constant-factor-gap subproblem.

The direct reverse embedding is false as designed: a hard marker outside the target cofactor makes the full z high, but any low row must disagree with that marker, so the DAG can shortcut its search there. To use cofactor hardness, preserve agreement outside the target while amplifying its complexity; if that cannot be done, quantify a direct lower bound on the cyclic fusion states instead.

## Idea 277 - Shift the exponent parameter using ignored-input padding

C-117 proves exact monotonicity of mismatch rect-DAG size under adding unused Boolean inputs, at unchanged circuit thresholds. Re-expressing the smaller instance gives \(\beta'=\beta n/(n-k)\), \(c'=cn/(n-k)\). For a fixed \(\beta'>\beta\), the smaller truth-table dimension is \(N'=N^{\beta/\beta'}\), so a lower-bound exponent \(\gamma\) transfers to \((\beta/\beta')\gamma\).

This is a valid bridge only if the stronger-\(\beta'\) result has enough exponent margin and is uniform for the transformed \(c'\). It gives no transfer from the constant-gap cofactor relation and no direct \(\rho\) lower bound.

## Idea 278 - Transfer \(\rho\) by pulling back filters

C-118 is stronger than rect-DAG padding for the project measure. Restrict a large cover's endpoints to the embedded smaller high class. Any surviving small semi-filter pulls back by \(A\mapsto A\cap Z^\iota\), preserving upward closure, matching slices, and pair intersections. Thus \(\rho_{\rm small}\le\rho_{\rm big}\) directly, without cubic loss.

Use this only with a direct lower bound at shifted parameters. For fixed \(\beta'>\beta\), the small dimension is \(N'=N^{\beta/\beta'}\), so exponent \(1+\epsilon'\) becomes \((\beta/\beta')(1+\epsilon')\); it must still exceed the desired \(1+\epsilon\).

## Idea 279 - Treat padding as a parameter ray, not an amplification

C-119 audits the exact ignored-input map. For rational lambda=p/q>1, compare arities pt and qt; the thresholds match exactly when (beta,c) is sent to (lambda beta,lambda c). A direct cover lower-bound exponent is divided by lambda. The OPS premise still quantifies over every sufficiently small fixed beta, so a single hard parameter cannot be stretched into the needed interval. If the source lower bound is uniform at the shifted constant lambda c0, its low class is smaller and hardness already transfers to c0 at the same beta by monotonicity; padding adds no advantage to magnification.

The exact rational schedule avoids threshold rounding.
