For a lower bound known only infinitely often, its hard arities must align with the selected subsequence; an all-large-arities bound avoids this issue. Empty endpoints created by restricting a cover pair are allowed in the source model, and are vacuous if a variant forbids them. Keep the transfer lemma, close the parameter-bookkeeping branch, and spend effort on the missing direct cyclic-state lower bound.

## Idea 280 - One-cell concentration is the sharp gate-signature stress test

For a fixed low circuit and kâ‰ˆ(1/2)log s2 selected wires including the output, take a largest joint-signature cell F. Its size is at least N/sqrt(s2). Alter the low table arbitrarily only on F. Because 2^|F| exceeds the number of size-s2 circuits for fixed beta<2/3, a completion is high. The constant-on-F completions are computed by the original low circuit plus a k-wire signature test, so a high completion must vary inside F. It agrees with the low row everywhere else. By sparse-point patching, it has Omega(s2/n) mismatches, all in this one cell.

This proves that C-115's total minority mass can concentrate completely; counting mixed cells or relying on several witnesses fails. The cell itself varies with the low circuit and high completion, so the shared-DAG challenge is still to identify it adaptively. No lower bound follows yet. See C-120.

## Idea 281 - The common-partition escape is fully characterized

Suppose all low rows are constant on a fixed partition into m cells. If the partition label plus an arbitrary m-cell lookup costs below s2, then every high table is mixed on some cell. Bob selects a mixed cell using O(m) states, Alice reveals the row's constant bit there, and Bob scans the cell for an opposite value. Total size is O(N).

For the full low class, point-indicator circuits of size O(n) separate every pair of truth-table positions. Thus any partition respected by all low rows must be discrete, with N cells; the lookup no longer fits below s2. This explains why the C-80 adaptive escape works for a structured subfamily but cannot be made universal by choosing one better fixed partition. The remaining challenge is sharing across row-dependent partitions. See C-121.

## Idea 282 - Joint signatures make every small anchor set easy

Fix r<=eta n low rows. Their joint output W(x) gives at most 2^r cells. A high z cannot be constant on all those cells: otherwise z is an r-bit lookup after the r low circuits, with total size r s1+O(r2^r)<s2 for sufficiently small eta. Thus one cell is mixed for z and constant for every row in the set. Bob finds such a cell, Alice tells her bit, and Bob scans for the opposite bit, giving an O(N)-vertex DAG for the whole set.

This strengthens C-109 by supplying the actual shared router and closes small-anchor fooling families based only on common-fiber incompatibility. The group partition depends on the chosen rows; covering all low tables by groups incurs exponential total size unless suffixes can be reused across groups. C-122 isolates that remaining reuse problem.
## Idea 283 â€” Short descriptions are existential witnesses, not shared states

For D circuit descriptions mapping onto Y, lifting each row predicate by G^-1 maps any table-domain rect-DAG to DÃ—Z. Choosing a section Yâ†’D maps it back without changing the graph. So descriptor inputs have exactly the same minimum DAG size. The DAG is Î˜ the circuit size of a promise separator h(Y)=1,h(Z)=0.

A universal circuit efficiently evaluates one supplied description, but table membership is âˆƒdâˆ€x[t_x=G(d)(x)]. The direct exact separator enumerates all descriptions and costs O(NÂ·2^ell), ell=O(s1 log(s1+n)); it is a valid baseline, not near-linear. Searching an interval for a mismatch also fails as a DAG transition because the joint mismatch predicate is nonrectangular. The lesson is precise: syntax helps a protocol communicate, but it neither proves nor disproves graph reuse. Any small DAG would be a new separator upper bound; any lower bound must attack that separator or the cyclic cover directly. See C-123.
## Idea 284 â€” Succinct MCSP hardness does not directly imply explicit DAG hardness

The 2026 Gap-ImpMCSP result operates on sampler circuits, with conditional NP-hardness under randomized half-Levin reductions. The C-75 relation and C_sep operate on explicit N-bit tables; expanding a sampler may cost exponential size. The SoS MCSP degree result is per fixed hard table, while a rect-DAG lower bound needs a single separator for all YÃ—Z pairs. Neither transfers to q without a new reduction. See C-124.

## Idea 285 - Partial-table embeddings may transfer cyclic lower bounds directly

Compose the q-state cyclic separator with a monotone map phi from a hard f into the dual-rail table cube. YES inputs should contain a full code for a low table; NO inputs should specify a consistent partial table with a high completion. Then phi's a AND gates plus q closure gates compute f, so q >= CycAnd(f)-a. For triangle, OR-only phi is impossible when the cyclic bound exceeds N; the obvious witness expansion costs O(r^3), so it does not beat Omega(r^3/log^4(r)). Learning: composition is easy; the open problem is a cheap, variable low-code family. This is an alternate direct-q route, not the primary shared-DAG route. See C-125/O-106.


## Idea 286 - The partial-code reduction has two separate obligations

For a rail vector u, let LowExt_Y(u) mean that some full signed code e(w) of a low truth table lies below u. C-126 proves f=LowExt_Y(phi) for any C-125 transfer: a NO input cannot contain a low code and also lie below a high code, because full one-hot codes are an antichain. But this alone is insufficient: the NO image also needs a high completion, since the fusion separator's medium values are free. Thus seek a low-AND reduction to LowExt_Y and separately certify a high completion for every NO. NO images are consistent; YES images may carry extra conflicts outside a chosen low code. This is the exact asymmetry left after the OR-only no-go.

## Idea 287 - Variable low-table witnesses need conflict spread

For YES x,y, monotonicity sends both chosen low codes below phi(x OR y). If the codes differ at coordinate k, both rails must be active there at the join. Therefore all witness variation is carried by YES-side conflict coordinates. If those coordinates lie in S of size delta, all witnesses agree outside S; enumerating at most 2^delta low tables yields a circuit for f with at most a+N+delta*2^delta AND gates. A transfer proving q>N^(1+epsilon) needs delta >= (1+epsilon)log2(N)-O(log log N). This gives a necessary shape for variable-witness maps, not a lower bound on q. Explore conflict incidence or a map with spread-out conflicts and high NO completions.

## Idea 288 - PRG lower bounds transfer through the promise, not through DAG sharing

Uniform N-bit tables lie outside SIZE(s2) with probability 1-2^{-N+o(N)} for s2=N^beta, beta<1. Any local PRG whose output tables have size <=s1 is entirely accepted by a valid promise separator, regardless of its medium-band values. Therefore the Cheraghchi-Kabanets-Lu-Myrisiotis local PRGs give promise formula lower bounds N^(3beta-o(1)) above beta=1/3 and arbitrary-basis formula/BP lower bounds N^(2beta-o(1)) above beta=1/2. This is useful exact model matching for trees, but the exponents are not superlinear at sufficiently small beta, and it does not constrain a shared rect-DAG. Need a PRG for that DAG model or a sharing-preserving simulation; see C-128/O-109.

## Idea 289 - Make every shared state pay for its excluded high fibers

C-129: A valid rect-DAG node with k descendant output coordinates and r distinct low-row signatures must omit at least r(2^(N-k)-M2) high tables from its column side whenever this quantity is positive. The proof is exact: each row signature's K-fiber contains that many high completions, and none can share the state rectangle with that row. This is a candidate non-shareability invariant tied to actual low/high tables. Try to charge these excluded columns globally through the DAG, accounting for overlaps and adaptive shrinking. If the charge can be made near-linear per state, it may produce a Tier-3 or stronger DAG theorem; without that step it gives no q bound.

## Idea 290 â€” Borrow bottleneck counting, but repair the root collapse

C-131 imports the shape of the 2025 Beame--Whitmeyer bottleneck argument for Search-BPHP triangle-DAGs. Define h_v(w) as the minimum number of descendant mismatch coordinates needed to hit every high column in a rect-DAG state A_v x B_v, for a fixed low row w in A_v. The completion-count argument gives h_root(w)>=N-log2|SIZE(s2)| for every low row: any smaller coordinate set has a high completion agreeing with w on all of it. Thus each low row must have nearly all output coordinates reachable somewhere in its subgraph.

This does not give a superlinear vertex lower bound; the invariant only counts distinct coordinates (at most N for fixed w), while context-specific leaves may still be needed. It also identifies why the published endpoint-to-bottleneck assignment does not directly work: the root itself crosses every natural width threshold, so it would absorb all rows. The BPHP proof's per-node capacity comes from equality/collision geometry, which is absent here. Next, search for a pair-distribution or multiscale statistic that avoids the root collapse and charges only actual first divergence. C-130 rules out raw sums of excluded high-table volumes because one table is excluded by Omega(N) reachable off-path states. See C-131/O-111.

## Idea 291 â€” A dense promise rectangle defeats width-only bottleneck capacity

C-132: choose I of size 3N/4, let P=pi_I(Y), and let B be high tables whose I-restriction is outside P. Every pair in Y x B differs inside I, so a valid subprotocol can output only in I. For any row w and S subset I of size at most N/2, the completion fiber has at least 2^(N/2) tables, while non-high tables plus all tables with a low prefix number only M2+|P|2^(N/4)=2^o(N)+2^(N/4+o(N)); therefore a high completion in B matches w on S. The node's width lies in (N/2,3N/4] for every low row.

Split the full root into Y x B and Y x (Z minus B). Its root width is N-o(N), so the B-child is a valid half-width-preserving move into the band [0.4N,0.8N) for every row. One in-band node can therefore see all |Y| rows. This kills the direct capacity lemma based on width alone, not a more careful global assignment. The next statistic must remember which column fibers were removed or use first-path context, and must survive C-130's repeated off-path charges. See C-132/O-112.

## 2026-09-26 - C-133: local richness defeats exact-restriction sharing

Tested the C-78 dyadic universal mismatch DAG against the low-circuit language itself. For any k coordinates, every bit pattern is realized by a low table when k=O(s1/n): make the table the OR of the selected point minterms, costing O(kn) gates. Thus at dyadic block size k=Theta(s1/n), the construction needs (N/k)2^k distinct interval-pattern rectangles, i.e. 2^(Omega(N^beta/n^2)) states. Different interval-pattern keys really have different row sides, so simple rectangle deduplication does not fix it.

**Learning:** short individual circuit descriptions do not help this architecture because its reuse key is the output restriction, and those restrictions are maximally rich on small blocks. This is not a lower bound on arbitrary shared DAGs. A general DAG may filter high columns or use non-interval semantic states; C-132 already shows width-only routing does not force a restriction context. Next: prove a routing lemma for arbitrary residual rectangles, or build a different DAG that compresses these patterns without creating invalid cross-pairs. Do not promote C-133 to a rho or P-vs-NP bound. See research/CURRENT_STATE.md and research/OPEN_OBLIGATIONS.md (O-113).

## 2026-09-26 - C-134: maximal local variation can be easy to route

Take all low tables supported on a small coordinate block I. This gives 2^k rows and every possible pattern on I. Still, every high table must have a 1 outside I, because any table supported on I has an O(kn) circuit. All rows are zero there, so a single Bob scan of the outside coordinates routes every pair to a valid mismatch in O(N) DAG states.

**Learning:** C-133's local-surjectivity fact cannot become a general DAG lower bound without accounting for the high-column residual. A common mismatch region can let Bob avoid learning which low row he has. For the full low class no such large common region is available; the unresolved question is whether adaptive semantic filters can manufacture comparable shortcuts. Track row and column sides together, and stress-test against C-132 and C-130. See O-114.

## 2026-09-26 - C-135: low-variation row families have a common router

For a row family A, let V be its nonconstant truth-table coordinates. All rows agree with one low row w0 outside V. If a table z agrees there too, patch w0 on V using point minterms; this costs O(n|V|) gates. Thus when |V|<=Theta((s2-s1)/n)=Theta(s1) in the OPS gap, no high table can agree on the common coordinates. Every high table exposes a mismatch where every row in A has the same bit, and Bob can scan those positions using an O(N)-state DAG.

**Learning:** the common-witness shortcut is much broader than a fixed zero block. But this only classifies easy row rectangles; the root varies on all N coordinates, and the number/sharing of small-variation states is uncontrolled. Large variation support does not itself imply hardness. Next try to use this dichotomy jointly with the column residual, keeping C-132 and C-130 as countertests. See O-115.

## 2026-09-26 - C-136: dense mismatch witnesses do not solve deterministic sharing

The C-135 patching estimate applies to every low/high pair: if w and z differed on at most d=Theta(s1) positions, patching w at those points would compute z below s2. Thus each pair has at least d+1 valid mismatch labels. Weighting each of the 2N coordinate/sign rectangles by 1/(d+1) gives a fractional cover of the ordinary search relation with total weight O(N/d). Any label-conflict fooling family is at most 2N/(d+1). C-138 later improves the explicit C-129 witness-family lower bound to Omega(N/s2), leaving a factor Theta(n) to this method ceiling. Public-coin sampling finds a mismatch in expected O(N/d) bits.

However, any fixed coordinate sample of size below N-log2|SIZE(s2)| misses some pair: choose the zero low table and complete its unqueried positions to a high table. So random sampling is not a universal deterministic schedule. The unresolved cost is the adaptive history: after equal answers, a deterministic continuation must preserve a rectangle, and compressing distinct histories may introduce invalid cross-pairs.

**Learning:** mismatch scarcity is not the obstruction. Fractional covers, standard label-conflict fooling sets, and fixed samples cannot reach a superlinear deterministic rect-DAG bound. The next proof attempt needs a routing-sensitive invariant or a construction that reuses equality histories safely. This is not a DAG lower bound and not a fusion/P-vs-NP result; see C-136/O-116/Q96.

## 2026-09-26 - C-137: a tiny cyclic scanner violates rectangle semantics

Tried a direct O(N)-state loop: at coordinate i, output if w_i differs from z_i; otherwise continue, merging equal outcomes 00 and 11. It terminates on every promised low/high pair, but the merged continuation is the union of two diagonal rectangles, not a rectangle. The product hull adds cross pairs. So the machine has joint access to both bits and discards a transcript distinction that a rect-DAG must preserve.

For a fixed-order scan, keeping that distinction forces 2^k nonempty equal-prefix contexts by k=Theta(s1/n): every prefix is realized by a low table and has a high completion. This is another falsification of the fixed-prefix architecture, consistent with C-133, not a general DAG lower bound.

**Learning:** cycles do not erase the rectangle invariant. A generic cyclic pair transducer is not the C-74 fusion closure game, and its state bound does not transfer without a simulation. Continue seeking a deterministic rectangle-preserving adaptive merge; see C-137/O-117/Q97.

## 2026-09-26 - C-138: sparse high supports improve the fooling baseline

For r=A s2, the sphere of r-subsets of [N] has more elements than the entire SIZE(s2) class, by the circuit-count bound and log binom(N,r)â‰ˆA(1-beta)s2 n. A random partition into r-blocks therefore contains a choice where every support indicator is high. Against the zero low table these pairs have disjoint mismatch labels, giving Omega(N/s2) leaves and a deterministic communication lower bound (1-beta)n-O(1). This sharpens C-129 by a factor Theta(n).

**Learning:** C-136's maximum for label-conflict families is O(N/s1), leaving only a logN factor above this stronger construction; both are still sublinear in N. Output-label packing cannot prove the desired superlinear DAG bound. The next step is state routing, not a larger disjoint-support packing. See C-138/O-118/Q98.

## 2026-09-26 - C-139: the closure proof is a ranked cyclic rectangle game

For each fusion rule i, use the rectangle R_i=(Y intersect X_i) x (Z minus X_i). If (w,z) is in it, the inactive rule at z has at least one unsupported side. At the first round when the rule activates on w, that side had either a matching literal witness or an already-active predecessor rule. The former is a mismatch, because z cannot have the same matching literal while the endpoint is absent. The latter is inactive at z by upward closure and has strictly smaller first-activation rank on w. Each transition splits along a z-local false side and a w-local true support, so the search preserves rectangles. Static rule edges may cycle, but no fixed-pair path does.

This proves an exact Q-to-ranked-cyclic-search transformation with q reusable rule states, at most 2N mismatch terminals, and O(q^2+qN) support arcs. The Q-witness relation is total iff Q covers all low anchors; plain mismatch is total regardless. It is not a standard rect-DAG because Sokolov's model requires a globally acyclic graph of outdegree at most two. Rank layering and binary support routing give O(q^2(q+N))=O(q^3), which does not beat the saved O(q^3/log q) compiler. The actual open step is sharing support routers among different activation-rank thresholds without adding cross-pairs.

**Learning:** C-75's useful resource is indeed shared state, but the closure already gives that resource only in a ranked cyclic model. Turning it into a standard DAG costs for input-dependent ranking and support choice. There is no reverse equivalence for arbitrary cyclic rectangle games unless they retain the C-74 seed and containment syntax. Also, by vertex count a tree cannot be smaller than the DAG it contains; the meaningful gap is short bit-depth versus many graph vertices. No superlinear q/DAG bound or P-vs-NP proof follows. See C-139/O-117/Q99.

## 2026-09-26 - C-140: rank-layer cost can belong to the witness, not the output

Tried to turn the q^2 rank layers from C-139 into a non-shareability lower bound. The two-state recurrence x1=(s1 OR x2) AND c, x2=(s2 OR x1) AND c kills that inference: the activation order reverses between seed inputs 10 and 01, but the least fixed point is just c AND (s1 OR s2), with a constant-size acyclic circuit.

**Learning:** the closure's ranked support path may be much more complicated than the separator it computes. A lower bound on unrolling or path preservation alone does not lower-bound S_rect or rho; the DAG may use a different proof/computation. This is an abstract C-74-shaped recurrence only, not yet a legal endpoint construction or a Gap-MCSP reduction. Next test realizability, then require any state-merging obstruction to survive alternative output circuits. See C-140/O-117/Q100.

## 2026-09-26 - C-141: legal endpoint realization of input-ranked cycles

Resolved Q100's local endpoint test. On the five-bit cube, take A={a=0}, B={b=0}, C={c=1}, P=C intersect(A union B), two distinct markers p1,p2 with a=b=1,c=0, and endpoints E1=A union P union {p1,p2}, H1=C union {p1}, E2=B union P union {p1,p2}, H2=C union {p2}. Then T1=P union {p1}, T2=P union {p2}; T2 is supported in E1 but not H1, and T1 in E2 but not H2. The only literal seeds are A, B, C, giving the C-140 equations exactly after self-loop deletion.

**Learning:** the dynamic rank reversal is not just an artifact of arbitrary Boolean equations; legal semantic fusion endpoints can produce it. But this two-rule fragment has no empty carrier, is not a promise cover, and its output reduces to C AND (A OR B). So it still cannot support a q or DAG lower bound. ## 2026-09-26 - C-142: a successful cover can contain a dispensable cyclic SCC

Built a three-pair finite promise cover around C-141's cycle. On four-bit anchors, Y={(0,1,1,0),(1,0,1,0)} and Z has five points. The two nonempty carriers are the distinct markers p1,p2; each rule supports the other on its E side, while an empty root pair uses E0={p1}, H0={p2}. The seed table gives x1=(a0 OR x2) AND (c1 OR f1), x2=(b0 OR x1) AND c1, x0=x1 AND x2. The two low anchors activate the SCC in opposite orders and both activate x0; all five high points leave x0 inactive.

**Learning:** even a successful fusion cover can have real input-dependent cyclic paths whose unrolling looks context-heavy, while an unrelated two-gate separator h=c AND (NOT a OR NOT b) solves the same promise. This closes the finite toy embedding but shows a lower bound on Q-path histories is not a separator lower bound. O-117 must attack the minimum output computation on the actual MCSP promise. See C-142/Q102.

## 2026-09-26 - C-143: a large cyclic rank profile can be output-small

Scaled the toy cover to a q-state directed cycle with q low anchors. State i has carrier p_i, E_i contains p_i and predecessor p_(i-1) plus a unique seed slice z_i, and H_i contains p_i plus a common control point. An empty rule combines p1 and p2. The lows each activate one seed with control c=1, inducing all q rotations; high seed points have c=0, control-only high point has no seed, and markers have c=0. Balanced unique tag bits block accidental literal seeds.

**Learning:** the rank-layer protocol has q(q-1)+1 distinct rectangles, since each low seed gives a different activation rank at every state. Yet h=c AND OR_i t_i is an O(q)-size separator. Thus even a successful cover with a large SCC and maximally diverse rank profiles can have a small unrelated DAG. This kills rank-profile counting as a standalone lower bound. The actual Gap-MCSP promise must force hardness of every separator, not just the closure path. See C-143/O-117/Q103.

## 2026-09-26 - C-144: a deletion-minimal q-cycle list has a one-pair alternative

Audited the C-143 promise beyond its displayed q-cycle list. One pair E*={z_i:i in [q]}, H*={r} covers every low anchor: w_i has literal slices {z_i} and {r} inside the two disjoint endpoints. No high anchor generates both: for z_i, the only matching t_j=1 singleton is {z_i}, not {r}; p_i has only large matching t-slices; neither matches c=1. At r, every matching slice contains r, so none lies in E*. Hence the promise's optimum cover is rho=1.

The displayed q-cycle list is still deletion-minimal: deleting rule i strands its only seed anchor w_i, and deleting the root leaves no empty carrier. So irredundancy within a fixed list is not a proxy for minimum semantic cover size. This is a stronger calibration of the earlier lesson: rank-layer complexity can be Theta(q^2) while the optimum cover uses one pair. It does not establish anything about optimal covers or the OPS promise. Future lower-bound arguments must be invariant under replacing Q with entirely different endpoint pairs.

## 2026-09-26 - C-145: OPS forces broad high-side bootstrap carriers

Used the circuit-count shattering property quantitatively. For any two distinct truth-table coordinates and any prescribed bits, the cylinder has 2^(N-2) tables and fewer than M2=2^o(N) low/medium tables, so it contains at least 2^(N-2)-M2 high tables. A successful closure must activate some rule in round one on each low anchor; otherwise iteration from zero never moves. Its two endpoint memberships must then come from matching literal slices. Their intersection lies in T_i=E_i intersect H_i, so the carrier contains that many high tables, and all of them activate the same state at round one.

**Learning:** finite marker cycles exploit a seed pair with no high common extension. OPS forbids that: every first state coactivates on a constant fraction of high inputs. This shifts the live target from bootstrap to downstream routingâ€”how can later supports shrink these high regions for low anchors without creating empty outputs on high tables? The local mass fact is not a global q lower bound; the same high columns may recur across many states. See C-145/O-119/Q105.

## 2026-09-26 - C-146: cofactor restrictions expose sharing, not a direct sum

A seed state from C-145 is constant on the cylinder determined by its two seed literals, so on that restriction its cyclic recurrence can drop one AND-state by substituting the constant. This is only a statement about the induced recurrence; restricting the high universe can change endpoint-containment edges, so I do not infer a smaller legal cover automatically.

Tried to amplify the drop by summing hard cofactors. The finite exact-one promise kills that: Y is the set of r weight-one vectors, Z all other r-bit vectors. It has a two-coordinate-dense high side, rho=Theta(r) (O(r) via prefix/suffix zero tests, Omega(r) from one-anchor literal width), while each of the binom(r,2) cofactors fixing two bits to 00 is another exact-one instance with Omega(r) complexity. The global circuit shares across all of them. The OPS route therefore needs a specific obstruction to cofactor sharing, not a generic direct-sum claim.

## 2026-09-26 - C-150 first-excluded carrier scan

For each low anchor w, order Q's active states by first-activation rank. For any high table z, the first active carrier T_i omitting z cannot rely on an earlier carrier to support the endpoint z misses: that earlier carrier would also omit z. Therefore that endpoint was seeded by a literal matching w and immediately supplies a differing coordinate. This replaces the support-path witness by a canonical first-missing-carrier selector.

The selector does not automatically compile to a small rect-DAG. After scanning t carriers, the residual column region is their intersection P_t(w), which depends on the row. Merging different row histories can create a product hull containing cross-pairs that should have exited on an earlier missing carrier. C-142 realizes this failure in a legal successful toy, but a one-pair alternative cover bypasses it. Keeping residual contexts may restore quadratic/cubic overhead; counting them only lower-bounds the chosen scan, since another separator may bypass Q. Next: seek a factorization theorem for OPS residual intersections or a cross-pair lemma that applies to every separator. See bridge section 76 and O-122/O-121.

## Idea 292 - Canonical selector cost can disappear when outputs are projected

Take A_S=[k]\\S and B_T=T union {k}. Every pair has common element k; the least common element is k on diagonal pairs, but any two diagonal pairs in one k-labelled rectangle force a cross-pair whose least common element is below k. Thus the unique-minimum relation needs 2^(k-1) k-labelled leaves, while the relation accepting any common element has one leaf. This is the sharp warning for C-150: first-missing-carrier selection is useful only if a lower bound survives the signed-mismatch relation's freedom to output any differing coordinate. Exact transfer test: every valid solver leaf must have one selector value, or a decoder/reduction must enforce it. The example is not a Gap-MCSP bound.

## Idea 293 - A successful toy lets mismatch merge selector fibers

In C-142, both low anchors have c=1 and columns p1,p2 have c=0. Their product is therefore a valid rectangle whose mismatch output is always c. However, the first-excluded C-150 carrier is state 2 on p1 and state 1 on p2, giving selector matrix [[2,1],[2,1]]. This disproves generic leaf-homogeneity transfer even inside a successful fusion toy. Only an OPS-specific restriction could recover the selected carrier; absent one, drop this route and search for an invariant of the full mismatch relation. This is not an OPS bound.

## Idea 294 - Import colourful-sunflower lifting only through a valid-output map

The CCC 2025 colourful-sunflower lifting theorem lower-bounds rect-DAG size for Index-lifted CSP search by (m/(A|Sigma|w log(mn)))^w. It is the right model family to inspect for shared-state lower bounds. But reducing it to Gap-MCSP requires separate maps into low-circuit and high tables, plus a decoder proving every mismatch leaf yields a violated constraint throughout its rectangle. No such reduction is known. C-151/C-153 warn that arbitrary mismatch outputs can project away a selector; they do not rule out a global CSP gadget. ## Idea 295 - RETRACTED: the partial-Index code obstruction was false

The old argument demanded agreement on invalid inputs y_x=0. SearchOR composed with Index is partial, so those pairs impose no condition. On legal inputs, a(x)=0^m and b(y)=y always mismatch at x, and every mismatch decodes to the sole valid output. Do not cite the old no-go. ## Idea 296 - Cyclic mismatch states need a progress condition

There is a tempting O(N)-state loop for any total mismatch relation: make every state the full input rectangle, put one signed mismatch leaf on one edge, and continue around a cycle on the other. Every pair has a finite path to a valid output, but also an infinite path, so this only works under vacuous existential-path semantics. It is not a terminating protocol or a fusion closure construction. A useful cyclic DAG model must expose a well-founded input-sensitive rank; in the fusion game, C-139's first-activation rank is the available candidate.

Also record the binary product-cover constraint: if two child rectangles cover A x B, one child must contain all of A or all of B. This forces a locally deterministic party choice at each standard Boolean-game state. It clarifies why a wide mismatch-leaf star is not a binary rect-DAG and why state sharing must preserve rectangle continuations. The lemma alone supplies no global lower bound; test any proposed charge against C-130/C-132.

## Idea 297 - Treat the rectangle trichotomy as circuit syntax, not a lower bound

C-159 checked Sokolov's primary proof: every binary Boolean-game node is AND-like, OR-like, or redundant/copy-like according to how its two child rectangles cover the parent. This explains the standard circuit correspondence and shows C-158 is known. A lower bound needs a global theorem about how many nonredundant states remain after arbitrary sharing; local gate classification alone cannot establish it. Combine only with a quantitatively new state-reuse invariant, and keep C-130/C-132 counterexamples active.

## Idea 301 - Charge source outputs against the low/high mismatch distance

C-136 gives a gap Delta=Theta(N^beta/n): every low/high table pair differs in at least Delta positions. For a total source relation R, define chi_out*(R) as the minimum total weight on answer labels so that every source pair is covered by valid-answer weight at least one. If partywise encodings map source pairs to low/high tables and each signed mismatch type is decoded through at most r output-labelled terminals, then
chi_out*(R) <= 2Nr/Delta = O(r n N^(1-beta)).

Proof: a source pair creates at least Delta mismatches; each mismatch decoder path must reach a valid source answer. Across the 2N signed types there are at most 2Nr answer incidences. Weight each incidence by 1/Delta; these weights cover every source pair. For a unique-answer relation with M used outputs, this forces r >= M Delta/(2N).

A calibration uses the relation whose unique answer is Alice's k=floor((1-beta/2)n)-bit input. It has M=Theta(N^(1-beta/2))<2N outputs, and each input can be encoded by putting its bits at k fixed truth-table positions, giving a low circuit of size O(n^2). Yet a mismatch-based decoder needs Omega(N^(beta/2)/n) output terminals per signed mismatch type. This shows output alphabet size alone misses the repetition forced by the OPS distance gap.

Use this before attempting the C-154 Index-lifting map: if the source's chi_out* exceeds the budget for the proposed decoder refinement, that transfer cannot work. Passing the test is only necessary; C-156's paired-cut rectangles must still be valid. This is a reduction no-go criterion, not a DAG or rho_prom lower bound. Full statement: bridge C-163.

## Idea 302 - Use Index rectangle density to price output decoding

C-164: for the lifted cPHP search relation, any rectangle whose pairs all admit the fixed pigeon-pair answer (p,q) has uniform mass at most 1/(m^2 d). Alice's two pointers must lie in a support S of size at most m^2; Bob's selected array cells must obey partial-matching constraints along S, whose equality graph gives probability at most d^(-rank). The component edge count bounds |S| by d^(rank-1).

Because every OPS low/high pair has Delta=Theta(N^beta/n) mismatches, any coordinatewise table embedding with r valid source-output rectangles per signed mismatch type must have r>=Delta m^2d/(2N). The simple fractional output-cover filter C-163 misses this extra Index geometry. Compare the required r to the colourful-sunflower lower bound before investing in a full reduction. This is only a decoder-cost lower bound; it does not prove the target DAG or fusion cover is large, and it may be dominated by the lifted bound. The low/high maps remain the main unresolved construction.

## Idea 303 - The sign of a mismatch is a real reduction cost

C-165 specializes C-156 to the Index-lifted cPHP source. For fixed Alice pointers, every fixed output pair of distinct pigeons occurs on at most a 1/d fraction of Bob arrays. At one table coordinate, if Alice's encoded bit takes both values, then the two Bob mismatch classes must each be covered by valid outputs; with r decoder leaves per sign their measures are at most r/d. Thus r>=d/2. If r<d/2, all Alice bits are constant, and a balanced Bob input makes every output valid on at most 1/d of Alice inputs, preventing the decoder from covering the rows. So no fixed signed decoder works for d>=3.

This does not contradict the CCC lifting paper: its clique-colouring reduction decodes only one monotone mKW orientation. Keep a larger input-aware signed decoder as a live possibility, with r>=max(d/2, Delta*m^2*d/(2N)). The key next question is whether one can construct such a decoder cheaply enough that the lifted lower bound still clears N^(3+3epsilon)/log N, or prove that the selected mismatch rectangles require much larger refinement.


## Idea 304 - C-166 rechecks the known interval-router obstruction

C-166 rechecked the C-78 universal rect-DAG whose states are (interval I, low restriction r). A short description lets Alice evaluate r locally, but a state remains a product rectangle. If another low restriction s has a high extension z_s, merging the two states introduces the cross-pair (w_s,z_s) that agrees on I, so it cannot be solved by descendants restricted to I. Point-indicator circuits give all 2^L patterns on L selected table entries for L=O(s1/n), and counting ensures high extensions for short enough I. C-133 already proves the full (N/L)2^L profile-router count with distinct row sides across intervals. The C-110 product-hull rule explains why same-interval merging fails. This is a reconciliation with existing work, not new lower-bound progress.

Learning: this is the known C-133 scanner lower bound plus a direct C-110 specialization, not a new theorem. It gives no non-shareability result for arbitrary DAGs. An arbitrary DAG can output a mismatch outside I, and no normalization forces it to preserve interval progress. Next task: either design such an adaptive bypass compactly or prove any low-size DAG has enough interval-local states to inherit the cross-pair obstruction. Do not convert the profile bound into an OPS DAG lower bound without that step.
## Idea 305 - C-160 kills generic interval normalization

C-167 specializes the easy two-tail threshold calibration to the exact O-127 question. Let I have L<=a=floor(N^beta/n) coordinates. Any restriction r extends to a low table by filling the rest with zeros, and also extends to a high middle-weight table by filling the rest to total weight floor(N/2). Hence all 2^L restriction contexts exist and have high extensions. Product-hull merging of two contexts introduces a low/high cross-pair that agrees on I, so an interval-local scanner needs 2^L states. At L=a this is 2^a, while a global Hamming-weight threshold circuit gives an O(N log N) rect-DAG.

Learning: this decisively falsifies a promise-independent polynomial-loss normalization from arbitrary rect-DAGs to interval routers. It narrows O-127 to an OPS-specific theorem using a feature absent from the threshold calibration, or retirement of interval-profile charging. The result does not lower-bound the actual Gap-MCSP DAG or rho_prom. Next work should attack arbitrary rectangle-state merging or find a genuinely OPS-specific invariant; no interval-state profile sum transfers without it.
## Idea 306 - A circuit description cannot preselect a short mismatch sample

C-168 allows the candidate coordinate set S(w) to depend on the exact low truth table, or on any description d that computes it. If every high table had to differ from w on S(w), all 2^(N-|S(w)|) completions of w|S(w) would be non-high. Since there are only M2=|SIZE(s2)| non-high tables, |S(w)|>=N-log2(M2)=N-o(N).

Learning: even row-specific, description-aware but nonadaptive sampling needs almost the whole truth table. This does not constrain Bob-dependent routing in a shared DAG. The surviving construction would need to use both parties' information through rectangle-valid state transitions; next seek such a joint adaptive construction or a state-reuse lower bound.

## Idea 307 - One-switch description protocols are too large

C-170 pushes the short-description objection to both fixed-order one-way architectures. If Alice sends a message and Bob finishes, every message class must be Hamming-diameter at most log|SIZE(s2)|. The existing C-80 block-constant subcode has 2^Theta(s1) low tables with pairwise distance Theta(N/s1), larger than that diameter for beta<1/2. So a one-switch DAG needs at least 2^Theta(s1) frontier states even if Bob's suffix is shared.

If Bob sends first and Alice finishes, every Bob message class is constant on a coordinate set that separates its columns from every low row. Low circuits can realize any pattern on t=Theta(s1/n) coordinates, so such a set must have more than t coordinates. Each message class then occupies a cylinder of size at most 2^(N-t-1), forcing 2^Omega(s1/n) messages to cover Z.

Learning: Alice's circuit description does make communication bits cheap, but it does not create shared topology; Bob cannot finish from one description state with a near-linear DAG, and Bob cannot send one compact synopsis either. The missing resource is repeated alternation. The result is architecture-specific; an arbitrary rect-DAG may alternate many times. Next define an alternation-sensitive rectangle potential or construct a multi-round DAG that evades this barrier. No OPS DAG or fusion lower bound follows yet.

**Countercheck.** C-80's block-constant low family has an O(N)-state B-to-A-to-B router: any high z is mixed in one common block, while each low row is constant there. This erases the one-switch lower bound for that subpromise. C-121 blocks only extending one fixed partition to all low circuits. The real candidate obstruction is therefore the cost of selecting and reusing circuit-dependent fibers.

## Idea 308 - Affine-flat test for fixed fiber-pair menus

C-171 turns the output-fiber idea into a graph problem. Let G be a fixed set of candidate coordinate pairs. For a low table w, keep only G-edges inside its 0- and 1-fibers. If the resulting graph has c components, every z constant on those components defeats every candidate pair. Since the high side is the complement of SIZE(s2), coverage forces c<=log|SIZE(s2)|.

Low circuit indicators of affine subspaces provide a uniform stress test. For every affine H of size mâ‰ˆ2log|SIZE(s2)|, G[H] must have at least m-log|SIZE(s2)| edges. A random affine-flat average then forces |G|=Omega(N^2/log|SIZE(s2)|)=Omega(N^(2-beta)/n). This is a real lower bound for a fixed output-pair menu and for the stronger Fib relation's leaf labels.

Learning: output-strengthening creates a lower bound but does not automatically help the original relation. Fib-to-mismatch is easy; mismatch-to-Fib has an O(N^2) context loss, making the quantitative implication useless. Keep this only as a nonadaptive-menu obstruction unless a cheaper reverse map is found.

## Idea 309 - Count all row-signature cylinders against one global budget
C-172 sharpens the state-volume inequality. At any shared DAG state, each distinct low-row pattern on the descendant output coordinates determines a disjoint full truth-table cylinder. Every high table in those cylinders must be excluded from the state, because it agrees with a low row on every output the suffix can use. The number of non-high tables across the union is at most M2 total, not M2 per signature, so

    excluded high columns >= r*2^(N-k)-M2.

At the root this yields |pi_K(Y)|*2^(N-k)<=M2. Point-minterm circuits realize 2^t patterns on any t=Theta(s1/n) selected coordinates, strengthening the root output-support floor by t. The improvement remains N-o(N), and C-135 patching gives a common N-Theta(s1) candidate-coordinate set that already hits every low/high pair. Thus the hard part is routing to one such coordinate through rectangles, not making a candidate list. The unresolved obstacle is overlap: many states may exclude the same high columns. Seek a potential charging that overlap across owner switches, stress-tested on C-80's adaptive router and C-160's easy threshold separator; otherwise keep C-172 as a local constraint only. See O-131/Q129.

## Idea 310 - Rectangle decision-list alternation and the C-75 state gap
The 2025 Rect-DL model is adjacent but not equivalent. A C-75 rect-DAG gives a list of leaf rectangles labelled by valid mismatches, but the direct multi-output list measure is at most 2N because the 2N signed mismatch rectangles cover the promise. The Rect-DL alternation results concern Boolean output changes, not which party owns the next protocol move.

The exact compile-back obstruction is the failed rectangle query: testing A x B requires Alice's and Bob's separate checks, and the union of failure cases (A^c x Y) union (A x B^c) is nonrectangular. Merging them forgets a bit of joint history that the DAG must preserve. This is another view of C-137's equal-outcome merge failure. The direct literature transfer is retired; only pursue a forced hard bit of every valid output or a context-sensitive list measure. Sources are linked in bridge C-173.

## Idea 311 - A forced output bit is a short rectangle list
If a bit h(i,b) has the same value on every valid mismatch for each input pair, the induced function is exactly the OR of the mismatch rectangles assigned value 1. There are at most 2N such rectangles, so the function has a Rect-DL of length <=2N. This makes the 2025 Rect-DL size hierarchy too weak for the project target. Sign-only h reduces to Hamming-weight comparison after bit flips. A block-index-only h forces every row/column block vector pair to have Hamming distance one; a complete bipartite family is constant in its differing block or collapses to a 2x2 square. Close O-132 as a Rect-DL-size route, but keep direct DAG lower bounds logically separate.

## Idea 312 - Owner-sensitive conflict cylinders still overcount
For each DAG state v, C_v is the set of tables agreeing with some feasible low row on every output coordinate below v. At an Alice split C_v is contained in the union of child conflict sets; at a Bob split it is contained in their intersection. C-172 bounds each high conflict set, but C-80 shows why their sizes cannot be summed: an O(N)-state block router has m=Theta(s1/n) candidate-block states, each with almost all high columns outside its feasible column set. The same high table can be counted at m-1 states it never reaches. Any global charge must be conditional on the parent rectangle or on actual path reach probability. See C-175/Q131.

## Idea 313 - Residual-history complexity instead of conflict mass (C-176)

Try to classify a DAG state by (row residual, column residual, allowed descendant output support) and record every distinct history rectangle that enters it. A merge is safe only if the shared suffix can find an output for the full product hull of those histories. This targets the real shared-DAG resource. The proposed parent-conditioned cross-conflict mass itself failed: C-80 has a high table mixed in every block whose path immediately selects a valid mismatch and incurs zero sibling-conflict charges. Learning: path weights remove the C-175 overlap artifact but do not force difficult paths to pay. Need a family of incompatible residual contracts, not a sum of local exclusions. Still only an idea; no lower bound.

## Idea 314 - Gap local-PRG route and its exponent loss (C-177)

Adapt the local-PRG MCSP argument directly to a promise separator: if every generator output is low, H accepts all seeds; a random table is high with probability 1-2^(-N+o(N)), so any PRG fooling H must have output locality greater than s1. The available general-branching-program generator has locality about S^(1/2+o(1)), giving only S>=N^(2beta-o(1)), below N for the magnification regime beta<1/2. Also, standard branching programs do not model C-75's unrestricted circuit-equivalent rect-DAG. The remaining PRG target must fool general separator circuits, which is essentially the hard part. This is a quantified route closure, not a new lower bound.


### 315 - Sparse envelopes and existential projection
A Gap-MCSP separator is a circuit that accepts every size-s1 table while accepting no table outside SIZE(s2); its 1-set is a sparse envelope between the two circuit classes. Short descriptions express low membership as exists d: TT(C_d)=x. A universal circuit computes the fixed-description verifier, not the existential projection. OR-ing descriptions costs N*2^(O(N^beta)); sending a description proves only short communication, with an exponential one-switch frontier. The useful next question is whether residual product hulls at shared DAG states have separator complexity that can be lower-bounded and charged. This is a sharpened target, not a breakthrough or a proof of non-shareability.



### 316 - One-shot parity fingerprints still need N-o(N) bits
Fix any low row w and let an affine sketch be L_w(x)=A_wx+b_w. If all high tables must have a sketch value different from L_w(w), then the whole coset w+ker(A_w) contains no high table. Its size is 2^(N-rank(A_w)), which is at most |SIZE(s2)|. Therefore rank(A_w)>=N-log2|SIZE(s2)|=N-o(N), even if the sketch matrix is selected from w. This rules out a broad class of fixed fingerprints, but not adaptive DAGs or general nonlinear summaries. A mismatch coordinate still has to be recovered.



### 317 - Count shared predicate cost, not fingerprint bits
A one-bit equality test separates any fixed low table w from all high tables, so nonlinear synopsis output length can be tiny. But the test h_w(x)=1[x=w] costs O(N) gates and varies with w. This sharpens the target: lower-bound the cost of sharing these row-dependent tests across all pairs, not the number of summary bits. It does not rule out adaptive nonlinear compression.



### 318 - Adaptive parity queries still need near-N depth
For a separator decision tree using parity tests, fix a low table w. The path to its leaf imposes t affine equations, so at least 2^(N-t) tables follow the same path. They must all be non-high, giving 2^(N-t)<=|SIZE(s2)| and t>=N-log2|SIZE(s2)|. The proof allows adaptive query selection. It does not lower-bound a DAG: an N-deep path can reuse O(N) nodes. The useful hard part is merging residual contexts.



### 319 - Nondeterministic BP local PRGs do not bridge the beta gap
The STACS 2021 local PRG with locality S^(2/3+o(1) yields, for the gap promise, only S>=s1^(3/2-o(1))=N^(3beta/2-o(1)). At beta<1/2 this is sublinear and remains in the BP model. The useful gap is not between exact and promise MCSP here; it is between the small OPS threshold and the output-locality exponent, plus the missing BP-to-rect-DAG transfer. Do not cite the N^1.5 exact-MCSP result as an OPS separator lower bound.


### C-196 - Q-output exits are constrained by tail overlap
At a product-rectangle state, split descendant outputs into coordinates in Q and coordinates outside Q. Whenever a low-signature fiber and a high-signature fiber share a tail projection, their Q signatures must differ on a coordinate the state can output; otherwise their cross-pair agrees on every descendant output. If r signatures appear on both sides, their disjoint cylinders jointly exclude at least max(0,r*2^(N-|Q|-t)-M2) high completions when t tail coordinates are available.

Learning: this formalizes the local exit-versus-tail tradeoff, but it does not solve the sharing problem. The high-column exclusions can overlap among many nodes, and an entire Q-output subgraph can be shared while diagonal pairs go to a tail subgraph. C-80/C-160 remain adversarial counterchecks. Next, seek a path-sensitive charge that prices both pieces together; stop this line if it collapses to raw exclusion volume or fails either calibration. No global DAG lower bound follows yet.
### C-197 - Artificial communication/DAG separation calibrates the resource
For any m-bit Boolean f, sending Alice's input solves its KW Bit relation with O(m) bits, while Sokolov's correspondence makes the minimum rect-DAG size Theta(C(f)); circuit counting gives examples of size 2^(Omega(m)). A separate parity example has an O(m) DAG but Omega(m^2) tree/formula nodes. This corrects a possible ambiguity: communication can be small relative to DAG size, but tree node complexity cannot be smaller than DAG complexity. Neither example transfers a lower bound to Gap-MCSP. See bridge C-196.

### C-198 - A partial-monotone KW lifting route has a hard-image bottleneck
The one-hot rail embedding makes C-75 exactly a restricted monotone KW relation: high rails are Alice's 0-inputs, low rails are Bob's 1-inputs, and a rising rail is a signed mismatch. This matches the rectangle-DAG model in the CCC 2025 colourful-sunflower lifting theorem. If a lifted CSP search relation reduced answer-preservingly to the actual low/high promise, its DAG lower bound would transfer with no state loss. The missing map must output high-complexity Bob tables and make every mismatch coordinate a valid CSP witness; ordinary succinct output maps are too small and therefore cannot land in SIZE(s2)^c. A tempting affine-code/coset embedding is easy by parity and yields only O(N) states. Takeaway: look for nonlinear, provably high images, not another code-coset gadget. No lower bound or proof has been obtained. Details: research bridge Â§123.



### C-199 - Dense-column lifting removes the need to construct every high table
The proof of ECCC 2024's triangle-DAG lifting theorem can be adapted by starting its error-column removal with all omitted Bob columns. If the omission density is <1/4, the argument retains enough root columns and the same resolution-width contradiction, up to constants. The OPS non-high set has density 2^(-N+o(N)), so Bob inputs may map to raw truth tables and be restricted to high ones. The unresolved step is not high-table generation: each signed mismatch orientation must decode to a valid lifted witness, and the low image must avoid an O(N)-size range separator. A blockwise one-hot pointer image fails because range membership is linear size. This narrows the lifting route but gives no DAG lower bound. See bridge Â§124.



### C-200 - The colourful-sunflower clique image has an O(N log N) separator
Alice's graph in the standard cPHP-to-clique-colouring reduction is a single k-clique on one selected vertex per part. Recognize it by computing vertex degrees and checking k active vertices of degree k-1, one per part, with all other vertices isolated. The circuit has O(N logN) gates and rejects all c-colourable Bob graphs, so its C-75 image promise is easy even after high-table filtering. Also, signed mismatch permits reverse edges that the monotone KW decoder does not accept. Close this specific reduction route; require hard low-image envelope and both-orientation output compatibility next time.

### C-201 - Correct the triangle-DAG lifting exponent
The ECCC 2024 lifting theorem says size at most one-half times m^((1-delta)w), not m to half that exponent. The paper confirms this with its near-tight comparison at delta=1/120. The dense-column adaptation with a quarter constant preserves Omega(m^((1-delta)w)) when fewer than one quarter of Bob columns are omitted. At mr=N this can exceed the N^(3+3epsilon)/log N compiler threshold for polylogarithmic source variable count and suitable fixed width. The hard low-image embedding and two-orientation witness decoder remain unresolved, so this is not a C-75 lower bound or breakthrough. See bridge C-201.

### C-202 - Unique-output lifting sources are too costly to decode
The full-clause formula with one falsified clause per assignment gives a unique-output Search(F) relation. In Search(F) composed with IND_m^v, any rectangle contained in one answer fiber has uniform measure at most (1/(2m))^v. A decoder refining each of 2N mismatch types therefore needs Omega(m^(v-1)) output leaves per type for N=mv. At v=16,w=15,delta=0.1, the lifted lower bound is Omega(m^13.5), while the decoder needs Omega(m^15); no useful lower-bound transfer survives. Avoid unique-output source relations here; next look for answer-rich relations with a decoder bound below the lifted-DAG lower bound. See bridge C-202.


### C-203 - cPHP passes the necessary decoder-cost exponent screen, conditionally

The constant-degree cPHP lifting source on an expander has width W=Omega(k) and lower bound L=(m/(A d W log(mk)))^W. With target length N=Theta(mk), the C-164 minimum decoder refinement is r_min=Omega(dN^(1+beta)/(k^2 logN)). For fixed base width W>4+3epsilon+beta, L exceeds T r_min for T=N^(3+3epsilon)/logN. So the unique-answer decoder failure in C-202 does not generalize to answer-rich cPHP.

This is only a parameter pass: r_min is a lower bound, and no decoder upper bound r<L/T or source-to-table maps exist. Its usual clique-colouring reduction still has the O(N logN) low-image recognizer in C-200. No target lower bound follows.

### C-204 - Restrict cPHP Bob inputs to high truth tables using the CCC proof

The CCC 2025 Full Range Lemma accepts arbitrary sufficiently dense Bob-column subsets, while the triangle-error union bound charges structured error columns. Adapting the extraction, the high-table subset survives deletion of eta=2^(-N+o(N)) columns when N=Theta(mk) and W log(mk)=o(N); the lifted cPHP triangle-DAG lower bound remains m^(Omega(W)) up to constants. With a power-of-two alphabet and compatible N=log2(d)*mk, flattening Bob's d-ary array is a bijection onto all N-bit tables, so filtering to high tables is exact.

This closes O-143 at the OPS deletion density and removes explicit high-table generation from the cPHP route. It does not construct Alice's low-table map, a hard low-image envelope, an all-sign mismatch decoder, or the decoder upper bound r<L/T. No S_rect, rho, or P-vs-NP bound follows. See bridge C-204.

### C-205 - A dense mismatch slab kills the raw/type-only cPHP decoder

For every Alice table encoding and every output bit, one Alice bit fiber has density at least one half. If Bob is the raw flattening bijection, the opposite bit fiber remains density one half up to the exponentially small low-table deletion. The CCC colourful-sunflower lifting extraction still works on that restricted rectangle: with a smaller constant size cap, row errors leave at least three eighths of the address cube, giving blockwise min-entropy log(m/8), and Bob error columns remove only o(1) density. So any decoder fixed only by mismatch coordinate/sign must solve cPHP at the source lower-bound scale L.

Learning: the previous C-203 check only compared L with the *minimum number of decoder leaves*. It missed that an entire type-decoder DAG is itself a hard lifted search protocol on a dense slab. Copying such a decoder per target sink gives no useful amplification. This closes raw Bob flattening plus type-only decoding, independent of the low-table map. It does not close sink-conditioned decoders: target sinks can fragment the slab, and we need a global state/context charge. Non-raw Bob encodings also remain open. See research bridge C-205 and O-144.

### C-206 - Sparse sink rows regularize after only a few address fixes

For a row set A of density rho in `[m]^k`, repeatedly condition on any address pattern whose probability is too large. Each step fixes coordinates and multiplies density by more than `m^(1-delta)` per coordinate. The final slice has blockwise min-entropy `delta log m`, after fewer than `log_m(1/rho)/(1-delta)` fixed addresses. For any polynomial-size DAG and fixed cPHP base parameters, this is O(1) addresses.

With complete cPHP, a distinct selected-value prefix leaves an online-matching-hard residual problem; a repeated value is already a witness. This gives a concrete local fork for sink decoders. It does not yield a global state count: the high-entropy row slices can overlap or miss most rows, and Bob's sink set can be concentrated on collision patterns. The next task is to charge those collision/address contexts under product-hull-safe sharing (O-145), not to sum the slices naively. No C-75 lower bound yet.

### C-207 - Circuit syntax does not shrink shared-DAG size

Tested the direct use of Alice's short circuit description. For any surjection from descriptions to low truth tables, pullback of Alice state predicates lifts a table-DAG to a description-DAG unchanged, and a section from each table back to one description converts every description-DAG to a table-DAG unchanged. Syntax gives a short communication message but no separate DAG-size saving. A description-aware universal DAG of size `N^(1+o(1))` would itself yield a sparse-envelope circuit of that size. The direct OR over descriptions remains `N*2^(O(s1 log(n+s1)))`; it is not a near-linear construction. This closes the syntax-only shortcut, not the shared-DAG lower-bound route. The missing result remains a global product-hull-safe charge on the actual `Y x Z` DAG, strong enough to beat `N^(3+3epsilon)/log N` under the current cover compiler. See research bridge C-207 and O-141/O-133. No breakthrough or P-vs-NP proof.

### C-208 - Local rectangle capacity is only a mismatch hitting-set fact

For a rect-DAG state v, let K_v be all output coordinates below it. Every pair in the state's product rectangle must reach an output leaf, so the row and column K_v-projections are disjoint. This is equivalent to â€œevery pair has some mismatch in K_v,â€ and immediately yields the local density inequality. It is not a new promise-specific hardness lemma: it holds for all mismatch search problems. At the root, high-table counting gives near-full support; internally the excluded high columns can repeat at many states. C-80/C-175 kill direct summation. The next candidate must price the parent-conditioned routing needed to choose an output while preserving product rectangles. No superlinear C-75 bound. See bridge C-208/O-141.

### C-209 - Cross-history product-hull condition

A state shared by path histories `A_h x B_h` must solve `(union A_h) x (union B_h)`, the full cross-product hull. If K is its descendant output-coordinate set, then the union of row K-projections and union of column K-projections must be disjoint. This gives the exact safety test for merging histories, without assuming any bound on anchors per state. It is not yet a size bound: the C-80 router passes it with O(N) states, and Q-output exits still permit cross-signature merges in C-191. Next derive an amortized residual-separator cost for many distinct hulls while allowing shared suffixes. No superlinear C-75 bound. See bridge C-209/O-141.

## C-210 - Rank-lifting reveals the cost hidden by cyclic fusion states

A successful q-pair cover gives q rule states only in a ranked cyclic model: for a fixed low/high pair, each chosen support rule has strictly smaller least-fixed-point activation rank. To make the protocol acyclic, index states by `(rule i, rank ceiling r)`. The rectangles `{w: tau_i(w)<=r} x {z: tau_i(z)=infinity}` route to a literal mismatch or a lower layer, giving q^2 multiway states. Each state still has up to O(q+N) support choices, so the edge/router cost is O(q^2(q+N))=O(q^3) in the OPS range q>=N/2. Counting the q^2 vertices while ignoring fan-out is not a standard binary-DAG bound; the best recorded binary compiler remains O(q^3/log q).

This confirms the exact distinction: the fusion cover is the promise's cyclic intersection complexity, while Sokolov/GGKS measure acyclic binary product-rectangle DAGs. Reverse transfer remains `rho_prom<=O(S_rect)`, and `S_rect=Theta` sparse-envelope separator circuit size. A description-aware shared DAG has the same minimum as a truth-table DAG, so universal circuit evaluation does not remove the existential search over descriptions. No universal near-linear DAG, superlinear C-75/cover lower bound, or P-vs-NP proof has been obtained. Next investigate whether product-hull-safe mergers can share support routers across rank layers; C-80/C-160 are required counterchecks. See research bridge C-210/O-141.

## C-211 - Near-linear hitting sets do not route a shared protocol

If z is high circuit complexity and w has size at most s1, patching their r truth-table disagreements costs O(rn) gates, so their Hamming distance is Omega(s2/n). A probabilistic set-cover argument gives a family of coordinate subsets of total incidence O(N logN) that hits every low/high mismatch set. This is a support-coverage lemma only: the event â€œQ contains a mismatchâ€ is a union of product rectangles, not a valid single state in a binary rect-DAG. A scan confined to one sample that discards its tested prefix breaks at the cross-history product hull; a composite protocol that reuses earlier coordinates or other samples may evade that narrow obstruction. This yields no S_rect/rho lower bound or P-vs-NP proof. See research bridge C-211/O-141.


## C-212 â€” shared decoders improve the local geometry, not the global DAG bound

For any r truth-table addresses in `{0,1}^n`, the exact indicator of that set has a fan-in-two circuit of `O(n+r*n/log(r+1))` gates. Split address bits into width-`Theta(log r)` blocks, share all equality decoders inside each block, AND the matching block codes for each selected address, then OR the r terms. Consequently the low circuit class realizes every labeling on every fixed `Theta(s1)` coordinate set, and pointwise patching improves the OPS low/high distance from `Omega(s2/n)` to `Omega(s2)`.

I learned that several old bounds were paying for each minterm independently. The improvement strengthens fixed-order context counts to `2^(Omega(s1))`, raises the local low-variation router threshold to `Theta(s2)`, and raises the Bob-chosen mismatch-certificate floor to `Omega(s1)`. It also enlarges the C-191 diagonal signature family to `2^(Omega(s1 log n))` and the C-195 triangle-state cover to `2^(Theta(s1))`.

These are not lower bounds for all C-75 DAGs. The exact break remains the same: a merged state must solve cross-history pairs in the full product hull, and cross-signature pairs may leave through Q-coordinate mismatch outputs. No global cost for those exits has been proved. Keep O-141 active, retain C-80/C-160 counterchecks, and do not change the `q -> S_rect=O(q^3/log q)` or `S_rect>N^(3+3epsilon)/logN` transfer without a new router theorem. See bridge C-212 for the full proof, literature comparison, and quantitative audit. No P-vs-NP proof or superlinear C-75 bound follows.


## C-213 â€” a cyclic scan kills the broad cyclic-DAG lower-bound route

A product-rectangle protocol can solve mismatch for every disjoint pair of N-bit families with 5N states if cycles are allowed and the protocol follows a deterministic local strategy: at scan state i, Alice selects her bit side; Bob outputs on a mismatch and otherwise moves to i+1, with the last state wrapping to the first. The deterministic walk terminates within N tests because every promised pair differs somewhere. Revisiting old coordinates lets a shared suffix solve cross-history pairs in its full product hull.

This is a useful counterexample to broad cyclic state lower bounds, but it does not imply a small fusion cover. Protocol states use independent free predicates of Alice's and Bob's inputs. A fusion state is one unary activation set generated by its endpoint/support closure; representing a general rectangle as a semantic cut is easy, but generating that cut with legal pair rules is not. The root scan state would require `X=Y`, the sparse-envelope separator itself. So the cycle closes only the broader-model lower-bound avenue; it does not touch the standard acyclic rect-DAG target or `rho_prom`. Continue O-141 / native closure work. No P-vs-NP proof follows. Full proof: bridge C-213.

### Idea 340 â€” Count the effective closure program, not semantic endpoints (C-214)

A q-rule closure's behavior on anchors is fully determined by two OR-clauses over the 2N signed literals per rule, two predecessor subsets per rule, and which rules have empty carrier. This is at most 4Nq+2q^2+q bits. Counting over all q up to 2^(N/2-1) leaves fewer systems than full Boolean partitions; therefore some partition needs Omega(2^(N/2)) fusion pairs, despite having the universal 5N-state cyclic mismatch protocol. This gives a direct native-fusion versus cyclic-rectangle separation and kills generic polynomial compiler claims.

The failed transfer lesson is precise: generic counting cannot name the fixed explicit sparse-envelope promise, and the medium band lets a separator choose its own values. To use the idea for Gap-MCSP, an encoding must force every promise separator to expose a closure-hard function with controlled loss. No such encoding is known. Keep O-141 active; C-214 is not an OPS lower bound. Full proof: research/C75_SHARED_DAG_CONTINUATION_2026-09-27.md.

## C-215 â€” Q-exit overlap graph audit

A state-local signature graph clarifies that cross-signature reuse is legal only when descendant Q labels separate every pair whose tail projections overlap. Root high-completion counting recovers near-full tail support, but static graph edge counts do not aggregate: tail support shrinks down paths and side filtering changes which signature pairs survive. Keep O-141 open for a parent-conditioned history-flow invariant; do not count signature pairs or excluded columns without an overlap-safe charge. The 2026 monotone-learning lifting paper is conditional/sample-based and has no map into the actual OPS promise. Details: research/C215_Q_EXIT_GRAPH_AUDIT_2026-09-27.md.

### Idea 344 â€” Uniform shattering kills every fixed-order mismatch scan (C-217)

For any permutation of table coordinates, the first `t=Theta(s1)` coordinates are shattered by the low class. Every one of their `2^t` patterns has a high completion because a prefix cylinder has `2^(N-t)>|SIZE(s2)|` points. In a fixed-order scanner, each matched prefix needs its own continuation state: merging two would make the state rectangle contain a cross-pair whose mismatch is in an already-passed coordinate. Thus short circuit descriptions do not make the straightforward shared scan small; it has `2^(Theta(s1))` states. The obstruction is only for scans that cannot revisit coordinates and cannot constrain arbitrary rect-DAGs. A general DAG may route through earlier-output leaves, use adaptive supports, or revisit information in another suffix. Next seek either a compact adaptive/revisiting construction or a justified reduction from general DAGs to an ordered model. No arbitrary-DAG or fusion lower bound follows.

**Scope correction for Idea 344:** the proof requires immediate first-mismatch termination. It does not rule out a deferred-output scan that merges prefix histories and later finds a mismatch in the remaining coordinates. Continue testing this possibility and keep C-80/C-160 as controls.


### C-218 ? Shrink the low class to expose certificate slack

For any `gamma<beta`, analyze `SIZE(N^gamma)` against the original high side. A lower bound for this smaller low set transfers to the original promise. Its circuit-description entropy/VC dimension is `O(N^gamma n)`, but its distance from high tables remains `Omega(N^beta)`. Hence every high table has a mismatch-hitting coordinate certificate of size `O(N^(1-beta+gamma)n)=o(N)`. A fixed `O(N^gamma n)`-coordinate block also has a constant fraction of patterns missing from the low projection, and every pair retains a large mismatch tail off the block.

This opens a projected-class routing test, but certificate size is not DAG size. We still need a product-rectangle-safe way to choose the certificate and find the mismatch coordinate, accounting for cross-history hulls. No superlinear C-75/fusion bound or P-vs-NP proof follows. Full derivation: `research/C218_DISTANCE_DIMENSION_CERTIFICATES_2026-09-27.md`.


### C-218-A - Fixed-order routing inside the certificate block still fails

For a block Q of size twice the VC dimension of the reduced low class, take a prefix J of size Theta(N^gamma) that the low class shatters. In every prefix slice, Sauer-Shelah leaves a missing suffix pattern because the remaining block has more than v coordinates. Each missing block pattern has a high full-table completion. Therefore the product-hull cross-prefix argument forces 2^(Theta(N^gamma)) states for any fixed-order first-mismatch scanner on Q. This is only a restricted scanner lower bound; deferred/adaptive routing remains open. Full proof: C-218 report, section C-218-A.


### Idea 346 - Residual separators are the unit of DAG reuse (C-220)

For a shared state `v`, merge all histories into the state rectangle `A_v x B_v`; every cross-pair must be solved by the common suffix. With descendant output coordinates `K_v`, correctness forces `pi_Kv(A_v) intersect pi_Kv(B_v)=empty`. A lower-bound route should count distinct residual separator functions across states and prove an overlap-safe global charge. A construction route should exploit the same residual function to share across descriptions and coordinates. Short circuit descriptions alone do not shrink the graph: replacing a table by one of its circuit descriptions preserves minimum rect-DAG size exactly. The root support argument yields only `N-o(N)` states, and the known compiler still needs `S_rect > N^(3+3epsilon)/log N` to force the target q lower bound. C-80/C-160/C-209 remain mandatory counterchecks.

**Correction:** for matching vertex measures, `DAGsize<=Treesize`; do not seek a small tree with a larger DAG. The meaningful resource gap is communication bits/depth versus graph vertices. GGKS triangle-DAGs are stronger than rectangle-DAGs, so their lower bounds would transfer, but C-194 gives a universal `4N-1`-state triangle-DAG for every disjoint mismatch promise. This rules out superlinear lower bounds in that stronger model; C-195's expansion of one chosen triangle state is not a rect-DAG lower bound.

The proposed interval binary search does not give a shared rect-DAG state: for `I={1,2}`, pairs `(00,10)` and `(01,00)` have a mismatch in I, but their cross-pair `(00,00)` does not. A single rectangle containing both histories is therefore not wholly in the â€œmismatch in Iâ€ relation. A multi-rectangle refinement remains possible and its cost is open.


### Idea 347 - Separate seed-feature dimension from closure-readout cost (C-221)

For q fusion pairs, form the 2q seed-clause feature vector `sigma_Q(x)`. The successful positive least-fixed-point readout must be 1 on low tables and 0 on high tables. Monotonicity forces every pair `w in Y,z in Z` to have some feature bit 1 on w and 0 on z. Each feature is an OR of signed literals, so its zero set is a subcube and the features give an oriented subcube-cut cover. This feature cover has a universal 2N construction from signed literals and a promise lower bound `N-log|SIZE(s2)|`, so this line cannot yield a superlinear q bound by itself.

The real target is the **closure readout interaction**: each pair-rule must AND two supports, reuse predecessor carriers, and avoid making any high table activate an empty carrier. Seek a lower bound on that structured readout beyond the linear feature cover, or a compact construction that exploits it. This sharpens O-141 and kills any proposed argument that uses only pairwise seed separation. Full derivation: `research/C221_SEED_FEATURE_VS_CLOSURE_READOUT_2026-09-27.md`.

**C-221-A refinement:** every satisfiable minimal activation certificate is a set of at least `N-log|SIZE(s2)|` seed clauses. Its clause conjunction is high-free, so fixing one true literal per clause gives the width bound. Every low table contains such a certificate; no high table does. The width yields only q=Omega(N), so focus next on how the rule graph generates/overlaps this certificate family, not just certificate size. See section C-221-A in the C-221 report.



### Idea 348 - Keep C-115 signatures adaptive; fixed menus explode (C-222)

A k-bit address signature partitions the N truth-table positions into at most K=2^k fibers. For a point-indicator table 1_S to be a lookup of that signature, S must be a union of fibers. There are `binom(N,t)` low t-sparse indicators with `t=Theta(N^beta/n)`, while one signature with K<=N^beta cells represents at most `sum_{j<=t} binom(K,j)` of them. Thus any menu that covers all low indicators needs `2^(Omega(N^beta))` signatures. The C-115 witness is useful because its signature depends on the specific low circuit; replacing that choice by a public polynomial menu fails.

Next look for an adaptive selector whose routing states share across circuit-dependent signatures without violating product-hull safety, or a different invariant that avoids factorization through a signature. C-219's coordinate certificate menu is not contradicted: it does not require low tables to factor through each item. Full proof: `research/C222_FIXED_SIGNATURE_MENU_LOWER_BOUND_2026-09-27.md`.



**C-222-A caveat:** the fixed-menu count does not imply an adaptive-selector lower bound. For the t-sparse indicators used in C-222, a bitonic sorting network extracts support addresses and outputs a point-indicator circuit description in `O(N log^3N)` size. General low-circuit synthesis remains unresolved. Any next claim must target all of `SIZE(s1)` and account for product-hull-safe state sharing. See C-222-A in the C-222 report.


### Idea 349 - Explicit adaptive signatures invoke circuit search (C-223)

An exact selector S that outputs a size-`s1` circuit for each low table yields a promise separator by evaluating that circuit on all N addresses. Its size is `O(|S|+N s1 log(s1+n))`, or `O(|S|+N^(1+beta))` in the OPS scaling. This sufficient route is stronger than a general rect-DAG, and has a nontrivial verification overhead. A separator need not output any circuit; no reverse implication follows without a search-to-decision theorem, and the classical exact MCSP search-to-decision question is listed as open in the cited literature. Thus a selector lower bound alone does not prove DAG hardness. Preserve O-141 as the general product-hull reuse target. See `research/C223_ADAPTIVE_SIGNATURE_SEARCH_MCSP_BOUND_2026-09-27.md`.


### Idea 350 - Approximation error versus within-fiber variation (C-224)

If a selected low-table circuit C is wrong on e addresses, and k of its wires (including the output) define address fibers, approximate each high table z by a lookup bit on each fiber. If m good addresses disagree with the cell majority, correcting the bad and minority points gives a circuit for z of size `|C|+O(k*2^k+(e+m)n)`. Since high z has complexity at least s2, either the approximation errors consume the gap or many good addresses vary within fibers. A mixed fiber contains two addresses where low w agrees and high z differs. This is a robust local witness, not a DAG lower bound; the missing work is selector-free discovery and product-hull-safe global charging. See C-224.

## C-225 - Approximate signatures have a one-cell adversary

Let C approximate low w correctly on at least half the truth-table addresses. Among its k-wire signatures (including C's output), one good cell F has at least `N/2^(k+1)` points. If k=`kappa*n` with `kappa<min(beta,1-beta)`, then for `s2=N^beta` this cell contains more points than the description count for size-s2 circuits. Flipping w on subsets of F gives 2^|F| completions, one high. The two constant-on-F endpoints are low: w itself, and w with all of F flipped, whose indicator is computed by checking the signature and `C=w` using circuits for w and C. The high completion is far from both endpoints by point-patching, so at least `Omega(s2/n)` minority points all lie in this one cell.

This extends the C-120 concentration obstruction to approximate selectors and every fixed beta in (0,1). It kills any route that needs many mixed cells. It leaves exactly the hard part: identify a pair-dependent cell without a circuit selector and charge the suffix across full product hulls. See `research/C225_APPROXIMATE_SIGNATURE_ONE_CELL_CONCENTRATION_2026-09-27.md`.

## C-226 - Fusion closure is an alternating reachability program

Each fusion rule requires two sides, so a winning activation proof has a universal fork at the rule and an existential support choice on each side. With infinite plays rejecting, the winning region is exactly the least activation fixed point. Thus q pairs give O(q) cyclic alternating states and O(q^2) support transitions on the active promise. This is a sharper model identification, but it does not make the object a standard NBP/rect-DAG: standard MCSP BP lower bounds apply only after a compiler that we do not have. Local PRG arguments yield an NBP promise-separator lower bound of roughly s1^{3/2}; at s1=N^beta/(cn), this crosses linear only for beta>2/3, outside our target. The missing theorem is a direct lower bound for the alternating closure at small beta, or a special compiler with controlled cost. C-226.


## C-227 - Context/subproof splicing, not bare state reuse

The native positive closure has a finite AND/OR proof grammar. Every E-side support can pair with every H-side support, and a proof subtree at a shared state can be replaced by another proof rooted at that state. The mixed proof is syntactically valid, but seed labels are dual-rail: opposite signs on one coordinate make its support unrealizable. If it is consistent, soundness forces it to fix at least N-log2(M2) coordinates, so its cylinder may contain only non-high tables. The target is to force a shared occurrence whose context and replacement supports are consistent and leave more than log2(M2) coordinates free.
